plain: Valve auscultation landmarks (PAM) in the dog → Left side: pulmonic ICS 2–4, aortic ICS 3–5, mitral ICS 5–6 (apex); tricuspid at right ICS 3–5. A systolic murmur at the right sternal border → tricuspid regurgitation or VSD. Not tricuspid at right 5–6 — it sits at 3–5.

plain: Most common congenital heart defect in dogs; most common acquired heart disease? Congenital: patent ductus arteriosus (then subaortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis). Acquired: myxomatous mitral valve disease (~75% of canine heart disease); DCM second, in large breeds.

plain: Puppy, continuous "machinery" murmur loudest at left heart base, bounding water-hammer pulses → Left-to-right PDA; aorta-to-PA shunt volume-overloads the left atrium and left ventricle (pulmonary overcirculation). Close early by surgical ligation or transcatheter occluder (ACDO); ~65% untreated die within 1 year. Females, Poodles, Maltese, Pomeranians, Shelties; heritable — do not breed.

plain: Soft grade I–II systolic murmur in a puppy that fades by 4–6 months → Innocent (physiologic) murmur; no workup if it disappears. Loud, continuous or persistent murmurs need echocardiography.

plain: Young Boxer/Golden/Newfoundland/Rottweiler, systolic ejection murmur at left base (ICS 3–4) radiating to carotids, weak late-rising pulses → Subaortic stenosis — the congenital defect most often causing exertional syncope and sudden death (ischemic ventricular arrhythmias); predisposes to endocarditis. Doppler >4.5 m/s = severe; atenolol.

plain: Young Bulldog/Boxer/Beagle, systolic murmur at left base (ICS 2–3), right axis deviation/RV hypertrophy, normal femoral pulses → Pulmonic stenosis; balloon valvuloplasty when gradient >50–80 mmHg (caution: anomalous coronary artery in Bulldogs). Not weak femoral pulses — those point to subaortic stenosis.

plain: Young Keeshond (or English Bulldog), cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen, exercise intolerance, polycythemia; small pulmonary vessels, RV enlargement → Tetralogy of Fallot: pulmonic stenosis, RV hypertrophy, VSD, overriding (dextropositioned) aorta → right-to-left shunt. Palliative β- blockers; phlebotomy/hydroxyurea for PCV >65%; avoid vasodilators.

plain: German Shepherd/Irish Setter puppy regurgitates solid food from weaning; esophagus dilated cranial to the heart base → Persistent right aortic arch: right-sided aorta, ligamentum arteriosum left and dorsal, heart base ventral entrap the esophagus. Ligate the ligamentum via left 4th ICS thoracotomy early (<6 months); elevated feeding; aspiration pneumonia limits prognosis.

plain: Older small-breed dog (CKCS, Dachshund, Poodle), left apical systolic murmur → Myxomatous mitral valve disease (endocardiosis): left atrial enlargement → cough, pulmonary edema, left CHF. CKCS is the MMVD breed, not a DCM breed.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
section: Mitral valve disease, endocarditis and congestive heart failure

spans.text: ACVIM staging of MMVD — when does pimobendan start?
(CHF) → add furosemide, ACE inhibitor, spironolactone. D (refractory) →

plain: ACVIM staging of MMVD — when does pimobendan start? B1 murmur without enlargement → monitor. B2 (LA:Ao ≥1.6, LVIDdN ≥1.7, VHS >10.5) → pimobendan 0.25–0.3 mg/kg PO q12h (EPIC: delays CHF ~15 months). C (CHF) → add furosemide, ACE inhibitor, spironolactone. D (refractory) → torsemide, sildenafil.

respiratory rate falls, plus pimobendan; butorphanol sedation; nitroglycerin/
dobutamine if hypotensive. IV crystalloids are contraindicated; edema cannot
be drained — thoracocentesis only for pleural effusion.
propranolol or diltiazem — not acute CHF drugs.

plain: Dog in acute left CHF with pulmonary edema, oxygen already given → next drug? Furosemide 2–4 mg/kg IV, repeated q1–2h or CRI until respiratory rate falls, plus pimobendan; butorphanol sedation; nitroglycerin/ dobutamine if hypotensive. IV crystalloids are contraindicated; edema cannot be drained — thoracocentesis only for pleural effusion. Not digoxin, propranolol or diltiazem — not acute CHF drugs.

spans.text: Right-sided CHF (ascites, jugular distension, hepatomegaly) → first-line
drug, and what about IV fluids? Furosemide 1–4 mg/kg
and an ACE inhibitor; spironolactone if refractory; abdominocentesis if ascites
impairs breathing. Fluids are withheld; if unavoidable, low-sodium crystalloid

plain: Right-sided CHF (ascites, jugular distension, hepatomegaly) → first-line drug, and what about IV fluids? Furosemide 1–4 mg/kg with pimobendan and an ACE inhibitor; spironolactone if refractory; abdominocentesis if ascites impairs breathing. Fluids are withheld; if unavoidable, low-sodium crystalloid (0.45% NaCl/2.5% dextrose) at ≤1 mL/kg/h. Not acetazolamide — a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor for glaucoma.

plain: Dog with advanced heart disease collapses briefly on exertion or coughing, recovers in seconds, no aura or postictal phase → Syncope: low forward output, tachyarrhythmia (AF; VT in Boxers/Dobermans), bradyarrhythmia, or cough/vasovagal syncope in small breeds with mitral disease. Holter plus echo; distinguish from seizure.

plain: Boxer with fever, shifting-leg lameness and a new murmur at the left 5th ICS → Infective endocarditis (mitral/aortic vegetations; immune-complex polyarthritis; predisposed by subaortic stenosis, Bartonella). Echo plus three blood cultures; 6–8 weeks bactericidal antibiotics; guarded. MMVD is afebrile and slowly progressive.

furosemide, ACE inhibitor, spironolactone; sotalol/mexiletine for ventricular

plain: Doberman/Great Dane/Irish Wolfhound, exercise intolerance, weak pulses, soft murmur, AF or VPCs; echo dilated poorly contracting LV (fractional shortening <20–25%) → DCM. Tx pimobendan 0.25–0.3 mg/kg q12h, furosemide, ACE inhibitor, spironolactone; sotalol/mexiletine for ventricular arrhythmias; diltiazem + digoxin for AF. Median survival after CHF ~6–12 months; sudden death risk.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Asymptomatic middle-aged Doberman: Holter >50 VPCs/24 h, echo
(PROTECT); sotalol or mexiletine for arrhythmias. Screen Dobermans
annually from 3 years with Holter and echo.

plain: Asymptomatic middle-aged Doberman: Holter >50 VPCs/24 h, echo reduced LV systolic function → Occult DCM (autosomal dominant PDK4/ titin variants; 25–30% die suddenly). Pimobendan delays CHF onset (PROTECT); sotalol or mexiletine for arrhythmias. Screen Dobermans annually from 3 years with Holter and echo.

plain: Which breeds/diets get nutritionally responsive DCM, and what is supplemented? Taurine: American Cocker Spaniel, Golden Retriever, Newfoundland, grain-free/legume or lamb-and-rice diets (whole blood <200 nmol/mL, plasma <40); taurine 500–1,000 mg q8–12h plus diet change, recovery 3–6 months. L-carnitine 50–100 mg/kg q8h: Boxers, Cockers. Cats: taurine (classic). Not English Cocker — American.

rhythm in dogs (often with wandering pacemaker, brachycephalics); abnormal
in a cat examined in clinic (suggests respiratory disease). No treatment.

plain: Heart rate speeds on inspiration and slows on expiration, normal P-QRS- T (even in a Boxer) → Respiratory sinus arrhythmia — normal vagal rhythm in dogs (often with wandering pacemaker, brachycephalics); abnormal in a cat examined in clinic (suggests respiratory disease). No treatment.

plain: Dog ECG with PR interval <0.1 s, otherwise normal → Normal: canine PR 0.06–0.13 s (cat 0.05–0.09 s). PR <0.06 s with a delta wave → ventricular pre- excitation (WPW); PR >0.13 s → first-degree AV block.

plain: Auscultated heart rate 110 bpm but femoral pulse rate 70 → Pulse deficit — beats with inadequate ventricular filling produce no pulse (atrial fibrillation, frequent VPCs). Next step: ECG.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Clinical signs that suggest an arrhythmia in a dog, and the next step?
Syncope/episodic collapse, exercise intolerance, weakness, pulse deficits,
irregular or very fast/slow rhythm, sudden death.

plain: Clinical signs that suggest an arrhythmia in a dog, and the next step? Syncope/episodic collapse, exercise intolerance, weakness, pulse deficits, irregular or very fast/slow rhythm, sudden death. ECG; 24-h Holter for intermittent episodes (Boxers, Dobermans).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Irregularly irregular R-R, no P waves, undulating f-wave baseline, narrow
QRS, rapid rate in a Great Dane →
entrant wavelets (not the SA node), usually with atrial enlargement (DCM,
advanced MMVD; lone AF in giant breeds). Narrow QRS confirms
supraventricular origin; in 2nd-degree block P waves are present and regular.

plain: Irregularly irregular R-R, no P waves, undulating f-wave baseline, narrow QRS, rapid rate in a Great Dane → Atrial fibrillation — multiple atrial re- entrant wavelets (not the SA node), usually with atrial enlargement (DCM, advanced MMVD; lone AF in giant breeds). Narrow QRS confirms supraventricular origin; in 2nd-degree block P waves are present and regular.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: AF in a dog with DCM at 220 bpm → goal, drugs, prognosis? Rate control,
amiodarone if refractory; treat CHF. Rate >125 bpm → median survival
months; lone AF tolerated for years.

plain: AF in a dog with DCM at 220 bpm → goal, drugs, prognosis? Rate control, not conversion: diltiazem + digoxin (target Holter mean <125 bpm); amiodarone if refractory; treat CHF. Rate >125 bpm → median survival months; lone AF tolerated for years. Not β-blocker + calcium blocker — the canine pairing is diltiazem + digoxin.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: electrical cardioversion; quinidine toxicity (QRS widening >25%, colic,
quinidine toxicity — it is the alternative to quinidine.

plain: AF drug approach by species? Dog: diltiazem + digoxin. Cat: diltiazem (or atenolol). Horse with lone AF: quinidine sulfate conversion or transvenous electrical cardioversion; quinidine toxicity (QRS widening >25%, colic, hypotension) → stop drug, sodium bicarbonate. Not cardioversion for quinidine toxicity — it is the alternative to quinidine.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia >200 bpm, P waves buried in preceding T waves → Supraventricular tachycardia: vagal maneuver (ocular/carotid pressure), then IV diltiazem 0.1–0.25 mg/kg or esmolol; long- term diltiazem or sotalol.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Premature wide bizarre QRS, no preceding P wave, large opposite-polarity
GDV, splenic disease, traumatic myocarditis, Boxer ARVC, Doberman DCM,
hypokalemia; look for an abdominal mass.

plain: Premature wide bizarre QRS, no preceding P wave, large opposite-polarity T wave, compensatory pause → Ventricular premature complex. Causes: GDV, splenic disease, traumatic myocarditis, Boxer ARVC, Doberman DCM, hypokalemia; look for an abdominal mass.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Occasional VPCs, rate <180, no pulse deficits, no clinical signs →
multiform complexes, pulse deficits or hemodynamic compromise

plain: Occasional VPCs, rate <180, no pulse deficits, no clinical signs → recommendation? No antiarrhythmic now; Holter, echo, electrolytes, abdominal imaging. Treat when sustained VT >160–180 bpm, R-on-T, multiform complexes, pulse deficits or hemodynamic compromise.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: 12–36 h after GDV surgery or splenectomy: wide-complex tachycardia
with pulse deficits → rhythm and DOC?
then CRI 25–80 µg/kg/min; procainamide second; correct K and Mg —
Not AV block; not mexiletine acutely — oral

plain: 12–36 h after GDV surgery or splenectomy: wide-complex tachycardia with pulse deficits → rhythm and DOC? Ventricular tachycardia (ischemia- reperfusion; ~40% of GDVs). Lidocaine 2 mg/kg IV bolus (repeat to 8 mg/kg) then CRI 25–80 µg/kg/min; procainamide second; correct K and Mg — lidocaine fails with hypokalemia. Not AV block; not mexiletine acutely — oral maintenance only.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: only; esmolol is the alternative for feline ventricular arrhythmias.

plain: Lidocaine in cats? Cats are lidocaine-sensitive (neurotoxicity): 0.25–0.5 mg/ kg only; esmolol is the alternative for feline ventricular arrhythmias.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Boxer with syncope; frequent VPCs upright in lead II (LBBB morphology,
q8h ± atenolol, fish oil; sudden death risk; screen breeding dogs.

plain: Boxer with syncope; frequent VPCs upright in lead II (LBBB morphology, right ventricular origin) → Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (Boxer cardiomyopathy; striatin mutation). Dx 24-h Holter (>100–300 VPCs/day); Tx sotalol 1–2 mg/kg q12h or mexiletine 5–8 mg/kg q8h ± atenolol, fish oil; sudden death risk; screen breeding dogs.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Collapsed dog: bradycardia, tall tented T waves, flattened/absent P waves
(cardioprotective, does not lower K), regular insulin
0.25–0.5 U/kg with dextrose, 0.9% saline; then ACTH stimulation test.

plain: Collapsed dog: bradycardia, tall tented T waves, flattened/absent P waves (atrial standstill), wide QRS → Hyperkalemia (>7–8 mEq/L: Addisonian crisis, urethral obstruction, uroabdomen, AKI). 10% calcium gluconate 0.5– 1.5 mL/kg IV slowly (cardioprotective, does not lower K), regular insulin 0.25–0.5 U/kg with dextrose, 0.9% saline; then ACTH stimulation test.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Open-mouth-breathing dog: tall peaked P waves (>0.4 mV), sinus
heartworm, brachycephalic airway); low-voltage QRS suggests pleural/
pericardial effusion or obesity. Radiographs and echo; sildenafil for pulmonary

plain: Open-mouth-breathing dog: tall peaked P waves (>0.4 mV), sinus tachycardia, small QRS → P pulmonale = right atrial enlargement from chronic pulmonary disease/pulmonary hypertension (chronic bronchitis, heartworm, brachycephalic airway); low-voltage QRS suggests pleural/ pericardial effusion or obesity. Radiographs and echo; sildenafil for pulmonary hypertension.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia → DOC? Atropine 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV
glycopyrrolate 0.005–0.01 mg/kg); run an atropine response test first — vagal
bradycardia responds, sick sinus syndrome or AV block may not and needs

plain: Symptomatic sinus bradycardia → DOC? Atropine 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV (or glycopyrrolate 0.005–0.01 mg/kg); run an atropine response test first — vagal bradycardia responds, sick sinus syndrome or AV block may not and needs pacing.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Intermittent P waves not followed by QRS — Mobitz I vs II?
constant PR with sudden dropped beats
often wide QRS; infranodal, may progress to complete block → pacemaker if
symptomatic. In fit horses resting 2nd-degree block is normal and vanishes

plain: Intermittent P waves not followed by QRS — Mobitz I vs II? Mobitz I (Wenckebach): progressive PR lengthening then dropped beat; vagal, benign, atropine-responsive. Mobitz II: constant PR with sudden dropped beats, often wide QRS; infranodal, may progress to complete block → pacemaker if symptomatic. In fit horses resting 2nd-degree block is normal and vanishes with exercise.

disease, digoxin toxicity. Theophylline/terbutaline temporize only.

plain: P waves marching independently of slow wide escape complexes at 30–40 bpm, syncope → Third-degree AV block; atropine response negative; permanent transvenous pacemaker. Rule out Lyme carditis, infiltrative disease, digoxin toxicity. Theophylline/terbutaline temporize only.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Treatment by AV block grade; sick sinus syndrome?
Mobitz I: none unless symptomatic. Mobitz II, high-grade or 3rd degree with
syncope/CHF: pacemaker. SSS (long pauses, syncope — Miniature Schnauzer,

plain: Treatment by AV block grade; sick sinus syndrome? 1st degree: none. Mobitz I: none unless symptomatic. Mobitz II, high-grade or 3rd degree with syncope/CHF: pacemaker. SSS (long pauses, syncope — Miniature Schnauzer, West Highland White, Cocker): pacemaker.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: ACE inhibitor (± spironolactone). MMVD B2: pimobendan. AF: diltiazem ±
digoxin. VT: lidocaine IV, sotalol/mexiletine PO. SVT: vagal maneuver,

plain: Standard canine cardiac drug matches? CHF: furosemide + pimobendan + ACE inhibitor (± spironolactone). MMVD B2: pimobendan. AF: diltiazem ± digoxin. VT: lidocaine IV, sotalol/mexiletine PO. SVT: vagal maneuver, diltiazem. Feline HCM: atenolol/diltiazem, clopidogrel; no pimobendan in obstructive HCM.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Muffled heart sounds, jugular distension, weak pulses with pulsus
paradoxus, ascites; globoid sharply marginated silhouette; electrical
Electrical alternans = heart swinging in fluid. Confirm by echocardiography,

plain: Muffled heart sounds, jugular distension, weak pulses with pulsus paradoxus, ascites; globoid sharply marginated silhouette; electrical alternans with small QRS → Pericardial effusion with cardiac tamponade. Electrical alternans = heart swinging in fluid. Confirm by echocardiography, which also finds a mass.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Immediate treatment of tamponade? Pericardiocentesis at the right 4th–

plain: Immediate treatment of tamponade? Pericardiocentesis at the right 4th– 5th ICS, ECG-monitored (avoids coronary arteries and lung). Diuretics and vasodilators are contraindicated — output is preload-dependent; give fluids, not furosemide, before the tap.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Causes of pericardial effusion in dogs; differentials for a globoid heart?
mesothelioma. A globoid silhouette also results from extreme generalized

plain: Causes of pericardial effusion in dogs; differentials for a globoid heart? Right auricular hemangiosarcoma (Golden, GSD; MST ~2–4 months), idiopathic, heart-base chemodectoma (Boxers, brachycephalics), mesothelioma. A globoid silhouette also results from extreme generalized cardiomegaly (DCM, tricuspid dysplasia); echo distinguishes.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Recurrent idiopathic pericardial effusion despite pericardiocentesis →
2nd–3rd recurrence; excellent long-term prognosis once hemangiosarcoma is

plain: Recurrent idiopathic pericardial effusion despite pericardiocentesis → definitive Tx? Subtotal pericardiectomy (open or thoracoscopic) after the 2nd–3rd recurrence; excellent long-term prognosis once hemangiosarcoma is excluded by echo.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Muffled heart sounds and dyspnea persist after thoracocentesis drains
heart failure produces pleural effusion), then pericardiocentesis; fluid cytology

plain: Muffled heart sounds and dyspnea persist after thoracocentesis drains pleural fluid → Echocardiography for pericardial effusion/tamponade (right heart failure produces pleural effusion), then pericardiocentesis; fluid cytology for neoplasia. Not calcium channel blockers.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cough, exercise intolerance; radiographs show enlarged tortuous blunted
caudal lobar pulmonary arteries, main PA bulge, "reversed-D" right heart
(positive 6–7 months post-infection; heat-treat if negative with suspicion) plus
modified Knott's; echo shows parallel double-lined worms only with heavy

plain: Cough, exercise intolerance; radiographs show enlarged tortuous blunted caudal lobar pulmonary arteries, main PA bulge, "reversed-D" right heart → Heartworm disease (Dirofilaria immitis). Antigen test is most sensitive (positive 6–7 months post-infection; heat-treat if negative with suspicion) plus modified Knott's; echo shows parallel double-lined worms only with heavy burdens.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: IM on day 60, then two doses 24 h apart on days 90–91
Not day 1 + day 30 — AHS begins melarsomine at day 60.

plain: Adulticide protocol (American Heartworm Society)? Strict exercise restriction; doxycycline 10 mg/kg q12h × 4 weeks (Wolbachia); monthly macrocyclic lactone; prednisone taper; melarsomine 2.5 mg/kg deep epaxial IM on day 60, then two doses 24 h apart on days 90–91; antigen retest 9 months after. Not day 1 + day 30 — AHS begins melarsomine at day 60.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Heartworm dog with hemoglobinuria, new murmur, collapse →
surgical worm extraction via the jugular vein first

plain: Heartworm dog with hemoglobinuria, new murmur, collapse → Caval syndrome; surgical worm extraction via the jugular vein first, adulticide afterward.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Define cor pulmonale; classic canine cause?
pulmonary hypertension from lung or pulmonary
pulmonary fibrosis, PTE (cattle: high-altitude brisket disease). Jugular
distension, ascites, hepatomegaly, split S2. Treat the lung cause, oxygen,

plain: Define cor pulmonale; classic canine cause? Right ventricular hypertrophy/ failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension from lung or pulmonary vascular disease — classically heartworm; also chronic bronchitis, pulmonary fibrosis, PTE (cattle: high-altitude brisket disease). Jugular distension, ascites, hepatomegaly, split S2. Treat the lung cause, oxygen, sildenafil 1–3 mg/kg q8–12h, cautious diuretics.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Dog with IMHA, PLN or hyperadrenocorticism: sudden severe dyspnea
pancreatitis, heartworm). Increased A-a gradient, D-dimer, CT angiography;
echo shows pulmonary hypertension. Oxygen, heparin/LMWH then
clopidogrel or rivaroxaban; thromboprophylaxis is standard in IMHA.

plain: Dog with IMHA, PLN or hyperadrenocorticism: sudden severe dyspnea and hypoxemia with near-normal radiographs → Pulmonary thromboembolism (hypercoagulable: antithrombin loss, sepsis, neoplasia, pancreatitis, heartworm). Increased A-a gradient, D-dimer, CT angiography; echo shows pulmonary hypertension. Oxygen, heparin/LMWH then clopidogrel or rivaroxaban; thromboprophylaxis is standard in IMHA.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Dog with a thrombus at the aortic trifurcation → signs and underlying
Acute painful hindlimb paresis, cold limbs, absent femoral pulses,
cyanotic pads. In dogs ATE reflects

plain: Dog with a thrombus at the aortic trifurcation → signs and underlying causes? Acute painful hindlimb paresis, cold limbs, absent femoral pulses, cyanotic pads. In dogs ATE reflects hypercoagulable states (PLN, hyperadrenocorticism, IMHA, neoplasia), not cardiac disease as in cats. Analgesia, clopidogrel/heparin, treat the cause.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Excited, panting dog with SBP 220 mmHg and a normal exam →
in a quiet room, 5–7 Doppler readings (discard the first, average), or recheck at

plain: Excited, panting dog with SBP 220 mmHg and a normal exam → Situational (white-coat) hypertension: re-measure after 5–10 min acclimation in a quiet room, 5–7 Doppler readings (discard the first, average), or recheck at another visit/at home. Treat only persistent SBP ≥160 mmHg or target-organ damage (retina, kidney, brain, LVH).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Enalapril indications in dogs; antihypertensive of choice in cats?
proteinuric nephropathy, CHF, mild hypertension in dogs. Cats:
retinopathy/acute blindness; ACE inhibitors are too weak as sole feline

plain: Enalapril indications in dogs; antihypertensive of choice in cats? Enalapril: proteinuric nephropathy, CHF, mild hypertension in dogs. Cats: amlodipine 0.625–1.25 mg/cat PO q24h (target SBP <160), including hypertensive retinopathy/acute blindness; ACE inhibitors are too weak as sole feline antihypertensives.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Breathing pattern of upper airway obstruction? Prolonged, labored
with stridor or stertor, extended head and neck, often hyperthermia.
Expiratory effort/wheeze = intrathoracic or lower airway disease; rapid shallow

plain: Breathing pattern of upper airway obstruction? Prolonged, labored inspiration with stridor or stertor, extended head and neck, often hyperthermia. Expiratory effort/wheeze = intrathoracic or lower airway disease; rapid shallow breathing = restrictive pleural/parenchymal disease.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
plain: Stertor vs stridor? Stertor: low-pitched snoring from nasopharynx/soft palate (brachycephalic syndrome). Stridor: high-pitched from laryngeal or tracheal narrowing (laryngeal paralysis).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Brachycephalic dog (Pug, Bulldog) with stertor, exercise/heat intolerance,
stenotic nares, elongated soft palate (>80%), hypoplastic trachea
aberrant turbinates. Secondary to chronic negative pressure: everted laryngeal
saccules, tonsillar eversion, laryngeal collapse; hiatal hernia.
paralysis — older large breeds; not "laryngeal hypoplasia".

plain: Brachycephalic dog (Pug, Bulldog) with stertor, exercise/heat intolerance, gagging, regurgitation → Brachycephalic obstructive airway syndrome. Primary: stenotic nares, elongated soft palate (>80%), hypoplastic trachea, aberrant turbinates. Secondary to chronic negative pressure: everted laryngeal saccules, tonsillar eversion, laryngeal collapse; hiatal hernia. Not laryngeal paralysis — older large breeds; not "laryngeal hypoplasia".

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: English Bulldog with elongated soft palate → breed-specific component
fold resection — cosmetic, not an airway procedure.

plain: English Bulldog with elongated soft palate → breed-specific component and its radiographic criterion? Tracheal hypoplasia: tracheal lumen:thoracic inlet ratio <0.16 on lateral film (normal ≥0.20; Bulldog mean 0.13). Congenital, not surgically correctable, raises anesthetic risk. Not nasal- fold resection — cosmetic, not an airway procedure.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: BOAS surgery: which first, which least important? Alar wedge resection
early (3–6 months), usually with staphylectomy to the
epiglottis tip; resect everted saccules if present; stage III laryngeal collapse
Perioperative steroids, maropitant, avoid heat and stress.

plain: BOAS surgery: which first, which least important? Alar wedge resection of stenotic nares early (3–6 months), usually with staphylectomy to the epiglottis tip; resect everted saccules if present; stage III laryngeal collapse may need permanent tracheostomy. Tonsillectomy contributes least. Perioperative steroids, maropitant, avoid heat and stress.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Laryngoscopy in a Bulldog shows pale everted tissue rostral to the vocal
— the first stage of laryngeal collapse;
correcting nares and palate early halts progression.

plain: Laryngoscopy in a Bulldog shows pale everted tissue rostral to the vocal folds → Everted laryngeal saccules — the first stage of laryngeal collapse; correcting nares and palate early halts progression.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Gagging dog with bilateral enlarged rounded masses in the caudal
Tonsillitis (usually secondary — treat the cause) or tonsillar
neoplasia (SCC, lymphoma — biopsy). Tonsillectomy only for neoplasia or

plain: Gagging dog with bilateral enlarged rounded masses in the caudal oropharynx → Tonsillitis (usually secondary — treat the cause) or tonsillar neoplasia (SCC, lymphoma — biopsy). Tonsillectomy only for neoplasia or persistent obstruction.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Old Labrador/Golden with inspiratory stridor, voice change, exercise/heat
intolerance, collapse in hot weather, later hindlimb weakness →

avoid heat, exertion, neck leads, swimming.

plain: Old Labrador/Golden with inspiratory stridor, voice change, exercise/heat intolerance, collapse in hot weather, later hindlimb weakness → Acquired laryngeal paralysis — geriatric-onset laryngeal paralysis polyneuropathy (GOLPP); check hypothyroidism. Congenital form: Bouvier, Husky. Owner: avoid heat, exertion, neck leads, swimming. Not heat stroke — a consequence, not the diagnosis.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Confirming laryngeal paralysis? Laryngoscopy under light anesthesia
breathing: arytenoids fail to abduct on inspiration (watch for paradoxical

plain: Confirming laryngeal paralysis? Laryngoscopy under light anesthesia (propofol to effect, ~4 mg/kg) with doxapram 1–2 mg/kg IV to stimulate deep breathing: arytenoids fail to abduct on inspiration (watch for paradoxical movement). Thoracic radiographs for aspiration/megaesophagus.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Laryngeal paralysis crisis (cyanosis, collapse) → initial management?

plain: Laryngeal paralysis crisis (cyanosis, collapse) → initial management? Sedation (butorphanol/acepromazine), oxygen, active cooling, dexamethasone; intubate or tracheostomy if obstructed. Not stenotic nares correction — irrelevant in a Labrador.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Definitive surgery for laryngeal paralysis and its most serious
megaesophagus/polyneuropathy); elevated feeding, no swimming, prompt

plain: Definitive surgery for laryngeal paralysis and its most serious complication? Unilateral arytenoid lateralization (tie-back); bilateral is avoided. MSC aspiration pneumonia, ~10–20% lifelong (higher with megaesophagus/polyneuropathy); elevated feeding, no swimming, prompt antibiotics. Not facial nerve paralysis.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Maltese/small dog: 1-minute episodes of loud snorting inspirations with neck extended, stopped by rubbing the throat, normal between → Reverse sneezing (paroxysmal inspiratory effort from nasopharyngeal irritation); benign, no treatment. Persistent stertor or discharge → nasal mites (Pneumonyssoides caninum), foreign body, nasopharyngeal polyp or mass; rhinoscopy.

plain: Dolichocephalic dog with unilateral epistaxis, depigmentation and ulceration of the nasal planum, nasal pain → Nasal aspergillosis (A. fumigatus): CT turbinate destruction without a mass; rhinoscopic fungal plaques. Topical clotrimazole 1% or enilconazole infusion under anesthesia (1 h), repeated as needed. Nasal tumors: older dogs, facial deformity; both begin unilateral with discharge.

plain: Best radiographic views of the canine nasal cavity? Open-mouth (intraoral) ventrodorsal and rostrocaudal frontal-sinus skyline views; lateral is least useful (superimposition). CT is the modality of choice.

plain: Obese middle-aged Yorkie/Pomeranian/Chihuahua with chronic "goose- honk" cough worse with excitement or collar pressure → Tracheal collapse (dorsal membrane laxity, cartilage weakness). Cervical trachea collapses on inspiration, intrathoracic on expiration. Confirming tracheal collapse when static radiographs look normal? Fluoroscopy during coughing (most sensitive non-invasive; static films miss ~40%); tracheobronchoscopy is definitive and grades I–IV. Inspiratory/ expiratory lateral films are the first screen.

plain: Management of tracheal collapse? Medical first (70–90% respond): weight loss, harness instead of collar, antitussives (hydrocodone 0.22 mg/kg, butorphanol), short steroid courses, bronchodilators, treat concurrent bronchitis, avoid heat/excitement. Refractory grade III–IV: intraluminal stent (intrathoracic) or extraluminal rings (cervical).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Tracheal-collapse dog becomes cyanotic and distressed after excitement → first treatment? Oxygen plus sedation (butorphanol 0.2–0.4 mg/kg ± acepromazine), cool quiet room, single dexamethasone dose; intubate only if arrest is imminent. Not terbutaline — bronchodilators are adjuncts, not rescue drugs.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Dog recently from a kennel, honking dry cough, otherwise bright →
doxycycline 5 mg/kg q12h if systemic signs; intranasal/oral vaccine gives

plain: Dog recently from a kennel, honking dry cough, otherwise bright → Canine infectious respiratory disease complex; Bordetella bronchiseptica (with parainfluenza, adenovirus-2, Mycoplasma). Self-limiting 1–2 weeks; doxycycline 5 mg/kg q12h if systemic signs; intranasal/oral vaccine gives mucosal IgA within days.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Middle-aged small dog, daily cough >2 months, crackles; transtracheal
wash shows nonseptic neutrophilic inflammation, abundant mucus

plain: Middle-aged small dog, daily cough >2 months, crackles; transtracheal wash shows nonseptic neutrophilic inflammation, abundant mucus (Curschmann spirals), no organisms → Canine chronic bronchitis.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: terbutaline, hydrocodone for non-productive cough, weight loss, harness;
antibiotics only if culture-positive. Irreversible but controllable.

plain: Prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day tapered (or inhaled fluticasone), theophylline/ terbutaline, hydrocodone for non-productive cough, weight loss, harness; antibiotics only if culture-positive. Irreversible but controllable.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Chronic cough, radiographs done → next diagnostic to characterize
airway disease? Transtracheal wash or bronchoscopy with BAL
cytology and culture (eosinophilic vs neutrophilic vs infectious) before

plain: Chronic cough, radiographs done → next diagnostic to characterize airway disease? Transtracheal wash or bronchoscopy with BAL for cytology and culture (eosinophilic vs neutrophilic vs infectious) before committing to long-term steroids.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Young dog with chronic dry cough; bronchoscopy shows pale nodules at
pathognomonic; L1 with kinked tail on Baermann or zinc sulfate (intermittent

plain: Young dog with chronic dry cough; bronchoscopy shows pale nodules at the carina → Oslerus (Filaroides) osleri — carinal nodules are near- pathognomonic; L1 with kinked tail on Baermann or zinc sulfate (intermittent shedding); direct dam-to-pup transmission. Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg × 10–14 days or ivermectin.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Alveolar pattern (air bronchograms, lobar sign) — causes and how
Alveoli filled with fluid or cells.
ARDS; atelectasis shifts the mediastinum toward the lesion; also hemorrhage,

plain: Alveolar pattern (air bronchograms, lobar sign) — causes and how distribution helps? Alveoli filled with fluid or cells. Cranioventral = bronchopneumonia/aspiration (right middle lobe); perihilar/caudodorsal = cardiogenic edema (dogs); caudodorsal = non-cardiogenic edema, contusion, ARDS; atelectasis shifts the mediastinum toward the lesion; also hemorrhage, neoplasia, lobe torsion.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Puppy chewed an electric cord → where is the noncardiogenic edema on
Not cranioventral — that is the aspiration

plain: Puppy chewed an electric cord → where is the noncardiogenic edema on radiographs? Caudodorsal lung fields (also seizures, head trauma, strangulation, smoke inhalation). Not cranioventral — that is the aspiration pattern.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Febrile coughing dog with a cranioventral alveolar pattern →
wash culture; broad-spectrum antibiotics, nebulization and coupage.

plain: Febrile coughing dog with a cranioventral alveolar pattern → Bronchopneumonia (bacterial or aspiration — gravity-dependent). Airway wash culture; broad-spectrum antibiotics, nebulization and coupage.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Radiograph: heart elevated off the sternum, lung lobes retracted with
sharp borders, peripheral lucency without vascular markings, flattened
subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum and rib fractures accompany
trauma. Mediastinal shift with flattened diaphragm = tension pneumothorax —

plain: Radiograph: heart elevated off the sternum, lung lobes retracted with sharp borders, peripheral lucency without vascular markings, flattened diaphragm → Pneumothorax. The heart is elevated, not enlarged; subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum and rib fractures accompany trauma. Mediastinal shift with flattened diaphragm = tension pneumothorax — emergency decompression.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Point-of-care ultrasound findings diagnostic of pneumothorax? Absent
(pathognomonic); M-mode shows the barcode/stratosphere sign instead

plain: Point-of-care ultrasound findings diagnostic of pneumothorax? Absent glide (lung-sliding) sign and absent B-lines, A-lines persist, with a lung point (pathognomonic); M-mode shows the barcode/stratosphere sign instead of the seashore sign.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Treatment of pneumothorax and when to escalate?
thoracocentesis at the dorsal third of the 7th–9th ICS
Chest tube if air re-accumulates after 2–3 taps or continuously; thoracotomy

plain: Treatment of pneumothorax and when to escalate? Oxygen and thoracocentesis at the dorsal third of the 7th–9th ICS, bilateral if needed. Chest tube if air re-accumulates after 2–3 taps or continuously; thoracotomy for a persistent leak.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Spontaneous pneumothorax (no trauma) in a dog → cause and Tx?

plain: Spontaneous pneumothorax (no trauma) in a dog → cause and Tx? Ruptured pulmonary bullae/blebs (Siberian Husky, deep-chested breeds); also neoplasia, abscess, heartworm, Paragonimus. CT to locate; usually lung lobectomy via median sternotomy.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: 7th–9th ICS, dorsal third for air, ventral
third for fluid, needle on the cranial border of the rib
caudally). Horse and cattle: standing, 6th–7th ICS.

plain: Thoracocentesis positioning and site? Sternal (or standing/lateral) with oxygen and minimal restraint; 7th–9th ICS, dorsal third for air, ventral third for fluid, needle on the cranial border of the rib (vessels and nerve run caudally). Horse and cattle: standing, 6th–7th ICS. Not the 4th–5th ICS.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Radiograph: retracted lobes, interlobar fissure lines, ventral fluid opacity
count, cytology, triglyceride; then treat the cause (CHF, pyothorax,

plain: Radiograph: retracted lobes, interlobar fissure lines, ventral fluid opacity obscuring the cardiac silhouette → Pleural effusion. In a dyspneic patient, thoracocentesis before radiographs — diagnostic and therapeutic: protein, cell count, cytology, triglyceride; then treat the cause (CHF, pyothorax, chylothorax, neoplasia).

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
plain: Pleural fluid classification? Transudate: protein <2.5 g/dL, cells <1,500/µL. Modified transudate: protein 2.5–5 g/dL, cells 1,000–7,000/µL. Exudate: protein >3 g/dL, cells >5,000–7,000/µL; degenerate neutrophils with bacteria = pyothorax.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Milky effusion, triglyceride higher than serum, small lymphocytes
(chronic cases turn exudative). Idiopathic is MCC; also cardiac
disease, cranial mediastinal mass. Medical: drainage, low-fat diet, rutin 50 mg/

plain: Milky effusion, triglyceride higher than serum, small lymphocytes predominate → Dx, class, Tx? Chylothorax — classically a modified transudate (chronic cases turn exudative). Idiopathic is MCC; also cardiac disease, cranial mediastinal mass. Medical: drainage, low-fat diet, rutin 50 mg/ kg q8h. Definitive: thoracic duct ligation + pericardectomy (± cisterna chyli ablation), ~80–90% resolve; chronic → fibrosing pleuritis.

chapter: Chapter 1 — Canine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Pyothorax confirmed (septic exudate), culture pending → next therapeutic
with warm saline lavage q6–12h plus IV
clindamycin + enrofloxacin) for 4–6 weeks; surgery if no improvement in 3–7
days or a grass awn/abscessed lobe is found.

plain: Pyothorax confirmed (septic exudate), culture pending → next therapeutic step? Bilateral thoracostomy tubes with warm saline lavage q6–12h plus IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering anaerobes (ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin + enrofloxacin) for 4–6 weeks; surgery if no improvement in 3–7 days or a grass awn/abscessed lobe is found. Not repeated needle thoracocentesis — inadequate drainage.

plain: Dog regurgitating (passive, no retching); radiograph shows diffusely gas/ food-dilated esophagus displacing trachea ventrally → Megaesophagus. Work up acquired causes: AChR antibody (myasthenia gravis, ~25%, the MC treatable cause), ACTH stim (hypoadrenocorticism), thyroid panel, lead; most adult cases idiopathic.

plain: Management of canine megaesophagus and its MCCOD? Upright Bailey- chair feeding of calorie-dense small meals held vertical 10–15 min; treat the underlying cause. Aspiration pneumonia is the usual cause of death. Not metoclopramide/cisapride — canine esophagus is striated muscle, prokinetics ineffective.

esophagus dilated only cranial to heart base →

Uniform generalized dilation in a puppy = congenital idiopathic

plain: 4–5-month-old GSD/Irish Setter puppy regurgitating since weaning; esophagus dilated only cranial to heart base → Persistent right aortic arch (vascular ring; ligamentum arteriosum entraps esophagus). Barium shows focal cranial dilation. Tx: ligate ligamentum via left 4th intercostal thoracotomy. Uniform generalized dilation in a puppy = congenital idiopathic megaesophagus.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Acute regurgitation, gagging, drooling; radiograph shows esophageal

promptly — retrieve or push into stomach; thoracotomy only if endoscopy fails

plain: Acute regurgitation, gagging, drooling; radiograph shows esophageal foreign body (thoracic inlet, heart base or hiatus) → Esophagoscopy promptly — retrieve or push into stomach; thoracotomy only if endoscopy fails or perforation. Avoid barium if perforation suspected (use iohexol). Follow with soft food, sucralfate/PPI; stricture is a late complication.

plain: Vomiting dog that swallowed a toy; gastric foreign body suspected → first step and contraindicated drug? Two-view abdominal radiographs first (± ultrasound/contrast), then endoscopic retrieval or gastrotomy.

plain: Chronic projectile vomiting hours after eating; hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria → Pyloric/ proximal duodenal (high) obstruction — HCl lost without duodenal bicarbonate. Ultrasound or barium/endoscopy to confirm; correct with 0.9% NaCl + KCl before surgery. Distal SI obstruction gives acidosis with mixed losses.

plain: Melena vs hematochezia — origin? Melena = digested blood from stomach/ small intestine (ulcers, NSAIDs, tumors) or swallowed blood (epistaxis, oral, pulmonary — check when no GI lesion found); hematochezia = fresh blood from colon/rectum/anus (whipworms, colitis, polyps).

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Dog on NSAIDs with melena, hematemesis, abdominal pain, falling PCV
(superior to famotidine), sucralfate 0.5–1 g q8h given 2 h apart from
other drugs, misoprostol for NSAID ulcers (

plain: Dog on NSAIDs with melena, hematemesis, abdominal pain, falling PCV → Gastroduodenal ulceration. Stop NSAID; omeprazole/pantoprazole 1 mg/ kg q12h (superior to famotidine), sucralfate 0.5–1 g q8h given 2 h apart from other drugs, misoprostol for NSAID ulcers (contraindicated in pregnancy); never combine NSAIDs with corticosteroids. Not famotidine — H2 blockers weaker, develop tolerance.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Large deep-chested dog, non-productive retching, tympanic distended
(caudal vena cava is compressed), then gastric
decompression, then right lateral radiograph, ECG, then surgery: derotation,

plain: Large deep-chested dog, non-productive retching, tympanic distended abdomen, shock → management sequence? Shock fluids via two large-bore cephalic (forelimb) catheters (caudal vena cava is compressed), then gastric decompression, then right lateral radiograph, ECG, then surgery: derotation, assess gastric/splenic viability, incisional gastropexy.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Shock fluid dose for GDV (or any hypovolemic dog)?
total (cats 40–60), given as 20–30 mL/kg boluses over 15 min to
perfusion endpoints; or hypertonic 7% saline 4 mL/kg then crystalloids; add

plain: Shock fluid dose for GDV (or any hypovolemic dog)? Isotonic crystalloid 90 mL/kg total (cats 40–60), given as 20–30 mL/kg boluses over 15 min to perfusion endpoints; or hypertonic 7% saline 4 mL/kg then crystalloids; add colloid/blood if no response.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Radiographic view and sign confirming volvulus (not simple dilatation)?
separated by a soft-tissue fold ("double bubble", reverse C, Popeye arm).
Simple dilatation shows one gas-filled stomach with pylorus ventral.

plain: Radiographic view and sign confirming volvulus (not simple dilatation)? Right lateral: gas-filled pylorus displaced craniodorsal to the fundus, separated by a soft-tissue fold ("double bubble", reverse C, Popeye arm). Simple dilatation shows one gas-filled stomach with pylorus ventral. Radiograph after decompression/stabilization.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

plain: Orogastric tube will not pass → Percutaneous trocarization: 14–16 g catheter at the point of greatest tympany, usually the right paracostal flank (percuss to avoid displaced spleen); then retry the tube. Not fixed left side — trocarize where the ping is loudest, typically right.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: GDV with plasma lactate 7 mmol/L — significance?
failure to fall >50% with fluids, predicts

plain: GDV with plasma lactate 7 mmol/L — significance? Lactate >6 mmol/L, or failure to fall >50% with fluids, predicts gastric necrosis and worse survival. Resuscitate before anesthesia regardless.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Most common post-GDV complications, and what gastropexy prevents?
necrosis/perforation, septic peritonitis, reperfusion injury, DIC, hypokalemia,
splenic infarction. Gastropexy (pyloric antrum to right body wall) cuts

plain: Most common post-GDV complications, and what gastropexy prevents? Ventricular arrhythmias (~40–50%, peak 12–72 h; lidocaine), gastric necrosis/perforation, septic peritonitis, reperfusion injury, DIC, hypokalemia, splenic infarction. Gastropexy (pyloric antrum to right body wall) cuts recurrent volvulus from 50–80% to <5% but does not prevent dilatation.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Vomiting dog with cranial abdominal pain after a fatty meal (Mini
Schnauzer, lipemic serum) → most sensitive/specific test? Spec cPL >400
enlarged pancreas, hyperechoic peripancreatic fat, ± effusion (~68% sensitive).

plain: Vomiting dog with cranial abdominal pain after a fatty meal (Mini Schnauzer, lipemic serum) → most sensitive/specific test? plain: Supportive lab/radiographic findings in canine pancreatitis? Leukocytosis, prerenal azotemia (BUN increased), raised ALP/ALT, hyperlipidemia, hypocalcemia (poor prognosis); radiographs: loss of right cranial serosal detail, static "sentinel" duodenal loop. Not low BUN — dehydration raises it.

plain: Treatment and nutrition for acute canine pancreatitis? IV crystalloids, opioid analgesia, maropitant, early enteral low-fat feeding within 24–48 h once vomiting controlled (esophagostomy/jejunostomy tube if needed); antibiotics only for infected necrosis; manage hypertriglyceridemia, stop KBr/ azathioprine. Not prolonged NPO — worsens gut barrier and outcome.

spans.text: How are uroabdomen, bile and chylous effusions confirmed?

plain: How are uroabdomen, bile and chylous effusions confirmed? Uroabdomen: fluid creatinine >2× serum (or fluid:serum K >1.4 dogs, >1.9 cats; urea equilibrates, unreliable). Bile: fluid bilirubin >2× serum, green fluid. Chylous: fluid triglyceride > serum (>100 mg/dL), milky; managed medically (low-fat diet, rutin).

plain: Young Boxer/French Bulldog with chronic hematochezia, mucoid diarrhea, weight loss, hypoalbuminemia; colonic biopsy shows PAS- positive macrophages → Histiocytic ulcerative colitis (adherent-invasive E. coli; FISH/culture). Tx enrofloxacin 10 mg/kg q24h 6–8 weeks; prognosis good if sensitive strain. Not diet/steroids or "grave prognosis" — E. coli- driven, fluoroquinolone-responsive.

plain: Intact male GSD with painful ulcerated draining perianal sinus tracts, tenesmus, dyschezia → Perianal fistula (anal furunculosis), immune- mediated. Tx of choice cyclosporine 5 mg/kg q12–24h; ketoconazole 5–10 mg/kg added halves cyclosporine dose/cost; topical tacrolimus 0.1% for mild/ maintenance; novel-protein diet; surgery last (incontinence). ~85–90% remission. Not prednisolone — less effective than calcineurin inhibitors.

plain: Intact male dog straining with thin ribbon-like feces → Extraluminal compression of the pelvic canal: prostatomegaly, sublumbar lymphadenopathy, perineal hernia, healed pelvic fracture. Rectal palpation of prostate and sublumbar nodes plus radiographs.

plain: Dietary cause of canine constipation and correction? Insufficient fiber (plus low water intake, bone/hair ingestion). Add psyllium 1–4 tsp/meal, canned pumpkin or high-fiber diet; ensure hydration.

plain: Soft painless fluctuant intermandibular/cervical swelling; aspirate viscous blood-tinged mucoid fluid → Sialocele (salivary mucocele), usually from the sublingual gland/duct. Excise the ipsilateral mandibular + sublingual gland complex (dog on its back — swelling shifts to the affected side) ± marsupialization. Drainage alone recurs.

plain: Definition and treatment of a ranula? A sublingual sialocele — saliva extravasated into tissue beside the tongue after duct/acinar rupture, not saliva inside the gland and not a true cyst. Remove mandibular + sublingual glands and marsupialize. Not saliva accumulated within the gland — it is leaked saliva in a granulation-tissue cavity.

spans.text: ALT/AST vs ALP/GGT vs liver function — and next step with marked
for extrahepatic bile duct obstruction or

plain: ALT/AST vs ALP/GGT vs liver function — and next step with marked ALP/GGT? ALT/AST = hepatocellular leakage; ALP/GGT = cholestasis/ induction (steroids, phenobarbital, Cushing's); function = paired pre/2-h postprandial bile acids (postprandial >25–30 µmol/L abnormal) or ammonia. High ALP/GGT → ultrasound for extrahepatic bile duct obstruction or mucocele.

spans.text: Mildly elevated liver enzymes, asymptomatic dog → next step?

plain: Mildly elevated liver enzymes, asymptomatic dog → next step? Assess function (bile acids), review drugs and endocrine causes, recheck 4–6 weeks; ultrasound next; biopsy with coagulation panel if persistently >2–3× upper limit. Treat function, not enzymes.

plain: Lab pattern of hepatic synthetic failure? Low BUN, albumin, glucose, cholesterol; prolonged PT/PTT; high bilirubin, bile acids, ammonia; enzymes may be normal in end-stage disease. Albumin falls late (half-life ~8 days). Not hypobilirubinemia or hypoalbuminemia from muscle disease — muscle raises CK/AST.

Hemolytic icterus: anemia, dark orange feces/urine; hepatic: normal feces. Ultrasound the biliary tree. Not hemolysis/hepatitis — no bile pigment reaches the gut.

plain: Young small-breed dog (Yorkie, Maltese) stunted, post-prandial dullness/ head pressing, ptyalism, microhepatica, ammonium biurate crystals, low BUN, microcytosis → Congenital portosystemic shunt. Screen with paired fasting/2-h postprandial bile acids (often >100 µmol/L) or ammonia; localize with ultrasound Doppler, CT angiography (best) or scintigraphy. Hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia common.

intrahepatic (patent ductus venosus) in large breeds (Irish Wolfhound,

plain: Congenital vs acquired shunts — number, location, breeds? Congenital: single; extrahepatic (portocaval/portoazygos) in toy breeds and cats, intrahepatic (patent ductus venosus) in large breeds (Irish Wolfhound, Labrador); signs <1–3 years. Acquired: multiple extrahepatic shunts from portal hypertension (cirrhosis) in older dogs — never ligated.

chapter: Chapter 2 — Canine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

traps NH3 as NH4+, speeds transit; warm retention enema in crisis) plus
seizures; treat GI bleeding/hypokalemia. Avoid benzodiazepines, methionine.

plain: Medical management of hepatic encephalopathy (DOC and mechanism)? Lactulose 0.5–1 mL/kg PO q8h to 2–3 soft stools/day (colonic acidification traps NH3 as NH4+, speeds transit; warm retention enema in crisis) plus metronidazole 7.5 mg/kg q12h, neomycin or amoxicillin; levetiracetam for seizures; treat GI bleeding/hypokalemia. Avoid benzodiazepines, methionine.

plain: Diet in hepatic failure/encephalopathy — what to avoid? Avoid severe protein restriction (muscle catabolism releases ammonia) and red/organ meat and fish. Feed moderate, highly digestible dairy/soy protein (~2–2.5 g/kg/day dogs), restricting only while encephalopathic; cats never below maintenance, with taurine and arginine.

Gradual surgical attenuation (ameroid constrictor or cellophane band) after medical stabilization — allows hypoplastic portal vasculature to develop, avoids acute portal hypertension; ~85% long-term survival. Not lactulose + neomycin — that is stabilization, not definitive therapy.

plain: Nerve block for mandibular teeth? Inferior alveolar (mandibular) block at the mandibular foramen anesthetizes the whole hemimandible including the canine (risk: lingual nerve block → tongue self-trauma). Middle mental block (foramen ventral to PM2 mesial root) reliably covers only incisors/rostral lip — fine for 403, less reliable for the canine whose root extends caudal to the foramen. Feline symphyseal separation: cerclage wire around canines.

Daily toothbrushing (plaque re-forms within 24 h) with VOHC- accepted products/diets, soft food several days after extractions, analgesia, recheck 2 weeks. Antibiotics not routine — only severe periodontitis or systemic risk.

plain: Dehydrated dog given large crystalloid volumes develops limb/ventral edema with persistent hypovolemia → next fluid class? Synthetic colloid (hetastarch 5–10 mL/kg bolus, ≤20 mL/kg/day) or plasma/albumin if hypoalbuminemic — crystalloids redistribute 75% to interstitium within an hour. HES carries AKI/coagulopathy risk.

plain: Anemic dog — will crystalloids raise PCV? What does? No — crystalloids dilute PCV further. Packed RBCs ~1 mL/kg raise PCV ~1%; whole blood ~2 mL/kg raises 1%. Volume = kg × blood volume (dog 90, cat 60–66 mL/kg) × (desired − recipient PCV)/donor PCV. Transfuse for signs, typically PCV <20% acute or <12–15% chronic.

plain: ECG: tall tented T waves, flat/absent P waves, wide QRS, bradycardia; K+ 8.5 (urethral obstruction, Addisonian crisis) → first drug and sequence? 10% calcium gluconate 0.5–1.5 mL/kg slow IV over 5–10 min with ECG — cardioprotective within minutes, does not lower K+; then regular insulin 0.25–0.5 U/kg IV + dextrose (2 g/U, then 2.5% CRI) to shift K+ in, 0.9% NaCl, ± bicarbonate; then treat the cause. Atrial standstill when K+ >8.

plain: Dog on dextrose-containing fluids or insulin (DKA) → electrolyte to anticipate? Hypokalemia (and hypophosphatemia): insulin drives K+ intracellularly via Na/K-ATPase. Supplement KCl by sliding scale, max 0.5 mEq/kg/h, recheck q2–4 h.

plain: Patient returning 7% dehydrated with heart rate 60 → first action? Stabilize before any financial discussion: deficit 0.07 × kg × 1,000 mL over 6– 24 h plus maintenance; relative bradycardia with hypovolemia suggests hyperkalemia/Addison's — ECG and electrolytes.

plain: Small bitch 1–4 weeks post-whelping a large litter: panting, restlessness, tremors, stiff gait, tetany, 41°C → Eclampsia (puerperal hypocalcemia; total Ca <7 mg/dL, iCa <0.8 mmol/L). 10% calcium gluconate 0.5–1.5 mL/kg slow IV over 15–30 min with ECG (stop if bradycardia), cool, diazepam if seizuring; then oral calcium/vitamin D, wean or supplement pups. Do not supplement calcium during pregnancy (suppresses PTH).

plain: Essential amino acids limiting muscle protein synthesis? Leucine (BCAA triggering mTOR-driven synthesis) and lysine (first-limiting in cereal-based diets); dogs have 10 essential amino acids, cats 11 (adding taurine).

plain: Growing dog on unbalanced all-meat/raw BARF diet → system most at risk and infectious hazard? Skeletal — nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism (Ca-poor, P-rich meat → PTH-driven bone resorption, folding fractures); excess bone → obstipation, tooth fractures. Zoonotic Salmonella /Listeria/ E. coli shedding. Feed AAFCO-complete diets.

Epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IM (0.1 mL/kg of 1:10,000; IV in shock), repeat q5–15 min; IV crystalloids, oxygen. Diphenhydramine 1–2 mg/kg IM and dexamethasone are adjuncts only (late-phase). Shock organ: liver/GI in dogs, lungs in cats. Mild urticaria alone: antihistamine ± steroid.

plain: Dog in status epilepticus (>5 min) → protocol? Diazepam 0.5–1 mg/kg IV (1–2 mg/kg rectal) or midazolam 0.2–0.3 mg/kg IV/IM/IN, up to 3 doses; then load levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV or phenobarbital 16–24 mg/kg IV divided (4 mg/kg q20–30 min); refractory → propofol/ketamine CRI, intubate. Check glucose, calcium; cool if >40°C.

plain: RECOVER CPR basics and survival to discharge? Compressions 100–120/ min, 1/3–1/2 chest width, uninterrupted 2-min cycles; intubate, 10 breaths/ min; epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IV every other cycle, atropine 0.04 mg/kg for asystole/PEA, defibrillate VF; ETCO2 >15 mmHg = effective compressions. ROSC 35–45% but survival to discharge <10% (~6% dogs, ~3–4% cats); anesthesia-related arrests up to 50%.

plain: Dog hit by car, dyspneic and aggressive → first step? Minimize handling: oxygen (flow-by/cage), light sedation (butorphanol ± low-dose benzodiazepine), analgesia; thoracocentesis if pneumothorax suspected; radiographs only after stabilization.

Effusion: ventral third. Horses: 6th–7th ICS above costochondral junction.

Thorax after stabilization: pulmonary contusions (worsen 12–24 h), pneumothorax, hemothorax, rib fractures, diaphragmatic hernia; abdomen/ultrasound for free fluid; retrograde cystourethrogram or effusion creatinine/K+ if not urinating (bladder rupture); pelvic films.

ABCs and shock first, then the globe (e-collar, lubricant, no pressure; repair within hours — prolapsed iris plugs the wound), skin last. Not the eye first — hypovolemia kills sooner than a plugged corneal wound.

Oxygen + sedation (butorphanol 0.2–0.4 mg/kg ± acepromazine), cooling, minimal handling, ± short-acting steroid; intubate/tracheostomy if failing. Antitussives/bronchodilators are maintenance, not first.

plain: Porcupine quills → management and MSC? Remove all quills promptly under general anesthesia with hemostats, pulling straight; never cut (they retract and migrate); check mouth, pharynx, eyes, interdigital spaces. plain: Dog with generalized seizures every ~2 months for 6 months — start maintenance therapy? Yes: start at ≥2 seizures within 6 months, cluster seizures, status epilepticus or severe post-ictal signs (ACVIM consensus). DOC phenobarbital 2–3 mg/kg PO q12h; alternatives potassium bromide, levetiracetam.

Never stop phenobarbital abruptly (withdrawal seizures); autoinduction lowers levels over time.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Paraparesis or tetraparesis: UMN vs LMN pattern → segment? C1–C5: UMN all four limbs. C6–T2: LMN thoracic limbs (reduced reflexes, atrophy), UMN pelvic. T3–L3: normal thoracic, UMN pelvic. L4–S3: LMN pelvic, reduced patellar/withdrawal, flaccid tail and bladder.

plain: Tetraparesis with exaggerated pelvic-limb reflexes — how are C1–C5 and C6–T2 separated? By thoracic-limb reflexes: reduced tone/reflexes (± Horner's, absent cutaneous trunci) → C6–T2; normal-to-exaggerated in all four limbs → C1–C5.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Hindlimb paralysis with flaccid, easily expressed bladder, reduced anal and tail tone → L4–S3 (LMN) lesion; pelvic and pudendal nerves arise from the sacral segments. A T3–L3 lesion gives spastic paralysis with a firm, hard- to-express UMN bladder.

plain: Pinching the medial (first) digit vs the lateral digits of the hindlimb tests which nerves? Medial digit/medial leg: femoral (saphenous), L4–L6; lateral digits: sciatic, L6–S2. Withdrawal flexion needs sciatic motor function; the patellar reflex tests femoral.

Surgery (trochleoplasty, tibial tuberosity transposition, imbrication) for symptomatic grade II and above.

plain: Of CCL rupture, hip dysplasia and Legg-Calvé-Perthes, which is least likely bilateral? Legg-Calvé-Perthes (bilateral only 12–16%) — a focal vascular event. Hip dysplasia is bilateral in most dogs; cruciate disease becomes bilateral in 40–60% within 1–2 yr.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: After stifle surgery (patellar luxation or CCL) → recovery instructions? Controlled, progressive exercise: confinement with short leash walks and passive range-of-motion or underwater treadmill for 6–8 weeks; no running, jumping or stairs until radiographic healing. Free activity → implant failure/ reluxation; no motion → quadriceps contracture.

plain: Femoral head or neck fracture (capital physeal slip) in a young dog → options? Fresh reducible: K-wires or lag screw. Otherwise salvage: FHO (best <20 kg, also cats) or total hip replacement in large dogs; a neck fracture devascularizes the head.

plain: When is a cast or splint appropriate? Closed, stable, minimally displaced fractures distal to the elbow or stifle (radius/ulna, tibia, metacarpals/tarsals) in young animals with ≥50% cortical contact; immobilize the joint above and below. Not humerus/femur, open, comminuted or articular fractures; fine for transport.

plain: Toy-breed dog with distal radius/ulna fracture → fixation? Bone plate (or ESF), not coaptation alone — toy breeds have a high nonunion rate from poor distal radial blood supply and minimal soft tissue.

plain: Humeral shaft fracture with ≥3 fragments → classification and fixation principle? Comminuted diaphyseal fracture (segmental = two fracture lines with an intact middle piece). Bridging osteosynthesis (plate-rod, interlocking nail, ESF) preserving the soft-tissue envelope; heals by callus — do not strip fragments to reconstruct every piece.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Fracture through a growth plate → classification, most common type, fixation? Salter-Harris I physis only; II physis + metaphysis (most common); III physis + epiphysis (articular); IV through all three; V crush (growth arrest, eg distal ulna). Repair early (<3–5 days) with smooth cross-pins or Rush pins; no screws or threaded implants across the physis.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Young dog, sudden lameness after exertion; fragment pulled off a tendon/ ligament insertion (tibial tuberosity, supraglenoid tubercle) → Avulsion fracture through an open apophysis — apophyseal cartilage is weaker than tendon. Early fixation with pin and tension-band wire or lag screw.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Dog cannot open its mouth (even sedated, ~2 cm), painful swollen then atrophied temporalis/masseter, limbs normal → Masticatory muscle myositis: autoantibodies to type 2M fibers (masticatory muscles only). Confirm with serum 2M antibody (~85–90% sensitive; false negative after steroids) ± temporalis biopsy; CK mildly high. Not EMG — supportive only.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Treatment of masticatory muscle myositis → Immunosuppressive prednisone 2 mg/kg/day tapered over months; never force the jaw open (mandibular fracture). Early treatment preserves range; chronic fibrosis → permanent trismus. Contrast: a jaw that cannot close = trigeminal neuritis or TMJ luxation.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

spans.text: Adult dog: generalized weakness, stiff gait, myalgia, atrophy, high CK;
biopsy shows lymphocytic-plasmacytic infiltrates and myonecrosis →

plain: Adult dog: generalized weakness, stiff gait, myalgia, atrophy, high CK; biopsy shows lymphocytic-plasmacytic infiltrates and myonecrosis → Immune-mediated polymyositis; may accompany megaesophagus, MG, SLE, polyarthritis, thymoma/lymphoma. Rule out Neospora/Toxoplasma, then prednisone 1–2 mg/kg q12h and taper; azathioprine adjunct.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Suspected myositis not improving on treatment → next step? Muscle biopsy (histopathology, immunohistochemistry, culture) to separate immune- mediated from infectious (Neospora, Toxoplasma, Hepatozoon) or paraneoplastic myositis; add CK, serology, EMG.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Synovial fluid in immune-mediated polyarthritis → High cell count of non- degenerate neutrophils, no bacteria (sterile), low viscosity, high protein. Septic arthritis: degenerate neutrophils ± bacteria. DJD: mononuclear cells, near-normal counts.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

(subchondral lysis, joint collapse), small breeds, rheumatoid factor often

plain: Chronic polyarthritis: rheumatoid arthritis vs SLE? RA: erosive (subchondral lysis, joint collapse), small breeds, rheumatoid factor often positive. SLE: non-erosive, multisystem (skin, glomerulonephritis/proteinuria, cytopenias), ANA positive. Both give sterile neutrophilic fluid; immunosuppression.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

plain: Radiographic hallmarks of osteoarthritis → Periarticular osteophytes/ enthesophytes, subchondral sclerosis, effusion, narrowed joint space, intra- articular mineralization, soft-tissue swelling. Radiographic severity correlates poorly with pain.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

spans.text: Overweight senior dog with hip/stifle OA → management cornerstones
Never combine NSAIDs with corticosteroids or

plain: Overweight senior dog with hip/stifle OA → management cornerstones and key contraindication? Weight loss (most effective single measure), controlled exercise/rehab, NSAIDs (carprofen, meloxicam, grapiprant), omega-3, gabapentin/amantadine, anti-NGF antibody (bedinvetmab; frunevetmab in cats). Never combine NSAIDs with corticosteroids or another NSAID; 5–7 day washout when switching.

chapter: Chapter 3 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 1)

spans.text: Bilateral symmetric painful distal-limb swelling; palisading periosteal new
bladder tumor, heartworm). Removing the mass resolves the bone lesions

plain: Bilateral symmetric painful distal-limb swelling; palisading periosteal new bone on long bones → Hypertrophic osteopathy (Marie disease), paraneoplastic → thoracic radiographs for a lung mass (also Spirocerca, bladder tumor, heartworm). Removing the mass resolves the bone lesions (vagally mediated).

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: UMN vs LMN signs on a dog's neuro exam →
tone, slow disuse atrophy. LMN (lesion in the intumescence or nerve): flaccid

plain: UMN vs LMN signs on a dog's neuro exam → UMN (lesion cranial to the limb's intumescence): paresis with normal-to-exaggerated reflexes, increased tone, slow disuse atrophy. LMN (lesion in the intumescence or nerve): flaccid paresis, absent/reduced reflexes, rapid neurogenic atrophy.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

Causes: cervical IVDD, atlantoaxial instability (toy breeds), Wobbler (C5–C7);

plain: Tetraparesis with UMN signs in all four limbs, neck pain → C1–C5. Causes: cervical IVDD, atlantoaxial instability (toy breeds), Wobbler (C5–C7); respiratory compromise possible.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Flaccid, hyporeflexic, atrophied forelimbs with UMN hindlimbs after
without hindlimb signs suggest brachial plexus injury rather than cord; check

plain: Flaccid, hyporeflexic, atrophied forelimbs with UMN hindlimbs after trauma → C6–T2 (cervicothoracic intumescence). Pure forelimb deficits without hindlimb signs suggest brachial plexus injury rather than cord; check cutaneous trunci and Horner.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Paraparesis, exaggerated patellar reflexes, crossed extensor reflex, normal
trunci cut-off 1–2 vertebrae caudal to the lesion.
pelvic signs localize cranial to L4.

plain: Paraparesis, exaggerated patellar reflexes, crossed extensor reflex, normal forelimbs, thoracolumbar pain → T3–L3 UMN myelopathy; cutaneous trunci cut-off 1–2 vertebrae caudal to the lesion. Not "cranial to L6" — UMN pelvic signs localize cranial to L4.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Hit-by-car dog: paralyzed hindlimbs, rigidly extended forelimbs with
severe T3–L3 lesion (loss of ascending border-cell inhibition). Not prognostic

plain: Hit-by-car dog: paralyzed hindlimbs, rigidly extended forelimbs with normal forelimb proprioception → Schiff-Sherrington posture = acute severe T3–L3 lesion (loss of ascending border-cell inhibition). Not prognostic by itself; deep pain decides prognosis.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Decreased patellar reflex plus reduced anal tone/flaccid tail →
(lumbosacral intumescence): patellar = L4–L6 femoral; withdrawal = L6–S1
Not L4–S1 or L4–S4 — dogs have

plain: Decreased patellar reflex plus reduced anal tone/flaccid tail → L4–S3 (lumbosacral intumescence): patellar = L4–L6 femoral; withdrawal = L6–S1 sciatic; perineal/anal = S1–S3 pudendal. Not L4–S1 or L4–S4 — dogs have three sacral segments.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Atonic distended bladder, dilated unresponsive anus, flaccid tail, hindlimb

lumbosacral stenosis and sacrocaudal fracture are classic causes.

plain: Atonic distended bladder, dilated unresponsive anus, flaccid tail, hindlimb reflexes normal → S1–S3 and caudal segments (cauda equina), which lie within the L5–L6 vertebral bodies; roots cross the L7–S1 junction, so lumbosacral stenosis and sacrocaudal fracture are classic causes.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

plain: UMN vs LMN bladder: location, findings, drugs? UMN (lesion cranial to sacral cord): large, firm, hard to express → prazosin/phenoxybenzamine (urethral smooth muscle) ± diazepam (striated sphincter) + bethanechol (detrusor). LMN (S1–S3/cauda equina): large flaccid, dribbling, easily expressed → manual expression ± bethanechol. Not S1–S3 for UMN — sacral lesions give LMN bladder.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Hindlimb knuckling, lost hock extension but still weight-bearing vs no
supports weight, sciatic flexes stifle/extends hock.

plain: Hindlimb knuckling, lost hock extension but still weight-bearing vs no weight-bearing with absent patellar reflex → Sciatic nerve injury (eg, IM injection, pelvic fracture) vs femoral nerve (L4–L6) injury; quadriceps supports weight, sciatic flexes stifle/extends hock.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Forelimb monoparesis after trauma: absent triceps reflex, absent
, the commonest form; radial nerve, lateral thoracic nerve (C8–T1)
and T1–T3 sympathetics lost. Absent deep pain with no improvement in 1–2

plain: Forelimb monoparesis after trauma: absent triceps reflex, absent ipsilateral cutaneous trunci, Horner → Caudal brachial plexus avulsion (C8–T2), the commonest form; radial nerve, lateral thoracic nerve (C8–T1) and T1–T3 sympathetics lost. Absent deep pain with no improvement in 1–2 months → amputation.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Miosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, third-eyelid protrusion → pathway and

postganglionic through middle ear to eye.

Not CN II/III/IV/VI — Horner is sympathetic

plain: Miosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, third-eyelid protrusion → pathway and localizing test? Sympathetic three-neuron pathway: hypothalamus → T1–T3; preganglionic via vagosympathetic trunk → cranial cervical ganglion; postganglionic through middle ear to eye. Phenylephrine 1% dilates within ~20 min in third-order (postganglionic) lesions. Causes: otitis media, plexus avulsion, idiopathic (Goldens). Not CN II/III/IV/VI — Horner is sympathetic denervation.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Head tilt, horizontal/rotary nystagmus not changing with head position, no
VIII): head tilt toward the lesion,
paralysis/Horner (middle ear) but never CP deficits.

plain: Head tilt, horizontal/rotary nystagmus not changing with head position, no proprioceptive deficits, normal mentation → Peripheral vestibular (CN VIII): head tilt toward the lesion, fast phase away. May carry ipsilateral facial paralysis/Horner (middle ear) but never CP deficits.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Head tilt with vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, ipsilateral

plain: Head tilt with vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, ipsilateral proprioceptive deficits, depressed mentation → Central vestibular (brainstem/cerebellum). Causes: neoplasia, MUO/GME, distemper, RMSF, thiamine deficiency, metronidazole toxicity. Head tilt opposite the CP-deficit side = paradoxical (caudal cerebellar peduncle/flocculonodular).

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Old dog, acute head tilt, nystagmus, falling, otherwise normal → Dx,
resolves over 2–3 weeks, residual head tilt possible. Supportive care
absent CP deficits exclude central disease.

plain: Old dog, acute head tilt, nystagmus, falling, otherwise normal → Dx, prognosis? Idiopathic geriatric vestibular disease: improves within 72 h, resolves over 2–3 weeks, residual head tilt possible. Supportive care (maropitant, meclizine); no steroids. Not cerebellum/cerebrum/neoplasm — absent CP deficits exclude central disease.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Head tilt and nystagmus plus ipsilateral facial paralysis and Horner →
