Otoscopy, bulla imaging, myringotomy culture; systemic antibiotics 6–8
weeks, bulla osteotomy if refractory; avoid ototoxic drops.

plain: Head tilt and nystagmus plus ipsilateral facial paralysis and Horner → Otitis media/interna: CN VII and sympathetic fibers traverse the middle ear. Otoscopy, bulla imaging, myringotomy culture; systemic antibiotics 6–8 weeks, bulla osteotomy if refractory; avoid ototoxic drops.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Hypermetria, intention tremor, truncal sway, wide-based stance, normal
strength, menace deficit with intact vision →
no paresis). Causes: hypoplasia (in utero parvovirus/panleukopenia),

plain: Hypermetria, intention tremor, truncal sway, wide-based stance, normal strength, menace deficit with intact vision → Cerebellum (ipsilateral signs, no paresis). Causes: hypoplasia (in utero parvovirus/panleukopenia), abiotrophy, neoplasia, infarct.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Behavior change, circling, normal gait but hopping/proprioceptive and
menace deficits on one side, seizures →
deficits; circling toward the lesion. Causes: meningioma, encephalitis,

plain: Behavior change, circling, normal gait but hopping/proprioceptive and menace deficits on one side, seizures → Forebrain lesion contralateral to the deficits; circling toward the lesion. Causes: meningioma, encephalitis, hydrocephalus, hepatic encephalopathy.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Which nerves mediate the palpebral reflex?
branch medial canthus, maxillary lateral); efferent
Menace adds cortical and cerebellar pathways.

plain: Which nerves mediate the palpebral reflex? Afferent CN V (ophthalmic branch medial canthus, maxillary lateral); efferent CN VII to orbicularis oculi. Menace adds cortical and cerebellar pathways.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Light in left eye: no PLR in either eye; light in right eye: both constrict →
oculomotor — a CN III lesion leaves the left pupil fixed whichever eye is lit.

plain: Light in left eye: no PLR in either eye; light in right eye: both constrict → Left optic nerve/retina (afferent, CN II) lesion, left eye blind. Not left oculomotor — a CN III lesion leaves the left pupil fixed whichever eye is lit.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Cannot blink one eye, same-side lip and ear droop, drooling →
hypothyroidism, trauma. Lubricate the cornea and check

plain: Cannot blink one eye, same-side lip and ear droop, drooling → Facial nerve (CN VII) paralysis: idiopathic (Cockers), otitis media/interna, hypothyroidism, trauma. Lubricate the cornea and check Schirmer tear test (lacrimal parasympathetics travel with VII).

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Dog suddenly cannot close its mouth (dropped jaw), drools, can swallow,
limiting in 2–4 weeks. Assisted feeding, tape muzzle; rule out rabies and

plain: Dog suddenly cannot close its mouth (dropped jaw), drools, can swallow, no pain → Idiopathic trigeminal neuritis (bilateral motor CN V); self- limiting in 2–4 weeks. Assisted feeding, tape muzzle; rule out rabies and lymphoma.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Bilateral symmetric temporalis/masseter atrophy vs unilateral atrophy

plain: Bilateral symmetric temporalis/masseter atrophy vs unilateral atrophy with absent facial sensation → Bilateral = chronic masticatory muscle myositis; unilateral with sensory loss = trigeminal neuropathy/neoplasia.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Which breeds get Hansen type I vs type II IVDD; which get Wobbler?
Type I (acute nucleus extrusion, mineralized disc):
Dachshund (~25% lifetime), Beagle, Pekingese, French Bulldog. Type II
(chronic annular protrusion): older large breeds (German Shepherd). Wobbler:

plain: Which breeds get Hansen type I vs type II IVDD; which get Wobbler? Type I (acute nucleus extrusion, mineralized disc): chondrodystrophic — Dachshund (~25% lifetime), Beagle, Pekingese, French Bulldog. Type II (chronic annular protrusion): older large breeds (German Shepherd). Wobbler: Doberman (disc-associated, middle-aged), Great Dane (osseous, young).

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Dachshund with acute thoracolumbar disc extrusion → Tx by grade and
(NSAID or steroid, never both). Non-ambulatory/progressive: MRI/CT then
; deep pain present → >90% recover; absent → ~50% if

plain: Dachshund with acute thoracolumbar disc extrusion → Tx by grade and prognosis? Pain or ambulatory paresis: strict cage rest 4–6 weeks + analgesia (NSAID or steroid, never both). Non-ambulatory/progressive: MRI/CT then hemilaminectomy; deep pain present → >90% recover; absent → ~50% if decompressed within 24–48 h. Not steroid alone — high-dose methylprednisolone no longer recommended.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Middle-aged Doberman/young Great Dane: wide-based pelvic ataxia,
short-strided forelimbs, neck pain worse on extension →
inflammatories, harness; surgery (ventral slot, distraction-fusion, dorsal
laminectomy for osseous) ~80% improve; adjacent "domino lesion" recurs.

plain: Middle-aged Doberman/young Great Dane: wide-based pelvic ataxia, short-strided forelimbs, neck pain worse on extension → Cervical spondylomyelopathy (C5–C7); MRI. Medical: restricted activity, anti- inflammatories, harness; surgery (ventral slot, distraction-fusion, dorsal laminectomy for osseous) ~80% improve; adjacent "domino lesion" recurs.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: German Shepherd >8 y: slowly progressive non-painful pelvic ataxia,
mutation, autosomal recessive, incomplete penetrance (also Boxers, Corgis,
Ridgebacks). Exclusion Dx (normal MRI/CSF) + SOD1 test; no treatment,
physiotherapy slows decline; non-ambulatory in ~6–12 months, euthanasia
Not tetraparesis at onset — paraparesis first, forelimbs late.

plain: German Shepherd >8 y: slowly progressive non-painful pelvic ataxia, scuffed nails, normal-to-brisk reflexes → Degenerative myelopathy: SOD1 mutation, autosomal recessive, incomplete penetrance (also Boxers, Corgis, Ridgebacks). Exclusion Dx (normal MRI/CSF) + SOD1 test; no treatment, physiotherapy slows decline; non-ambulatory in ~6–12 months, euthanasia within 1–3 years. Not tetraparesis at onset — paraparesis first, forelimbs late.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Chihuahua/toy breed with neck pain, screams when neck flexed → first
diagnostic? Cervical radiographs in neutral position
(dens hypoplasia); never force flexion — risk of cord compression.

plain: Chihuahua/toy breed with neck pain, screams when neck flexed → first diagnostic? Cervical radiographs in neutral position for atlantoaxial instability (dens hypoplasia); never force flexion — risk of cord compression.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Spinal pain, arched back, fever, lysis of adjacent vertebral endplates →
(test all intact dogs — zoonotic), Streptococcus, E. coli, Aspergillus
(GSD). Blood/urine culture; antibiotics ≥8 weeks, often months.

plain: Spinal pain, arched back, fever, lysis of adjacent vertebral endplates → Discospondylitis: MCC Staphylococcus pseudintermedius; also Brucella canis (test all intact dogs — zoonotic), Streptococcus, E. coli, Aspergillus (GSD). Blood/urine culture; antibiotics ≥8 weeks, often months. Not S. aureus — pseudintermedius is the canine staphylococcus.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Dog 1–5 y, generalized seizures months apart, normal interictal exam and
bloodwork → Dx; when to treat? Idiopathic epilepsy
in 24 h) or status, severe postictal signs, or structural cause.

plain: Dog 1–5 y, generalized seizures months apart, normal interictal exam and bloodwork → Dx; when to treat? Idiopathic epilepsy (exclusion; MRI/CSF if atypical). Start maintenance when ≥2 seizures in 6 months, any cluster (≥2 in 24 h) or status, severe postictal signs, or structural cause.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: First-line maintenance anticonvulsant in dogs: dose, range, effects?
Alternatives/add-ons: KBr (loading needed), levetiracetam (preferred with liver

plain: First-line maintenance anticonvulsant in dogs: dose, range, effects? Phenobarbital 2–3 mg/kg PO q12h; trough 15–35 µg/mL, steady state 10–14 days. Sedation, PU/PD/PP, ↑ALP, hepatotoxicity >35 µg/mL, rare dyscrasias. Alternatives/add-ons: KBr (loading needed), levetiracetam (preferred with liver disease), zonisamide.

plain: Rapidly ascending flaccid tetraparesis over 24–72 h, hyporeflexia, intact sensation, normal mentation → first action; US vs Australia? Search coat and remove ticks — tick paralysis. US (Dermacentor variabilis/andersoni): recovery within 24–72 h after removal. Australia (Ixodes holocyclus): respiratory failure; tick antiserum, oxygen/ventilation.

plain: Ascending flaccid tetraparesis 7–10 days after raccoon contact, hyperesthesia, bladder spared → Dx; vs botulism and tick paralysis? Acute polyradiculoneuritis (coonhound paralysis), immune-mediated; recovers over weeks with nursing. Botulism: descending flaccid paralysis with cranial nerve signs (megaesophagus, mydriasis) after carrion. Tick paralysis resolves 24–72 h after removal. Not tick-borne or myotonic — coonhound is immune; botulism is flaccid.

plain: Puppy <6 months with progressive ascending hindlimb paresis → rigid hyperextension, dam asymptomatic → Neosporosis (Neospora caninum, transplacental; dog definitive host). IFAT serology, muscle biopsy; clindamycin ± TMS/pyrimethamine early — contracture irreversible. Toxoplasma is the differential.

plain: "Chewing-gum" jaw myoclonus, hyperkeratotic footpads/nose, prior respiratory and GI illness → Canine distemper (morbillivirus): eosinophilic intracytoplasmic and intranuclear inclusions; thymic atrophy and lymphoid depletion at necropsy; MLV vaccination prevents; no specific Tx.

plain: Collapsed pigmenturic animal with markedly elevated CK and BUN → Rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuric AKI: CK half-life 2–4 h means ongoing damage; exertional myopathy (horses, greyhounds), heat stroke, seizures, recumbency. Aggressive IV fluids, alkalinize urine, analgesia.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Swollen painful temporalis/masseter, cannot open the mouth even under
anesthesia → Dx, most specific test, Tx? Masticatory muscle myositis
supportive only. Not "type II fibers" — 2M specifically.

plain: Swollen painful temporalis/masseter, cannot open the mouth even under anesthesia → Dx, most specific test, Tx? Masticatory muscle myositis (acute): autoantibodies against type 2M fibers (only in masticatory muscles); serum 2M antibody ~85–90% sensitive, highly specific; biopsy if seronegative/on steroids. Prednisone 2 mg/kg/day tapered over months; azathioprine steroid-sparing; never force the jaw open. Not CK/AST — supportive only. Not "type II fibers" — 2M specifically.

plain: Marked masticatory atrophy with trismus, no fever → Chronic MMM (fibrosis locks the jaw shut). Not trigeminal injury — dropped jaw cannot CLOSE; not tetanus — trismus with risus sardonicus, no atrophy.

plain: Dog presented with mouth locked wide open, cannot close, otherwise normal → TMJ luxation (usually rostrodorsal) or open-mouth jaw locking (coronoid on zygomatic arch). Radiograph/CT first; reduce under anesthesia with a wooden dowel fulcrum between caudal molars while closing the jaw.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

swelling, periosteal proliferation of mandible and tympanic bullae →
NSAIDs/prednisolone, soft food/feeding tube; self-limiting at growth arrest

plain: 4-month West Highland White/Scottish/Cairn terrier: painful mandibular swelling, periosteal proliferation of mandible and tympanic bullae → Craniomandibular osteopathy (autosomal recessive in WHWT). Palliative NSAIDs/prednisolone, soft food/feeding tube; self-limiting at growth arrest ~11–13 months; guarded if TMJ ankylosis.

spans.text: Large-breed puppy 2–6 months (Weimaraner, Great Dane, Irish Setter)

plain: Large-breed puppy 2–6 months (Weimaraner, Great Dane, Irish Setter) with fever, painful swollen distal radius/ulna metaphyses, radiolucent line parallel to the physis ("double physis") → Dx, Tx? Hypertrophic osteodystrophy: NSAIDs/analgesia, rest, balanced large-breed diet, stop calcium/vitamin supplementation; Weimaraners with severe systemic form respond to corticosteroids. Self-limiting, may relapse; sequelae angular limb deformity, premature physeal closure.

palpation, medullary opacity on radiographs → Dx, Tx, other shifting-
rest; self-limiting by ~18–20 months; avoid excess dietary supplementation.
Not hydrotherapy — analgesia and rest are standard.

plain: German Shepherd 5–18 months, shifting-leg lameness, pain on long-bone palpation, medullary opacity on radiographs → Dx, Tx, other shifting- lameness causes? Panosteitis (diaphyseal, not metaphyseal): NSAIDs and rest; self-limiting by ~18–20 months; avoid excess dietary supplementation. Other causes: Lyme, Anaplasma, Bartonella, immune-mediated polyarthritis/ SLE, HOD. Not hydrotherapy — analgesia and rest are standard.

plain: Young Labrador/Rottweiler/GSD with forelimb lameness, elbow pain on flexion/supination → components, best view, Tx? Elbow dysplasia: fragmented medial coronoid process (MCC; arthroscopic removal), ununited anconeal process (GSD; flexed mediolateral view after 20–24 weeks; lag screw + proximal ulnar osteotomy), OCD medial humeral condyle, incongruity (ulnar osteotomy). CT most sensitive; heritable, worsened by over- nutrition; OFA screen breeding stock.

plain: Growing dog with carpal valgus, cranial radial bowing and elbow incongruity after forelimb trauma → Premature closure of the distal ulnar physis (cone-shaped, prone to Salter-Harris V crush); radius keeps growing and bows. Ulnar ostectomy ± corrective radial osteotomy. Distal radial closure instead shortens the radius/subluxates the elbow.

spans.text: Fracture through a growth plate → classification, most common type,
(crush) worst for growth arrest; III/IV cross the articular

plain: Fracture through a growth plate → classification, most common type, worst type, fixation? Salter-Harris; type II (physis + metaphysis) most common; type V (crush) worst for growth arrest; III/IV cross the articular surface and need anatomic reduction. Fix with smooth crossed K-wires; threaded pins, lag screws or plates across the physis arrest growth.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Toy/terrier breed 4–12 months, unilateral hindlimb lameness, hip pain,

plain: Toy/terrier breed 4–12 months, unilateral hindlimb lameness, hip pain, femoral head flattening/lysis → Dx, Tx? Legg-Calvé-Perthes (avascular necrosis; autosomal recessive in Manchester Terriers/Westies); bilateral only 12–17%. Femoral head and neck ostectomy + early physiotherapy — excellent prognosis; conservative succeeds in <25%.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Surgical options for hip dysplasia by age and DJD status? Juvenile pubic

plain: Surgical options for hip dysplasia by age and DJD status? Juvenile pubic symphysiodesis 14–20 weeks; triple/double pelvic osteotomy <10–12 months with laxity but no DJD; total hip replacement in mature dogs with DJD after failed medical Tx; FHO salvage, best <20 kg.

plain: Young dog with bilateral hindlimb lameness: CCL rupture vs Legg-Calvé- Perthes vs hip dysplasia → most likely bilateral? Hip dysplasia (large breeds, usually bilateral, Ortolani sign). CCL rupture becomes bilateral in 30– 60% eventually; LCP is rarely bilateral.

plain: Large dog, acute non-weight-bearing hindlimb lameness, positive cranial drawer and tibial thrust, medial buttress → Dx, Tx by size, contralateral risk? Cranial cruciate ligament rupture (tibia slides cranially on femur). Medium–large: TPLO or TTA; small <15 kg: lateral fabellotibial suture/ TightRope. 40–60% rupture the other side within 2 years.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Chronic CCL rupture with an audible "click" on stifle flexion →

chronic ruptures): fixed to tibia and medial collateral, crushed by the femoral

plain: Chronic CCL rupture with an audible "click" on stifle flexion → concurrent injury and why? Caudal horn of the medial meniscus (~50% of chronic ruptures): fixed to tibia and medial collateral, crushed by the femoral condyle during cranial tibial thrust; lateral meniscus is mobile and spared. Partial meniscectomy at stabilization.

plain: Small-breed dog with intermittent skipping lameness, patella displaced medially on radiographs → Medial patellar luxation (toy breeds; lateral luxation in large breeds). Versus CCL rupture: tibial instability, effusion compressing the infrapatellar fat pad, osteophytes; the two often coexist.

plain: Patellar luxation grades? Grade I: luxates with pressure, returns spontaneously. Grade II: luxates intermittently/with flexion, stays out until manually reduced. Grade III: permanently luxated, manually reducible, reluxates on release. Grade IV: permanent, irreducible. Surgery for lame grade ≥II.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

, trochlear block/wedge recession sulcoplasty, lateral retinacular
imbrication + medial release; femoral corrective osteotomy for severe

plain: Surgical components for grade III MPL? Lateral tibial tuberosity transposition, trochlear block/wedge recession sulcoplasty, lateral retinacular imbrication + medial release; femoral corrective osteotomy for severe deformity; weight management.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

(~90% of hip luxations); round ligament ruptured; VD/

plain: Acute non-weight-bearing hindlimb after trauma, limb shortened and externally rotated, thumb pushed out of ischiatic notch → Craniodorsal coxofemoral luxation (~90% of hip luxations); round ligament ruptured; VD/ lateral pelvic radiographs before reduction.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Craniodorsal hip luxation, no fracture → Tx sequence and
contraindications? Closed reduction under anesthesia within 72 h
~50% → open reduction (toggle pin, capsulorrhaphy, iliofemoral suture);
salvage FHO/THR. Closed reduction contraindicated with hip dysplasia or

plain: Craniodorsal hip luxation, no fracture → Tx sequence and contraindications? Closed reduction under anesthesia within 72 h, then Ehmer sling (flexion, abduction, internal rotation) 10–14 days, skin checks daily, recheck radiographs; caudoventral luxation gets hobbles. Reluxation ~50% → open reduction (toggle pin, capsulorrhaphy, iliofemoral suture); salvage FHO/THR. Closed reduction contraindicated with hip dysplasia or acetabular fracture.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Puppy hit by car 2 h ago: craniodorsal hip luxation plus incidental medial
patellar luxation → treat first? The hip
before muscle contracture, cartilage erosion and avascular necrosis; the patellar

plain: Puppy hit by car 2 h ago: craniodorsal hip luxation plus incidental medial patellar luxation → treat first? The hip — closed reduction within 24–72 h before muscle contracture, cartilage erosion and avascular necrosis; the patellar luxation is elective.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

common), DJD, implant failure, sciatic nerve injury, infection/osteomyelitis,
persistent lameness; salvage FHO or THR.

plain: Complications after open reduction of hip luxation? Reluxation (most common), DJD, implant failure, sciatic nerve injury, infection/osteomyelitis, persistent lameness; salvage FHO or THR.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Pelvic trauma with SI luxation, acetabular, ischial and pubic fractures →
which repair is prioritized? Acetabular fracture
bearing; anatomic reduction and plating prevent DJD. Ilial fractures/SI luxation
also stabilized; ischial and pubic fractures heal conservatively.

plain: Pelvic trauma with SI luxation, acetabular, ischial and pubic fractures → which repair is prioritized? Acetabular fracture — articular and weight- bearing; anatomic reduction and plating prevent DJD. Ilial fractures/SI luxation also stabilized; ischial and pubic fractures heal conservatively.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Dropped hock (plantigrade) but still weight-bearing with toes flexed/
gives dropped hock with flat toes. Tenorrhaphy + tarsal

plain: Dropped hock (plantigrade) but still weight-bearing with toes flexed/ clawed → structure ruptured? Gastrocnemius tendon with intact superficial digital flexor (SDFT curls the toes). Complete common calcaneal (Achilles) rupture gives dropped hock with flat toes. Tenorrhaphy + tarsal immobilization in extension 6–8 weeks.

spans.text: Acute unilateral plantigrade stance after exertion vs bilateral plantigrade

plain: Acute unilateral plantigrade stance after exertion vs bilateral plantigrade stance in a cat → Achilles rupture or calcaneal fracture (palpation, radiographs) vs diabetic neuropathy in cats.

plain: Lateral malleolus (distal fibula) fracture with tarsal instability → repair? Open reduction with lag screw or pin and tension-band wire (or lateral collateral prosthesis) — it is the origin of the lateral collateral ligament; splinting alone is inadequate.

chapter: Chapter 4 — Canine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal (part 2)

spans.text: Fracture pattern classification and typical cause? Comminuted
fragments; high-energy — gunshot, treat as open, plate/interlocking nail/ESF,
do not chase pellets); spiral (torsion); transverse (bending); greenstick (one

plain: Fracture pattern classification and typical cause? Comminuted (≥3 fragments; high-energy — gunshot, treat as open, plate/interlocking nail/ESF, do not chase pellets); spiral (torsion); transverse (bending); greenstick (one cortex intact, immature animals).

weeks with radiographic rechecks when stable and the joints above and below

plain: Minimally displaced stable closed tibial fracture in a small dog vs large displaced comminuted fracture → External coaptation (cast/splint) 6–8 weeks with radiographic rechecks when stable and the joints above and below can be immobilized; displaced/comminuted → internal fixation or external skeletal fixator.

plain: Long bone with irregular periosteal new bone, lysis, a sequestrum and draining tract → Chronic bacterial osteomyelitis (post-traumatic/surgical, Staphylococcus). Culture deep tissue, debride with sequestrectomy, remove loose implants once healed, culture-based antibiotics 4–8 weeks; biopsy to exclude osteosarcoma if no sequestrum.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Middle-aged dog, PU/PD, polyphagia, pot belly, panting, bilateral
symmetric truncal alopecia, thin skin, recurrent UTI/pyoderma →
functional adrenal tumor. Cortisol excess drives protein catabolism,
gluconeogenesis, insulin antagonism and ADH antagonism.

plain: Middle-aged dog, PU/PD, polyphagia, pot belly, panting, bilateral symmetric truncal alopecia, thin skin, recurrent UTI/pyoderma → Hyperadrenocorticism; ~85% pituitary-dependent (PDH), remainder functional adrenal tumor. Cortisol excess drives protein catabolism, gluconeogenesis, insulin antagonism and ADH antagonism.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Typical bloodwork of a Cushingoid dog? Stress leukogram
(steroid isoenzyme), mild ALT rise, hypercholesterolemia, mild
hyperglycemia, USG <1.015–1.020. Hypothyroidism lacks the leukogram and
ALP surge; Addison's shows the reverse leukogram.

plain: Typical bloodwork of a Cushingoid dog? Stress leukogram (mature neutrophilia, lymphopenia, eosinopenia, monocytosis), markedly elevated ALP (steroid isoenzyme), mild ALT rise, hypercholesterolemia, mild hyperglycemia, USG <1.015–1.020. Hypothyroidism lacks the leukogram and ALP surge; Addison's shows the reverse leukogram.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

inhibit fibroblast collagen synthesis and follicular cycling;

plain: Paper-thin hypotonic skin, visible veins, comedones, calcinosis cutis in a dog → Hyperadrenocorticism (spontaneous or iatrogenic). Glucocorticoids inhibit fibroblast collagen synthesis and follicular cycling; calcinosis cutis is pathognomonic when present.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Most sensitive screening test for naturally occurring Cushing's, and its
h cortisol >1.4 µg/dL = failure to suppress
sensitive (~80% PDH, ~60% adrenal tumor; post >22 µg/dL) but the only test
for iatrogenic disease and for monitoring. Normal UCCR rules out.

plain: Most sensitive screening test for naturally occurring Cushing's, and its thresholds? LDDST (0.01 mg/kg dexamethasone IV): sensitivity ~90–95%; 8- h cortisol >1.4 µg/dL = failure to suppress. ACTH stimulation is less sensitive (~80% PDH, ~60% adrenal tumor; post >22 µg/dL) but the only test for iatrogenic disease and for monitoring. Normal UCCR rules out.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: LDDST shows no suppression at 4 or 8 h; which test next?
in adrenal tumor, normal/high in PDH), adrenal ultrasound (bilateral vs
unilateral with contralateral atrophy), or HDDST.

plain: LDDST shows no suppression at 4 or 8 h; which test next? Diagnosis is made; now differentiate PDH from adrenal tumor: endogenous ACTH (low in adrenal tumor, normal/high in PDH), adrenal ultrasound (bilateral vs unilateral with contralateral atrophy), or HDDST. Not ACTH stim or UCCR — screening tests, not differentiating ones.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Does HDDST or ultrasound confirm Cushing's?
pituitary from adrenal origin after a positive screen;
they never confirm the disease. Partial suppression (<50% baseline) at 4 h on
the LDDST already indicates PDH; adrenal tumors never suppress.

plain: Does HDDST or ultrasound confirm Cushing's? No — HDDST and ultrasound differentiate pituitary from adrenal origin after a positive screen; they never confirm the disease. Partial suppression (<50% baseline) at 4 h on the LDDST already indicates PDH; adrenal tumors never suppress.

Adrenalectomy is reserved for a unilateral tumor with a small contralateral
gland; hypophysectomy/radiation for macroadenoma with neurologic signs.
Ketoconazole is a weak third line; selegiline is FDA-approved but rarely

plain: Dog with confirmed Cushing's and bilaterally symmetric adrenomegaly on ultrasound → PDH: trilostane (DOC; 3β-HSD inhibitor) or mitotane. Adrenalectomy is reserved for a unilateral tumor with a small contralateral gland; hypophysectomy/radiation for macroadenoma with neurologic signs. Ketoconazole is a weak third line; selegiline is FDA-approved but rarely effective.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Medical options for PDH and their shared major adverse effect?
(lethargy, vomiting, hyperkalemia/hyponatremia); monitor ACTH stim or pre-
pill cortisol 10–14 days after every change.

plain: Medical options for PDH and their shared major adverse effect? Trilostane (reversible enzyme inhibitor) or mitotane (o,p'-DDD, adrenocorticolytic, 25–50 mg/kg/day induction). Both can cause iatrogenic hypoadrenocorticism (lethargy, vomiting, hyperkalemia/hyponatremia); monitor ACTH stim or pre- pill cortisol 10–14 days after every change.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Miniature Poodle with acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, near-normal
radiographs; PTE suspected → most likely underlying endocrinopathy?

obesity; other PTE causes are PLN, IMHA, neoplasia, sepsis, heartworm.
hypothyroidism — not a recognized PTE cause. Not thrombocytosis —
mechanism is clotting factors, not platelets.

plain: Miniature Poodle with acute dyspnea, hypoxemia, near-normal radiographs; PTE suspected → most likely underlying endocrinopathy? Hyperadrenocorticism: hypercoagulability from increased factors II, V, VII– X, XII and fibrinogen with decreased antithrombin, plus hypertension and obesity; other PTE causes are PLN, IMHA, neoplasia, sepsis, heartworm. Not hypothyroidism — not a recognized PTE cause. Not thrombocytosis — mechanism is clotting factors, not platelets.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Young–middle-aged dog (Standard Poodle, Portuguese Water Dog, often female), waxing-waning vomiting/lethargy, bradycardia despite hypovolemic shock, Na 128, K 7.1 → Hypoadrenocorticism ("great pretender", mimics renal/GI disease). Na:K <27 (<24 highly suggestive); aldosterone loss wastes Na and retains K, cortisol loss removes the stress response.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Other classic lab clues for Addison's? Absence of a stress leukogram
sick dog (lymphocytosis/eosinophilia), hypoglycemia, prerenal azotemia with

plain: Other classic lab clues for Addison's? Absence of a stress leukogram in a sick dog (lymphocytosis/eosinophilia), hypoglycemia, prerenal azotemia with inappropriately dilute urine, mild hypercalcemia (~30%), hypochloremia, non-regenerative anemia, microcardia. Atypical (glucocorticoid-only) Addison's has normal electrolytes.

plain: Is Na:K <27 specific for Addison's? No — whipworms (pseudo-Addison's), uroabdomen, renal failure, effusions and GI disease also lower it; always confirm with ACTH stimulation.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

stimulation: pre- and post-ACTH cortisol <2 µg/dL
cortisol >2 µg/dL essentially rules it out
prednisone/hydrocortisone, if steroids are needed before testing — it does not

plain: Confirmatory test for hypoadrenocorticism and its thresholds? ACTH stimulation: pre- and post-ACTH cortisol <2 µg/dL confirms; a basal cortisol >2 µg/dL essentially rules it out. Give dexamethasone, not prednisone/hydrocortisone, if steroids are needed before testing — it does not cross-react with the cortisol assay.

plain: Collapsed dog, no P waves, bradycardia, tall tented T waves, wide QRS → Hyperkalemia (atrial standstill); in a young dog think Addison's. Protect the heart with 10% calcium gluconate 0.5–1.5 mL/kg slow IV (no effect on K), then regular insulin + dextrose or bicarbonate, and treat the cause.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Dog in Addisonian crisis (shock, K 7.5, Na 125) → first treatment and

plain: Dog in Addisonian crisis (shock, K 7.5, Na 125) → first treatment and glucocorticoid of choice? Rapid IV 0.9% NaCl boluses (restores volume, dilutes K) then dexamethasone 0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV (assay-neutral), dextrose if hypoglycemic, calcium gluconate only for severe arrhythmia. Raise Na no faster than ~0.5 mEq/L/h (myelinolysis risk).

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Lifelong maintenance for typical Addison's? DOCP 1.5–2.2 mg/kg SC/IM

Prognosis excellent. Atypical cases need prednisone alone.

plain: Lifelong maintenance for typical Addison's? DOCP 1.5–2.2 mg/kg SC/IM every 25–28 days (mineralocorticoid only, adjusted by electrolytes) plus prednisone 0.1–0.25 mg/kg/day, doubled to 5× during stress; alternative oral fludrocortisone 0.01–0.02 mg/kg/day (has some glucocorticoid activity). Prognosis excellent. Atypical cases need prednisone alone.

plain: Dog on months of prednisone/dexamethasone develops PU/PD, pot belly, alopecia; ACTH stim shows low baseline and low post-ACTH cortisol → Iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism: Cushingoid signs with a flat/low ACTH response (adrenal atrophy from suppressed endogenous ACTH), small adrenals on ultrasound, steroid hepatopathy with hepatomegaly. Spontaneous HAC gives a normal-to-exaggerated response. Treat by slow taper.

plain: Dog on glucocorticoids for 2 months stopped abruptly; a week later weak, vomiting, hypotensive → Iatrogenic secondary hypoadrenocorticism: HPA suppression → zona fasciculata atrophy; glucocorticoid deficiency only, so electrolytes stay normal (aldosterone is RAAS-driven). Low cortisol with low endogenous ACTH. Prevent by tapering; treat with fluids and physiologic prednisone.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

iatrogenic Cushing's; HPA axis suppressed, so abrupt withdrawal precipitates

plain: Dog on long-term steroids for arthritis develops PU/PD, polyphagia and glucosuria → Steroid-induced diabetes mellitus (insulin resistance) alongside iatrogenic Cushing's; HPA axis suppressed, so abrupt withdrawal precipitates adrenal insufficiency.

Rarer signs: facial nerve paralysis, vestibular disease, laryngeal paralysis, megaesophagus, myxedema coma. Lab: fasting hypercholesterolemia (~75%), mild non-regenerative anemia, elevated CK.

plain: Lab pattern that confirms canine hypothyroidism? Low total T4 + low free T4 by equilibrium dialysis + elevated canine TSH; TSH is elevated in only ~70–75% of cases. Test only otherwise healthy dogs — glucocorticoids, phenobarbital, sulfonamides and NSAIDs depress T4.

plain: Dog with low total T4, normal TSH, concurrent illness or on phenobarbital/prednisone → next step? Free T4 by equilibrium dialysis (± antithyroglobulin antibodies); euthyroid sick syndrome has low TT4 but normal fT4ED and normal TSH — retest after recovery. Never treat on total T4 alone. Not L-tyrosine or metronidazole — no role in canine thyroid disease.

Treat with porcine GH or progestins plus levothyroxine. A normal-sized GSD with generalized alopecia → deep-scrape for demodicosis first, then hypothyroidism/HAC.

plain: Classic presenting signs of canine diabetes, and the complication that separates dogs from cats? PU/PD, polyphagia with weight loss; bilateral cataracts in ~75–80% of dogs within a year (lens aldose reductase → sorbitol swelling). Cats rarely form cataracts and instead develop plantigrade stance (neuropathy); 30–50% of cats remit, dogs are permanently insulin- dependent.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Newly diagnosed uncomplicated diabetic dog → initial insulin?
porcine lente (Vetsulin) or NPH 0.25–0.5 U/kg SC q12h
with a consistent diet, 12-h glucose curve after 7–14 days.
those are first-line in cats, not dogs.

plain: Newly diagnosed uncomplicated diabetic dog → initial insulin? Intermediate-acting porcine lente (Vetsulin) or NPH 0.25–0.5 U/kg SC q12h with a consistent diet, 12-h glucose curve after 7–14 days. Not glargine/PZI — those are first-line in cats, not dogs.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Diet for a diabetic dog versus a diabetic cat?
diet fed at fixed times with insulin.

plain: Diet for a diabetic dog versus a diabetic cat? Dog: consistent-composition, complex-carbohydrate, increased-fiber diet fed at fixed times with insulin. Cat: high-protein (>40% ME), low-carbohydrate (<12% ME) diet, which can induce remission.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: How is a 12-h blood glucose curve interpreted? Sample q2h; target nadir 80–150 mg/dL, duration 10–12 h, most values <250–300. Adjust on nadir and duration, never a single reading; fructosamine reflects the preceding 2–3 weeks.

plain: Curve: all values 240–440 mg/dL, nadir 240–250 at 8 h, duration adequate, signs persist → Underdosed: increase insulin 10–25%, re-curve in 7–14 days. Short duration means change insulin type, not dose. Nadir ~100, peak ~240, signs controlled → no change.

plain: Morning hyperglycemia and glucosuria that worsen as insulin is increased → Somogyi overswing: nadir <80 mg/dL then counter-regulatory rebound (glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol). Run a full curve, then decrease insulin 10– 25%; exclude Somogyi before ever raising a dose.

plain: Diabetic dog well regulated for 3 months suddenly hyperglycemic with rising ALP → Insulin resistance from concurrent disease — classically hyperadrenocorticism (steroid hepatopathy) or exogenous steroids; also UTI, pancreatitis, hypothyroidism, diestrus progesterone. Exclude insulin handling and Somogyi first; LDDST once glucose is stable.

plain: Diabetic dog with Cushing's starts trilostane/mitotane → effect on insulin need? Requirement falls as cortisol resistance resolves — reduce the dose and have owners check glucose daily for hypoglycemia. Not stopped — canine beta-cell loss is permanent.

plain: Dog with vomiting, glucose 450 mg/dL, ketonuria, high anion gap acidosis, K 3.2, P 1.8 → treatment order? DKA: isotonic fluids first (0.9% NaCl or balanced), potassium before insulin (K ≥3.5 mEq/L), phosphate (hemolysis <1.5 mg/dL), then insulin; bicarbonate only if pH <7.0–7.1; treat the precipitating disease (pancreatitis, UTI, HAC).

plain: Which insulin for DKA, and how? Regular (short-acting) crystalline insulin as IV CRI 0.05–0.1 U/kg/h (2.2 U/kg/day dog, 1.1 cat in 250 mL saline) or hourly IM, started 1–6 h after fluids; lower glucose 50–75 mg/dL/h, add dextrose below 250 mg/dL. Switch to long-acting insulin once eating and ketone-free.

Hyposthenuria proves active tubular dilution; USG ~1.014 is isosthenuric and with azotemia points to renal disease, not DI.

plain: When is the water deprivation test contraindicated? In azotemic or dehydrated animals and before secondary causes (CKD, Cushing's, hypercalcemia, pyometra, hyperthyroidism) are excluded; dehydrating a kidney that cannot concentrate risks hypernatremia and acute renal decompensation. Reserve it for DI vs psychogenic polydipsia.

plain: Most common cause of hypercalcemia in dogs, and the PTH-dependent cause? Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (lymphoma, anal sac adenocarcinoma: PTH suppressed, PTHrP high) is most common; primary hyperparathyroidism is PTH-dependent. Others: hypoadrenocorticism, renal failure, vitamin D toxicosis.

plain: Older Keeshond, clinically well, Ca 14 mg/dL, low-normal phosphorus, PU/PD, calcium oxalate stones/UTI, PTH high-normal → Primary hyperparathyroidism (parathyroid adenoma; Keeshond autosomal dominant). An inappropriately detectable PTH with hypercalcemia confirms; PTHrP negative; cervical ultrasound nodule >4 mm. Parathyroidectomy or ethanol/ heat ablation; watch for post-op hypocalcemia (calcitriol).

plain: Young dog with azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, demineralized lytic bones, soft "rubber jaw" → Renal secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal osteodystrophy; juvenile CKD/renal dysplasia). Phosphorus retention and low calcitriol drive PTH, resorbing mandible/maxilla. Phosphate restriction, binders, calcitriol; prognosis poor. Nutritional secondary HPT (all-meat diet) looks identical with normal kidneys.

plain: Small-breed bitch 2–3 weeks postpartum nursing a large litter, panting, tremors, stiff gait, hyperthermia → Eclampsia (puerperal tetany, ionized hypocalcemia). 10% calcium gluconate 0.5–1.5 mL/kg slow IV over 10–30 min with ECG/auscultation, stop for bradycardia/arrhythmia; then oral calcium/vitamin D, wean pups if recurrent. Do not supplement calcium during pregnancy (suppresses PTH).

plain: Dog with facial rubbing, muscle tremors, stiff gait, seizures; ionized Ca <~0.8 mmol/L → causes? Eclampsia, primary hypoparathyroidism, post- thyroid/parathyroid surgery, ethylene glycol, acute pancreatitis, protein-losing enteropathy, phosphate enema. Same slow IV calcium gluconate, then oral calcium plus calcitriol for hypoparathyroidism.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

hypophysectomy or radiation (pasireotide medical option). Dogs are rarely true

plain: Treatment of acromegaly in the bitch versus the cat? Bitch: ovariohysterectomy and stop progestins — diestrus progesterone induces GH from mammary tissue. Cat: GH-secreting pituitary adenoma → hypophysectomy or radiation (pasireotide medical option). Dogs are rarely true pituitary acromegalics.

Renal: azotemia with isosthenuria 1.008–1.012 or inadequately concentrated urine (~75% nephrons lost; concentrating ability lost at ~66%). plain: Dog with markedly elevated BUN/creatinine → appropriate next step? Localize (USG, hydration, bladder palpation/ultrasound), stage and treat the cause with fluids. Not euthanasia — many acute azotemias are reversible.

plain: Dog with pale mucous membranes, non-regenerative anemia, azotemia, isosthenuria, hyponatremia/hypochloremia, small irregular kidneys → Chronic kidney disease: EPO deficiency anemia; small kidneys = chronic, enlarged suggest acute disease, lymphoma, FIP, PKD. Irreversible; aim to slow progression. Differential Addison's needs hyperkalemia with Na:K <27 and flat ACTH stim.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Mainstay of therapy for IRIS stage 2–3 CKD? Renal therapeutic diet (phosphorus/protein restricted) — the only intervention proven to prolong survival; add phosphate binders, SC fluids, RAAS blockade for proteinuria, amlodipine for hypertension, antiemetics, potassium (cats). Controlling phosphorus slows renal secondary hyperparathyroidism.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: CKD dog with UPC >0.5 and SBP 175–190 mmHg → which drug for

plain: CKD dog with UPC >0.5 and SBP 175–190 mmHg → which drug for which problem? Proteinuria: ACE inhibitor (benazepril/enalapril 0.5 mg/ kg) or telmisartan (target UPC <0.5 dog, <0.4 cat; accept <30% creatinine rise, monitor K). Hypertension (persistent SBP >160): dogs ACEi/ARB first, add amlodipine 0.1–0.5 mg/kg q24h; cats amlodipine first. Avoid NSAIDs and glucocorticoids.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Dehydrated azotemic CKD dog → IV fluid?

plain: Dehydrated azotemic CKD dog → IV fluid? A balanced isotonic crystalloid (LRS, Plasma-Lyte) over 12–24 h; 0.9% NaCl acceptable when hyperkalemic but acidifying and chloride-rich. Reassess weight, urine output, electrolytes; avoid overhydration. (Both are accepted answers — balanced preferred unless hyperkalemic.) Indication for recombinant EPO/darbepoetin in veterinary patients? Non- regenerative anemia of CKD (PCV <~20–25% with signs); darbepoetin preferred (fewer anti-EPO antibodies) with iron supplementation. Not marrow aplasia — no precursors to stimulate.

exception? Hyperphosphatemia with normal-to-low ionized calcium
calcitriol → renal secondary HPT); total Ca may be mildly high, 10–30% of
Horses with chronic renal failure are

plain: Effect of CKD on calcium and phosphorus in dogs/cats, and the species exception? Hyperphosphatemia with normal-to-low ionized calcium (low calcitriol → renal secondary HPT); total Ca may be mildly high, 10–30% of CKD cats hypercalcemic. Horses with chronic renal failure are hypercalcemic (kidney is the main equine calcium route).

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Dog after pelvic trauma: abdominal effusion, azotemia, hyperkalemia, no urine → confirm and manage uroabdomen? Effusion creatinine >2× serum (or K >1.4× serum) confirms; positive-contrast retrograde cystourethrography locates the leak. Stabilize first — fluids, treat hyperkalemia, urinary catheter plus peritoneal drain — then surgical repair; small tears may heal with drainage.

plain: Hallmark lab finding of glomerular disease? Persistent proteinuria with inactive sediment (UPC >0.5 dog, >0.4 cat); severe cases → hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, edema (nephrotic syndrome) and hypercoagulability.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Protein-losing nephropathy → drug to reduce proteinuria and the most serious complication? ACE inhibitor (enalapril/benazepril 0.5 mg/kg q12– 24h) or telmisartan, plus clopidogrel/low-dose aspirin; thromboembolism from antithrombin III loss, hypertension, edema, progression to renal failure.

chapter: Chapter 5 — Canine — Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Interpret urinary casts: hyaline, granular/cellular, waxy, RBC, WBC? Hyaline: Tamm-Horsfall protein, few normal, more with proteinuria/ dehydration. plain: Red urine: how are hematuria, hemoglobinuria and myoglobinuria differentiated? Centrifuge: hematuria clears with a red RBC pellet; pigmenturias stay red (dipstick positive, no RBCs). plain: Pseudomonas aeruginosa UTI in a dog → antibiotic? Culture-guided fluoroquinolone — enrofloxacin (high end of dose) or marbofloxacin; alternatives amikacin, ceftazidime. Not ciprofloxacin — poor, variable oral bioavailability (~40%) in dogs.

plain: Struvite in dogs versus cats — cause and prevention? Dogs: almost always infection-induced → prevention is UTI control and culture monitoring. Hyperkalemic cardiac arrest (bradycardia, absent P waves, tented T, wide QRS, atrial standstill), worsened by metabolic acidosis shifting K out of cells. All of them, and people: zoophilic but not host-restricted; cats are the primary reservoir; ruminants, camelids, horses and humans (especially young/immunocompromised) are susceptible. Surgical replacement of the prolapsed nictitans gland — Morgan pocket (conjunctival imbrication) or orbital- rim anchoring; recurrence ~5–20%. plain: Unilateral miosis, ptosis, enophthalmos, third-eyelid protrusion → Dx, pathway, localization? Horner syndrome (sympathetic denervation): first- order brain→T1–T3; second-order preganglionic T1–T3 via brachial plexus/ vagosympathetic trunk; third-order postganglionic cranial cervical ganglion through the middle ear. Dilute phenylephrine: dilation within ~20 min → postganglionic (denervation hypersensitivity); idiopathic common in Golden Retrievers.

Topical broad-spectrum antibiotic (neomycin-polymyxin- bacitracin or ofloxacin q6–8h), topical atropine 1% for ciliary spasm/miosis, E-collar, systemic NSAID, recheck 5–7 days, find the cause (distichia, KCS, entropion, foreign body). Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated; systemic antibiotics unnecessary for simple ulcers.

plain: Why are topical steroids contraindicated on a corneal ulcer? They delay epithelial healing, potentiate collagenase (melting) and suppress local immunity → bacterial/fungal keratitis and perforation. Topical NSAIDs also slow epithelialization. Not glaucoma — steroid glaucoma is not the reason.

plain: Rapidly progressive gelatinous grey "melting" ulcer within 24–48 h → organisms and Tx? Keratomalacia from Pseudomonas aeruginosa or β- hemolytic Streptococcus collagenases plus host MMPs. Culture; topical fluoroquinolone or tobramycin every 1–2 h, anticollagenase (autologous serum, EDTA, N-acetylcysteine) every 1–2 h, atropine, systemic doxycycline; conjunctival graft if >50% stromal depth; no steroids.

Descemetocele — only Descemet's membrane and endothelium remain; the hydrophobic membrane does not stain while surrounding stroma does. Imminent perforation: conjunctival pedicle graft, no steroids, no pressure on the globe, E-collar.

plain: Full-thickness corneal laceration with iris prolapse → sequelae if not repaired promptly? Anterior synechiae and dyscoria, secondary glaucoma, cataract if the lens capsule is torn, endophthalmitis, phthisis bulbi, blindness. The iris plugs the wound; refer for surgical repair within hours, E-collar, no topical steroids.

plain: Boxer with superficial ulcer unhealed for weeks and a loose epithelial lip at the edge → Dx and Tx; species caveat? Spontaneous chronic corneal epithelial defect (indolent/Boxer ulcer) — epithelium fails to adhere to abnormal basement membrane. Debride loose epithelium with a cotton swab under topical anesthesia, then grid/punctate keratotomy or diamond-burr, topical antibiotic ± contact lens; heals in 2–3 weeks. Grid keratotomy is contraindicated in cats (corneal sequestrum; feline indolent ulcers are often herpetic).

Prevented by CAV-2 vaccines, which cross-protect against infectious canine hepatitis.

plain: Dull lusterless cornea, thick mucoid discharge, recurrent conjunctivitis, corneal neovascularization/pigmentation, STT <10 mm/min → Dx and Tx of choice? Keratoconjunctivitis sicca, usually immune-mediated lacrimal adenitis (Westie, Cocker, Bulldog). Topical cyclosporine 0.2% q12h (or tacrolimus 0.02–0.03%) — lacrimostimulant and immunomodulator, lifelong, response in 4–8 weeks (~80%); tear replacement and antibiotics are adjuncts only; parotid duct transposition if medical therapy fails (mineral deposits, moist dermatitis).

plain: Which commonly used drugs cause KCS in dogs? Sulfonamides (trimethoprim-sulfa, sulfadiazine, sulfasalazine for colitis), especially small dogs and long courses — may be irreversible; also etodolac, atropine (transient), general anesthesia, and removal of the third-eyelid gland; distemper and neurogenic causes. Monitor STT on chronic sulfonamides.

Oral pilocarpine (1–2 drops of 2% per 10 kg in food BID, titrated below GI side effects) plus topical cyclosporine and lubricants; many recover in months.

plain: Red painful eye: uveitis vs glaucoma vs keratitis, and why the distinction matters? Uveitis: IOP <10, miosis, flare → steroid + atropine. Glaucoma: IOP >25–30, fixed dilated pupil, corneal edema, episcleral injection → latanoprost, dorzolamide, mannitol. Keratitis: corneal lesion with normal IOP and pupil. Atropine is contraindicated in glaucoma; latanoprost in uveitis. Red painful eye with mydriasis, corneal edema, episcleral congestion → most appropriate next diagnostic step? Tonometry: normal canine/feline IOP 10–25 mmHg; >25–30 mmHg with signs = glaucoma. Uveitis presents similarly with low IOP, so measure before treating.

plain: Cocker/Basset, acute painful red eye, diffuse corneal edema, fixed dilated pupil, IOP 55 mmHg → Dx and emergency Tx? Acute primary (goniodysgenesis) glaucoma. IV mannitol 1–2 g/kg over 20–30 min (withhold water 2–4 h), topical latanoprost (rapid, ↑uveoscleral outflow), dorzolamide ± timolol; same-day referral. Retinal ganglion cells die within hours; vision loss is permanent after 24–72 h. Start prophylactic dorzolamide/ timolol in the fellow eye.

plain: Latanoprost → species caveat and key contraindications? Ineffective in cats (lack the receptor), contraindicated with anterior lens luxation and uveitis (miosis traps the lens, prostaglandins worsen inflammation). Pilocarpine is a miotic that increases conventional outflow; CAIs (dorzolamide, methazolamide) and timolol reduce aqueous production.

plain: Which sign is NOT characteristic of glaucoma? Miosis — glaucoma causes a fixed dilated pupil, buphthalmos, corneal edema, episcleral congestion, pain; miosis means uveitis. Sustained IOP destroys retinal ganglion cells and cups the optic disc.

plain: Breed predisposed to primary glaucoma → which exam evaluates the drainage angle? Gonioscopy (goniolens on the cornea) shows pectinate ligament dysplasia/narrow angle; primary glaucoma is bilateral, so the normotensive fellow eye receives prophylaxis. Secondary glaucoma follows uveitis, lens luxation, hyphema or neoplasia blocking a normal angle.

plain: Buphthalmic globe with diffuse blue edema, episcleral congestion, deeply cupped dark optic disc → Chronic end-stage glaucoma — irreversibly blind (Haab striae, lens subluxation). Comfort procedures: enucleation, intrascleral prosthesis or ciliary body ablation; prophylaxis for the fellow eye.

plain: Terrier, 3–6 years, aphakic crescent seen → what it indicates and Tx? Lens luxation/subluxation — the crescent is the gap between displaced lens equator and pupil margin; primary zonular degeneration (ADAMTS17) in terriers, or secondary to glaucoma, uveitis, trauma. Anterior luxation is an emergency (acute glaucoma): lower IOP with dorzolamide ± timolol and mannitol, avoid miotics and latanoprost, then intracapsular lens extraction (couching if blind); posterior luxation → miotics.

chapter: Chapter 6 — Canine — Dermatology & Ophthalmology

plain: Dog with mature cataract develops a sudden red painful eye, IOP 45 mmHg → complication? Lens-induced (phacolytic) uveitis with secondary glaucoma — leaking lens protein incites uveitis that obstructs the angle. Lower IOP (mannitol, dorzolamide/timolol; latanoprost unless luxation), treat uveitis with topical steroids/NSAIDs, refer for phacoemulsification.

chapter: Chapter 6 — Canine — Dermatology & Ophthalmology

bilateral bluish haze in dogs >6–7 years,

plain: White/grey lens opacity: cataract vs nuclear sclerosis? Nuclear sclerosis: bilateral bluish haze in dogs >6–7 years, tapetal reflex and fundus view preserved, vision intact (fiber compaction, not opacity). Cataract: blocks the tapetal reflex/fundus on retroillumination, any age (inherited, diabetic), impairs vision.

chapter: Chapter 6 — Canine — Dermatology & Ophthalmology

plain: Cataract stages → mature vs hypermature? Mature: whole lens opaque, no tapetal reflex, smooth capsule, blind. Hypermature: wrinkled capsule, liquefied cortex, reflex may return, high risk of lens-induced uveitis. Incipient/ immature retain the reflex.

plain: Most common causes of cataract in dogs vs cats and horses? Dogs: inherited first, diabetes mellitus second (~75–80% of diabetic dogs within 1– 2 years). Cats and horses: secondary to chronic uveitis (equine recurrent uveitis). Diabetic cats rarely form cataracts (low lens aldose reductase).

plain: Diabetic dog with rapid bilateral cataracts → mechanism? Lens aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, which cannot leave the lens → osmotic water influx ruptures fibers; a cataract is often the owner's first sign of canine diabetes.

confirm a functional, attached retina. No medical cure; topical NSAIDs/

plain: Definitive treatment for canine cataracts and timing? Phacoemulsification ± intraocular lens — 90–95% success, best done before hypermaturity and lens-induced uveitis; pre-op electroretinogram and ocular ultrasound confirm a functional, attached retina. No medical cure; topical NSAIDs/ steroids control lens-induced uveitis if surgery is deferred.

plain: Poodle/Labrador/Cocker/Irish Setter with progressive night blindness, dilated poorly responsive pupils, tapetal hyperreflectivity, attenuated retinal vessels, later bilateral cataracts → Progressive retinal atrophy — inherited (autosomal recessive prcd) photoreceptor degeneration, rods first (nyctalopia) then cones; bilateral, symmetric, painless. Confirm with ERG/ DNA test; no treatment; never remove secondary cataracts without an ERG; remove from breeding.

SARDS (sudden acquired retinal degeneration syndrome): flat/extinguished ERG with an initially normal fundus; optic neuritis has a normal ERG and swollen disc. Cushing- like signs often transient; no effective treatment; blindness permanent.

plain: Collie puppy at 6–8 weeks: pale patch with abnormal choroidal vessels temporal to the optic disc, ± coloboma → Dx, inheritance, pathognomonic lesion? Collie eye anomaly — autosomal recessive (NHEJ1 deletion), congenital, non-progressive; choroidal hypoplasia temporal to the disc is pathognomonic; optic nerve coloboma (grey pit into which vessels dip), retinal detachment and hemorrhage mark severe cases. Screen before 8–12 weeks — pigment can mask mild lesions ("go normal"). Also Shelties, Aussies, Border Collies; no treatment.

The right pupil still constricts consensually, proving the right oculomotor (efferent, CN III/Edinger-Westphal) pathway is intact.

plain: Normal canine cycle: lengths, interestrous interval, seasonality? Monoestrous, non-seasonal; proestrus ~9 days, estrus ~9 days, diestrus ~2 months, obligatory anestrus 4–5 months; interestrous interval ~7 months (range 4–12). Basenjis cycle once yearly. Mandatory anestrus allows endometrial repair after progesterone-dominated diestrus.

plain: Bitch with serosanguineous vulvar discharge and vulvar swelling, not yet accepting the male → Proestrus (~9 days); cytology shows parabasal → intermediate cells with RBCs (estrogen-driven diapedesis). Bleeding in proestrus is normal.

plain: Vaginal smear: >90% anuclear, angular cornified superficial cells, no neutrophils, clear background → Estrus; the bitch stands to be bred. Breed 2–4 days after the LH surge. Not nucleated superficial cells — those predominate in late proestrus.

plain: Vaginal smear: abrupt return of parabasal/small intermediate cells with a flood of neutrophils ("metestrum cells") → Day 1 of diestrus, ~6 days after the LH surge; superficial cells fall abruptly below 50%. Whelping follows in 57 ± 1 days. Anestrus shows parabasal/intermediate cells with few neutrophils and scant debris.

plain: Most reliable practical method to time ovulation and breeding? Serial serum progesterone: ~2 ng/mL marks the LH surge, 4–10 ng/mL marks ovulation (2 days after the surge); oocytes mature 2–3 days later, fertile period 2–5 days post-ovulation. Not vaginal cytology — confirms estrus but cannot pinpoint ovulation.

plain: Bitch bred while showing bloody discharge, did not conceive, receptive estrus ~1 month later → Bred in proestrus, before ovulation. Optimal breeding is 2–3 days after the LH surge (progesterone 4–10 ng/mL, cytology >90% cornified).

plain: Bitch with persistent or prolonged estrus (nymphomania) → ovarian causes? Follicular ovarian cysts or an estrogen-secreting granulosa cell tumor; confirm with persistent cornification, estradiol and ultrasound; OHE (or hCG/GnRH to luteinize cysts if breeding). Not Sertoli cell tumor — a testicular tumor causing feminization in males.

plain: Pregnancy diagnosis in the bitch: method and earliest positive day? Serum relaxin (the only pregnancy-specific canine hormone) from ~day 22–27; ultrasound gestational sacs from day 20–25, heartbeats day 23–25; radiographs from day 42–45 when fetal skeletons mineralize (count pups after day 55). Progesterone cannot diagnose pregnancy — luteal phase is identical in pregnant and non-pregnant bitches. Not 29 days for radiographs — bones are not radiopaque before ~day 42.

plain: Ultrasound of a pregnant bitch: thin echogenic ring/fluid compartment immediately surrounding the fetus → Amniotic sac (amnion); the outer, larger fluid compartment is the allantoic (chorioallantoic) cavity.

plain: Predicting whelping date from the LH surge, ovulation, diestrus onset, or breeding? 65 ± 1 days from the LH surge; 63 ± 1 from ovulation; 57 ± 1 from first day of cytologic diestrus; only 57–72 days from a breeding because sperm survive up to 7 days and ova mature 2–3 days. Gestation is fixed from ovulation, variable from mating.

plain: Most reliable sign that whelping will occur within 24 h? Rectal temperature drop of ~1 °C to below 99–100 °F (37.2–37.8 °C) 12–24 h before whelping, caused by progesterone falling below 2 ng/mL (progesterone is thermogenic). Monitor temperature twice daily from day 56; nesting, inappetence and milk let-down also occur.

plain: Pregnant bitch given griseofulvin for ringworm (and an MLV vaccine); pups born with cleft palate and skeletal defects → cause? Griseofulvin — teratogen contraindicated in pregnancy (cleft palate, skeletal and ocular defects; disrupts microtubules in dividing fetal cells). MLV vaccines in pregnancy risk fetal infection and abortion, not malformations.

plain: Termination of a confirmed pregnancy (>25–30 days) → protocol? Natural PGF2α (dinoprost) 0.1 mg/kg SC q8h for 2 days, then 0.2 mg/kg q8h until ultrasound confirms all fetuses expelled; side effects vomiting, panting, defecation. Cloprostenol 1–3 µg/kg SC q24–48h has fewer side effects; aglepristone where available (not US). The bitch is CL-dependent throughout gestation, so luteolysis ends pregnancy. Not estrogens (ECP) — no longer recommended for mismating.

plain: Bitch resting quietly >2 h after two normal pups, more fetuses present, no straining or distress → Monitor; up to 2–4 h between pups is acceptable in a resting bitch with normal fetal heart rates. Intervene if >4 h, weak unproductive contractions, or fetal distress.

plain: Day 65, strong active contractions for 30–60 min with no pup; radiograph available → oxytocin, PGF2α or C-section? C-section if the radiograph shows obstruction (oversize, malposition, fetal-pelvic mismatch) or after 30–60 min of strong unproductive straining. Oxytocin is contraindicated during active contractions or obstruction (uterine rupture); PGF2α has no role in inducing canine parturition. If the radiograph shows no obstruction, allow natural whelping and monitor.

plain: One pup delivered; second lodged at the pelvic inlet, malpositioned (transverse, head deflected, true breech) → Oxytocin is contraindicated with obstruction. Gentle digital repositioning/traction with lubrication if reachable per vaginum (forceps only on a reachable last or dead pup); otherwise cesarean section. Waiting is not an option.

chapter: Chapter 7 — Canine — Theriogenology

plain: Single oversized fetus or transverse presentation on a term radiograph → Cesarean section; fetal oversize (single-puppy syndrome) and transverse presentation are absolute indications. Obstructive dystocia cannot be relieved medically.

plain: Dystocia; radiographs show one dead and two live fetuses → next step? Cesarean section — fetal death with live siblings remaining signals prolonged or obstructed labor; surgery saves the viable pups. Oxytocin is reserved for uncomplicated inertia with open cervix, no obstruction and normal fetal heart rates.

plain: Term radiograph: intrafetal gas, overlapping skull bones, collapsed spine → interpretation? Fetal death; intrafetal gas is the earliest radiographic sign (≥6 h after death), skull overlap (Spalding sign) and spinal collapse appear later. With dead fetuses and uterine inertia: emergency C-section (or OHE).

plain: Suture pattern for closing the uterus after cesarean or hysterotomy? Inverting pattern — Cushing or Lembert (often over a continuous appositional first layer), absorbable monofilament (eg 2-0/3-0 PDS or poliglecaprone), without penetrating the lumen; serosa-to-serosa contact seals rapidly with fibrin and limits leakage and adhesions.

plain: Can a bitch be spayed at the time of C-section; effect on pups? Yes — OHE (en bloc or after pup removal) if no future litters are wanted; lactation and maternal behavior are not impaired because milk production depends on prolactin, not the ovaries. Drawbacks: longer anesthesia, hemorrhage from enlarged vessels.

Do not supplement calcium during pregnancy — it suppresses PTH and predisposes.

plain: Bitch ~10 days post-whelping: fever, firm hot red painful mammary gland, discolored milk; pups weak or dying → Acute septic mastitis (E. coli, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus); pups die of hypoglycemia/sepsis when they cannot nurse. Nursing-safe antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate, cephalexin, clindamycin), warm compresses, stripping, analgesia; lance abscesses, mastectomy for gangrene. Not routine weaning — pups keep nursing unless the gland is abscessed/gangrenous or the drug is unsafe.

plain: Young bitch >6 weeks postpartum with persistent intermittent brownish serosanguineous discharge, otherwise well → Subinvolution of placental sites (SIPS) — persistent trophoblasts delay involution; usually self-limiting; OHE only for hemorrhage/anemia or no future breeding. Fever or foul discharge indicates metritis instead. Not first-line OHE — most resolve spontaneously.

plain: Poor lactation in a bitch → galactagogues? Dopamine (D2) antagonists metoclopramide 0.1–0.5 mg/kg PO q8h or domperidone raise prolactin (dopamine is the prolactin brake); oxytocin for let-down. Cabergoline does the opposite (suppresses prolactin).

Closed- cervix form is more septic.

plain: Why PU/PD in pyometra? E. coli endotoxin causes renal tubular insensitivity to ADH (secondary nephrogenic DI), reversible after surgery. Not renomegaly — the renal clue is the concentrating defect.

plain: Dog with only one scrotal testis at 6 months (or an adult unilateral cryptorchid stud) → which side, risks, advice? Cryptorchidism; the right testis is more often retained (inguinal or abdominal); descent should be complete by 8 weeks, certainly by 6 months. Heritable (sex-limited autosomal recessive) — do not breed, even though unilateral cryptorchids are usually fertile (bilateral are sterile). Remove both testes: the retained testis has ~10–13× risk of Sertoli cell tumor/seminoma and torsion (body temperature blocks spermatogenesis but not hormone production or neoplasia). Orchiopexy, hCG/GnRH therapy and prosthetic implants for show are ineffective or unethical; registries disqualify affected dogs.

Direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test detects IgG/complement on RBCs; IMHA needs 2 of 3: spherocytosis, persistent saline autoagglutination, positive Coombs. plain: Plasma protein lost in protein-losing nephropathy that predisposes to thrombosis → Antithrombin (III) — albumin-sized, so it leaks with albumin; its loss removes the main inhibitor of thrombin and factor Xa.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

detects recipient antibodies against donor cells. Minor = donor plasma +

plain: What is a major crossmatch? Donor RBCs + recipient plasma/serum — detects recipient antibodies against donor cells. Minor = donor plasma + recipient RBCs. Dogs lack significant natural alloantibodies: no crossmatch needed for a first transfusion, required >4 days after any prior one; cats must always be typed (type B has strong anti-A).

plain: Patient at greatest risk of an acute transfusion reaction → A previously transfused (sensitized) animal, or a type B cat receiving type A blood even on first transfusion. A first DEA 1 mismatch in a dog is tolerated but sensitizes.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Severe anemia plus thrombocytopenic bleeding needing transfusion → best product? Fresh whole blood (<8 h old, never refrigerated) — supplies RBCs, functional platelets and clotting factors together. Stored/frozen RBCs lack platelets; plasma alone does not raise PCV; platelet-rich plasma suits isolated thrombocytopenia.

plain: Volume of whole blood to transfuse → mL = BW (kg) × blood volume (90 mL/kg dog, 60–70 mL/kg cat) × (desired PCV − recipient PCV) ÷ donor PCV; rule of thumb 2 mL/kg whole blood (1 mL/kg pRBC) raises PCV ~1%.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Circulating blood volume per kg: dog, cat, horse →

plain: Circulating blood volume per kg: dog, cat, horse → Dog 80–90 mL/kg; cat 55–66 mL/kg; horse ~72–100 mL/kg (hot-blooded higher). Safe donation ~20% of volume (dog 15–20 mL/kg, cat 10–12 mL/kg). Not 40 mL/kg for the cat — too low.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
plain: Components of the glucocorticoid (stress) leukogram → SMILED: Segmented (mature) neutrophilia, Monocytosis (dogs), Lymphopenia, Eosinopenia, Decreased. Lymphopenia is the most consistent; a sick dog with normal/high lymphocytes and eosinophils → suspect hypoadrenocorticism.

plain: Dog collapses with pale gums, vomiting and hypotension minutes after vaccination → first drug? Anaphylaxis → epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg IM (or IV), then IV crystalloids and oxygen; antihistamines and glucocorticoids are adjuncts only. Shock organ: dog = liver/GI (vomiting, diarrhea, hepatic congestion); cat = lungs (bronchospasm).

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

Not a live attenuated lepto — lepto vaccines are killed bacterins.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Classify the hypersensitivity type: pemphigus, IMHA/ITP, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis → Pemphigus foliaceus/vulgaris (anti-desmoglein; acantholytic cells) = type II; IMHA and ITP = type II; SLE, RA, glomerulonephritis = type III (immune complex). Not discoid lupus for acantholytic cells — those mean pemphigus.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Shifting-leg lameness, fever, carpal/tarsal polyarthritis; arthrocentesis

plain: Shifting-leg lameness, fever, carpal/tarsal polyarthritis; arthrocentesis non-septic neutrophilic, culture negative → Immune-mediated polyarthritis (non-erosive idiopathic most common; erosive rheumatoid-like if subchondral lysis). Rule out tick-borne disease; immunosuppressive prednisone ± cyclosporine/leflunomide.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Chemotherapy drug that is cardiotoxic in dogs, and the limit → Doxorubicin: cumulative >180–240 mg/m² → irreversible dilated cardiomyopathy (Dobermans, Boxers at higher risk; echo before starting). In cats it is nephrotoxic instead. Both: myelosuppression at 7–10 days, GI toxicity, perivascular slough if extravasated, anaphylactoid reaction (pretreat diphenhydramine).

plain: Key toxicities of vincristine → Peripheral neuropathy, paralytic ileus/ constipation, severe vesicant if extravasated, mild myelosuppression. Species flag: doxorubicin targets heart in dogs, kidney in cats.

(doxorubicin, vincristine) through a questionable catheter or a vein punctured

plain: Preferred vein for IV chemotherapy in a dog → Cephalic (lateral saphenous alternative) via a clean first-stick peripheral catheter; never give vesicants (doxorubicin, vincristine) through a questionable catheter or a vein punctured in the last 24 h. Jugular reserved for central lines.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Dog with lymphoma on chemotherapy losing weight, refusing the

— a diet the dog eats outranks any

plain: Dog with lymphoma on chemotherapy losing weight, refusing the prescribed high-fat low-carb diet → most important dietary parameter? Palatability/adequate caloric intake — a diet the dog eats outranks any macronutrient ratio; switch to an energy-dense palatable diet and treat nausea.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

cutaneous MCT, also used in urothelial carcinoma →
inhibitor — cytostatic); in TCC mostly stable disease, often combined with an

plain: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor FDA-approved for recurrent grade II/III cutaneous MCT, also used in urothelial carcinoma → Toceranib phosphate (Palladia) 2.5–2.75 mg/kg PO every other day (KIT, VEGFR, PDGFR inhibitor — cytostatic); in TCC mostly stable disease, often combined with an NSAID (watch GI toxicity).

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Middle-aged dog, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, otherwise well
larger than a neutrophil, prominent nucleoli, lymphoglandular bodies; reactive
nodes are >75–90% small mature lymphocytes with plasma cells.

plain: Middle-aged dog, generalized painless lymphadenopathy, otherwise well → Multicentric lymphoma (most common canine hematopoietic tumor). Dx FNA cytology: monomorphic large lymphoblasts >50% of cells, nucleus larger than a neutrophil, prominent nucleoli, lymphoglandular bodies; reactive nodes are >75–90% small mature lymphocytes with plasma cells.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: clonality if equivocal; stage with CBC, chemistry, thoracic/abdominal imaging.

plain: Next step after cytologic lymphoma → Immunophenotype by flow cytometry or IHC (B-cell ~70%, better prognosis; T-cell worse), PARR for clonality if equivocal; stage with CBC, chemistry, thoracic/abdominal imaging.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Expected survival of canine multicentric lymphoma on CHOP →
Prednisone alone 1–3 months; untreated 4–6 weeks. Better: B-cell, substage a,
Not a 2-year median — 2 years is the upper tail.

plain: Expected survival of canine multicentric lymphoma on CHOP → Median ~12 months (10–14), 80–90% remission; ~20–25% alive at 2 years. Prednisone alone 1–3 months; untreated 4–6 weeks. Better: B-cell, substage a, no hypercalcemia. Not a 2-year median — 2 years is the upper tail.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

after diagnosis — they are lympholytic and obscure cytology.

plain: Lymphoma with hypercalcemia, azotemia and nonregenerative anemia → phenotype and mechanism? T-cell (often mediastinal) lymphoma secreting PTHrP; hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI and renal injury. Steroids only after diagnosis — they are lympholytic and obscure cytology.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Feline low-grade small-cell GI lymphoma treatment →

plain: Feline low-grade small-cell GI lymphoma treatment → Chlorambucil 2 mg/cat PO q48h + prednisolone; MST 2–3 years (usually T-cell). Contrast CHOP for canine multicentric disease.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Older dog, incidental lymphocytosis 45,000/µL of small mature
(usually CD8+ T-cell). Confirm flow cytometry/PARR; marrow
>30% lymphocytes. Indolent — treat when symptomatic, cytopenic or
Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (blasts, cytopenias) carries a poor prognosis.

plain: Older dog, incidental lymphocytosis 45,000/µL of small mature lymphocytes, mild anemia, no lymphadenopathy → Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (usually CD8+ T-cell). Confirm flow cytometry/PARR; marrow >30% lymphocytes. Indolent — treat when symptomatic, cytopenic or >60,000/µL with chlorambucil 0.2 mg/kg PO + prednisone; MST 1–3 years. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (blasts, cytopenias) carries a poor prognosis.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Monoclonal gammopathy, punched-out lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia,

plain: Monoclonal gammopathy, punched-out lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, azotemia, hyperviscosity (retinal hemorrhage) → Multiple myeloma — 2 of 4: monoclonal spike on serum electrophoresis, Bence Jones proteinuria (dipstick-negative), osteolysis, >10–20% marrow plasma cells. Melphalan + prednisone, MST ~18 months. IgM spike = Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, not lymphoma.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Most common cause of hypercalcemia in dogs; mechanism; feline

causes: hypoadrenocorticism, renal failure, vitamin D toxicosis, primary

plain: Most common cause of hypercalcemia in dogs; mechanism; feline counterpart → Lymphoma (esp. T-cell mediastinal) via PTHrP — humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy; second anal sac apocrine gland adenocarcinoma; also multiple myeloma, thymoma, bone metastasis. Other causes: hypoadrenocorticism, renal failure, vitamin D toxicosis, primary hyperparathyroidism. In cats idiopathic hypercalcemia is most common, then CKD and neoplasia.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

high with low PTH and high PTHrP
total calcium misleads with hypoalbuminemia or acid-base shifts. CKD usually

plain: True statement about ionized calcium → It is the biologically active fraction (~50% of total) and is high with low PTH and high PTHrP in malignancy; total calcium misleads with hypoalbuminemia or acid-base shifts. CKD usually has normal ionized calcium despite high total.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Work-up and treatment of a hypercalcemic dog →
lymph node aspirates, thoracic radiographs, ionized Ca/PTH/PTHrP.
NaCl, furosemide only after rehydration, bisphosphonates
withheld until a diagnosis is made.

plain: Work-up and treatment of a hypercalcemic dog → Rectal exam (anal sacs), lymph node aspirates, thoracic radiographs, ionized Ca/PTH/PTHrP. 0.9% NaCl, furosemide only after rehydration, bisphosphonates; steroids withheld until a diagnosis is made.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

plain: Boxer/Boston Terrier dermal mass that reddens and swells when handled (Darier sign); FNA round cells with purple cytoplasmic granules, eosinophils → Mast cell tumor (most common canine cutaneous malignancy). Granules are metachromatic on toluidine blue and may not stain with Diff- Quik; histamine/heparin cause GI ulceration and delayed wound healing.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

spans.text: Surgical margins for a canine cutaneous MCT →
recurrent; proportional margins (lateral = tumor diameter, max 4 cm)
Microscopic tendrils extend beyond the palpable mass.
adenocarcinoma as the "indistinct-margin" tumor — MCT and soft-tissue

plain: Surgical margins for a canine cutaneous MCT → 2 cm lateral + one fascial plane deep for low-grade (Patnaik I/II, Kiupel low); 3 cm for high-grade or recurrent; proportional margins (lateral = tumor diameter, max 4 cm) acceptable. When offered 1.5/3/5 cm, choose 3 cm; never less than 2 cm. Microscopic tendrils extend beyond the palpable mass. Not mammary adenocarcinoma as the "indistinct-margin" tumor — MCT and soft-tissue sarcomas are.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

hypotension). Famotidine is an H2 blocker, not a classical antihistamine.

plain: Perioperative drugs for MCT, and the anesthetic to avoid → Pretreat with H1 (diphenhydramine) and H2 (famotidine) blockers against degranulation; avoid manipulating the tumor; avoid morphine (histamine release, hypotension). Famotidine is an H2 blocker, not a classical antihistamine.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

spans.text: Chemotherapy for high-grade, node-positive or non-resectable MCT →
for recurrent/non-resectable grade II–III, especially c-KIT mutant
(~25–30% of high-grade). Incomplete margins → re-excision or radiation.
Palladia as the general DOC — it is the targeted option.

plain: Chemotherapy for high-grade, node-positive or non-resectable MCT → Vinblastine + prednisone (standard first-line), lomustine; toceranib (Palladia) for recurrent/non-resectable grade II–III, especially c-KIT mutant (~25–30% of high-grade). Incomplete margins → re-excision or radiation. Not Palladia as the general DOC — it is the targeted option.

plain: What determines MCT prognosis → Histologic grade (Patnaik I good, III poor; Kiupel low vs high), mitotic index >5/10 hpf, c-KIT mutation, location (mucocutaneous, inguinal, preputial worse), stage/node involvement. Feline cutaneous MCT is usually benign. Recheck every 3–6 months.

plain: Swollen popliteal node; FNA round cells with abundant purple granules → Metastatic MCT to the node — stage, excise with margins; grade decides prognosis.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
