perinuclear clear zone — usually benign, cured by excision),

plain: List the canine round cell tumors and how cytology separates them → MCT (granules, eosinophils), histiocytoma (young dog, pale blue cytoplasm, no granules), cutaneous lymphoma, plasmacytoma (eccentric nucleus, perinuclear clear zone — usually benign, cured by excision), TVT (punctate vacuoles). Lipoma: adipocytes, oily slide.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

spans.text: Button-like raised alopecic nodule on head/limb of a dog <3 years; round
only if ulcerated or persistent beyond 3 months.

plain: Button-like raised alopecic nodule on head/limb of a dog <3 years; round cells without granules → Cutaneous histiocytoma — benign Langerhans cell tumor; regresses spontaneously in 1–3 months via T-cell response. Excise only if ulcerated or persistent beyond 3 months.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Mast cell tumor and other skin/round cell tumors

spans.text: Older dog, wart-like yellowish lobulated skin mass; cytology shows foamy
(very common, benign, excision curative), epithelioma (low-grade), carcinoma

plain: Older dog, wart-like yellowish lobulated skin mass; cytology shows foamy sebocytes → Sebaceous gland tumors — nodular hyperplasia and adenoma (very common, benign, excision curative), epithelioma (low-grade), carcinoma (rare, locally invasive, low metastasis).

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

periosteal reaction and Codman's triangle, not crossing the joint →
away from the elbow, toward the knee

plain: Large-breed dog, lytic-proliferative metaphyseal lesion with sunburst periosteal reaction and Codman's triangle, not crossing the joint → Appendicular osteosarcoma. Sites "away from the elbow, toward the knee ": distal radius (most common), proximal humerus, distal femur, proximal tibia; forelimbs 2× hindlimbs; median age ~7 years. Confirm by Jamshidi biopsy of the lesion center, through tissue the amputation will remove. Not the elbow.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: How to tell primary bone tumor from osteomyelitis radiographically →
Osteosarcoma is monostotic, metaphyseal and does not cross the joint
(articular cartilage barrier); lesions on both sides of a joint suggest
(sequestra, cloacae, draining tracts; fungal forms polyostotic) or

plain: How to tell primary bone tumor from osteomyelitis radiographically → Osteosarcoma is monostotic, metaphyseal and does not cross the joint (articular cartilage barrier); lesions on both sides of a joint suggest osteomyelitis (sequestra, cloacae, draining tracts; fungal forms polyostotic) or synovial cell/histiocytic sarcoma. Biopsy ± culture confirms. Not "crossing joint = neoplasia" — reversed.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Metastatic rate and survival of appendicular OSA with amputation alone
months; amputation + carboplatin (300 mg/m² IV q3wk × 4–6), cisplatin

plain: Metastatic rate and survival of appendicular OSA with amputation alone vs with chemotherapy → ~90% have pulmonary micrometastasis at diagnosis, though <15% visible on radiographs. Amputation alone MST 4–5 months; amputation + carboplatin (300 mg/m² IV q3wk × 4–6), cisplatin or doxorubicin ~10–12 months; 1-year survival ~45–50%. Stage with 3-view thoracic radiographs/CT.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Laboratory finding that worsens OSA prognosis →
(total or bone isoenzyme) pre-amputation, or failure to normalize after. Other
negatives: proximal humeral site, large tumor, high grade, metastasis at
diagnosis, very young/old age, high monocyte count.

plain: Laboratory finding that worsens OSA prognosis → Elevated serum ALP (total or bone isoenzyme) pre-amputation, or failure to normalize after. Other negatives: proximal humeral site, large tumor, high grade, metastasis at diagnosis, very young/old age, high monocyte count.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Dog amputated for OSA a year ago, now pulmonary nodules →
— palliative care (analgesia/NSAID, ± metronomic chemotherapy or palliative

plain: Dog amputated for OSA a year ago, now pulmonary nodules → Metastasis — palliative care (analgesia/NSAID, ± metronomic chemotherapy or palliative radiation); prognosis weeks to months.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Large-breed dog, firm mandibular swelling; dental radiograph shows lysis
mandibular OSA metastasizes later and less
than appendicular, so surgery alone gives long survival; carboplatin for

plain: Large-breed dog, firm mandibular swelling; dental radiograph shows lysis with sunburst new bone → Oral (axial) osteosarcoma — wide mandibulectomy/maxillectomy; mandibular OSA metastasizes later and less than appendicular, so surgery alone gives long survival; carboplatin for incomplete margins.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Older German Shepherd/Golden, acute collapse, pale gums, HR 176,
distended abdomen; abdominocentesis yields non-clotting blood →
of serosal detail, splenic mass, displaced bowel; confirm with AFAST/

plain: Older German Shepherd/Golden, acute collapse, pale gums, HR 176, distended abdomen; abdominocentesis yields non-clotting blood → Ruptured splenic hemangiosarcoma with hemoabdomen. Radiographs: loss of serosal detail, splenic mass, displaced bowel; confirm with AFAST/ abdominocentesis (effusion PCV near peripheral). Stabilize (fluids, transfusion) before surgery.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Most common primary site of canine HSA, and staging before splenectomy
echocardiography (right atrial mass in up to 25%)
expect VPCs. HSA is the most common neoplastic cause of pericardial effusion

plain: Most common primary site of canine HSA, and staging before splenectomy → Spleen (~50%), then right atrium/auricle, skin/subcutis, liver. Stage with thoracic radiographs and echocardiography (right atrial mass in up to 25%); expect VPCs. HSA is the most common neoplastic cause of pericardial effusion and of hemoabdomen in dogs.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Treatment and prognosis of splenic HSA →
based chemotherapy: MST 5–7 months vs 1–3 months surgery alone;

plain: Treatment and prognosis of splenic HSA → Splenectomy + doxorubicin- based chemotherapy: MST 5–7 months vs 1–3 months surgery alone; <10% alive at 1 year. Histopathology is required — about one-third of splenic masses are benign (hematoma, nodular hyperplasia). Brain metastasis = disseminated stage III, grave.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Oral, nasal, ear, eyelid, digit and thyroid tumors

spans.text: Older small-breed dog with pigmented (or amelanotic) gingival mass,
>70% and early lung spread. Then SCC and fibrosarcoma.

plain: Older small-breed dog with pigmented (or amelanotic) gingival mass, halitosis, loose teeth → Oral malignant melanoma — most common malignant oral tumor of dogs; one-third amelanotic; regional node metastasis >70% and early lung spread. Then SCC and fibrosarcoma. In cats: SCC (sublingual/mandibular, poor prognosis), fibrosarcoma second.

plain: First staging step for oral melanoma → FNA of mandibular lymph nodes even if normal size (~40% metastatic) plus thoracic radiographs/CT, then mandibulectomy/maxillectomy ± radiation and the Oncept xenogeneic DNA vaccine. Tumor >2 cm, caudal location and bone invasion worsen prognosis; pulmonary metastasis within a year is the expected course (MST 6–12 months).

plain: Rostral gingival SCC vs tonsillar SCC in dogs → Nontonsillar/rostral mandibular SCC: locally invasive, low metastasis, good prognosis (>80– 90% 1-year survival after segmental mandibulectomy with 1–2 cm margins; radiation if incomplete). Tonsillar SCC: highly metastatic, poor. Fibrosarcoma recurs locally, rarely metastasizes.

plain: Most common benign oral tumor of dogs → Canine acanthomatous ameloblastoma (formerly acanthomatous epulis): invades bone locally, never metastasizes — needs 1 cm bony margins or radiation. Peripheral odontogenic fibromas are the other common gingival masses.

chapter: Chapter 8 — Canine — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Young dog with multiple cauliflower-like oral papillary lesions →
spontaneously in 1–3 months; excise only lesions that interfere with eating.

plain: Young dog with multiple cauliflower-like oral papillary lesions → treatment? None — oral papillomatosis (papillomavirus) regresses spontaneously in 1–3 months; excise only lesions that interfere with eating.

— benign; ~75% of canine lid tumors are benign. Full-thickness

Antigen–antibody complexes (resolve by heat-treating serum), infection <6–7 months (immature females), male-only or very light burdens. Repeat heat-treated antigen, Knott's test, echocardiography. plain: T. cati: transmammary only, no prenatal infection. Toxascaris leonina: neither — only ingested eggs or paratenic hosts, gut-wall migration, older animals.

Pups still dewormed from 2 weeks.

plain: Whipworm transmission and why kennels cannot clear it → Ingestion of embryonated eggs from soil/feces; direct cycle, no intermediate host, no transplacental/transmammary route. plain: Proglottids seen on the stool but routine fecal flotation negative → why? Tapeworms (Dipylidium, Taenia, Echinococcus) pass eggs inside intact proglottids, so flotation is often falsely negative; Dipylidium egg packets float poorly. Diagnose by proglottid identification.

chapter: Chapter 9 — Canine — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Dog passing proglottids; fecal shows thick-walled, radially striated taeniid eggs with a six-hooked embryo → Taenia spp. — eggs identical to Echinococcus, so handle feces as potentially zoonotic (hydatid disease). Acquired from rabbits, rodents or raw viscera; stop hunting and offal access.

chapter: Chapter 9 — Canine — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

chapter: Chapter 9 — Canine — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

Acetaminophen (dogs: centrilobular necrosis; cats: methemoglobinemia dominates — N- acetylcysteine), xylitol (dogs), carprofen (idiosyncratic), azathioprine, ketoconazole/itraconazole, chronic phenobarbital, TMS, lomustine, oral diazepam in cats, methimazole, iron, sago palm (cycasin), aflatoxin, blue- green algae.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Several dogs on the same moldy corn-based commercial diet; icterus,
hepatomegaly, markedly ↑ ALT and bilirubin, coagulopathy →
hepatocyte DNA). Remove source, SAMe, vitamin K, plasma;

plain: Several dogs on the same moldy corn-based commercial diet; icterus, hepatomegaly, markedly ↑ ALT and bilirubin, coagulopathy → Aflatoxicosis (Aspergillus flavus/parasiticus B1; CYP450 epoxide binds hepatocyte DNA). Remove source, SAMe, vitamin K, plasma; poor prognosis once icteric; test the feed.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Owner treating a dog's otitis externa with tea tree oil and vinegar →
melaleuca oil is neuro- and hepatotoxic
(ataxia, tremors, hypothermia); vinegar is irritating and ototoxic through a
ruptured tympanum. Examine the TM, cytology, then an appropriate otic

plain: Owner treating a dog's otitis externa with tea tree oil and vinegar → advice? Stop both: melaleuca oil is neuro- and hepatotoxic to dogs and cats (ataxia, tremors, hypothermia); vinegar is irritating and ototoxic through a ruptured tympanum. Examine the TM, cytology, then an appropriate otic antimicrobial/antifungal.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with mild anemia, many nucleated RBCs and basophilic stippling out
of proportion to the anemia, GI signs and seizures →

nucleotidase so ribosomal RNA persists; confirm

plain: Dog with mild anemia, many nucleated RBCs and basophilic stippling out of proportion to the anemia, GI signs and seizures → Lead poisoning (plumbism). Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase and pyrimidine 5'- nucleotidase so ribosomal RNA persists; confirm whole-blood lead > 0.35 ppm (0.6 ppm definitive).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia
plain: Lead poisoning treatment? Remove source (radiograph for paint chips/ objects, GI decontamination); chelate with CaEDTA 25 mg/kg SC q6h × 5 days or succimer 10 mg/kg PO q8h × 10 days; control seizures; screen children in the household (shared exposure).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with hemolytic anemia, icterus, hepatosplenomegaly and vomiting
after swallowing pennies or a galvanized nut →
foreign body. Remove endoscopically or surgically, transfuse as needed;
chelation rarely needed once the source is out.

plain: Dog with hemolytic anemia, icterus, hepatosplenomegaly and vomiting after swallowing pennies or a galvanized nut → Zinc toxicosis (US pennies minted after 1982 are 97.5% zinc); radiograph shows the metallic gastric foreign body. Remove endoscopically or surgically, transfuse as needed; chelation rarely needed once the source is out.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Melarsomine overdose with vomiting, collapse, hepatic and renal injury →
arsenic, plus aggressive fluids. Melarsomine itself is dosed by lean weight

plain: Melarsomine overdose with vomiting, collapse, hepatic and renal injury → antidote? Dimercaprol (BAL in oil) IM, a sulfhydryl chelator of trivalent arsenic, plus aggressive fluids. Melarsomine itself is dosed by lean weight 2.5 mg/kg deep epaxial IM; AHS 3-dose protocol (day 60, then 90 and 91).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

bradycardia, muscle tremors after pesticide exposure → toxin class and
(¼ IV, rest IM/SC) titrated to drying of

plain: Dog with salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, miosis, bradycardia, muscle tremors after pesticide exposure → toxin class and first drug? Organophosphate/carbamate acetylcholinesterase inhibition (SLUDGE). Atropine 0.2–0.5 mg/kg (¼ IV, rest IM/SC) titrated to drying of secretions; bathe to decontaminate; diazepam for seizures. Atropine does not treat the tremors (nicotinic).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Role and timing of pralidoxime (2-PAM) in organophosphate toxicosis? 20
mg/kg IM/slow IV q8–12h within 24–48 h
nicotinic signs before the enzyme-OP bond "ages" irreversibly.

plain: Role and timing of pralidoxime (2-PAM) in organophosphate toxicosis? 20 mg/kg IM/slow IV q8–12h within 24–48 h to reactivate cholinesterase for nicotinic signs before the enzyme-OP bond "ages" irreversibly. Not for carbamates — reversible inhibition, oxime unnecessary.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog ate snail/slug bait; severe tremors, hyperesthesia, seizures,

plain: Dog ate snail/slug bait; severe tremors, hyperesthesia, seizures, hyperthermia ("shake and bake") → Metaldehyde (a molluscicide, not an insecticide; lowers brain GABA).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: seizures, active cooling, fluids; watch for acidosis and later hepatic injury.
strychnine — rigid extensor seizures triggered by stimuli.

plain: No antidote: decontaminate, methocarbamol 55–220 mg/kg IV for tremors, diazepam/barbiturates for seizures, active cooling, fluids; watch for acidosis and later hepatic injury. Not strychnine — rigid extensor seizures triggered by stimuli.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog in Florida, Texas or Hawaii mouths a large toad; profuse drooling,
brick-red gums, then seizures and arrhythmias →

plain: Dog in Florida, Texas or Hawaii mouths a large toad; profuse drooling, brick-red gums, then seizures and arrhythmias → Bufotoxins (bufadienolides: digoxin-like Na/K-ATPase inhibition plus catecholamines).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia
plain: Flush mouth 10–15 min head down, diazepam for seizures, ECG and potassium monitoring. Both cane toad (Rhinella marina) and Colorado River toad (Incilius alvarius) are potentially lethal; other native toads are mild.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Toad-poisoned dog with second-degree AV block/bradycardia →
lidocaine, esmolol or propranolol; hyperkalemia or refractory arrhythmia →

plain: Toad-poisoned dog with second-degree AV block/bradycardia → arrhythmia treatment? Atropine 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV; tachyarrhythmias → lidocaine, esmolol or propranolol; hyperkalemia or refractory arrhythmia → digoxin-specific Fab.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Collie, Australian Shepherd or Sheltie given ivermectin develops ataxia,
mydriasis, blindness, tremors, coma → mechanism? ABCB1 (MDR1)
: defective P-glycoprotein blood-brain-barrier efflux lets ivermectin
potentiate GABA- and glutamate-gated chloride channels
Supportive care, IV lipid emulsion; recovery days–weeks.

plain: Collie, Australian Shepherd or Sheltie given ivermectin develops ataxia, mydriasis, blindness, tremors, coma → mechanism? ABCB1 (MDR1) deletion: defective P-glycoprotein blood-brain-barrier efflux lets ivermectin accumulate and potentiate GABA- and glutamate-gated chloride channels. Supportive care, IV lipid emulsion; recovery days–weeks. Not GABA inhibition — ivermectin enhances it.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: What is safe and what is avoided in MDR1-mutant dogs? Heartworm-
preventive doses of ivermectin, milbemycin, moxidectin and selamectin are
; avoid high-dose ivermectin (horse paste, treated-horse feces),
, and reduce vincristine/doxorubicin; caution with acepromazine

plain: What is safe and what is avoided in MDR1-mutant dogs? Heartworm- preventive doses of ivermectin, milbemycin, moxidectin and selamectin are safe; avoid high-dose ivermectin (horse paste, treated-horse feces), loperamide, and reduce vincristine/doxorubicin; caution with acepromazine and butorphanol.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog on metronidazole 2 weeks develops vertical nystagmus, ataxia, head
tilt → Dx, central or peripheral, management?

plain: Dog on metronidazole 2 weeks develops vertical nystagmus, ataxia, head tilt → Dx, central or peripheral, management? Metronidazole neurotoxicity, central vestibular/cerebellar (vertical nystagmus marks a central lesion); usually > 60 mg/kg/day or prolonged courses. Stop drug; diazepam 0.5 mg/kg IV then PO q8h × 3 days speeds recovery (1–2 weeks).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog's ear flushed with chlorhexidine; head tilt, nystagmus, deafness;
otoscopy shows ruptured tympanum → central or peripheral? Peripheral
vestibular disease from ototoxicity: the agent crosses the round window and
destroys inner-ear hair cells. Avoid chlorhexidine and aminoglycosides when
the TM is not intact; flush with saline.
Not a treatment for vestibular disease —

plain: Dog's ear flushed with chlorhexidine; head tilt, nystagmus, deafness; otoscopy shows ruptured tympanum → central or peripheral? Peripheral vestibular disease from ototoxicity: the agent crosses the round window and destroys inner-ear hair cells. Avoid chlorhexidine and aminoglycosides when the TM is not intact; flush with saline. Not a treatment for vestibular disease — these drugs cause it.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Why is enrofloxacin avoided in growing dogs, and the feline-specific
Fluoroquinolones erode articular cartilage during rapid growth —
enrofloxacin > 5 mg/kg/day causes acute irreversible retinal degeneration

plain: Why is enrofloxacin avoided in growing dogs, and the feline-specific toxicity? Fluoroquinolones erode articular cartilage during rapid growth — avoid until ~8 months (small breeds) or 12–18 months (large/giant). In cats, enrofloxacin > 5 mg/kg/day causes acute irreversible retinal degeneration and blindness; use ≤ 5 mg/kg q24h or marbofloxacin/pradofloxacin.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Why are tetracyclines avoided in pregnant bitches and puppies?
chelate calcium in mineralizing enamel, dentin and bone →
gestation until permanent teeth have mineralized (
Not just 8–12 weeks — the whole mineralization window.

plain: Why are tetracyclines avoided in pregnant bitches and puppies? They chelate calcium in mineralizing enamel, dentin and bone → permanent yellow-brown teeth and enamel hypoplasia; the window runs from mid- gestation until permanent teeth have mineralized (~6 months). Doxycycline binds calcium least. Not just 8–12 weeks — the whole mineralization window.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Adverse effects of potentiated sulfonamides (TMS) in dogs?

plain: Adverse effects of potentiated sulfonamides (TMS) in dogs? Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (monitor Schirmer), reversible hypothyroidism (thyroid peroxidase inhibition), idiosyncratic hepatopathy, immune-mediated polyarthritis/fever/skin eruptions (Dobermans), blood dyscrasias, crystalluria in dehydrated patients.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Parvovirus puppy on antibiotics for septic diarrhea develops rising
— proximal tubular necrosis, worst in dehydrated/
hypovolemic puppies; dose once daily only when euhydrated, monitor urine

plain: Parvovirus puppy on antibiotics for septic diarrhea develops rising creatinine → which antibiotic is nephrotoxic? Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin) — proximal tubular necrosis, worst in dehydrated/ hypovolemic puppies; dose once daily only when euhydrated, monitor urine casts. Sulfonamides can add crystalluria. Not penicillin/ampicillin — not nephrotoxic.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog on amphotericin B → what to monitor? BUN/creatinine and
; nephrotoxicity is dose-limiting — hold if BUN
> 50 mg/dL; saline loading and lipid formulations reduce it.

plain: Dog on amphotericin B → what to monitor? BUN/creatinine and urinalysis before every dose; nephrotoxicity is dose-limiting — hold if BUN > 50 mg/dL; saline loading and lipid formulations reduce it.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Main adverse effect of long-term ketoconazole? Hepatotoxicity
anorexia, vomiting); also inhibits cortisol and testosterone synthesis, cataracts
with chronic use, CYP3A4 inhibition (raises cyclosporine levels), teratogenic.

plain: Main adverse effect of long-term ketoconazole? Hepatotoxicity (↑ ALT, anorexia, vomiting); also inhibits cortisol and testosterone synthesis, cataracts with chronic use, CYP3A4 inhibition (raises cyclosporine levels), teratogenic.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Griseofulvin: what increases absorption and the key adverse effects?
, especially in FIV-positive cats and kittens.

plain: Griseofulvin: what increases absorption and the key adverse effects? Give with a fatty meal (lipophilic); teratogenic (contraindicated in pregnancy) and bone marrow suppression, especially in FIV-positive cats and kittens.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with a heart murmur or CHF needs chemotherapy; which CHOP
drug is contraindicated and why? Doxorubicin: cumulative cardiotoxicity
Boxers, dexrazoxane protective. Also anaphylactoid reaction (slow infusion,

plain: Dog with a heart murmur or CHF needs chemotherapy; which CHOP drug is contraindicated and why? Doxorubicin: cumulative cardiotoxicity (DCM, arrhythmias) above ~180–240 mg/m² total; echo-screen Dobermans/ Boxers, dexrazoxane protective. Also anaphylactoid reaction (slow infusion, pre-treat diphenhydramine), perivascular slough, nephrotoxic in cats.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Estrogen (ECP/DES) given for mismating or incontinence → most
short term, and dose-dependent, potentially irreversible

plain: Estrogen (ECP/DES) given for mismating or incontinence → most important adverse effects? Pyometra (cervix opens, endometrial hyperplasia) short term, and dose-dependent, potentially irreversible bone marrow suppression (aplastic anemia/pancytopenia).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Most common adverse effect of NSAIDs in dogs? GI ulceration/erosion
(vomiting, melena) from COX-1 prostaglandin loss; then nephrotoxicity (with
combine with corticosteroids or another NSAID.
Role of tramadol for canine osteoarthritis?
and trials show no benefit over
placebo; NSAIDs are first-line. Tramadol has better evidence in cats.

plain: Most common adverse effect of NSAIDs in dogs? GI ulceration/erosion (vomiting, melena) from COX-1 prostaglandin loss; then nephrotoxicity (with hypotension/dehydration) and idiosyncratic hepatopathy (carprofen). Never combine with corticosteroids or another NSAID. Role of tramadol for canine osteoarthritis? Minimal: dogs form little of the active M1 (O-desmethyltramadol) metabolite and trials show no benefit over placebo; NSAIDs are first-line. Tramadol has better evidence in cats. Not a first-line OA analgesic in dogs.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

plain: Prednisone/prednisolone dose tiers in dogs? Physiologic replacement 0.1– 0.25 mg/kg/day; anti-inflammatory 0.5–1 mg/kg/day; immunosuppressive 2– 4 mg/kg/day (commonly 2.2 mg/kg = 1 mg/lb; cap ~50–60 mg/day or 40–50 mg/m² in large dogs), then taper ~25% every 2–4 weeks. Not 1–2 mg/kg for immunosuppression — that is sub-therapeutic.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: 30-kg Labrador with IMHA → immunosuppressive prednisone amount?
, usually capped near 50–60 mg/day in large dogs. In cats
at roughly double doses (prednisone is poorly converted

plain: 30-kg Labrador with IMHA → immunosuppressive prednisone amount? 30 × 2.2 = 66 mg/day, usually capped near 50–60 mg/day in large dogs. In cats use prednisolone at roughly double doses (prednisone is poorly converted hepatically).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Most common adverse effects of glucocorticoids in dogs? PU/PD
chronic: muscle wasting, pot belly, thin skin/alopecia, calcinosis cutis, steroid
hepatopathy (↑ ALP), insulin resistance, GI ulceration (especially with
NSAIDs), iatrogenic Cushing's. Cats relatively resistant but risk diabetes/CHF.
Not renal insufficiency — not a glucocorticoid effect.

plain: Most common adverse effects of glucocorticoids in dogs? PU/PD (earliest and most frequent; ADH antagonism), polyphagia with weight gain, panting; chronic: muscle wasting, pot belly, thin skin/alopecia, calcinosis cutis, steroid hepatopathy (↑ ALP), insulin resistance, GI ulceration (especially with NSAIDs), iatrogenic Cushing's. Cats relatively resistant but risk diabetes/CHF. Not renal insufficiency — not a glucocorticoid effect.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog on prednisolone, cephalexin, miconazole and lime sulfur starts eating
manifests as coprophagia or pica; antibiotics, azoles and lime sulfur do not
stimulate appetite. Phenobarbital and benzodiazepines also cause polyphagia.

plain: Dog on prednisolone, cephalexin, miconazole and lime sulfur starts eating feces → responsible drug? Prednisolone — steroid-induced polyphagia manifests as coprophagia or pica; antibiotics, azoles and lime sulfur do not stimulate appetite. Phenobarbital and benzodiazepines also cause polyphagia.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Common silent complication of chronic glucocorticoid therapy? Occult
plus dilute urine) — culture urine periodically.

plain: Common silent complication of chronic glucocorticoid therapy? Occult bacterial UTI in ~20–40% of dogs, often without pyuria (immunosuppression plus dilute urine) — culture urine periodically.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: First-line empirical antibiotic for canine superficial pyoderma
cefadroxil, amoxicillin-clavulanate, clindamycin, TMS) for 3–4 weeks,
; culture if recurrent; fluoroquinolones and third-generation

plain: First-line empirical antibiotic for canine superficial pyoderma (Staphylococcus pseudintermedius)? Cephalexin 22–30 mg/kg PO q12h (or cefadroxil, amoxicillin-clavulanate, clindamycin, TMS) for 3–4 weeks, 1 week past clinical cure; culture if recurrent; fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins are second-tier.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Contaminated traumatic or bite wound → empirical antibiotic?
staphylococci, streptococci, anaerobes) after lavage and debridement;
cephalexin for simple skin wounds; add fluoroquinolone only if Gram-negative

plain: Contaminated traumatic or bite wound → empirical antibiotic? Amoxicillin-clavulanate 12.5–25 mg/kg PO q12h (covers Pasteurella, staphylococci, streptococci, anaerobes) after lavage and debridement; cephalexin for simple skin wounds; add fluoroquinolone only if Gram-negative sepsis suspected.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: cefpodoxime acceptable; fluoroquinolones reserved for complicated or

plain: Empirical antibiotic for uncomplicated E. coli cystitis in a dog? Amoxicillin (± clavulanate) or TMS first-line (ISCAID); cephalexin/ cefpodoxime acceptable; fluoroquinolones reserved for complicated or prostatic infections; base on culture.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Intact male dog with fever, painful prostate and hematuria → antibiotic?
basic drugs cross the blood-prostate barrier (chloramphenicol, erythromycin
also); beta-lactams penetrate poorly in chronic disease; castrate after resolution.

plain: Intact male dog with fever, painful prostate and hematuria → antibiotic? Enrofloxacin (fluoroquinolone) or TMS for 4–6 weeks — lipophilic, weakly basic drugs cross the blood-prostate barrier (chloramphenicol, erythromycin also); beta-lactams penetrate poorly in chronic disease; castrate after resolution.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Reliable anaerobic antimicrobials, and which fail?

plain: Reliable anaerobic antimicrobials, and which fail? Metronidazole, amoxicillin-clavulanate/penicillins, clindamycin, chloramphenicol (and carbapenems). Aminoglycosides (oxygen-dependent uptake) and most fluoroquinolones (except pradofloxacin) are ineffective. Not azithromycin — only limited anaerobic activity.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: , given with food or a water

plain: Cat with upper respiratory infection (Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Bordetella) → antibiotic? Doxycycline 5 mg/kg PO q12h, given with food or a water chaser to prevent esophageal stricture.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with weekly idiopathic epileptic seizures → maintenance drug of
choice and monitoring? Phenobarbital 2–3 mg/kg PO q12h
bile acids every 6 months. Alternatives: KBr, levetiracetam, zonisamide.

plain: Dog with weekly idiopathic epileptic seizures → maintenance drug of choice and monitoring? Phenobarbital 2–3 mg/kg PO q12h; trough level at 2–3 weeks, target 15–35 µg/mL (hepatotoxicity above 35); liver enzymes and bile acids every 6 months. Alternatives: KBr, levetiracetam, zonisamide.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Potassium bromide in dogs: dose, steady state, loading, diet interaction,
— load 400–600 mg/kg over 24 h if needed; therapeutic 1–3 mg/mL.

plain: Potassium bromide in dogs: dose, steady state, loading, diet interaction, adverse effects? 20–40 mg/kg/day; half-life ~25 days so steady state 3–4 months — load 400–600 mg/kg over 24 h if needed; therapeutic 1–3 mg/mL.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: High-chloride diets increase renal bromide excretion
Sedation, PU/PD, polyphagia, hindlimb weakness, pancreatitis.

plain: High-chloride diets increase renal bromide excretion (keep diet constant). Sedation, PU/PD, polyphagia, hindlimb weakness, pancreatitis.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Actively seizing dog → diazepam dose? 0.5–1 mg/kg IV
rectum without IV access), repeat up to three times; midazolam 0.2–0.3 mg/kg
IV/IM/IN alternative; follow with a loading anticonvulsant.

plain: Actively seizing dog → diazepam dose? 0.5–1 mg/kg IV (1–2 mg/kg per rectum without IV access), repeat up to three times; midazolam 0.2–0.3 mg/kg IV/IM/IN alternative; follow with a loading anticonvulsant. Avoid oral diazepam in cats (hepatic necrosis).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Sedative traditionally avoided in an epileptic dog?
(phenothiazine, said to lower seizure threshold; evidence weak) and ketamine;

plain: Sedative traditionally avoided in an epileptic dog? Acepromazine (phenothiazine, said to lower seizure threshold; evidence weak) and ketamine; benzodiazepines preferred.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Drug of choice for acquired myasthenia gravis, its class, and the most
common cause of death? Pyridostigmine 0.5–3 mg/kg PO q8–12h
for diagnosis); add prednisone/azathioprine/mycophenolate if poor response.

plain: Drug of choice for acquired myasthenia gravis, its class, and the most common cause of death? Pyridostigmine 0.5–3 mg/kg PO q8–12h, a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (neostigmine injectable; edrophonium for diagnosis); add prednisone/azathioprine/mycophenolate if poor response. MCCOD: aspiration pneumonia from megaesophagus — feed upright.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog or cat started on fluoxetine → most common adverse effects?
often irritability, urinary retention (cats), lowered seizure threshold. Allow 4–6

plain: Dog or cat started on fluoxetine → most common adverse effects? Anorexia/decreased appetite, lethargy, GI upset (vomiting, diarrhea); less often irritability, urinary retention (cats), lowered seizure threshold. Allow 4–6 weeks for effect.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog on selegiline or wearing an amitraz collar started on fluoxetine,
clomipramine, tramadol or trazodone → key interaction? Serotonin
supportive care; wash out before switching.

plain: Dog on selegiline or wearing an amitraz collar started on fluoxetine, clomipramine, tramadol or trazodone → key interaction? Serotonin syndrome (MAO inhibitor + reuptake blocker): agitation, tremors, hyperthermia, diarrhea, seizures. Stop drugs, cyproheptadine antidote, supportive care; wash out before switching.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Loperamide's effect on motility, and the breed caution?
increases segmental contractions and decreases propulsive peristalsis
mg/kg PO q8–12h); avoid in MDR1-mutant herding breeds (CNS depression).
Anticholinergics decrease all motility including segmentation.

plain: Loperamide's effect on motility, and the breed caution? Mu-opioid agonist: increases segmental contractions and decreases propulsive peristalsis (0.1 mg/kg PO q8–12h); avoid in MDR1-mutant herding breeds (CNS depression). Anticholinergics decrease all motility including segmentation. Not "slows segmentation" — it increases it.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Digoxin: class, actions and therapeutic range?
tone slowing SA rate and AV conduction (rate control in atrial fibrillation).

plain: Digoxin: class, actions and therapeutic range? Cardiac glycoside: Na ⁺ /K ⁺ - ATPase inhibition → ↑ intracellular Ca² ⁺ (positive inotrope) and ↑ vagal tone slowing SA rate and AV conduction (rate control in atrial fibrillation). Narrow index: 0.8–1.2 ng/mL sampled 6–8 h post-pill; hypokalemia, azotemia and quinidine increase toxicity.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Stable dog on digoxin begins vomiting, anorexia, lethargy → action?
Discontinue digoxin and measure serum level
GI signs are the earliest toxicity, followed by AV block and VPCs.

plain: Stable dog on digoxin begins vomiting, anorexia, lethargy → action? Discontinue digoxin and measure serum level, potassium and renal function; GI signs are the earliest toxicity, followed by AV block and VPCs.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: ACE inhibitors (enalapril, benazepril): mechanism and indications?
: less angiotensin II → vasodilation, less aldosterone Na/water
retention, lower glomerular efferent pressure. Proteinuric nephropathy, CHF
adjunct, mild hypertension in dogs; monitor creatinine/K; benazepril preferred
in renal disease (hepatic clearance). Spironolactone is the aldosterone-receptor

plain: ACE inhibitors (enalapril, benazepril): mechanism and indications? Block the RAAS: less angiotensin II → vasodilation, less aldosterone Na/water retention, lower glomerular efferent pressure. Proteinuric nephropathy, CHF adjunct, mild hypertension in dogs; monitor creatinine/K; benazepril preferred in renal disease (hepatic clearance). Spironolactone is the aldosterone-receptor antagonist. Not a direct cardiac drug.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: for SBP ≥ 160–180 mmHg, preventing retinal detachment/blindness;
telmisartan for proteinuria. Feline hypertension responds poorly to ACE

plain: First-line antihypertensive in cats? Amlodipine (calcium channel blocker) for SBP ≥ 160–180 mmHg, preventing retinal detachment/blindness; telmisartan for proteinuria. Feline hypertension responds poorly to ACE inhibitors alone.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with glaucoma secondary to anterior lens luxation → contraindicated
and safe topical classes? Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, travoprost,
— miosis traps the lens and worsens pupillary
anhydrase inhibitors) are safe; emergency IV mannitol 1–2 g/kg.

plain: Dog with glaucoma secondary to anterior lens luxation → contraindicated and safe topical classes? Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost) contraindicated — miosis traps the lens and worsens pupillary block (also avoid in uveitis). Dorzolamide 2%/brinzolamide 1% (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) are safe; emergency IV mannitol 1–2 g/kg.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Drug of choice for tapeworms, and which common dewormer fails against
7.5 mg/kg × 2 days in dogs); epsiprantel alternative.

plain: Drug of choice for tapeworms, and which common dewormer fails against Dipylidium ? Praziquantel 5 mg/kg PO/SC (higher for Echinococcus; Diphyllobothrium 7.5 mg/kg × 2 days in dogs); epsiprantel alternative.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Which flea product inhibits chitin synthesis, and what does it not do?
Not an adulticide; no activity against ticks or mites
pair with an adulticide in flea-allergic animals.

plain: Fenbendazole kills Taenia but not Dipylidium caninum or Echinococcus. Which flea product inhibits chitin synthesis, and what does it not do? Lufenuron (benzoylurea development inhibitor): blocks egg/larval development only. Not an adulticide; no activity against ticks or mites — pair with an adulticide in flea-allergic animals. Not a tick/mite treatment.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Mechanisms of the main ectoparasiticide classes?
chloride blockers (fleas, ticks, mites); pyrethrins/permethrin: sodium-channel

plain: Mechanisms of the main ectoparasiticide classes? Fipronil: blocks GABA- gated chloride channels; imidacloprid/nitenpyram: nicotinic ACh agonists (fleas only); isoxazolines (fluralaner, afoxolaner): GABA/glutamate-gated chloride blockers (fleas, ticks, mites); pyrethrins/permethrin: sodium-channel openers (permethrin toxic to cats); macrocyclic lactones: glutamate-gated chloride channels.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

; no analgesia, not reversible, hypothermia, splenic sequestration

plain: Acepromazine: receptor actions and main adverse effect? Phenothiazine D2 antagonist (sedation, antiemetic) and alpha-1 antagonist → vasodilation and hypotension; no analgesia, not reversible, hypothermia, splenic sequestration lowers PCV. Avoid in hypovolemic/shocky patients, caution in Boxers and giant breeds (syncope). Epinephrine can cause paradoxical hypotension (beta-2 unmasked).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Anesthetized dog develops severe bradycardia → anticholinergic, and
glycopyrrolate vs atropine? Glycopyrrolate 0.005–0.01 mg/kg IV
atropine 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV. Glycopyrrolate: slower onset (2–4 min), longer
quaternary — does not cross BBB or placenta
tachycardia. Alpha-2-agonist bradycardia → reverse, do not atropinize.

plain: Anesthetized dog develops severe bradycardia → anticholinergic, and glycopyrrolate vs atropine? Glycopyrrolate 0.005–0.01 mg/kg IV or atropine 0.02–0.04 mg/kg IV. Glycopyrrolate: slower onset (2–4 min), longer duration, quaternary — does not cross BBB or placenta, less initial tachycardia. Alpha-2-agonist bradycardia → reverse, do not atropinize.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog apneic immediately after propofol or other IV induction → first
action, and prevention? Intubate and ventilate with 100% oxygen
12 breaths/min, ≤ 15–20 cmH₂O) — post-induction apnea is transient; then
reverse reversible agents (naloxone, atipamezole, flumazenil). Prevent by pre-
oxygenating 3–5 min and titrating propofol over 60–90 s.
resort, never replaces ventilation; not tracheostomy.

plain: Dog apneic immediately after propofol or other IV induction → first action, and prevention? Intubate and ventilate with 100% oxygen (IPPV 8– 12 breaths/min, ≤ 15–20 cmH₂O) — post-induction apnea is transient; then reverse reversible agents (naloxone, atipamezole, flumazenil). Prevent by pre- oxygenating 3–5 min and titrating propofol over 60–90 s. Not doxapram — last resort, never replaces ventilation; not tracheostomy.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Reversal agents for pure mu-opioids, alpha-2 agonists and
re-sedation possible; butorphanol gives partial reversal keeping analgesia);

plain: Reversal agents for pure mu-opioids, alpha-2 agonists and benzodiazepines? Naloxone 0.01–0.04 mg/kg IV/IM (30–60 min duration; re-sedation possible; butorphanol gives partial reversal keeping analgesia); atipamezole for alpha-2 agonists; flumazenil for benzodiazepines.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog with chronic kidney disease → best maintenance anesthetic?
— pulmonary elimination, no renal clearance, rapid
aminoglycosides and alpha-2 agonists (reduce renal perfusion), reduce

plain: Dog with chronic kidney disease → best maintenance anesthetic? Isoflurane or sevoflurane — pulmonary elimination, no renal clearance, rapid adjustment. Pre-hydrate, keep MAP > 70 mmHg, avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides and alpha-2 agonists (reduce renal perfusion), reduce injectable doses.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Dog hit by a car with head trauma → anesthetic classically
mixed but still the exam answer). Prefer propofol or alfaxalone, intubate,
ventilate to normocapnia, head elevated 30°, mannitol or hypertonic saline,

plain: Dog hit by a car with head trauma → anesthetic classically contraindicated? Ketamine (raises cerebral blood flow/ICP; recent data mixed but still the exam answer). Prefer propofol or alfaxalone, intubate, ventilate to normocapnia, head elevated 30°, mannitol or hypertonic saline, avoid jugular compression.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Anesthetic plan for a GDV dog; is xylazine + propofol appropriate?
oxygenate, pure mu-opioid ± benzodiazepine, titrated propofol or etomidate/

plain: Anesthetic plan for a GDV dog; is xylazine + propofol appropriate? No — avoid alpha-2 agonists (bradycardia, arrhythmogenic, cardiovascular depression) and mask induction. Decompress and shock-dose fluids first, pre- oxygenate, pure mu-opioid ± benzodiazepine, titrated propofol or etomidate/ ketamine-diazepam, rapid intubation, inhalant maintenance, lidocaine 2 mg/kg IV then CRI for ventricular arrhythmias; no nitrous oxide.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Geriatric dog with chronic osteoarthritis; owner wants comfort → first-
meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg day 1 then 0.1 mg/kg PO
or carprofen — after renal/hepatic screening; adjuncts: weight control,

plain: Geriatric dog with chronic osteoarthritis; owner wants comfort → first- line drug? An NSAID — meloxicam 0.2 mg/kg day 1 then 0.1 mg/kg PO q24h or carprofen — after renal/hepatic screening; adjuncts: weight control, omega-3s, gabapentin/amantadine, bedinvetmab (anti-NGF mAb) monthly. Never combine with corticosteroids.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Puppy having retained deciduous teeth extracted during spay → best
addition to analgesia? Regional nerve block with bupivacaine 0.5%
buprenorphine 0.01–0.02 mg/kg is complementary systemic cover —

plain: Puppy having retained deciduous teeth extracted during spay → best addition to analgesia? Regional nerve block with bupivacaine 0.5% (infraorbital, inferior alveolar/mental; ≤ 2 mg/kg total), 6–8 h analgesia; buprenorphine 0.01–0.02 mg/kg is complementary systemic cover — multimodal.

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Buprenorphine: main adverse effects and what to monitor?
respiratory depression (ceiling effect), bradycardia, hyperthermia in cats,
hepatically metabolized — reduce dose in hepatic insufficiency
no significant renal or cardiac toxicity; hard to reverse with naloxone (high

plain: Buprenorphine: main adverse effects and what to monitor? Sedation, mild respiratory depression (ceiling effect), bradycardia, hyperthermia in cats, dysphoria; hepatically metabolized — reduce dose in hepatic insufficiency; no significant renal or cardiac toxicity; hard to reverse with naloxone (high receptor affinity).

chapter: Chapter 10 — Canine — Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

spans.text: Fentanyl transdermal patch: onset and duration? Onset 12–24 h in dogs
(6–12 h in cats) — bridge with another analgesic;
to ~5 days in cats; heat increases absorption; dispose carefully.

plain: Fentanyl transdermal patch: onset and duration? Onset 12–24 h in dogs (6–12 h in cats) — bridge with another analgesic; duration ~72 h in dogs, up to ~5 days in cats; heat increases absorption; dispose carefully.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

— every bite must engage it; mucosa and serosa tear, muscularis holds poorly.

plain: Holding layer of intestine, bladder and other hollow viscera; holding layer of a midline celiotomy → Submucosa (dense collagen) for all hollow viscera — every bite must engage it; mucosa and serosa tear, muscularis holds poorly. Celiotomy: external rectus sheath (linea alba); muscle and peritoneum add no strength.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Enterotomy or small-intestinal anastomosis closure — material, pattern,
continuous (modified Gambee if mucosa everts), bites 3–5 mm, engaging

plain: Enterotomy or small-intestinal anastomosis closure — material, pattern, needle → 3-0/4-0 monofilament absorbable (polydioxanone, poliglecaprone 25) on a taper needle, single-layer appositional simple interrupted or continuous (modified Gambee if mucosa everts), bites 3–5 mm, engaging submucosa; omentalize and leak-test. Not Lembert/Cushing or two-layer — inverting narrows the lumen.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

plain: Where is the enterotomy made, and where does anastomosis suturing start? Incise the antimesenteric border in healthy bowel aboral to a foreign body; begin the anastomosis at the mesenteric border (fat obscures it — commonest leak site) and work antimesenterically.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Instrument to occlude bowel atraumatically during enterotomy →
(non-crushing) intestinal forceps or an assistant's fingers; crushing clamps
(Kocher, Carmalt) go only on the segment being removed.

plain: Instrument to occlude bowel atraumatically during enterotomy → Doyen (non-crushing) intestinal forceps or an assistant's fingers; crushing clamps (Kocher, Carmalt) go only on the segment being removed.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: seromuscular (thick, vascular, must be watertight). Intestine: single-layer

plain: Gastrotomy closure versus enterotomy closure → Stomach: two layers — simple continuous mucosa/submucosa, then inverting Cushing or Lembert seromuscular (thick, vascular, must be watertight). Intestine: single-layer appositional only.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Cystotomy closure — suture material and pattern →
two-layer inverting, suture kept out of the lumen; bladder regains full strength

plain: Cystotomy closure — suture material and pattern → 3-0/4-0 synthetic absorbable monofilament (PDS, poliglecaprone), single-layer appositional or two-layer inverting, suture kept out of the lumen; bladder regains full strength in 14–21 days. Never nonabsorbable or braided — nidus for calculi.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Uterine closure after cesarean (bitch vs cow) →
absorbable, simple continuous then inverting Cushing/Lembert (or single
suture; inversion gives a serosa-to-serosa seal against lochia leakage.

plain: Uterine closure after cesarean (bitch vs cow) → Bitch: 3-0 monofilament absorbable, simple continuous then inverting Cushing/Lembert (or single inverting layer). Cow: continuous inverting Utrecht pattern with absorbable suture; inversion gives a serosa-to-serosa seal against lochia leakage.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Gallbladder or bile duct surgery — suture; which species has no
appositional simple continuous or interrupted; braided/nonabsorbable becomes
Horses (also rats, deer) have no gallbladder
continuously via the common bile duct.

plain: Gallbladder or bile duct surgery — suture; which species has no gallbladder? 4-0/5-0 absorbable monofilament (PDS, poliglecaprone), appositional simple continuous or interrupted; braided/nonabsorbable becomes a cholelith nidus. Horses (also rats, deer) have no gallbladder — bile drains continuously via the common bile duct. Not "larger PDS for the equine gallbladder" — it does not exist.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Routine skin closure — pattern, material, needle →
appositional (or cruciate; intradermal absorbable for cosmesis) with 3-0/4-0
needle; remove 10–14 days. Taper needles for muscle, viscera, vessels.
Horizontal mattress for tension or fragile skin.

plain: Routine skin closure — pattern, material, needle → Simple interrupted appositional (or cruciate; intradermal absorbable for cosmesis) with 3-0/4-0 monofilament nonabsorbable nylon or polypropylene on a reverse-cutting needle; remove 10–14 days. Taper needles for muscle, viscera, vessels. Horizontal mattress for tension or fragile skin.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Torn muscle or deep fascia in a laceration — suture →
(polyglactin 910, polyglycolic acid, poliglecaprone, PDS) in simple continuous

plain: Torn muscle or deep fascia in a laceration — suture → Absorbable (polyglactin 910, polyglycolic acid, poliglecaprone, PDS) in simple continuous or horizontal mattress, always incorporating fascia — muscle alone holds suture poorly.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Severed tendon — suture pattern and material →
with large monofilament nonabsorbable or slowly absorbable suture
(polypropylene, nylon, PDS); immobilize 3–6 weeks then load gradually.
"all others multifilament" — nylon and polypropylene are monofilament.

plain: Severed tendon — suture pattern and material → Tension-resisting three- loop pulley (strongest, round tendons), locking-loop (Kessler) or Krackow with large monofilament nonabsorbable or slowly absorbable suture (polypropylene, nylon, PDS); immobilize 3–6 weeks then load gradually. Not "all others multifilament" — nylon and polypropylene are monofilament.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Full-thickness eyelid laceration or wedge resection — closure →
layers: tarsoconjunctival 5-0/6-0 absorbable, buried knots; then a
and simple interrupted skin sutures (4-0 to 6-0; 7-0
acceptable), knots away from the cornea; up to one-third of lid length
Not simple continuous — misaligns the margin, causing

plain: Full-thickness eyelid laceration or wedge resection — closure → Two layers: tarsoconjunctival 5-0/6-0 absorbable, buried knots; then a figure-of- eight at the lid margin and simple interrupted skin sutures (4-0 to 6-0; 7-0 acceptable), knots away from the cornea; up to one-third of lid length removable primarily. Not simple continuous — misaligns the margin, causing notching and trichiasis.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: thickness; complex entropion/ectropion → refer to an ophthalmologist.

plain: Corneal suture size → 7-0 to 9-0 absorbable (polyglactin) or nylon, partial thickness; complex entropion/ectropion → refer to an ophthalmologist.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Full-thickness lip laceration crossing the mucocutaneous junction →
Lavage, minimal debridement, two layers: oral mucosa simple interrupted
(knots in the mouth), then first suture exactly aligning the
0 or 1-0 suture — far too large for the lip.

plain: Full-thickness lip laceration crossing the mucocutaneous junction → Lavage, minimal debridement, two layers: oral mucosa simple interrupted 4-0 absorbable (knots in the mouth), then first suture exactly aligning the mucocutaneous junction, skin 3-0/4-0 nonabsorbable simple interrupted. Not 0 or 1-0 suture — far too large for the lip.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry
section: Suture materials, patterns and holding layers

spans.text: Porcine small-intestinal submucosa (SIS) xenograft versus cyanoacrylate
SIS is an acellular collagen scaffold for
healing by second intention; glue only bonds epidermis — small, clean,
low-tension superficial wounds, never inside contaminated wounds.

plain: Porcine small-intestinal submucosa (SIS) xenograft versus cyanoacrylate tissue glue → SIS is an acellular collagen scaffold for large full-thickness defects healing by second intention; glue only bonds epidermis — small, clean, low-tension superficial wounds, never inside contaminated wounds.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Perioperative prophylactic antibiotic for clean or clean-contaminated
h; indicated when surgery exceeds 90 min, implants placed or wound clean-
Not every 2–3 h — redose at about two half-lives.

plain: Perioperative prophylactic antibiotic for clean or clean-contaminated surgery (Staphylococcus, E. coli) → Cefazolin 22 mg/kg IV 30–60 min before incision, redosed every 90–120 min intraoperatively, stopped within 24 h; indicated when surgery exceeds 90 min, implants placed or wound clean- contaminated. Not every 2–3 h — redose at about two half-lives.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Lavage solution and pressure for a contaminated wound →
dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% or povidone-iodine 0.1–1% acceptable. Avoid
hypertonic/hypotonic fluids, undiluted antiseptics and hydrogen peroxide

plain: Lavage solution and pressure for a contaminated wound → Large volumes of sterile isotonic saline or LRS at 7–8 psi (35 mL syringe + 18–19 g needle); dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% or povidone-iodine 0.1–1% acceptable. Avoid hypertonic/hypotonic fluids, undiluted antiseptics and hydrogen peroxide (cytotoxic).

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Contaminated penetrating wound over a joint →
penetrated, through-and-through joint lavage/arthroscopy plus cefazolin. Leave
open or delayed primary closure — wounds >6–8 h carry >10^5 bacteria/g.

plain: Contaminated penetrating wound over a joint → Clip, lavage, debride, culture; test joint penetration by arthrocentesis or sterile saline distension; if penetrated, through-and-through joint lavage/arthroscopy plus cefazolin. Leave open or delayed primary closure — wounds >6–8 h carry >10^5 bacteria/g.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Purpose of a Penrose or closed-suction drain in a wound →
closed-suction preferred for large wounds; remove at 3–5 days when output
falls. Drains do not replace debridement.

plain: Purpose of a Penrose or closed-suction drain in a wound → Removes fluid and eliminates dead space, preventing seroma, hematoma and abscess. Penrose exits a separate ventral stab incision (gravity), bandaged; active closed-suction preferred for large wounds; remove at 3–5 days when output falls. Drains do not replace debridement.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Sutured laceration becomes infected — most likely organism →
canine skin commensal; infections arise from the patient's own flora. Dog-bite

plain: Sutured laceration becomes infected — most likely organism → Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (formerly S. intermedius), the dominant canine skin commensal; infections arise from the patient's own flora. Dog-bite wounds in humans → Pasteurella.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Chronic firm mass with intermittent draining tract; FNA
nidus plus weeks of culture-based antimicrobials; biopsy to exclude neoplasia,
fungal or mycobacterial agents. Antibiotics alone rarely penetrate a walled-off

plain: Chronic firm mass with intermittent draining tract; FNA pyogranulomatous → Surgical excision/exploration for a foreign body or nidus plus weeks of culture-based antimicrobials; biopsy to exclude neoplasia, fungal or mycobacterial agents. Antibiotics alone rarely penetrate a walled-off granuloma.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Draining tract at the stifle after extracapsular CCL suture →

plain: Draining tract at the stifle after extracapsular CCL suture → Implant infection/foreign-body reaction (biofilm on nylon suture, S. pseudintermedius); culture, remove the implant (periarticular fibrosis maintains stability), culture-based antibiotics 4–6 weeks.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Thoracotomy incision partially dehisced at 1 week, granulating, no air
debride, moist dressings, bandage) with delayed secondary closure once a
healthy granulation bed forms. Pleural communication, subcutaneous

plain: Thoracotomy incision partially dehisced at 1 week, granulating, no air leak or pleural communication → Open wound management (lavage, debride, moist dressings, bandage) with delayed secondary closure once a healthy granulation bed forms. Pleural communication, subcutaneous emphysema, dyspnea or pyothorax → immediate surgical revision.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Post-operative management after FHO versus total hip replacement →
osseointegration and capsule healing before gradual return.

plain: Post-operative management after FHO versus total hip replacement → FHO: early, aggressive physical therapy — function depends on a mobile fibrous pseudarthrosis. THR: strict activity restriction 6–8 weeks for osseointegration and capsule healing before gradual return.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: When is a cast or splint acceptable as sole fixation? Closed, stable,
in young animals, where the joint above and below can be immobilized.
Not for humerus/femur, open, comminuted, unstable fractures or heavy adults.

plain: When is a cast or splint acceptable as sole fixation? Closed, stable, minimally displaced (transverse, greenstick) fractures distal to the elbow or stifle in young animals, where the joint above and below can be immobilized. Not for humerus/femur, open, comminuted, unstable fractures or heavy adults.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: interlocking nail, or IM pin tied in with plate/ESF (pin alone resists bending
only — add cerclage for long oblique).
— the hip/shoulder cannot be immobilized and the cast becomes

plain: Complete mid-diaphyseal femoral fracture → Internal fixation: bone plate, interlocking nail, or IM pin tied in with plate/ESF (pin alone resists bending only — add cerclage for long oblique). Casts are contraindicated for femur and humerus — the hip/shoulder cannot be immobilized and the cast becomes a fulcrum.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: — plate or plate-rod, locking plate, interlocking nail or ESF spanning

plain: Comminuted (non-reconstructable) diaphyseal fracture → Bridging fixation — plate or plate-rod, locking plate, interlocking nail or ESF spanning the comminution without disturbing fragments. Not IM pin alone — no rotational or axial stability.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Highly comminuted open radius/ulna fracture with contaminated wound
— pins away from the wound permit open-
wound management with no implant in contaminated tissue; plating is for

plain: Highly comminuted open radius/ulna fracture with contaminated wound → External skeletal fixation — pins away from the wound permit open- wound management with no implant in contaminated tissue; plating is for closed, reconstructable fractures.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Distal radius/ulna fracture: juvenile greenstick vs toy-breed adult →
— poor distal vascularity gives a high
rate with coaptation. Adult complete fractures → ORIF.

plain: Distal radius/ulna fracture: juvenile greenstick vs toy-breed adult → Aligned greenstick → splint/cast 3–4 weeks. Toy/miniature breeds (Yorkie, Pomeranian) → bone plate — poor distal vascularity gives a high nonunion rate with coaptation. Adult complete fractures → ORIF.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Plating a tibial fracture — where and how many screws?
compression plate for transverse/short oblique, bridging plate-rod or locking
plate for comminuted. Closed stable tibial fracture in a young dog may be cast

plain: Plating a tibial fracture — where and how many screws? On the medial (tension) surface, flat and subcutaneous, with ≥3 screws (6 cortices) per side; compression plate for transverse/short oblique, bridging plate-rod or locking plate for comminuted. Closed stable tibial fracture in a young dog may be cast (stifle and hock immobilized).

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Match the sling: Ehmer, Velpeau, Robert Jones, 90-90 flexion →
fracture; Robert Jones — temporary support distal to elbow/stifle; 90-90 —
prevents quadriceps contracture after distal femoral repair in young dogs.

plain: Match the sling: Ehmer, Velpeau, Robert Jones, 90-90 flexion → Ehmer — after reducing craniodorsal hip luxation; Velpeau — shoulder luxation/scapular fracture; Robert Jones — temporary support distal to elbow/stifle; 90-90 — prevents quadriceps contracture after distal femoral repair in young dogs. Not Ehmer for tibial fractures.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Simple diaphyseal fracture plated with good post-op alignment —
; adult healing 6–12 weeks, faster in puppies.
Worse with open comminuted fractures, articular involvement or distal radius

plain: Simple diaphyseal fracture plated with good post-op alignment — prognosis → Good to excellent; adult healing 6–12 weeks, faster in puppies. Worse with open comminuted fractures, articular involvement or distal radius in toy breeds.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Pelvic fracture — when is surgery indicated?

plain: Pelvic fracture — when is surgery indicated? Unstable or displaced fractures in the weight-bearing axis: acetabulum (articular), ilial body, unstable/painful sacroiliac luxation, and any pelvic canal narrowing >50% (later obstipation, dystocia).

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Mature large-breed dog, hip dysplasia with DJD, failed medical therapy
(>90% good outcomes). FHO is the salvage
alternative, best <20 kg; TPO/DPO only in dogs <~1 year without DJD;

plain: Mature large-breed dog, hip dysplasia with DJD, failed medical therapy → Total hip replacement (>90% good outcomes). FHO is the salvage alternative, best <20 kg; TPO/DPO only in dogs <~1 year without DJD; JPS at 12–20 weeks.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Ventral approach to the hip — most superficial medial muscle
(arises from the iliopubic eminence over the ventral
capsule), transected for pectineal myectomy/ventral capsulotomy; iliopsoas lies

plain: Ventral approach to the hip — most superficial medial muscle encountered → Pectineus (arises from the iliopubic eminence over the ventral capsule), transected for pectineal myectomy/ventral capsulotomy; iliopsoas lies lateral, adductor caudal.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: CCL rupture in a large-breed dog — procedure of choice and what TPLO
so the stifle is stable without the ligament; it does not
recreate the CCL. Inspect menisci and excise the torn medial caudal horn.

plain: CCL rupture in a large-breed dog — procedure of choice and what TPLO achieves → TPLO (or TTA): rotates the plateau to ~5–6.5°, neutralizing cranial tibial thrust so the stifle is stable without the ligament; it does not recreate the CCL. Inspect menisci and excise the torn medial caudal horn. Extracapsular suture acceptable <15 kg.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: Older intact male dog, perineal swelling lateral to anus, tenesmus,
, defect bounded by external anal sphincter; usually unilateral,
more often right-sided, rectal sacculation >90%; rare in bitches and cats.

plain: New-onset aggression in an adult dog → what to exclude before behavioral diagnosis? Pain (orthopedic, dental), hypothyroidism in dogs (total T4/free T4/TSH), neurologic disease, sensory decline, hyperadrenocorticism, drugs. In cats, hyperthyroidism causes irritability/aggression. Then classify, no punishment, desensitization/counter-conditioning ± fluoxetine, referral.

plain: Dog newly aggressive toward a housemate only when that dog eats → Food-related resource guarding; exclude polyphagia drivers — hyperadrenocorticism, exogenous glucocorticoids, diabetes mellitus. Hypoadrenocorticism causes anorexia, not polyphagia. Feed separately, behavior modification.

plain: Young dog urinates with lowered posture or rolls over when greeted, reached over or scolded → Submissive (appeasement) urination — a social signal, not marking or incontinence. Never punish; greet calmly at the dog's level, no looming or eye contact, ignore until settled, build confidence; most outgrow it by 1 year. Exclude UTI/sphincter incompetence.

plain: Intact male urinating small volumes on vertical surfaces, normal urinalysis → Urine marking — diagnosis of exclusion (UTI, cystoliths, polyuria). Castration reduces or eliminates marking in ~50–60% of dogs (~90% of cats); plus enzymatic cleaning, restrict targets, pheromones, behavior modification; punishment counterproductive.

plain: Dog or cat urinating throughout the house — most basic history question → Is the animal neutered? Marking is testosterone-driven in intact males (estrus females too); then separate marking (small volumes, vertical surfaces) from medical causes.

plain: Dog urinates on doors indoors; owners unsure whether marking or anxiety → After urinalysis, obtain video of the dog alone and with owners present: soiling at exits soon after departure → separation anxiety; vertical marking with owners home → territorial marking; low posture on greeting → submissive urination.

plain: Adult dog soils indoors, medical causes excluded → Behavior modification first: supervise/confine (crate, leash), scheduled trips outside (after meals, waking, play), reward outdoor elimination, enzymatic cleaning, no punishment. Not fluoxetine — reserved for documented anxiety-based soiling.

plain: Destruction, vocalization and elimination only when the owner leaves → Separation anxiety; graduated departures and independence training plus clomipramine or fluoxetine (4–6 weeks to effect) and pre-departure alprazolam or trazodone 30–60 min before leaving.

plain: Night-shift owner feeds the dog and sleeps; dog vocalizes repeatedly while owner is home → Attention-seeking behavior, reinforced by any response; ignore completely, structured exercise before bedtime, reward quiet. Exclude separation anxiety (owner absent), pain and cognitive dysfunction in old dogs.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

plain: Tail chasing on doorbell/noise; video shows it also about hourly when alone with no trigger → Compulsive (stereotypic) disorder — self- sustaining, out of context. Rx: desensitization/counter-conditioning, no punishment, clomipramine 1–3 mg/kg q12h or fluoxetine. Not noise phobia — needs a noise trigger; not separation anxiety — distress clusters after departure.

Recurrence common.

plain: Dog repeatedly licking its coat and vomiting hair → Overgrooming: pruritic skin disease (allergy, fleas, parasites) or psychogenic/stress-related licking — complete the dermatologic work-up before labeling it behavioral.

plain: Newly bought puppy shows fear-aggression toward the owner — what to ask the breeder? Whether it was socialized to people and novel stimuli during 3–12 (14) weeks of age; missed exposure predicts fear and aggression. Not 2–7 weeks — that is the feline window.

plain: Define desensitization, counter-conditioning, response substitution, flooding; which is contraindicated? Desensitization — graded exposure below threshold; counter-conditioning — pairing the stimulus with a positive state (food); response substitution — training an incompatible behavior (sit, not lunge). Flooding (forced full-intensity exposure) and punishment are contraindicated for fear/aggression.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

plain: Dog with generalized anxiety — owner action that worsens it → Punishment or flooding (water spray, shock collar, scolding) increases fear and can provoke aggression; use desensitization/counter-conditioning with anxiolytics as needed.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

— an aversive is added to decrease a

plain: Citronella or shock collar to stop barking — which category of modification? Positive punishment — an aversive is added to decrease a behavior (negative punishment removes something desired). Not recommended: risks fear and aggression.

plain: Dog scared by fireworks/storms, hides in bathtub for two years — best advice → Let it use and improve the safe haven (bedding, white noise, closed curtains), stay calmly present — comforting does not reinforce fear, never punish; situational anxiolytic 1–2 h before (Sileo, trazodone, alprazolam); off-season desensitization with recordings. First-line distraction: food toys.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

clomipramine for the season if severe. Benzodiazepine effect ~4–6 h.

plain: Long-standing severe thunderstorm phobia — most effective management → Desensitization/counter-conditioning plus medication: event alprazolam 0.02–0.1 mg/kg, trazodone or dexmedetomidine oromucosal gel (Sileo, FDA-approved for noise aversion) 30–60 min before; daily fluoxetine/ clomipramine for the season if severe. Benzodiazepine effect ~4–6 h. Not hydrocodone — an opioid antitussive.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

spans.text: FDA-approved canine behavior drugs and indications →

plain: FDA-approved canine behavior drugs and indications → Fluoxetine (Reconcile) and clomipramine (Clomicalm) — separation anxiety with behavior modification; selegiline (Anipryl) — cognitive dysfunction; dexmedetomidine oromucosal gel (Sileo) — noise aversion. Alprazolam, trazodone, diazepam are extra-label.

plain: Acepromazine: sedation only, not anxiolytic; may worsen noise phobia.

(1–3 mg/kg PO q12h) or fluoxetine with desensitization/
counter-conditioning and a safe place; no punishment; acepromazine is not

plain: Dog fearful when visitors come — long-term pharmacologic aid → Clomipramine (1–3 mg/kg PO q12h) or fluoxetine with desensitization/ counter-conditioning and a safe place; no punishment; acepromazine is not anxiolytic.

chapter: Chapter 11 — Canine — Surgery, Behavior & Husbandry

plain: Most common adverse effects of fluoxetine and amitriptyline → Fluoxetine: decreased appetite, lethargy, vomiting/diarrhea, may lower seizure threshold. Amitriptyline: sedation plus anticholinergic effects — dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, reduced tear production.

Overdue but with documented prior vaccination: same booster + 45 days. (NASPHV compendium) Not 45–90 days — the compendium interval is 45 days.

plain: Same exposure, dog or cat never vaccinated → Euthanasia recommended; if the owner refuses, one rabies vaccine within 96 h + strict 4-month quarantine (6 months for ferrets). Not a 3-dose series + 6 months — the 2016 compendium shortened dog/cat quarantine to 4 months.

chapter: Chapter 12 — Canine — Public Health, Welfare, Communication & Practice Law

plain: Healthy owned dog (any vaccination status) bites a person → Report to local public health/animal control and confine and observe 10 days; do not vaccinate during observation; if signs develop, euthanize and submit for dFA. Applies to dogs, cats and ferrets; strays may be euthanized and tested at once. Not revaccinate during the 10 days — vaccination is withheld.

chapter: Chapter 12 — Canine — Public Health, Welfare, Communication & Practice Law

observed 10 days; the employee seeks medical care and the injury goes in the

plain: Staff member bitten by a patient during a procedure → Report to local animal control/public health (rabies control) as state law requires, dog observed 10 days; the employee seeks medical care and the injury goes in the clinic's OSHA injury log.

plain: How do people acquire Toxocara, and why are fresh feces safe? Ingestion of embryonated eggs from soil/sandboxes contaminated with old feces — eggs need 2–4 weeks to become infective; secondary route is undercooked paratenic-host meat (rabbit, lamb, chicken liver). Nearly all pups are infected transplacentally/transmammary and shed from ~3 weeks.

Yes — by swallowing an infected flea (cysticercoid), not by flea bite or proglottid contact; human disease is uncommon and mild (perianal itch, proglottids). Prevent with year-round flea control + praziquantel. Not hemorrhagic enteritis — dipylidiasis is mild.

plain: Cat with murmur, gallop or arrhythmia → diagnostic test of choice? Echocardiography: diastolic LV wall ≥6 mm, left atrial enlargement, systolic anterior mitral motion (SAM). NT-proBNP screens for occult disease; radiographs show congestion (valentine-shaped biatrial enlargement on VD), not the muscle.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Why HCM produces signs → Concentric hypertrophy → diastolic dysfunction → raised LA pressure (edema, effusion); SAM outflow obstruction (murmur, syncope); ischemia (arrhythmia, sudden death); LA stasis (thromboembolism). Often silent until a murmur or gallop is found incidentally.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Older cat, new murmur, LV hypertrophy on echo — exclude before calling
dehydration give pseudohypertrophy. Commercial diet makes taurine DCM

plain: Older cat, new murmur, LV hypertrophy on echo — exclude before calling it primary HCM? Hyperthyroidism (total T4), systemic hypertension (SBP >160–180), acromegaly (IGF-1 in insulin-resistant diabetics); anemia/ dehydration give pseudohypertrophy. Commercial diet makes taurine DCM unlikely.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Gallop rhythm in a cat → heart sound and work-up? Audible S4 (sometimes S3) = stiff ventricle; always abnormal. Echo, T4 and blood pressure; IGF-1 if a diabetic cat. Not acromegaly first — only with insulin- resistant diabetes.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

Not congenital — hypertrophy develops postnatally, typically 1–

plain: Breeds with a validated heritable HCM mutation → Maine Coon (MYBPC3 A31P) and Ragdoll (MYBPC3 R820W), autosomal dominant, incomplete penetrance; Persian, Sphynx, British Shorthair, Bengal predisposed without a test. Not congenital — hypertrophy develops postnatally, typically 1– 4 years.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: HCM with left atrial enlargement, no CHF (ACVIM stage B2) →
no drug has proven to delay CHF, so atenolol/diltiazem are optional. Monitor
resting respiratory rate, echo/NT-proBNP every 6–12 months.

plain: HCM with left atrial enlargement, no CHF (ACVIM stage B2) → treatment? Clopidogrel 18.75 mg/cat PO q24h to prevent thromboembolism; no drug has proven to delay CHF, so atenolol/diltiazem are optional. Monitor resting respiratory rate, echo/NT-proBNP every 6–12 months.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
