Atenolol (preferred for LVOTO) or diltiazem to
Not verapamil — not used in cats.

plain: HCM with dynamic outflow obstruction → rate-control choice and contraindicated drugs? Atenolol (preferred for LVOTO) or diltiazem to lengthen diastolic filling; digoxin and positive inotropes (incl. pimobendan) worsen obstruction. Not verapamil — not used in cats.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Cat tachycardic (>200 bpm) in the clinic, otherwise normal → next step? Allow 5–10 min acclimation, quiet room, repeat HR/BP later in the visit (average 5–7 readings); stress tachycardia and situational hypertension are expected. Persistent tachycardia with weight loss → T4, echo.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Owner home-monitoring instruction for a cardiac cat →
daily from a distance, watching chest rise for 60 s

plain: Owner home-monitoring instruction for a cardiac cat → Count sleeping/ resting respiratory rate daily from a distance, watching chest rise for 60 s without touching: normal <30/min; sustained >40, open-mouth breathing, or hind-limb pain/weakness → come in immediately.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Known HCM, gallop, open-mouth breathing, cyanosis → emergency
minimal handling, butorphanol sedation, thoracocentesis if effusion, keep
Not diltiazem, enalapril or IV fluids —

plain: Known HCM, gallop, open-mouth breathing, cyanosis → emergency treatment? Oxygen + furosemide 1–2 mg/kg IV/IM repeated to effect, minimal handling, butorphanol sedation, thoracocentesis if effusion, keep warm; radiographs only once stable. Not diltiazem, enalapril or IV fluids — chronic-phase drugs; fluids worsen edema.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat in left-sided CHF with pleural effusion — difference from the dog? In
cats left-sided failure causes pleural effusion
as well as pulmonary edema; in
dogs effusion implies right-sided/biventricular failure. Ultrasound, then

plain: Cat in left-sided CHF with pleural effusion — difference from the dog? In cats left-sided failure causes pleural effusion as well as pulmonary edema; in dogs effusion implies right-sided/biventricular failure. Ultrasound, then therapeutic thoracocentesis before radiographs.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: LA enlarged, ± pimobendan (extralabel; avoid with outflow obstruction), ±
ACE inhibitor; beta-blockers are not started in decompensated failure.

plain: Chronic therapy after feline CHF → Furosemide long term, clopidogrel if LA enlarged, ± pimobendan (extralabel; avoid with outflow obstruction), ± ACE inhibitor; beta-blockers are not started in decompensated failure.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat screaming, acute bilateral hindlimb paralysis, cold pale/cyanotic pads,
absent femoral pulses, firm painful gastrocnemius, murmur/gallop →
from LA thrombus in HCM. Diagnosis is
clinical (pain, pulselessness, pallor, paresis, poikilothermy; no bleeding when a
nail is cut); echo confirms the cardiomyopathy.

plain: Cat screaming, acute bilateral hindlimb paralysis, cold pale/cyanotic pads, absent femoral pulses, firm painful gastrocnemius, murmur/gallop → Aortic (saddle) thromboembolism from LA thrombus in HCM. Diagnosis is clinical (pain, pulselessness, pallor, paresis, poikilothermy; no bleeding when a nail is cut); echo confirms the cardiomyopathy.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat acutely non-weight-bearing on one forelimb, paw cold, no brachial
ATE); most lodge at the aortic trifurcation.

plain: Cat acutely non-weight-bearing on one forelimb, paw cold, no brachial pulse, gallop → Same disease, brachial artery embolus (~10% of feline ATE); most lodge at the aortic trifurcation.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: ATE → treatment priorities and prognosis? Full mu-opioid analgesia first
(fentanyl CRI, methadone), then clopidogrel ± heparin/LMWH or rivaroxaban,

plain: ATE → treatment priorities and prognosis? Full mu-opioid analgesia first (fentanyl CRI, methadone), then clopidogrel ± heparin/LMWH or rivaroxaban, treat CHF, no aggressive fluids, no thrombolytics or surgery. Monitor K ⁺ (reperfusion hyperkalemia), renal values, CK. ~30–45% survive; worse if bilateral, hypothermic <37 °C, or in CHF.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Preferred long-term antithrombotic after ATE, and why? Clopidogrel
(P2Y12 blockade): FAT CAT trial median recurrence

plain: Preferred long-term antithrombotic after ATE, and why? Clopidogrel 18.75 mg/cat PO q24h (P2Y12 blockade): FAT CAT trial median recurrence 443 vs 192 days with aspirin. Not aspirin — inferior in cats.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Older cat, acute blindness, dilated fixed pupils, retinal hemorrhage/
idiopathic). Vision may return if retinas reattach within days.

plain: Older cat, acute blindness, dilated fixed pupils, retinal hemorrhage/ detachment, SBP >180 → Hypertensive choroidopathy (SBP ≥160 high risk, ≥180 severe), usually from CKD or hyperthyroidism (also aldosteronism, idiopathic). Vision may return if retinas reattach within days.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Hypertensive cat → drug of choice? Amlodipine 0.625–1.25 mg/cat PO
telmisartan or benazepril for proteinuria. Nitroprusside CRI only for
Not ACE inhibitor first — that is the

plain: Hypertensive cat → drug of choice? Amlodipine 0.625–1.25 mg/cat PO q24h (0.125–0.25 mg/kg); target SBP <160, recheck 1–2 weeks; add telmisartan or benazepril for proteinuria. Nitroprusside CRI only for hypertensive encephalopathy in hospital. Not ACE inhibitor first — that is the dog.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Hypertensive CKD cat cannot tolerate amlodipine → alternative?
Not benazepril alone — drops SBP only ~10 mmHg in cats.

plain: Hypertensive CKD cat cannot tolerate amlodipine → alternative? Telmisartan 1.5–2 mg/kg PO q24h (ARB, FDA-approved for feline hypertension). Not benazepril alone — drops SBP only ~10 mmHg in cats.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat on unsupplemented home-cooked or vegetarian diet develops DCM
with taurine 250 mg PO q12h, central retinal degeneration is irreversible. All-
meat diets also cause nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism.

plain: Cat on unsupplemented home-cooked or vegetarian diet develops DCM and hyperreflective retinal lesions → Taurine deficiency; DCM reverses with taurine 250 mg PO q12h, central retinal degeneration is irreversible. All- meat diets also cause nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: ECG of blocked male cat: tall tented T waves, flat/absent P waves, wide
peaked T → prolonged PR/atrial standstill → wide QRS → sine wave/asystole.

plain: ECG of blocked male cat: tall tented T waves, flat/absent P waves, wide QRS, bradycardia → Hyperkalemia (P waves lost at ~7–8 mEq/L); sequence peaked T → prolonged PR/atrial standstill → wide QRS → sine wave/asystole. Tx calcium gluconate 10% 0.5–1 mL/kg slow IV, regular insulin 0.25–0.5 U/ kg + dextrose, fluids, relieve obstruction.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat with cough/vomiting, suspected heartworm → diagnosis and why
with antigen test, echo (double-lined worms) and radiographs (enlarged
tortuous caudal lobar arteries). Cats carry 1–3 worms, often single-sex or
immature, so antigen and microfilaria tests are often negative.

plain: Cat with cough/vomiting, suspected heartworm → diagnosis and why harder than dogs? Combine antibody test (exposure, immature/male worms) with antigen test, echo (double-lined worms) and radiographs (enlarged tortuous caudal lobar arteries). Cats carry 1–3 worms, often single-sex or immature, so antigen and microfilaria tests are often negative.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Heartworm-positive cat with cough → treatment? No adulticide —
preventive, ± doxycycline, monitor; infection often self-limits in 2–4 years;
sudden death from worm death is a risk.

plain: Heartworm-positive cat with cough → treatment? No adulticide — melarsomine is toxic in cats. Prednisolone for respiratory signs, monthly preventive, ± doxycycline, monitor; infection often self-limits in 2–4 years; sudden death from worm death is a risk.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat radiograph with dorsal displacement of the trachea →
(lymphoma — FeLV-associated in young cats; thymoma) or
marked cardiomegaly; aspirate effusion/mass for cytology.

plain: Cat radiograph with dorsal displacement of the trachea → Cranioventral mediastinal mass (lymphoma — FeLV-associated in young cats; thymoma) or marked cardiomegaly; aspirate effusion/mass for cytology.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat with episodic cough, expiratory wheeze, abdominal push; radiographs
show bronchial "doughnuts and tramlines", hyperinflation, flattened
lobe atelectasis and aerophagia. Expiratory effort = lower airway; inspiratory

plain: Cat with episodic cough, expiratory wheeze, abdominal push; radiographs show bronchial "doughnuts and tramlines", hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm → Feline asthma (allergic bronchitis), often with right middle lobe atelectasis and aerophagia. Expiratory effort = lower airway; inspiratory stertor = upper airway.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Suspected asthma → confirmatory sample and what to rule out first? BAL
, Baermann) and heartworm (antibody test — antigen often

plain: Suspected asthma → confirmatory sample and what to rule out first? BAL or transtracheal wash with eosinophils >17–20%; exclude lungworm (Aelurostrongylus, Baermann) and heartworm (antibody test — antigen often negative in cats).

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Asthmatic cat in acute distress → emergency Rx?

plain: Asthmatic cat in acute distress → emergency Rx? Oxygen, minimal handling, terbutaline 0.01 mg/kg SC/IM or inhaled albuterol, dexamethasone SP 0.1–0.5 mg/kg IV/IM.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Chronic asthma → long-term treatment of choice? Glucocorticoids are the
: inhaled fluticasone 110–220 mcg q12h via spacer/mask (AeroKat)
terbutaline) for rescue; theophylline second line; reduce dust/smoke/litter
Not bronchodilators alone — they do not control inflammation.

plain: Chronic asthma → long-term treatment of choice? Glucocorticoids are the mainstay: inhaled fluticasone 110–220 mcg q12h via spacer/mask (AeroKat) or prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day tapering; bronchodilators (albuterol, terbutaline) for rescue; theophylline second line; reduce dust/smoke/litter aerosols. Not bronchodilators alone — they do not control inflammation.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: cause bronchoconstriction; atropine thickens secretions and is not

plain: Drugs contraindicated in feline asthma → Beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol) cause bronchoconstriction; atropine thickens secretions and is not used.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat with fever and cough after anesthesia, vomiting/regurgitation or
megaesophagus; alveolar pattern in the right middle/cranioventral lobes
airway wash first), nebulization/coupage; no corticosteroids or antitussives.

plain: Cat with fever and cough after anesthesia, vomiting/regurgitation or megaesophagus; alveolar pattern in the right middle/cranioventral lobes → Aspiration pneumonia (gravity-dependent lobes). Oxygen, fluids, ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± fluoroquinolone (culture airway wash first), nebulization/coupage; no corticosteroids or antitussives.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat open-mouth breathing with abducted elbows → meaning and first
point-of-care ultrasound; thoracocentesis if effusion, bronchodilator/steroid if
wheezes, furosemide if crackles; radiographs only once stable.

plain: Cat open-mouth breathing with abducted elbows → meaning and first action? Severe distress near arrest. Oxygen, minimal handling, butorphanol, point-of-care ultrasound; thoracocentesis if effusion, bronchodilator/steroid if wheezes, furosemide if crackles; radiographs only once stable.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Dyspneic cat; radiograph shows pleural fissure lines, retracted rounded
lung lobes, obscured cardiac silhouette → next step? Thoracocentesis first
(therapeutic and diagnostic). Fluid sorts chylothorax (TG > serum), FIP

plain: Dyspneic cat; radiograph shows pleural fissure lines, retracted rounded lung lobes, obscured cardiac silhouette → next step? Thoracocentesis first (therapeutic and diagnostic). Fluid sorts chylothorax (TG > serum), FIP (protein >3.5 g/dL), pyothorax (septic neutrophils), CHF (modified transudate), mediastinal lymphoma (young FeLV+), carcinomatosis (older cats).

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: (vessels/nerve run caudal to each rib); ventral third for fluid,
dorsal third for air; pre-oxygenate, 3-way stopcock.

plain: Thoracocentesis site → 7th–9th intercostal space, needle on the cranial border of the rib (vessels/nerve run caudal to each rib); ventral third for fluid, dorsal third for air; pre-oxygenate, 3-way stopcock. Not 5th–7th — risks the heart.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Cat radiograph: lungs retracted with no peripheral vascular markings,
oxygen; chest tube if repeated; tension pneumothorax (mediastinal shift) needs
immediate decompression; surgery for persistent leaks.

plain: Cat radiograph: lungs retracted with no peripheral vascular markings, heart elevated off the sternum → Pneumothorax (trauma most common; spontaneous from asthma/bullae/neoplasia). Dorsal-third thoracocentesis, oxygen; chest tube if repeated; tension pneumothorax (mediastinal shift) needs immediate decompression; surgery for persistent leaks.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: tubes with lavage + ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate ±

plain: Cat pyothorax → organisms and treatment? Oropharyngeal flora from bites/ aspiration: Pasteurella multocida + obligate anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus), Actinomyces/Nocardia. Bilateral chest tubes with lavage + ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate ± fluoroquinolone 4–6 weeks; surgery if no response.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Foul-smelling pleural fluid on thoracocentesis → cause? Anaerobic

plain: Foul-smelling pleural fluid on thoracocentesis → cause? Anaerobic pyothorax (volatile fatty acids). Chyle is odorless. Not Mycoplasma — uncommon and not malodorous.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Milky pleural fluid → confirm chylothorax? Fluid triglyceride > serum
, fluid cholesterol < serum, small lymphocytes predominate.
heartworm, trauma — echo and CT indicated.

plain: Milky pleural fluid → confirm chylothorax? Fluid triglyceride > serum triglyceride, fluid cholesterol < serum, small lymphocytes predominate. Causes: idiopathic (most), cardiomyopathy, mediastinal lymphoma, heartworm, trauma — echo and CT indicated.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Chylothorax → medical and definitive treatment; chronic sequela?

plain: Chylothorax → medical and definitive treatment; chronic sequela? Intermittent drainage, low-fat diet, rutin 50–100 mg/kg PO q8h, ± octreotide; if persistent 2–4 weeks → thoracic duct ligation + subtotal pericardiectomy ± cisterna chyli ablation (~80% success). Sequela: fibrosing pleuritis.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: diaphragmatic line, gas-filled bowel or liver/stomach in the thorax, displaced
heart, organs missing from the abdomen, effusion; ultrasound confirms viscera
crossing; positive-contrast peritoneography if equivocal. Stabilize before

plain: Diaphragmatic hernia after trauma → diagnosis? Radiographs: lost diaphragmatic line, gas-filled bowel or liver/stomach in the thorax, displaced heart, organs missing from the abdomen, effusion; ultrasound confirms viscera crossing; positive-contrast peritoneography if equivocal. Stabilize before repair.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Agents of the feline upper respiratory complex →

plain: Agents of the feline upper respiratory complex → FHV-1 and calicivirus (~90%), Chlamydia felis (conjunctivitis), Bordetella bronchiseptica (cross- infects dogs and cats), Mycoplasma felis. Supportive care; doxycycline for Chlamydia / Mycoplasma / Bordetella; famciclovir for severe FHV-1.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Best radiographic views of the feline nasal cavity →
superimposition; rostrocaudal skyline for frontal sinuses; lateral least useful.

plain: Best radiographic views of the feline nasal cavity → Intraoral (occlusal) DV and open-mouth VD (beam angled 20–30°) remove mandibular superimposition; rostrocaudal skyline for frontal sinuses; lateral least useful. CT is superior.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Young cat (<2–3 yr), inspiratory stertor, nasal discharge, dysphagia, otitis/
head tilt or Horner's; pink pedunculated mass above the soft palate or in
Not external ear canal origin — polyps only extend into

plain: Young cat (<2–3 yr), inspiratory stertor, nasal discharge, dysphagia, otitis/ head tilt or Horner's; pink pedunculated mass above the soft palate or in the horizontal ear canal → Inflammatory nasopharyngeal polyp, arising from middle ear/auditory tube mucosa. Dx: retract soft palate, otoscopy, bulla radiographs/CT. Not external ear canal origin — polyps only extend into it.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Nasopharyngeal polyp → treatment and recurrence? Traction-avulsion
os/ear plus tapering prednisolone (recurrence ~10–15% with steroids, 30–50%
regrowth; transient Horner's syndrome expected; benign, excellent prognosis.

plain: Nasopharyngeal polyp → treatment and recurrence? Traction-avulsion per os/ear plus tapering prednisolone (recurrence ~10–15% with steroids, 30–50% without); ventral bulla osteotomy (<5% recurrence) for bulla involvement or regrowth; transient Horner's syndrome expected; benign, excellent prognosis.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Does a nasopharyngeal polyp cause epistaxis?

plain: Does a nasopharyngeal polyp cause epistaxis? No — it obstructs rather than erodes. Feline epistaxis points to neoplasia (lymphoma, carcinoma), Cryptococcus, trauma, hypertension or coagulopathy.

chapter: Chapter 13 — Feline — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Ear-canal mass by age in cats →
cat → ceruminous gland adenocarcinoma or SCC.

plain: Ear-canal mass by age in cats → Young cat → inflammatory polyp; older cat → ceruminous gland adenocarcinoma or SCC.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Cat regurgitates/dysphagic 1–3 weeks after dry-pilled tablets →
stricture; Dx contrast esophagram/endoscopy; Tx repeated

plain: Cat regurgitates/dysphagic 1–3 weeks after dry-pilled tablets → Doxycycline hyclate (also clindamycin) esophagitis → benign esophageal stricture; Dx contrast esophagram/endoscopy; Tx repeated balloon dilation or bougienage, sucralfate, omeprazole. Prevent: chase every pill with 5–6 mL water or food, or use liquid doxycycline. Cats most at risk (slow esophageal transit).

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Cat regurgitating solids 2 weeks after general anesthesia →
esophagitis stricture; same Dx and dilation treatment (2–4 sessions ±

plain: Cat regurgitating solids 2 weeks after general anesthesia → Reflux- esophagitis stricture; same Dx and dilation treatment (2–4 sessions ± intralesional triamcinolone), slurry diet.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Passive, effortless expulsion of undigested tubular food right after eating
body, vascular ring anomaly in kittens); first test
, then contrast esophagram/fluoroscopy. No prodromal nausea or

plain: Passive, effortless expulsion of undigested tubular food right after eating → Regurgitation = esophageal disease (megaesophagus, stricture, foreign body, vascular ring anomaly in kittens); first test survey thoracic radiographs, then contrast esophagram/fluoroscopy. No prodromal nausea or retching.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Feline esophagram: mild deviation at thoracic inlet, oblique mucosal folds
left of the trachea and returns dorsally at the inlet; the caudal

plain: Feline esophagram: mild deviation at thoracic inlet, oblique mucosal folds in caudal esophagus, no dilation → Normal study; cervical esophagus lies left of the trachea and returns dorsally at the inlet; the caudal herringbone pattern is normal in cats.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Cat with acute vomiting, radiographs show gastric distension without
NPO 12–24 h then bland meals, IV fluids,
(or ondansetron); avoid metoclopramide until obstruction is

plain: Cat with acute vomiting, radiographs show gastric distension without obstruction → NPO 12–24 h then bland meals, IV fluids, maropitant 1 mg/ kg SC/IV q24h (or ondansetron); avoid metoclopramide until obstruction is excluded; no antibiotics.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Persistent vomiting with radiographic gastric wall thickening →
endoscopy/biopsy; check T4, renal values, FeLV/FIV; no empirical steroids
before excluding lymphoma or foreign body.

plain: Persistent vomiting with radiographic gastric wall thickening → Abdominal ultrasound (wall layering, foreign body, mass, pancreatitis) → endoscopy/biopsy; check T4, renal values, FeLV/FIV; no empirical steroids before excluding lymphoma or foreign body.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Repeated bilious vomiting and anorexia, initial diagnostic step →
Minimum database (CBC, chemistry with fPL, T4, urinalysis) plus
; contrast study or ultrasound only after plain films.

plain: Repeated bilious vomiting and anorexia, initial diagnostic step → Minimum database (CBC, chemistry with fPL, T4, urinalysis) plus survey abdominal radiographs; contrast study or ultrasound only after plain films.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Outdoor cat returns dull, vomiting 2 h →
for foreign body, bloodwork; do not induce emesis in a cat already

plain: Outdoor cat returns dull, vomiting 2 h → Toxin history (lilies, ethylene glycol, permethrin), check under tongue, abdominal radiographs ± ultrasound for foreign body, bloodwork; do not induce emesis in a cat already vomiting.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Vomiting dehydrated cat with palpable abdominal mass, owner declines
avoid prokinetics (metoclopramide, cisapride) with possible obstruction.
colloids — treat intravascular/oncotic deficit, not dehydration.

plain: Vomiting dehydrated cat with palpable abdominal mass, owner declines work-up; first step → IV isotonic crystalloids for interstitial dehydration; avoid prokinetics (metoclopramide, cisapride) with possible obstruction. Not colloids — treat intravascular/oncotic deficit, not dehydration.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Longhaired cat intermittently vomiting cylindrical hair masses →
up motility disease if frequent. In rabbits, trichobezoar/gastric stasis is treated
medically (fluids, syringe feeding, prokinetics), surgery last.

plain: Longhaired cat intermittently vomiting cylindrical hair masses → Trichobezoars: grooming, petrolatum lubricant, high-fiber hairball diet; work up motility disease if frequent. In rabbits, trichobezoar/gastric stasis is treated medically (fluids, syringe feeding, prokinetics), surgery last.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids

spans.text: Fluctuant, non-painful sublingual or cervical swelling in a cat; aspirate
Sialocele: viscous, stringy, clear to blood-tinged
low cellularity, PAS-positive; Tx excise mandibular + sublingual gland

plain: Fluctuant, non-painful sublingual or cervical swelling in a cat; aspirate contents → Sialocele: viscous, stringy, clear to blood-tinged mucoid saliva, low cellularity, PAS-positive; Tx excise mandibular + sublingual gland complex, marsupialize a ranula.

chapter: Chapter 14 — Feline — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Dental & Nutrition/Fluids
section: Linear and discrete foreign bodies, intussusception

exam step: lift the tongue for string around the
pylorus). Little bowel dilation, unlike discrete obstruction.

plain: Vomiting cat; radiograph shows centrally bunched, plicated small intestine with eccentric comma/teardrop gas bubbles → Linear foreign body; first exam step: lift the tongue for string around the frenulum (or anchored at pylorus). Little bowel dilation, unlike discrete obstruction.

spans.text: String found looped under the tongue; correct action →

plain: Cat recovering from URI develops crusting ulcers on nasal planum/face; biopsy: eosinophilic dermatitis with intranuclear inclusions → FHV-1 ulcerative dermatitis (stress reactivation). In cats, generalized Malassezia flags underlying disease: allergy, FIV, diabetes, thymoma exfoliative dermatitis, pancreatic paraneoplastic alopecia; Devon Rex/Sphynx predisposed. plain: Anemic cat; smear shows tiny cocci, rings or chains on the RBC surface (epicellular) → Mycoplasma haemofelis (feline infectious anemia, formerly Haemobartonella); extravascular immune-mediated hemolysis, often Coombs- positive. Cannot be cultured; organisms cycle and detach in EDTA, so PCR is the test of choice. Test FeLV/FIV. Not Mycoplasma felis — a conjunctival/ respiratory mycoplasma.

plain: Treatment of Mycoplasma haemofelis? Doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 2–4 weeks (give with water/food — esophageal stricture risk) or pradofloxacin/marbofloxacin; prednisolone only if an immune-mediated component (autoagglutination, Coombs-positive); transfuse if PCV <12–15%. Carriers persist after treatment.

plain: How is Mycoplasma haemofelis transmitted? Fleas (Ctenocephalides felis), also bite wounds/fighting, blood transfusion and transplacentally; outdoor intact males over-represented. Flea control is part of prevention.

plain: Mycoplasma haemofelis vs Cytauxzoon felis on a feline smear → M. haemofelis: epicellular cocci/rings on the RBC surface, regenerative anemia, doxycycline-responsive. Cytauxzoon: 1–2 µm signet-ring piroplasms inside RBCs plus schizont-laden macrophages in buffy coat/tissue, high fever, icterus, rapid death.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: South-central/southeastern US cat with fever, icterus, pancytopenia; intraerythrocytic signet-ring piroplasms → Cytauxzoon felis: Amblyomma americanum (lone star tick) vector, bobcat reservoir; schizont-filled macrophages occlude vessels. Atovaquone 15 mg/kg q8h + azithromycin 10 mg/kg q24h for 10 days plus supportive care (~60% survival vs <25% untreated); tick control prevents.

plain: Cat with anemia and numerous Heinz bodies → causes and treatment? Oxidative injury: acetaminophen (also methemoglobinemia; antidote N- acetylcysteine), onion/garlic, zinc, propylene glycol, methylene blue. Remove source, supportive care, transfuse if severe. Feline hemoglobin's eight sulfhydryl groups and non-sinusoidal spleen make cats uniquely susceptible; a few Heinz bodies are normal.

plain: Excited, struggling cat at venipuncture → expected leukogram? Physiologic (epinephrine) leukocytosis: mature neutrophilia with lymphocytosis (lymphocytes may exceed neutrophils in cats), no left shift, no eosinopenia; resolves within 30 min. Stress leukogram instead: neutrophilia, lymphopenia, eosinopenia, monocytosis.

plain: Classic hematologic finding in feline panleukopenia → Severe leukopenia/ neutropenia (often <2,000 WBC/µL) with lymphopenia; parvovirus destroys dividing marrow and crypt cells. Canine fecal parvo antigen tests cross-react.

plain: Firm subcutaneous mass at a cat's vaccination site; when to biopsy and how? 3-2-1 rule: biopsy if present >3 months, >2 cm, or still growing 1 month after injection. Use incisional (wedge/Tru-cut) biopsy, tract planned for later removal; FNA and excisional biopsy are inadequate.

plain: Confirmed feline injection-site sarcoma → treatment? CT/MRI for planning, then radical excision with 3–5 cm lateral margins and two fascial planes deep (often amputation or body-wall resection) by a surgical oncologist, plus pre- or post-op radiation ± doxorubicin. Not 2 cm margins — marginal excision recurs in most cats.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Metastatic behavior and staging of injection-site sarcoma? Locally invasive along fascial planes; metastasis low-to-moderate (10–25%), to lungs, late in the course; regional nodes uncommon. Stage with three-view thoracic radiographs or CT before radical surgery.

plain: Most serious vaccine-related complication in cats and how to reduce it? Injection-site sarcoma, ~1 in 10,000–30,000 doses, mostly adjuvanted FeLV/ rabies. AAFP sites: rabies distal right hindlimb, FeLV distal left hindlimb, FVRCP distal right forelimb (or tail), never interscapular, so amputation can be curative; prefer non-adjuvanted vaccines; report to manufacturer and USDA CVB.

plain: White or light-colored cat with crusted, erosive lesions on pinnal tips, nasal planum or eyelids → Cutaneous (actinic) SCC, UV-induced p53 damage in unpigmented sparsely haired skin via actinic keratosis; most common feline pinnal tumor. Biopsy; pinnectomy curative for pinnae; nosectomy, strontium-90, radiation, cryotherapy or photodynamic therapy for superficial lesions; UV avoidance.

plain: Old cat with ulcerated proliferative sublingual or mandibular mass, drooling, halitosis, loose teeth → Oral SCC, the most common feline oral tumor (60–70%); invades bone early, metastasizes late; MST 1–3 months with palliation, <10% alive at 1 year. Risk factors: tobacco smoke, flea collars, canned food. Fibrosarcoma is second.

plain: Cat missing two upper teeth; sockets abscessed, radiographs show bone lysis → next step? Biopsy/cytology before any definitive surgery — maxillary bone lysis with tooth loss is oral SCC until proven otherwise; culture if infection suspected. Treatment then follows histology (maxillectomy/ radiation vs extraction and debridement).

plain: Localized mandibular SCC with bone lysis confirmed on biopsy: extraction or mandibulectomy? Rostral/hemi-mandibulectomy with margins ± radiation — extraction alone is inadequate because bone is already invaded; small rostral lesions not crossing midline do best (up to ~1 year). Most cats present too advanced and receive palliation.

plain: Cat with a swollen, painful digit and nail loss; biopsy shows SCC → where to look next? Thoracic radiographs — digital SCC in cats is usually a metastasis from a primary pulmonary carcinoma (lung–digit syndrome) seeded by arterial spread; prognosis grave (weeks).

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Firm mammary mass in a cat → most important thing to tell the owner? 85–90% of feline mammary tumors are malignant (adenocarcinoma), vs ~50% in dogs; treat with radical (chain) mastectomy.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

unilateral or staged bilateral radical chain mastectomy

OHE at surgery does not improve survival once tumors exist; adjuvant

plain: Intact 10-year-old queen with multiple mammary masses; options OHE, mastectomy, chemotherapy → next step? Stage (thoracic radiographs, node cytology), then unilateral or staged bilateral radical chain mastectomy — en-bloc removal beats lumpectomy because spread follows chain lymphatics. OHE at surgery does not improve survival once tumors exist; adjuvant doxorubicin for tumors >3 cm or node-positive.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Most important prognostic factor after mastectomy for feline mammary

plain: Most important prognostic factor after mastectomy for feline mammary carcinoma? Tumor size: <2 cm, median survival >3 years; 2–3 cm, ~1–2 years; >3 cm, 4–6 months. Spaying before 6 months cuts risk ~91%. Not sex — size predicts survival.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: 9-year-old intact queen, kittens weaned 6 months ago, firm ulcerated
ulcerated/fixed mass. Mastitis fits a lactating queen; fibroepithelial hyperplasia
fits a young cycling or progestin-treated cat.

plain: 9-year-old intact queen, kittens weaned 6 months ago, firm ulcerated mammary mass → Mammary carcinoma — older intact, non-lactating, ulcerated/fixed mass. Mastitis fits a lactating queen; fibroepithelial hyperplasia fits a young cycling or progestin-treated cat. Not mastitis — no lactation for months.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Senior cat, chronic weight loss and vomiting, thickened intestinal muscularis; biopsy shows small-cell (lymphocytic) lymphoma → treatment? Chlorambucil 2 mg/cat PO q48–72h (or 20 mg/m² q2wk) plus prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day; 70–90% remission, median survival 2–3 years. Monitor CBC q2–4 weeks; supplement cobalamin; separate from IBD by immunohistochemistry/PARR clonality.

plain: Large-cell/intermediate-high-grade feline lymphoma (mediastinal, multicentric, large-cell GI) → treatment and prognosis? Multi-agent COP or CHOP (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, prednisolone ± doxorubicin 25 mg/ m²); ~50–70% remission, median 6–9 months. Nasal lymphoma: radiation, best prognosis (MST 1.5–3 years).

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Key prognostic factors in feline lymphoma? Response to induction, FeLV status (negative better), anatomic form (nasal best; mediastinal in young FeLV-positive cats worst) and histologic grade. Most current cases are FeLV- negative alimentary lymphoma in older cats.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

Chlorambucil for small-cell GI lymphoma; cyclophosphamide/

plain: Feline lymphoma on prednisolone; which drug is added, and its notable toxicity? Chlorambucil for small-cell GI lymphoma; cyclophosphamide/ vincristine ± doxorubicin for high-grade. Cyclophosphamide → sterile hemorrhagic cystitis (mainly dogs; morning dosing, furosemide); doxorubicin is nephrotoxic in cats, cardiotoxic in dogs.

plain: Young FeLV-positive cat, dyspnea, non-compressible cranial thorax, pleural effusion; radiograph: cranial mediastinal mass → Mediastinal (thymic) lymphoma, T-cell, Siamese/Oriental predisposed. Dx by effusion or FNA cytology (monomorphic lymphoblasts); treat with COP/CHOP, not surgery; FeLV-positive worsens prognosis.

plain: Cat radiograph: trachea elevated dorsally, heart displaced caudally, cranial thoracic soft-tissue opacity ± effusion → differentials? Cranial mediastinal mass: lymphoma (young, FeLV-positive) vs thymoma (older cats, paraneoplastic myasthenia gravis or exfoliative dermatitis; treated by excision); less often cranial lung lobe mass, abscess, cyst. Ultrasound-guided FNA distinguishes.

plain: Cat with a solitary cutaneous mast cell tumor on the head → treatment and prognosis? Surgical excision; wide margins are less critical than in dogs — most feline cutaneous MCTs are well-differentiated and benign, cured by excision. Atypical/histiocytic MCTs in young Siamese may regress spontaneously. Check the spleen.

plain: Older cat with vomiting, anorexia, splenomegaly; splenic aspirate shows sheets of mast cells → treatment? Splenectomy, even with mastocythemia or marrow involvement; pretreat with H1/H2 blockers; median survival ~12– 19 months. Lomustine or a TKI if systemic. Spleen is the most common feline visceral MCT site.

plain: Mast cells on a cat's peripheral blood smear → most likely cause? Mast cell tumor (visceral/splenic or disseminated) — cats rarely release mast cells except from neoplasia; buffy-coat smear screens. In dogs, mastocythemia more often reflects inflammation (parvovirus, pancreatitis, regenerative anemia) than MCT.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

plain: Most common splenic tumor of the cat and its characteristic complication? Mast cell tumor; histamine release causes gastroduodenal ulceration, vomiting and anorexia — give H2 blockers/PPI. Dog: hemangiosarcoma; horse: lymphosarcoma.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

Not MCT in cats — second, and

plain: Most common skin tumor of cats vs most common malignant skin tumor of dogs → Cats: basal cell tumor (pigmented, well-circumscribed dome on head/neck/ear, >90% benign, excision curative), then MCT, SCC, fibrosarcoma. Dogs: mast cell tumor (~20%). Not MCT in cats — second, and usually benign.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spindle (mesenchymal) cells and needs 3–5 cm margins.

plain: Cat with a 1 cm dermal mass; cytology shows cohesive clusters of small uniform epithelial cells → Basal cell tumor — cohesive clusters mean epithelial origin. Fibrosarcoma/injection-site sarcoma exfoliates individual spindle (mesenchymal) cells and needs 3–5 cm margins.

plain: Older cat, hindlimb lameness; aggressive lytic/proliferative lesion of distal femur or proximal tibia → Dx, prognosis? Appendicular osteosarcoma; confirm by biopsy (differentials fibrosarcoma, SCC, osteomyelitis, injection- site sarcoma at a vaccine site). Amputation alone is often curative (metastasis ~5–10% at diagnosis vs ~90% in dogs); median survival >2–4 years; chemotherapy adds little. Axial OSA recurs locally and does worse.

plain: Feline osteosarcoma amputated, then lung metastases documented 3 months later → prognosis? Poor — survival after documented metastasis is weeks to a few months; palliative care. When feline OSA does spread, it goes to the lungs.

plain: Progressive iris hyperpigmentation, pupil distortion, rising IOP in a cat → Diffuse iris melanoma, the most common feline primary intraocular tumor; metastasizes late to liver/lungs. Enucleate once the iris thickens or glaucoma develops; stage with thoracic radiographs. In dogs anterior uveal and limbal melanomas are usually benign; feline pinnal/dermal melanoma needs wide excision with node check.

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Most common primary intracranial tumor in cats →
axial, dural-based, contrast-enhancing, often multiple in cats; surgically

plain: Most common primary intracranial tumor in cats → Meningioma: extra- axial, dural-based, contrast-enhancing, often multiple in cats; surgically resectable with MST >2 years. Dogs: meningioma ~45%, gliomas second (brachycephalics).

chapter: Chapter 17 — Feline — Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Cat radiograph: pleural effusion (fissure lines, scalloped retracted lungs,
obscured heart) with multiple pulmonary nodules → Dx and first step?
Metastatic neoplasia (eg mammary carcinoma) or primary lung carcinoma with
fluid for cytology and unmasks the lung pattern; re-radiograph after drainage.

plain: Cat radiograph: pleural effusion (fissure lines, scalloped retracted lungs, obscured heart) with multiple pulmonary nodules → Dx and first step? Metastatic neoplasia (eg mammary carcinoma) or primary lung carcinoma with malignant effusion. Thoracocentesis first — stabilizes breathing, provides fluid for cytology and unmasks the lung pattern; re-radiograph after drainage.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Unvaccinated kitten, vomiting, hemorrhagic diarrhea, fever then
destroys dividing crypt epithelium (villous atrophy) and marrow precursors.

plain: Unvaccinated kitten, vomiting, hemorrhagic diarrhea, fever then hypothermia, dehydration, WBC 500–3,000/µL → Feline panleukopenia (feline parvovirus). Profound neutropenia/leukopenia is the hallmark; virus destroys dividing crypt epithelium (villous atrophy) and marrow precursors.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: In-clinic confirmation of panleukopenia? Canine parvovirus fecal antigen
with FPV: high specificity, moderate sensitivity (shedding
is brief, a negative does not exclude); recent MLV vaccine (5–12 days) can
give a weak false positive. PCR available.

plain: In-clinic confirmation of panleukopenia? Canine parvovirus fecal antigen SNAP cross-reacts with FPV: high specificity, moderate sensitivity (shedding is brief, a negative does not exclude); recent MLV vaccine (5–12 days) can give a weak false positive. PCR available.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Treatment of a panleukopenic kitten → Supportive: IV crystalloids with dextrose/potassium, maropitant, broad-spectrum antibiotics for neutropenic sepsis (ampicillin ± amikacin/enrofloxacin), early enteral nutrition, plasma/ whole blood if needed, strict isolation. Survival improves once WBC rebounds.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

queen); virus destroys the cerebellar external germinal layer. Fixed lesion —

plain: Kitten with non-progressive intention tremor, hypermetria, wide-based stance since it began walking; otherwise bright → Cerebellar hypoplasia from in-utero/perinatal FPV infection (or MLV vaccine given to a pregnant queen); virus destroys the cerebellar external germinal layer. Fixed lesion — neither worsens nor improves; good quality of life.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology
plain: Prevention of panleukopenia → Core MLV FVRCP from 6–8 weeks; never MLV in pregnant queens or kittens <4 weeks (cerebellar hypoplasia).

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Disinfectant for a surface or ward contaminated by feline parvovirus →
surface; also potassium peroxymonosulfate (Virkon S), accelerated hydrogen

plain: Disinfectant for a surface or ward contaminated by feline parvovirus → Sodium hypochlorite 1:32 (≈1,560 ppm), 10 min contact on a precleaned surface; also potassium peroxymonosulfate (Virkon S), accelerated hydrogen peroxide, formaldehyde/glutaraldehyde. Quaternary ammoniums, chlorhexidine, alcohol, phenolics fail. Not "phenolic" — bleach is a hypochlorite; phenolics are unreliable parvocides.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: How long does feline parvovirus persist in the environment? Months to >1
at room temperature (non-enveloped; survives freezing). Disinfect

plain: How long does feline parvovirus persist in the environment? Months to >1 year at room temperature (non-enveloped; survives freezing). Disinfect thoroughly before introducing unvaccinated kittens.

plain: Kitten with sneezing, ocular/nasal discharge, conjunctivitis, keratitis and a branching corneal ulcer → Feline herpesvirus-1 (rhinotracheitis); dendritic corneal ulcers are pathognomonic. Ocular involvement favors FHV-1; lingual ulcers favor calicivirus; Chlamydia gives chemosis only.

plain: Most sensitive confirmatory test for FHV-1? PCR on conjunctival/ oropharyngeal swabs (positive also in carriers and after MLV vaccine); IFA on conjunctival scrapings is less sensitive.

plain: Cat treated a month ago for FHV-1 dendritic ulcer, now clinically normal — state of infection? Latent in the trigeminal ganglion for life; stress or corticosteroids reactivate shedding. Not eliminated.

plain: Cat with ulcers on tongue/palate, sneezing, nasal discharge, shifting lameness ("limping kitten") → Feline calicivirus; oral ulceration and transient synovitis are its hallmarks. Persistent shedders develop chronic gingivostomatitis (test FIV too). Not FIV — kitten URI with oral ulcers is calicivirus first.

plain: Intranasal FIP vaccine — mechanism and status? Temperature-sensitive mutant FCoV replicating only in the cool upper airway → local secretory IgA and cell-mediated immunity; efficacy questionable, not recommended by AAFP.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: What does the in-clinic FeLV/FIV SNAP detect? FeLV: p27 core antigen (positive within ~30 days of infection); FIV: antibody (positive ~60 days post- infection). Vaccination does not cause FeLV false positives.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Why do progressively infected FeLV cats die, and are regressive cats
Progressive = lifelong viremia → death within ~3 years from

plain: Why do progressively infected FeLV cats die, and are regressive cats carriers? Progressive = lifelong viremia → death within ~3 years from lymphoma (mediastinal/multicentric), nonregenerative anemia/ myelosuppression, or opportunistic infection. Regressive cats hold provirus only and rarely shed.

plain: FeLV subgroups? A — the only naturally transmitted form, in every infected cat; B — recombinant with endogenous FeLV, lymphoma; C — pure red cell aplasia/non-regenerative anemia; T — T-cell depletion, immunodeficiency.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

(mutual grooming, shared bowls), bites, in utero
and milk; kittens most susceptible, age resistance by ~4–6 months. Test before

plain: How is FeLV transmitted and who is most susceptible? Saliva via prolonged friendly contact (mutual grooming, shared bowls), bites, in utero and milk; kittens most susceptible, age resistance by ~4–6 months. Test before vaccinating.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: FeLV-positive stray to join a household with other cats → Confirm (IFA/ PCR, retest 4–6 weeks); keep the positive cat separate; test residents and vaccinate negatives (two doses 3–4 weeks apart). Vaccination of an infected cat has no benefit. Not "vaccinate all" — vaccine protection is incomplete.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Owner's cat died of FeLV; how long before a new cat? No prolonged wait — enveloped retrovirus survives only minutes to hours and dies with any detergent; clean bowls and bedding, wait a few days, test and vaccinate the newcomer.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Which feline virus is hardest to transmit? FIV
inoculation of saliva; casual contact and shared bowls rarely transmit. FeLV
needs prolonged intimate contact; FPV and FCV spread readily and persist in

plain: Which feline virus is hardest to transmit? FIV — needs deep bite inoculation of saliva; casual contact and shared bowls rarely transmit. FeLV needs prolonged intimate contact; FPV and FCV spread readily and persist in the environment.

plain: Healthy adult cat FIV antibody-positive on in-clinic ELISA → Confirm with Western blot, IFA or PCR (false positives in low-prevalence cats; prior FIV vaccination gives antibody — Anigen/Witness are more specific than SNAP/VetScan in vaccinated cats). Then indoors, neuter, twice-yearly exams, no raw diets; no euthanasia.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Kitten under 6 months FIV antibody-positive, healthy → Maternal antibody — retest after 6 months of age; PCR can be used earlier. Not a rule for FIP — the retest rule is FIV only.

plain: Antiviral for FIV cats with stomatitis or neurologic signs → Zidovudine (AZT) 5–10 mg/kg PO/SC q12h; monitor CBC, stop if PCV <20% (nucleoside RT inhibitor, marrow-toxic). Otherwise supportive; feline interferon-omega alternative.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Drug to avoid in an FIV-positive cat with dermatophytosis → Griseofulvin — idiosyncratic severe neutropenia in retrovirus-positive cats; also teratogenic. Use itraconazole.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Core vaccines for all cats → FHV-1, calicivirus, panleukopenia (FVRCP) plus rabies where law or AAFP/AAHA require; FeLV core for kittens under 1 year. Chlamydia, Bordetella and FIP are non-core.

plain: Cat-fight abscess; smear shows small gram-negative bipolar coccobacilli → Pasteurella multocida (normal oral flora, with anaerobes). Lance, flush; amoxicillin-clavulanate DOC (penicillin/ampicillin, cefovecin alternatives); retest FeLV/FIV after 60 days. Not cephalexin, clindamycin, erythromycin or metronidazole — poor or no Pasteurella activity.

plain: Cat from southwestern US with fever and submandibular abscess; bipolar "safety-pin" gram-negative rods → Yersinia pestis (bubonic plague, from rodents/fleas). Gentamicin, doxycycline or enrofloxacin 10–21 days; penicillins ineffective. Isolate, flea control, masks/gloves (pneumonic zoonosis), report to public health. Pasteurella also stains bipolar.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Chronic draining tracts; branching filamentous rods, partially acid-fast →
Mycobacteria (feline leprosy, rapid growers in inguinal fat): strongly acid-fast,

plain: Chronic draining tracts; branching filamentous rods, partially acid-fast → Nocardia → trimethoprim-sulfonamide 1–3 months plus drainage. Actinomyces: branching, not acid-fast, sulfur granules → penicillin. Mycobacteria (feline leprosy, rapid growers in inguinal fat): strongly acid-fast, non-branching → fluoroquinolone/clarithromycin/doxycycline, surgery. Test FIV/FeLV.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Cat with regenerative hemolytic anemia, macroscopic autoagglutination, small epicellular cocci/rings on RBCs seen intermittently → Mycoplasma haemofelis (feline infectious anemia; fleas, bites, transfusion). PCR is the test of choice — uncultivable, parasitemia cycles so smears miss it. Immune- mediated extravascular hemolysis.

plain: Treatment of Mycoplasma haemofelis → Doxycycline 10 mg/kg PO q24h (or 5 mg/kg q12h) for 2–4 weeks with water/food (esophageal stricture), or pradofloxacin/marbofloxacin; transfuse if PCV <12–15%; glucocorticoids only for persistent immune-mediated hemolysis. Test FeLV/FIV; carriers persist. Not steroids first-line.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Fever, gingival petechiae, thrombocytopenia, hyperglobulinemia after brown dog tick (in dogs) → Ehrlichia canis (monocytic; pancytopenia when chronic) → doxycycline 10 mg/kg q24h for 28 days. Anaplasma platys causes cyclic thrombocytopenia.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Outdoor cat with firm swelling over the nasal bridge ("Roman nose"), chronic nasal discharge, nasal bone lysis, skin nodules ± neurologic signs, pigeon-dropping exposure → Cryptococcosis (C. neoformans; C. gattii with eucalyptus/Pacific Northwest) — most common systemic mycosis of cats. Not contagious to people or other animals.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Cytology: 5–15 µm round yeast with thick clear non-staining capsule and
Not Streptococcus — it is a yeast.

plain: Cytology: 5–15 µm round yeast with thick clear non-staining capsule and narrow-based budding → Cryptococcus (India ink/Diff-Quik halo). Blastomyces: 8–15 µm, thick wall, broad-based bud; Histoplasma: 2–4 µm intracellular. Confirm with serum latex cryptococcal antigen (sensitivity >90%). Not Streptococcus — it is a yeast.

plain: Treatment and endpoint for cryptococcosis → Fluconazole 50 mg/cat PO q12h (or itraconazole) for months, until latex antigen titer is repeatedly negative; amphotericin B ± flucytosine for CNS/disseminated disease (especially dogs); debulk granulomas. Prognosis good for nasal form, guarded with CNS.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Pigeon droppings are the classic source of which agent?
. Bird/bat guano in soil also harbors

plain: Pigeon droppings are the classic source of which agent? Cryptococcus neoformans. Bird/bat guano in soil also harbors Histoplasma; pigeons carry Chlamydia psittaci and Trichomonas gallinae (raptors).

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Outdoor cat (rose garden, fights) with ulcerated, crusted, draining nodules
on head, distal limbs, tail base following lymphatics, regional
pseudotuberculosis — enteric/hepatosplenic granulomas, not skin nodules.

plain: Outdoor cat (rose garden, fights) with ulcerated, crusted, draining nodules on head, distal limbs, tail base following lymphatics, regional lymphadenopathy, antibiotic-unresponsive → Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii/brasiliensis, dimorphic, inoculated by thorns/scratches). DDx Nocardia, mycobacterial panniculitis, Cryptococcus. Not Yersinia pseudotuberculosis — enteric/hepatosplenic granulomas, not skin nodules.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Cytology of feline nodule exudate: numerous cigar-shaped 3–10 µm yeasts
(unlike dogs/horses) so exudate, scratches and bites infect handlers

plain: Cytology of feline nodule exudate: numerous cigar-shaped 3–10 µm yeasts inside macrophages; zoonotic risk? Sporothrix — cats shed huge organism loads (unlike dogs/horses) so exudate, scratches and bites infect handlers directly: wear gloves, wash hands.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Treatment of feline sporotrichosis → Itraconazole 5–10 mg/kg PO q24h, continued ≥1 month beyond clinical cure (typically 3–6 months); terbinafine alternative; avoid steroids. Potassium iodide (SSKI) suits dogs but cats are iodide-sensitive.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

shows 2–4 µm round yeasts with thin halo inside macrophages →

plain: Cat with fever, weight loss, dyspnea, anemia; marrow/lymph node smear shows 2–4 µm round yeasts with thin halo inside macrophages → Disseminated histoplasmosis (Mississippi–Ohio valleys, bird/bat guano). Dx cytology or urine Histoplasma antigen EIA; itraconazole 10 mg/kg/day for 4– 6+ months, amphotericin B if severe; fluconazole less effective.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Kitten with patchy alopecia, scaling, crusting, broken hairs on face, ears, forelimbs → Microsporum canis (>90% of feline dermatophytosis). Wood's lamp fluoresces only ~50% of M. canis (negative does not exclude); DTM culture or PCR confirms. Itraconazole 5 mg/kg or griseofulvin with a fatty meal (teratogenic; myelosuppressive in FIV+); lime sulfur dips. Not "M. caninum"; Wood's lamp is used in cats.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Outdoor cat, south-central/southeastern US (Oklahoma, Arkansas, Louisiana), acute 106°F fever, icterus, dyspnea, pancytopenia; signet-ring piroplasms in RBCs, schizont-laden macrophages → Cytauxzoonosis (Cytauxzoon felis); vector Amblyomma americanum (lone star tick; also Dermacentor variabilis), bobcat reservoir. Dogs are not a source. Confirm PCR.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Which Cytauxzoon stage is transmitted and which kills? Sporozoites
venules of lung, liver, spleen → DIC, multi-organ failure. Erythrocytic
piroplasms appear late and are minor.

plain: Which Cytauxzoon stage is transmitted and which kills? Sporozoites in tick saliva infect the cat; schizonts in macrophages (tissue phase) occlude venules of lung, liver, spleen → DIC, multi-organ failure. Erythrocytic piroplasms appear late and are minor. Not schizont as infective stage.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: azithromycin 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 10 days
100% dead within a week. Survivors are carriers; prevent with isoxazoline

plain: Treatment of cytauxzoonosis → Atovaquone 15 mg/kg PO q8h + azithromycin 10 mg/kg PO q24h for 10 days plus fluids, heparin, transfusion, minimal handling: ~60% survive; imidocarb ~25%, untreated near 100% dead within a week. Survivors are carriers; prevent with isoxazoline acaricides, indoor housing. Not imidocarb — used for Hepatozoon/Babesia.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: DOC for clinical toxoplasmosis in cats and dogs; key public-health fact →
Clindamycin 10–12.5 mg/kg PO q12h for 4 weeks
undercooked meat is the main human source.

plain: DOC for clinical toxoplasmosis in cats and dogs; key public-health fact → Clindamycin 10–12.5 mg/kg PO q12h for 4 weeks (alternatives TMS, azithromycin). Cats shed oocysts once, for 1–3 weeks after first infection; oocysts sporulate in 1–5 days, so daily litter removal prevents exposure; undercooked meat is the main human source.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Fecal panel positive for Toxoplasma oocysts plus enteric coronavirus →
Toxoplasma with clindamycin (reduces shedding); no antiviral
for enteric coronavirus. Litter hygiene counseling.

plain: Fecal panel positive for Toxoplasma oocysts plus enteric coronavirus → treat which? Toxoplasma with clindamycin (reduces shedding); no antiviral for enteric coronavirus. Litter hygiene counseling.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Young cattery/pedigree cat with chronic malodorous large-bowel diarrhea,
mucus, fresh blood, fecal incontinence, metronidazole-unresponsive; pear-

plain: Young cattery/pedigree cat with chronic malodorous large-bowel diarrhea, mucus, fresh blood, fecal incontinence, metronidazole-unresponsive; pear- shaped flagellate with undulating membrane and jerky forward motion → Tritrichomonas foetus (T. blagburni). Dx fresh saline smear, InPouch TF culture or fecal PCR (most sensitive); no cyst stage, so flotation misses it. Giardia instead moves like a falling leaf.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Treatment of Tritrichomonas and its main adverse effect →
usually reversible. Metronidazole and fenbendazole ineffective; many self-

plain: Treatment of Tritrichomonas and its main adverse effect → Ronidazole 30 mg/kg PO q24h for 14 days (extralabel, compounded, handle with gloves); dose-dependent neurotoxicity (ataxia, tremors, seizures) — stop the drug, usually reversible. Metronidazole and fenbendazole ineffective; many self- resolve by ~2 years but stay carriers.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Cat with mucoid/bloody diarrhea or steatorrhea; piriform flagellates with
metronidazole 25 mg/kg BID 5–7 days; bathe to remove cysts.

plain: Cat with mucoid/bloody diarrhea or steatorrhea; piriform flagellates with falling-leaf motion → Giardia duodenalis (cysts on zinc sulfate float, fecal antigen ELISA). Fenbendazole 50 mg/kg PO q24h 3–5 days or metronidazole 25 mg/kg BID 5–7 days; bathe to remove cysts.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Kitten with diarrhea and Cystoisospora (Isospora) oocysts on float →
Sulfadimethoxine 50–60 mg/kg PO q24h for 5–20 days
ponazuril/toltrazuril extralabel; sanitation, oocysts sporulate in 1–2 days.
Coccidioides — a dimorphic fungus (Valley fever) treated with azoles for

plain: Kitten with diarrhea and Cystoisospora (Isospora) oocysts on float → Sulfadimethoxine 50–60 mg/kg PO q24h for 5–20 days (labeled) or ponazuril/toltrazuril extralabel; sanitation, oocysts sporulate in 1–2 days. Not Coccidioides — a dimorphic fungus (Valley fever) treated with azoles for months.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Which enteric protozoan is typically missed on routine fecal flotation in
centrifugation at high power, acid-fast stain, IFA, antigen or PCR. Giardia
floats with zinc sulfate; Cystoisospora and Besnoitia oocysts are large.

plain: Which enteric protozoan is typically missed on routine fecal flotation in cats? Cryptosporidium — oocysts 4–6 µm and few; needs Sheather's sugar centrifugation at high power, acid-fast stain, IFA, antigen or PCR. Giardia floats with zinc sulfate; Cystoisospora and Besnoitia oocysts are large.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Kitten fecal float: spherical 65–75 µm egg, thick pitted shell, single dark
ocular larva migrans. Pyrantel 20 mg/kg or fenbendazole; deworm from 3

plain: Kitten fecal float: spherical 65–75 µm egg, thick pitted shell, single dark cell → Toxocara cati; transmammary (not transplacental, unlike T. canis) and paratenic-host transmission; T. canis egg 85–90 µm. Zoonotic visceral/ ocular larva migrans. Pyrantel 20 mg/kg or fenbendazole; deworm from 3 weeks, every 2 weeks.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Owner sees a worm in the feces but flotation is negative; options

plain: Owner sees a worm in the feces but flotation is negative; options Ancylostoma vs Toxocara → Toxocara cati — large adults are visible and may pass before patency; Ancylostoma tubaeforme is tiny. Rice-grain segments instead → Dipylidium caninum (also flotation-negative).

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

spans.text: Hunting cat passing large single-pored tapeworm segments, no fleas →

plain: Hunting cat passing large single-pored tapeworm segments, no fleas → Taenia taeniaeformis from rodents carrying the strobilocercus (Cysticercus fasciolaris) in the liver; thick radially striated taeniid eggs. Praziquantel or fenbendazole; stop hunting. Fleas → Dipylidium.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

Snails/slugs are the intermediate host; rodents,
Adults in terminal bronchioles; Baermann beats

plain: Coughing cat; Baermann yields L1 larvae with kinked S-shaped tail and dorsal spine; nodular bronchointerstitial pattern → Aelurostrongylus abstrusus (feline lungworm). Snails/slugs are the intermediate host; rodents, birds, frogs paratenic. Adults in terminal bronchioles; Baermann beats flotation. Dictyocaulus are ruminant/equine lungworms. Not mice as intermediate host — they are paratenic.

chapter: Chapter 18 — Feline — Infectious Disease & Parasitology

plain: Why are cats uniquely sensitive to acetaminophen, aspirin, phenols, propofol and pyrethroids? Deficient hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 pseudogene) → slow glucuronidation, so phenolic compounds and their oxidative metabolites accumulate; feline hemoglobin (8 reactive sulfhydryl groups) is also unusually oxidant-prone. Aspirin is therefore dosed only q48–72h in cats.

Avoid phenolics/pine oils (Lysol, Pine-Sol) and essential oils → hepatotoxicity, methemoglobinemia, tremors.

plain: Treatment of anticoagulant rodenticide toxicosis in a cat? plain: Glucocorticoid preferred in cats and how feline doses compare with canine? Prednisolone (cats poorly convert prednisone); feline doses are roughly double canine — anti-inflammatory 1–2 mg/kg/day, immunosuppressive 2–4 mg/kg/day (up to 4.4). plain: Opioid selection in cats by pain severity, and species-specific cautions? Mild/visceral: butorphanol (1–2 h). Moderate: buprenorphine 0.02–0.03 mg/ kg IV/IM/OTM q6–8h — the standard feline choice (eg, painful footpads); fentanyl patch 25 µg/h for multi-day pain. plain: What does feline onychectomy remove, and what is cut? The entire third phalanx (P3) with the ungual crest/germinal epithelium, transecting the common digital extensor, dorsal elastic ligaments, collateral ligaments and deep digital flexor at the distal interphalangeal joint. Any retained P3 fragment → claw regrowth, chronic pain and draining tracts. AVMA discourages elective declawing (banned in several jurisdictions); multimodal analgesia with ring block is required.

Year-round flea control; also trim claws, avoid rough play, wash scratches promptly, keep indoors, screen feline blood donors. plain: Racehorse fading late in races; irregularly irregular rhythm, variable S1, absent S4; ECG no P waves, f waves, normal QRS → Atrial fibrillation — the most common performance-limiting arrhythmia in horses; large atrial mass + high vagal tone sustain "lone" AF without structural disease. Confirm with ECG, then echo before any conversion.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Why does S4 disappear in equine AF? S4 is produced by coordinated atrial contraction, normally audible in horses; fibrillating atria cannot generate it, so absent S4 + irregular rhythm → ECG for AF.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

Not quinidine sulfate IV — the IV form

plain: Horse with lone AF (no murmur, no CHF, normal echo) → treatment of choice? Quinidine sulfate 22 mg/kg via nasogastric tube q2h, max 4–6 doses, then q6h; or transvenous electrical cardioversion. Digoxin if ventricular rate >100 during quinidine. Not quinidine sulfate IV — the IV form is quinidine gluconate (recent-onset AF).

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Quinidine toxicity in the horse — stop when? QRS widening >25% of baseline, colic, diarrhea, nasal edema, urticaria, hypotension, laminitis. Class IA drug prolongs atrial refractoriness.

plain: Prognosis for conversion of equine AF depends on? Best if duration <4 months and no atrial enlargement or valvular disease (>80% convert); AF <24–48 h may convert spontaneously. Recurrence common with mitral regurgitation or long duration.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: AF treatment across species: horse vs dog vs cat? Horse: rhythm conversion (quinidine or cardioversion). Dog: rate control with diltiazem ± digoxin (AF accompanies DCM/MMVD; dilated atria will not hold sinus).

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Cat: diltiazem (rare, HCM). Not quinidine in dogs — conversion fails with structural disease.

plain: Fit horse at rest: regular dropped beats, isolated P waves without QRS, S4 followed by a pause; resolves with exercise or excitement → Second-degree AV block (Mobitz I) — the most common equine arrhythmia, physiologic from high resting vagal tone. Next step: nothing; no treatment or exercise restriction.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: When is second-degree AV block in a horse pathologic? If it persists during exercise, is high-grade (several consecutive blocked P waves), or accompanies poor performance/collapse → exercising ECG and echo. Third-degree block (bradycardia, collapse) is always pathologic.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

AF is the commonest pathologic arrhythmia; VT and VPCs are always

plain: Which rhythm is normal in a resting horse: VT, VPCs, AF or second- degree AV block? Second-degree AV block (also sinus arrhythmia, SA block). AF is the commonest pathologic arrhythmia; VT and VPCs are always abnormal.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Older horse (>10 yr), holodiastolic decrescendo murmur loudest left heart base, bounding (water-hammer) pulses → Aortic regurgitation — the most common acquired valvular disease and most common diastolic murmur of aged horses; degenerative nodular cusp thickening.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Mild–moderate aortic regurgitation in a horse → effect on performance and advice? Usually benign, slowly progressive, no effect on performance; safe to ride; monitor with annual echocardiography. Severe AR (LV dilation, ventricular arrhythmias, worsening bounding pulses) → collapse risk, retire from ridden work.

plain: Most common congenital cardiac defect in horses? Its murmur? Ventricular septal defect (perimembranous; Arabians, Welsh ponies). Loud pansystolic band-shaped murmur loudest right sternal border (right 4th ICS) with palpable thrill, softer left pulmonic ejection murmur; confirm by echo.

plain: Prognosis of equine VSD depends on? Defects <2.5 cm with shunt velocity >4 m/s (restrictive) are compatible with athletic use; large defects cause left- sided volume overload and failure.

plain: Murmur map in the horse: timing and location → valve? Left base diastolic decrescendo = aortic regurgitation; right pansystolic cranial = VSD; left apex holosystolic = mitral regurgitation; right apex = tricuspid regurgitation; soft early-systolic left-base murmur varying with heart rate = physiologic flow murmur.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

plain: Horse with pitting edema along ventral mandible/intermandibular space extending down the neck → best initial diagnostic? Ultrasound of the jugular veins (catheter-associated thrombophlebitis, Doppler shows occlusion) and thorax (pleuropneumonia, cranial mediastinal mass); then total protein, lymph nodes (strangles), check for purpura hemorrhagica.

plain: Horse with pitting edema of all four distal limbs and ventral abdomen → differentials and how to sort? Vasculitis (purpura hemorrhagica after S. equi exposure, EVA, EIA), hypoproteinemia (PLE, liver, PLN), right heart failure (jugular distension), lymphangitis (one hot limb), stocking up (resolves with exercise). Check petechiae, albumin, auscultation, Coggins.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Racehorse with gurgling EXPIRATORY noise, chokes down late in race,
normal at rest; endoscopy: epiglottis hidden beneath soft palate →

plain: Racehorse with gurgling EXPIRATORY noise, chokes down late in race, normal at rest; endoscopy: epiglottis hidden beneath soft palate → Dorsal displacement of the soft palate (intermittent). Confirm with dynamic (overground/treadmill) endoscopy — resting scope often normal. Caudal laryngeal retraction lets the palate flip over the epiglottis, obstructing expiration.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: DDSP → treatment options and surgery of choice?
Cornell collar, figure-8 noseband, rest, treat lower airway inflammation.

plain: DDSP → treatment options and surgery of choice? Conservative: tongue-tie, Cornell collar, figure-8 noseband, rest, treat lower airway inflammation. Surgical: laryngeal tie-forward (~80% success) is the procedure of choice; staphylectomy or sternothyrohyoid myectomy ~50–60%.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

grade on Havemeyer scale (grade III–IV abnormal), slap test.

plain: Tall young Thoroughbred with INSPIRATORY roaring/whistling at speed; endoscopy: left arytenoid fails to abduct → Left recurrent laryngeal neuropathy (laryngeal hemiplegia) — idiopathic distal axonopathy of the long left recurrent laryngeal nerve → cricoarytenoideus dorsalis atrophy; grade on Havemeyer scale (grade III–IV abnormal), slap test. Not DDSP — that is an expiratory gurgle.
