plain: Laryngeal hemiplegia → treatment and prognosis? Prosthetic laryngoplasty (tie-back) + ventriculocordectomy; ~70% of racehorses return to prior performance, better in non-racehorses. Complications: coughing/ aspiration from the permanently abducted arytenoid, loss of abduction.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Tie-back: where are the prosthetic sutures placed?
replicating cricoarytenoideus dorsalis action to hold the arytenoid abducted;

plain: Tie-back: where are the prosthetic sutures placed? Between the muscular process of the left arytenoid and the caudodorsal edge of the cricoid, replicating cricoarytenoideus dorsalis action to hold the arytenoid abducted; over-abduction → aspiration and cough.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Causes of BILATERAL laryngeal paralysis in horses? Lead toxicity
hepatic encephalopathy, organophosphates (unilateral left-sided disease is the

plain: Causes of BILATERAL laryngeal paralysis in horses? Lead toxicity, hepatic encephalopathy, organophosphates (unilateral left-sided disease is the idiopathic neuropathy).

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Endoscopy: epiglottis outline visible but covered by aryepiglottic fold
good prognosis unless epiglottic hypoplasia coexists. Causes exercise

plain: Endoscopy: epiglottis outline visible but covered by aryepiglottic fold mucosa, serrated edge obscured → Epiglottic entrapment. Tx axial division of the entrapping fold (transendoscopic laser or hooked bistoury); good prognosis unless epiglottic hypoplasia coexists. Causes exercise intolerance, cough, sometimes DDSP.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Horse with inspiratory noise, foul breath; endoscopy: swollen arytenoid
with granulation tissue → Dx and organism? Arytenoid chondropathy

plain: Horse with inspiratory noise, foul breath; endoscopy: swollen arytenoid with granulation tissue → Dx and organism? Arytenoid chondropathy (chondritis) — mixed infection, often Fusobacterium necrophorum / Streptococcus; antibiotics and anti-inflammatories, partial arytenoidectomy if chronic.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Which structures run through the medial vs lateral guttural pouch
compartment? Medial: internal carotid artery, CN IX, X, XI, XII, cranial
cervical (sympathetic) ganglion. Lateral: external carotid/maxillary artery
nerve runs with the lateral compartment.

plain: Which structures run through the medial vs lateral guttural pouch compartment? Medial: internal carotid artery, CN IX, X, XI, XII, cranial cervical (sympathetic) ganglion. Lateral: external carotid/maxillary artery and CN VII. Separated by the stylohyoid bone. Not CN VII medial — facial nerve runs with the lateral compartment.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Horse with severe spontaneous epistaxis AT REST, dysphagia, Horner
syndrome; endoscopy: diphtheritic plaque on roof of medial compartment
and CN IX/X. Dysphagia is the

plain: Horse with severe spontaneous epistaxis AT REST, dysphagia, Horner syndrome; endoscopy: diphtheritic plaque on roof of medial compartment → Guttural pouch mycosis (Aspergillus) eroding the internal carotid artery and CN IX/X. Dysphagia is the worst prognostic sign. Do not biopsy the plaque.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Guttural pouch mycosis → definitive treatment? Emergency surgical
to the lesion — retrograde flow from the
ligation alone fail; topical antifungals adjunctive. Fatal hemorrhage without

plain: Guttural pouch mycosis → definitive treatment? Emergency surgical arterial occlusion (balloon catheter or coil embolization) both proximal AND distal to the lesion — retrograde flow from the circle of Willis makes proximal ligation alone fail; topical antifungals adjunctive. Fatal hemorrhage without occlusion.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Horse found dead in stall with several liters of blood from both nostrils →
smaller bleeds. EIPH and ethmoid hematoma rarely exsanguinate.

plain: Horse found dead in stall with several liters of blood from both nostrils → source? Guttural pouch mycosis (internal carotid rupture), usually after prior smaller bleeds. EIPH and ethmoid hematoma rarely exsanguinate.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Weeks after strangles: intermittent unilateral mucopurulent discharge
worse when head lowered/eating, swelling in Viborg's triangle; lateral
Mycosis shows plaques and epistaxis instead.

plain: Weeks after strangles: intermittent unilateral mucopurulent discharge worse when head lowered/eating, swelling in Viborg's triangle; lateral radiograph fluid line in pouch → Guttural pouch empyema (retained S. equi equi) ± inspissated chondroids. Confirm by endoscopy (pus from ostium). Mycosis shows plaques and epistaxis instead.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Guttural pouch empyema → treatment and public-health significance?
Repeated saline lavage via indwelling (Chambers) catheter,
(~10% of recovered horses shed for months)

plain: Guttural pouch empyema → treatment and public-health significance? Repeated saline lavage via indwelling (Chambers) catheter, endoscopic basket or surgical chondroid removal (Viborg's triangle/hyovertebrotomy), topical penicillin gel. The carrier state (~10% of recovered horses shed for months) seeds new outbreaks — isolate until three negative PCR/culture washes.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Arabian filly foal with non-painful fluctuant parotid swelling, stertor,
dysphagia → Dx, most important complication, Tx? Guttural pouch
(one-way valve at pharyngeal ostium traps air). Complication:
into the normal pouch or laser

plain: Arabian filly foal with non-painful fluctuant parotid swelling, stertor, dysphagia → Dx, most important complication, Tx? Guttural pouch tympany (one-way valve at pharyngeal ostium traps air). Complication: aspiration pneumonia from dysphagia/milk reflux, dyspnea, secondary empyema. Tx fenestrate the median septum into the normal pouch or laser salpingopharyngeal fistula.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Horse with unilateral nasal discharge and intermittent epistaxis at rest →
most appropriate diagnostic? Upper airway endoscopy including guttural
Unilateral discharge localizes rostral to the nasopharynx.

plain: Horse with unilateral nasal discharge and intermittent epistaxis at rest → most appropriate diagnostic? Upper airway endoscopy including guttural pouches and ethmoid region; radiographs/CT for sinus disease follow. Unilateral discharge localizes rostral to the nasopharynx.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Epistaxis in the horse — localize by pattern?

plain: Epistaxis in the horse — localize by pattern? Bilateral after racing = EIPH (most common); profuse at rest ± dysphagia = guttural pouch mycosis; intermittent mild unilateral, older horse = ethmoid hematoma; also trauma, sinus disease/neoplasia, polyps; rarely coagulopathy.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Recurrent mild unilateral epistaxis at rest; endoscopy: smooth greenish-
yellow mass from the ethmoid region →
non-neoplastic encapsulated expanding hematoma that erodes bone. Tx

plain: Recurrent mild unilateral epistaxis at rest; endoscopy: smooth greenish- yellow mass from the ethmoid region → Progressive ethmoid hematoma — non-neoplastic encapsulated expanding hematoma that erodes bone. Tx repeated intralesional 4% formalin via endoscope, laser ablation or frontonasal flap removal; recurrence up to 50%.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Chronic unilateral FETID mucopurulent discharge, facial swelling, dull
sinus percussion → cause and first examination? Secondary (dental)
— apical infection of caudal maxillary cheek teeth
sit in the maxillary sinus. First:

plain: Chronic unilateral FETID mucopurulent discharge, facial swelling, dull sinus percussion → cause and first examination? Secondary (dental) sinusitis — apical infection of caudal maxillary cheek teeth 08–11 whose roots sit in the maxillary sinus. First: oral exam with speculum; then radiographs (fluid line, apical changes)/CT, sinoscopy, centesis.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory

spans.text: Equine sinusitis: primary vs secondary and treatment?
(streptococcal after URT infection, less odor): systemic antibiotics + sinus
lavage via trephination. Secondary (~50%, dental, fetid):
. Ethmoid hematoma and GP mycosis bleed

plain: Equine sinusitis: primary vs secondary and treatment? Primary (streptococcal after URT infection, less odor): systemic antibiotics + sinus lavage via trephination. Secondary (~50%, dental, fetid): extract the diseased tooth + lavage. Ethmoid hematoma and GP mycosis bleed without odor.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
section: Lower Airway — Equine Asthma and EIPH

spans.text: Middle-aged stabled horse on hay: chronic cough, nasal discharge,
expiratory effort with heave line, end-expiratory wheezes, afebrile, normal
dust molds and endotoxin → neutrophilic inflammation, bronchospasm,
mucus. Afebrile status differentiates from infectious pneumonia.

plain: Middle-aged stabled horse on hay: chronic cough, nasal discharge, expiratory effort with heave line, end-expiratory wheezes, afebrile, normal CBC → Severe equine asthma (RAO/heaves) — hypersensitivity to hay/barn dust molds and endotoxin → neutrophilic inflammation, bronchospasm, mucus. Afebrile status differentiates from infectious pneumonia.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
section: Lower Airway — Equine Asthma and EIPH

spans.text: How is severe equine asthma confirmed? BAL cytology with >25% non-
eosinophils or mast cells. Tracheal wash is for infectious culture.
eosinophilic — eosinophils mark mild asthma, not heaves.

plain: How is severe equine asthma confirmed? BAL cytology with >25% non- degenerate neutrophils (often >50%) ± Curschmann spirals; normal BAL <5% neutrophils. Mild/moderate asthma (IAD): 5–20% neutrophils, eosinophils or mast cells. Tracheal wash is for infectious culture. Not eosinophilic — eosinophils mark mild asthma, not heaves.

chapter: Chapter 21 — Equine — Cardiovascular & Respiratory
section: Lower Airway — Equine Asthma and EIPH

spans.text: Severe equine asthma → most important management step?

plain: Horse fed mostly grain/wheat bran: shifting lameness, hindlimb weakness, enlarged facial bones ("big head") → Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism (bran disease) — low Ca:P (also oxalate-rich tropical grasses) → PTH → fibrous osteodystrophy. Correct Ca:P to ≥1.1–2:1 with alfalfa or calcium carbonate/limestone, cut bran.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: HYPP horse — feeds to avoid and diet instead → Avoid high-potassium feeds: alfalfa, molasses (cane/beet), soybean meal, kelp, K-containing electrolytes. Feed grass hays (timothy, brome, bermuda), oats/corn, rinsed beet pulp; total diet <1% K, small frequent meals, regular exercise; acetazolamide 2–3 mg/kg PO q8–12h for prevention.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Liver-specific enzyme for hepatocellular injury in horses and cattle (ALT unreliable)? Sorbitol dehydrogenase (SDH) or GLDH — liver-specific leakage enzymes with short half-lives → acute injury; GGT marks biliary/ cholestatic and chronic disease; AST is elevated but also muscle-derived. ALT is useless in horses, ruminants and pigs.

plain: Colt 1–5 days old (often after dystocia), straining, progressive abdominal distension, depression, dribbling urine; Na 118, Cl 85, K 6.8, creatinine high → Uroperitoneum from ruptured bladder (dorsal tear during parturition; urachal necrosis in septic foals, including fillies). plain: Confirmed uroperitoneum in a foal → next step and pre-surgical priority? Stabilize before surgery: drain the abdomen slowly, IV 0.9% NaCl with dextrose (± insulin, bicarbonate, calcium gluconate for ECG changes), no LRS/K-containing fluids, no succinylcholine; anesthetize only when K <5.5 mEq/L; then cystorrhaphy. Survival ~80–90% when stabilized. Not surgery first — hyperkalemic arrest under anesthesia kills. Not a fixed K cutoff for prognosis — lower K, then operate.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: 10-day-old septic foal suddenly weak and ataxic, falls when stood; hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremia → Hyperkalemia from uroperitoneum (bladder/urachal rupture in recumbent septic foals) — K depolarizes muscle and myocardium. Confirm by ultrasound and peritoneal creatinine ≥2× serum. Not hypoglycemia — it does not produce this electrolyte triad.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Foal dripping urine from a moist umbilicus, urine scald on the ventral abdomen → Patent urachus (congenital, or acquired from omphalitis/ straining/recumbency). Dx is clinical plus ultrasound of umbilical remnants (enlarged urachus/vessels, abscess); contrast cystography rarely needed. Most acquired cases close with hygiene and antimicrobials; resect if persistent >1–2 weeks, infected or abscessed. Not contrast radiography as the standard confirmation.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Horse with markedly elevated CK after exertional rhabdomyolysis → most concerning complication? Myoglobinuric nephrosis (pigment acute kidney injury) — myoglobin is tubulotoxic, worst with dehydration and NSAIDs. IV fluids to keep urine flowing; monitor creatinine; hold NSAIDs/ aminoglycosides until hydrated. Not glomerulonephritis — myoglobin damages tubules.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Most common urolith in horses, and why cloudy urine is normal → Calcium carbonate (type I, yellow-green spiculated), mostly in the bladder of geldings → stranguria, post-exercise hematuria; cystotomy, perineal urethrotomy or lithotripsy. Normal equine urine is cloudy from physiologic calcium carbonate crystals and mucus; crystalluria alone is not disease.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Aged horse (>15 yr): long curly coat that fails to shed, PU/PD, muscle

Lesion is the pars intermedia, not the adrenal.

plain: Aged horse (>15 yr): long curly coat that fails to shed, PU/PD, muscle wasting, pot belly, recurrent laminitis/infections → Pituitary pars intermedia dysfunction (equine Cushing's) — loss of hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition → pars intermedia adenoma/hyperplasia → excess POMC peptides (ACTH, α-MSH). Hypertrichosis is near-pathognomonic. Lesion is the pars intermedia, not the adrenal.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: PPID — confirmatory test and its seasonal caveat? Resting endogenous plasma ACTH with seasonally adjusted reference ranges (physiologically higher Aug–Oct); TRH stimulation test (ACTH at 10 min after 1 mg TRH IV) for early/equivocal cases. Dexamethasone suppression is older (laminitis risk). Not an ACTH stimulation test — that assesses adrenal reserve, never used for PPID.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

Prascend); cyproheptadine is a weaker adjunct; body clipping, dental/parasite

plain: PPID — drug of choice? Pergolide 2 µg/kg PO q24h (dopamine agonist, Prascend); cyproheptadine is a weaker adjunct; body clipping, dental/parasite care, manage insulin dysregulation and laminitis. Not trilostane — the lesion is pituitary, unlike canine Cushing's.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Obese horse/pony, cresty neck, tailhead fat pads, high fasting insulin with normal glucose, recurrent laminitis → Equine metabolic syndrome (insulin dysregulation); most important complication is hyperinsulinemia- associated laminitis (insulin acts on lamellar IGF-1 receptors, independent of inflammation). Dx oral sugar test or basal insulin; hypertriglyceridemia and high leptin support. Rule out PPID.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: EMS vs PPID — how testing and body condition differ →

plain: EMS vs PPID — how testing and body condition differ → EMS: younger, gains weight/regional adiposity, test insulin (oral sugar test). PPID: aged, loses muscle/weight, hypertrichosis, test ACTH. The two can coexist.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: EMS horse, BCS 8/9, already laminitic → treatment plan? Soaked grass
hay with NSC <10–12% at 1.5% body weight

plain: EMS horse, BCS 8/9, already laminitic → treatment plan? Soaked grass hay with NSC <10–12% at 1.5% body weight, no grain or pasture, ration balancer; NSAIDs, sole support, radiographs for laminitis; exercise only once laminitis is stable; metformin or levothyroxine if diet fails. Not insulin — the horse is already hyperinsulinemic; insulin drives the laminitis.

chapter: Chapter 22 — Equine — Gastrointestinal, Hepatic, Nutrition, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Old horse (>15–20 yr) with a firm, mobile, asymptomatic nodule in the thyroid region → Thyroid adenoma (or C-cell adenoma) — very common incidental finding, almost always non-functional; no treatment, monitor; surgery only for dysphagia/airway compromise. Adult hypothyroidism is rare and over-diagnosed; never supplement on low T4 alone. Not hypothyroidism/ goiter — nodules are euthyroid.

plain: Horse incisor eruption schedule → Deciduous: central 6 days, intermediate 6 weeks, corner 6 months. Permanent: central 2.5 yr, intermediate 3.5 yr, corner 4.5 yr (in wear ~6–12 months later); "full mouth" at 5 yr; canines 4–5 yr (usually absent/vestigial in mares).

plain: Aging a horse after 5 years by wear → Lower cups disappear I1 6 yr, I2 7 yr, I3 8 yr (uppers 9, 10, 11); dental star ~8 yr; 7-year hook on upper corner incisor at 7 and again ~11; occlusal surface oval → triangular (11–15+) → rectangular (18–20+); incisor angle becomes more acute.

plain: Galvayne's groove — location and timeline → Labial surface of the upper corner incisor (103/203): appears at the gumline 10 yr, halfway 15, full length 20, gone from upper half 25, gone 30.

so it is the oldest and most worn cheek tooth in aged horses.

Hindlimb: hip hike — tuber coxae rises higher on the lame side; shortened cranial stride phase, toe drag; lameness worsens with the lame limb on the inside of a circle.

plain: Lameness exam: history and standing exam done, horse walked in a straight line → next step? Trot in a straight line on firm footing (most lameness shows only at the trot), then lunge in circles on hard and soft ground, then flexion tests, hoof testers and nerve blocks distal → proximal, then image the blocked region. Not circles straight after walking — trot straight first.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Hoof testers: focal sole/white-line pain vs frog/heel pain vs diffuse pain in

plain: Hoof testers: focal sole/white-line pain vs frog/heel pain vs diffuse pain in several feet → Focal → subsolar abscess, bruise, nail prick, keratoma; across the central frog/heels → navicular/palmar heel pain; diffuse toe pain in multiple feet with bounding pulses → laminitis. Always compare the contralateral foot.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

A block is positive if lameness improves ≥70% within 10–15 min. Not the low palmar block for navicular pain — that is the four-point.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

four-point (plantar + plantar metatarsal nerves) → high plantar (proximal

plain: Hindlimb block sequence? Plantar digital → abaxial sesamoid → low plantar four-point (plantar + plantar metatarsal nerves) → high plantar (proximal suspensory) → intra-articular tarsometatarsal/distal intertarsal (bone spavin) → tibial and peroneal (whole distal limb).

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Palmar digital block negative; high palmar (proximal metacarpal) block

plain: Palmar digital block negative; high palmar (proximal metacarpal) block abolishes lameness → next step? Ultrasound the proximal metacarpus — proximal suspensory desmitis is the leading Dx (also inferior check ligament, flexor tendons); radiograph proximal MC3. Tx rest, controlled exercise, shock wave, PRP; fasciotomy/neurectomy if chronic.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Laceration near a joint — how is joint involvement proven? Distend the

plain: Laceration near a joint — how is joint involvement proven? Distend the joint with sterile saline from a remote aseptic site and watch for egress from the wound, and/or synoviocentesis (± positive-contrast arthrography). Never probe blindly — probing inoculates a clean joint.

spans.text: Turbid synovial fluid: nucleated cells >30,000/µL, >80–90% neutrophils,

plain: Turbid synovial fluid: nucleated cells >30,000/µL, >80–90% neutrophils, total protein >4 g/dL → Septic arthritis (normal <500–1,000 cells/µL, TP <2.5 g/dL). Culture in blood-culture medium — only ~50% grow, so a negative culture never excludes it. Tx within 24–48 h: joint lavage (arthroscopic/ through-and-through), systemic + intra-articular or regional-perfusion antibiotics, NSAIDs.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Horse lacerated 8 cm above the fetlock on the palmar side 5 days ago, now

plain: Horse lacerated 8 cm above the fetlock on the palmar side 5 days ago, now severely lame with pastern/fetlock swelling → Septic digital flexor tendon sheath (the sheath, not the fetlock joint, lies under a palmar wound there): sample the sheath (same cytology thresholds as a joint), tenoscopic lavage, systemic + regional antibiotics, NSAIDs.

(or place a sterile probe in the tract) to show depth, direction

plain: Horse steps on a nail still embedded in the hoof → how to radiograph? Leave the nail in (or place a sterile probe in the tract) to show depth, direction and whether navicular bursa, DDFT or coffin joint are reached; then remove, flush, synoviocentesis ± contrast, tetanus prophylaxis, referral if a synovial structure is penetrated.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Pastured or grain-overfed horse, forelimbs camped forward, weight
rocked back, bounding digital pulses, heat in hooves, toe pain on hoof
points one toe, heel raised, and has heel pain.

plain: Pastured or grain-overfed horse, forelimbs camped forward, weight rocked back, bounding digital pulses, heat in hooves, toe pain on hoof testers → Laminitis; key history question is grain/concentrate intake and lush pasture (also retained placenta/metritis, SIRS, EMS/PPID). Lands heel- first; forelimbs (~60% of weight) affected first. Not navicular — that horse points one toe, heel raised, and has heel pain.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Acute laminitis → first treatment and imaging?
distal-limb cryotherapy (ice to below the carpus, 48–72 h)
developmental phase, frog/sole support, deep bedding, strict rest, remove the

plain: Acute laminitis → first treatment and imaging? NSAIDs, continuous distal-limb cryotherapy (ice to below the carpus, 48–72 h) in the developmental phase, frog/sole support, deep bedding, strict rest, remove the cause. Lateromedial radiograph with dorsal-wall marker: P3 rotation >5° (significant), sole depth <15 mm and founder distance/sinking >10–15 mm carry a poor prognosis.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Laminitic horse that is endotoxemic (enterocolitis) vs chronic laminitis in a
systemically well horse → NSAID of choice? Flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h
well horse (skip a day every 5–7 days — accumulates; right dorsal colitis, renal

plain: Laminitic horse that is endotoxemic (enterocolitis) vs chronic laminitis in a systemically well horse → NSAID of choice? Flunixin 1.1 mg/kg IV q12h when endotoxemic (anti-endotoxic effect); phenylbutazone for the chronic, well horse (skip a day every 5–7 days — accumulates; right dorsal colitis, renal papillary necrosis); firocoxib when renal/GI risk.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Therapeutic shoeing in laminitis vs navicular syndrome? Laminitis: heart- bar shoe or frog/sole support and raise the heel (wedge) to reduce DDFT pull on rotating P3. Navicular/underrun heels: egg-bar shoe, raised heel, eased breakover. Not egg-bar for laminitis — egg-bar is a heel-support (navicular) shoe. Not "raise the toe" — the heel is raised.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Acute severe single-limb lameness, bounding pulse, heat, focal hoof-tester

plain: Acute severe single-limb lameness, bounding pulse, heat, focal hoof-tester pain, red focus or draining tract on the sole → Subsolar abscess — the MCC of acute severe lameness in horses. Pare to establish ventral drainage, poultice/bandage 3–5 days, tetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics usually unnecessary. Not laminitis — that is bilateral, diffuse, toe-centred. "Sole ulcer" is the dairy-cow (Rusterholz) lesion.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

spans.text: Chronic intermittent bilateral forelimb lameness, short choppy toe-first

plain: Chronic intermittent bilateral forelimb lameness, short choppy toe-first stride, worse on hard ground and circles, points a toe, hoof testers positive over the frog → Navicular syndrome (podotrochlosis). PD block abolishes lameness and it switches to the other forelimb; radiographs (flexor cortex erosion, synovial invaginations), MRI definitive. Tx corrective shoeing, NSAIDs, intra-bursal steroids, bisphosphonates (clodronate, tiludronate); PD neurectomy as salvage. Not P3 fracture — acute, unilateral.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Radiographic views for the navicular bone and for a suspected P3 fracture? Navicular: lateromedial, 60–65° dorsoproximal-palmarodistal oblique (upright pedal) and palmaroproximal-palmarodistal "skyline" (flexor cortex). P3 fracture: 65° DPr-PaDiO plus 45° obliques with the frog sulci packed; repeat in 7–10 days if negative — fracture lines appear late.

plain: Acute severe unilateral lameness, positive hoof testers, lucent line through the distal phalanx → Pedal (P3) fracture: bar shoe with quarter clips or foot cast, stall rest 6–12 months; lag screw for articular fractures. The hoof capsule acts as a natural cast.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Long toe, low collapsed/underrun heels, broken-back hoof-pastern axis → predisposes to what, and the farriery fix? Navicular syndrome/palmar heel pain (delayed breakover raises DDFT tension on the navicular bone). Shorten the toe, move breakover caudally, support heels (egg-bar/wedge) to restore a straight axis.

plain: Hind shoe too small, not covering the heels; underrun heels → Reshoe with a full-fitting, wider shoe extending to the heels (wide-web or egg-bar). Short shoeing causes heel contraction, corns and palmar foot pain.

Debride necrotic frog, dry clean footing, daily cleaning, exercise, topical copper sulfate/dilute iodine/chlorine dioxide; if sensitive tissue is exposed use metronidazole paste and bandage rather than astringents.

plain: Which hoof structure, if destroyed, leaves a permanent hoof-wall defect? The coronary band (coronary corium) — sole and frog corium regenerate horn, but wall grows only from the coronary germinal epithelium (~6–10 mm/ month).

High ringbone: NSAIDs, intra-articular therapy, then pastern arthrodesis (~70–80% sound; low-motion joint tolerates fusion). Low ringbone: medical only, guarded — the high-motion coffin joint cannot be fused.

Not the fetlock — fetlock knuckling is SDFT → superior check desmotomy.

plain: Premature/dysmature foal: fetlock drops, toe tips up, no pain → Flexor tendon laxity (fetlock/coffin hyperextension). Controlled exercise and heel extensions; avoid bandaging/splints — they worsen laxity.

plain: Racehorse with heat, pain and convex "bowed" swelling of the palmar mid-metacarpus → Superficial digital flexor tendinitis. Ultrasound at 7–10 days grades the hypoechoic core lesion (% cross-sectional area). Acute: cold therapy 48–72 h, compression bandage, stall rest, phenylbutazone; then 6–12 months controlled exercise with serial ultrasound; PRP/stem cells adjunct. Re- injury 40–60%.

plain: Ultrasound: enlarged hypoechoic suspensory body/branches vs thickened plantar tarsal ligament at the distal hock → Suspensory desmitis (Standardbreds, hindlimb common) vs curb (long plantar ligament desmitis; sickle hocks). plain: Which soft-tissue structure inserts on the proximal sesamoid bones; what does sesamoiditis implicate? The suspensory (interosseous) ligament branches; distal sesamoidean ligaments continue to P1/P2; SDFT/DDFT only pass over them palmarly. Sesamoiditis = strain at the branch insertion — ultrasound the branches.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Proximal sesamoid fracture classification and significance? Apical, abaxial, mid-body, basilar, comminuted. Apical (upper third) most common → arthroscopic removal; mid-body/basilar and biaxial fractures compromise the suspensory apparatus (catastrophic breakdown, fetlock sinks).

plain: Toe lifts off the ground, fetlock normal or extended vs fetlock drops to the ground → Toe-up = DDFT rupture (or inferior check ligament; DDFT holds the toe down via P3). Fetlock to the ground = suspensory apparatus breakdown (suspensory + distal sesamoidean ligaments ± sesamoid fractures); SDFT rupture gives only mild fetlock drop. Not DDFT for a dropped fetlock — DDFT rupture elevates the toe.

plain: Acute fetlock breakdown (dropped fetlock) → emergency splint? Dorsal splint with the fetlock flexed (Kimzey Leg Saver or board, hoof to proximal cannon) aligning the dorsal cortices of hoof, pastern and cannon so bone bears the load, in a Robert Jones bandage. Not a palmar/caudal splint — it does not support hyperextension.

plain: Cast or splint for a pastern/fetlock/distal cannon injury — how far must it extend? Immobilize the joint above and below: half-limb cast including the hoof up to the proximal metacarpus/metatarsus just below carpus/hock. Injuries above mid-cannon need a full-limb cast; mid-radius fractures need a lateral splint to the elbow plus caudal splint. Change casts every 2–4 weeks; cast sores are the main complication.

plain: Complete fracture of the distal third metacarpus in an adult → Open reduction and internal fixation (double plating, lag screws) after splinted transport; external coaptation alone fails under adult weight-bearing. Guarded prognosis.

plain: Two-year-old in training, warm painful swelling on the medial proximal cannon (MC2), mild lameness → "Splints" — periostitis of the small metacarpal bone/interosseous ligament. Rest 4–6 weeks, NSAIDs, cold, bandage; radiograph to exclude fracture; remove only if the exostosis impinges on the suspensory. Medial fore splint = MC2, lateral hind = MT4.

plain: Splint bone fracture → treatment by location? Distal third (expendable): surgical removal of the fragment if non-union/sequestrum/persistent lameness (rest first if fresh and closed); ultrasound for suspensory desmitis. Proximal third: rest or internal fixation — it supports the carpometacarpal/ tarsometatarsal joint.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Soft, fluctuant, painless swellings around the fetlock of a working horse, sound → Wind galls (windpuffs) — effusion of the fetlock joint (articular) or digital flexor sheath (tendinous). Cosmetic; investigate only if lame.

(Cross-pinning/lag screws are for foal Salter-Harris physeal fractures, not chips.) Oblique carpal radiographs — DLPMO vs DMPLO highlight which bones? DLPMO profiles the dorsomedial surface: radial carpal bone, second and medial third carpal bones (classic chip/slab-fracture sites).

plain: DMPLO profiles the dorsolateral surface: intermediate carpal, lateral third and fourth carpal bones. Not the reverse — the view is named by beam entry; the opposite surface is in profile.

plain: Carpal joints — which communicate? Antebrachiocarpal (radiocarpal) and middle carpal joints are high-motion; carpometacarpal is low-motion. Middle carpal and carpometacarpal communicate; the antebrachiocarpal joint is separate — determines where injected drug or infection spreads.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Young horse, soft fluctuant swelling dorsomedial hock (tarsocrural joint), usually sound → Bog spavin — tarsocrural synovial effusion; radiograph young horses for OCD (distal intermediate ridge of the tibia). Not osteophytes — those are bone spavin. Thoroughpin = effusion of the tarsal (DDF) sheath plantar to the tibia above the point of the hock; capped hock = calcaneal bursa.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

Spavin/Churchill test is supportive only; confirm with intra-articular anesthesia and radiographs. Tx intra-articular corticosteroids ± hyaluronan, NSAIDs, corrective shoeing, continued work; refractory → facilitated ankylosis/arthrodesis (ethanol, drilling, laser) — curative because fused low-motion joints lose no function.

shoulder (worst prognosis); yearling with joint effusion → arthroscopic

plain: Most common OCD sites in the horse, and in the dog? Horse: femoropatellar (lateral trochlear ridge of femur), tarsocrural (distal intermediate ridge of tibia — DIRT), fetlock (sagittal ridge MC3/MT3), shoulder (worst prognosis); yearling with joint effusion → arthroscopic debridement. Dog: caudal humeral head, large-breed males 4–8 months.

chapter: Chapter 23 — Equine — Neurology & Musculoskeletal

plain: Young horse stifle radiograph: well-defined circular lucency in the medial femoral condyle → Subchondral cystic lesion — commonest equine cyst site, part of the osteochondrosis complex. Stifle OCD instead flattens/ fragments the lateral trochlear ridge.

plain: Young, unfit, straight-legged horse or pony intermittently locks a hindlimb in extension, drags the toe, then the stifle suddenly releases → Upward fixation of the patella (medial patellar ligament hooked over the medial trochlear ridge; not luxation). Conditioning and heel elevation first; medial patellar ligament splitting or desmotomy if refractory (desmotomy risks patellar fragmentation).

plain: Horse can extend the hock while the stifle is flexed; dimple in the slack gastrocnemius (common calcaneal) tendon; bears weight → Peroneus (fibularis) tertius rupture — loss of the reciprocal apparatus (stifle and hock normally flex together). 2–3 months stall rest, good prognosis. Gastrocnemius rupture instead → dropped, overflexed hock that cannot bear weight, poor prognosis in adults.

plain: Hindlimb slaps down abruptly before full protraction (goose-step), shortened cranial phase, firm band in caudal thigh → Fibrotic (ossifying) myopathy of the semitendinosus (± semimembranosus, biceps femoris, gracilis) after trauma or IM injection; mechanical, painless. plain: Involuntary exaggerated hyperflexion of one or both hindlimbs at the walk, worse backing/turning → Stringhalt. Classic unilateral form: lateral digital extensor myotenectomy (tenectomy with a segment of muscle); phenytoin adjunct. Australian (pasture) form — bilateral, Hypochaeris radicata (flatweed; sweet-pea lathyrism in the US), distal axonopathy — remove from pasture, resolves over months.

Rectal palpation (crepitus on rocking, displaced fragments, hematoma) plus transrectal/transcutaneous ultrasound — recumbent radiographs need anesthesia. Hip luxation requires rupture of the round (teres) ligament; limb shortened, stifle and toe turned out.

plain: Carpal valgus surgery — which side gets periosteal stripping, which gets the transphyseal bridge? The lateral (concave) side grows slowly → hemicircumferential periosteal transection laterally to accelerate; the medial (convex, fast) side → transphyseal bridging (screws/wire or single screw) medially to retard. Varus is the mirror image. Bandage 10–14 days, radiograph to confirm. Not strip medial/bridge lateral — reversed. Not the distal ulnar physis — that is the canine rule.

Overcorrection into carpal varus if implants are not removed the moment the limb is straight (recheck every 2 weeks); also implant failure, physeal infection, premature closure. Periosteal stripping is self-limiting — may undercorrect but does not overcorrect.

plain: Circular alopecic scaling crusted lesions in girth/saddle area, spread by tack; most common equine dermatophyte? Treatment? Trichophyton equinum (cattle: T. verrucosum). Lime sulfur or enilconazole rinses 1–2×/ week for 3–4 weeks, disinfect tack; self-limiting in 1–3 months, zoonotic. Not T. mentagrophytes — secondary in horses.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Horse with crusting, scaling, skin sloughing; cytology shows acantholytic
prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg tapered; adjunct gold salts/azathioprine; better

plain: Horse with crusting, scaling, skin sloughing; cytology shows acantholytic keratinocytes with neutrophils → Pemphigus foliaceus (anti-desmosomal autoantibodies). Immunosuppressive dexamethasone 0.05–0.2 mg/kg or prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg tapered; adjunct gold salts/azathioprine; better prognosis in horses <1 year.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Firm, non-pruritic, non-alopecic, non-painful dermal nodules over back/
saddle area in insect season; histology collagen degeneration with

plain: Firm, non-pruritic, non-alopecic, non-painful dermal nodules over back/ saddle area in insect season; histology collagen degeneration with eosinophils → Eosinophilic (collagenolytic) granuloma, the most common equine nodular skin disease. Intralesional triamcinolone 3–5 mg/lesion (≤20 mg total — laminitis risk); many lesions → prednisolone 1 mg/kg 2–3 weeks; excise solitary/mineralized nodules; fly control.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

plain: Multiple wheals on neck and trunk that pit on pressure and appear/ disappear within a day → Urticaria (type I: insects, penicillin, vaccines, feed, contact). Remove trigger; dexamethasone 0.05–0.1 mg/kg or hydroxyzine; epinephrine if angioedema. Not eosinophilic granuloma — firm, persistent, non-pitting.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

plain: Summer-only intense pruritus, alopecia and crusting of mane, tail head and ventral midline → Culicoides hypersensitivity (sweet itch, type I/IV to midge saliva). Stable at dusk/dawn, fine-mesh screens, fans, fly sheets, permethrin; glucocorticoids/antihistamines for flares.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Culicoides hypersensitivity, lice or Chorioptes, and a

plain: Horse rubbing tail head; pinworm (Oxyuris equi) excluded → other causes? Culicoides hypersensitivity, lice or Chorioptes, and a dirty sheath or udder — clean it; treatment follows the cause found.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Flat depigmented hyperkeratotic plaques inside the pinnae →
— equine papillomavirus spread by black flies (

plain: Flat depigmented hyperkeratotic plaques inside the pinnae → Aural plaques — equine papillomavirus spread by black flies (Simulium). Usually no treatment; topical imiquimod 5% for painful/head-shy horses; fly control.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Yearling with multiple small gray-white cauliflower growths on muzzle
; contagious to young naive horses. Adult facial nodules
are more often eosinophilic granuloma, sarcoid or habronemiasis.

plain: Yearling with multiple small gray-white cauliflower growths on muzzle and lips → Equine viral papillomatosis (papillomavirus 1); benign neglect, regress in 1–9 months; contagious to young naive horses. Adult facial nodules are more often eosinophilic granuloma, sarcoid or habronemiasis.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Young Quarter Horse (cutting lines) with loose, hyperextensible, fragile
skin over the back tearing and forming seromas under the saddle →
(cyclophilin B) mutation; genetic test; no cure, retire, do not breed

plain: Young Quarter Horse (cutting lines) with loose, hyperextensible, fragile skin over the back tearing and forming seromas under the saddle → HERDA (hereditary equine regional dermal asthenia) — autosomal recessive PPIB (cyclophilin B) mutation; genetic test; no cure, retire, do not breed carriers.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Appaloosa with recurrent episodes of blepharospasm, epiphora, miosis,
aqueous flare, corneal edema; later synechiae, cataract, phthisis →

plain: Appaloosa with recurrent episodes of blepharospasm, epiphora, miosis, aqueous flare, corneal edema; later synechiae, cataract, phthisis → Equine recurrent uveitis (moon blindness) — immune-mediated, leading cause of equine blindness; Appaloosas ~8× risk (leopard complex, ELA-A9).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Infectious agent most associated with equine recurrent uveitis?

plain: Infectious agent most associated with equine recurrent uveitis? Leptospira interrogans serovar Pomona (molecular mimicry with uveal/lens antigens); also Onchocerca.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: dexamethasone only after fluorescein excludes an ulcer
(mydriasis, prevents posterior synechiae, relieves ciliary spasm), systemic

plain: Active ERU flare → treatment? Topical prednisolone acetate or dexamethasone only after fluorescein excludes an ulcer, topical atropine 1% (mydriasis, prevents posterior synechiae, relieves ciliary spasm), systemic flunixin 1.1 mg/kg; taper over weeks.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: ERU: options to reduce recurrences when medical control is inadequate?

plain: ERU: options to reduce recurrences when medical control is inadequate? Suprachoroidal cyclosporine implant (US standard, quiet eyes) or pars plana vitrectomy (Europe, Leptospira-positive eyes). Blind, painful, phthisical eye → enucleation.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: (gammaherpesvirus). EHV-1 abortion/EHM, EHV-3 coital exanthema, EHV-4

plain: Equine herpesvirus causing punctate keratoconjunctivitis? EHV-2 (gammaherpesvirus). EHV-1 abortion/EHM, EHV-3 coital exanthema, EHV-4 rhinopneumonitis.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Horse with blepharospasm preventing exam → which block, and what
does it not do? Auriculopalpebral block (CN VII motor)
at supraorbital foramen; cornea needs topical

plain: Horse with blepharospasm preventing exam → which block, and what does it not do? Auriculopalpebral block (CN VII motor) over the zygomatic arch → eyelid akinesia, no analgesia. Sensory upper lid = supraorbital (frontal, CN V) block at supraorbital foramen; cornea needs topical proparacaine.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Subpalpebral lavage system: why and where?
of painful eyes (melting ulcer, stromal abscess, uveitis) that resist
+ supraorbital blocks, tubing braided into the mane.

plain: Subpalpebral lavage system: why and where? For q1–2h topical medication of painful eyes (melting ulcer, stromal abscess, uveitis) that resist handling; footplate in the dorsal conjunctival fornix under auriculopalpebral + supraorbital blocks, tubing braided into the mane. Not for nasolacrimal obstruction — that is flushed.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Unilateral epiphora, no pain, Schirmer normal, fluorescein negative, dye
flush retrograde via the nasal punctum
on the floor of the nostril;
dacryocystorhinography if flush fails; topical antibiotic-steroid once patent.
Foal: imperforate nasal punctum — open surgically, stent 2–4 weeks.

plain: Unilateral epiphora, no pain, Schirmer normal, fluorescein negative, dye does not reach nostril → Nasolacrimal duct obstruction (failed Jones test); flush retrograde via the nasal punctum on the floor of the nostril; dacryocystorhinography if flush fails; topical antibiotic-steroid once patent. Foal: imperforate nasal punctum — open surgically, stent 2–4 weeks.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology
plain: Rapidly "melting" gelatinous corneal ulcer; culture Pseudomonas aeruginosa → agents and treatment? Collagenase-producing Pseudomonas and β-hemolytic Streptococcus (fungi: Aspergillus, Fusarium). Topical tobramycin/gentamicin q1–2h + anticollagenase (autologous serum, EDTA, acetylcysteine), atropine, systemic flunixin; never topical steroids; conjunctival graft if >50% stromal loss.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Topical atropine in a horse with corneal ulcer → adverse effects? Ileus/
from systemic absorption (monitor gut sounds) and reduced tear
production impairing healing; use lowest effective frequency.

plain: Topical atropine in a horse with corneal ulcer → adverse effects? Ileus/ colic from systemic absorption (monitor gut sounds) and reduced tear production impairing healing; use lowest effective frequency.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Full-thickness eyelid laceration, presented 2 h later → repair? Minimal

plain: Full-thickness eyelid laceration, presented 2 h later → repair? Minimal debridement, two-layer primary closure, align margin first with figure-eight suture; never excise eyelid margin (lifelong corneal exposure).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Horse found to have a cataract → next step?
ERU is the most common acquired cause
ultrasound if fundus hidden, ERG before surgery. Congenital cataract in a

plain: Horse found to have a cataract → next step? Full ophthalmic exam for cause: ERU is the most common acquired cause (treat uveitis first), ocular ultrasound if fundus hidden, ERG before surgery. Congenital cataract in a normal eye → refer for phacoemulsification before ~6 months; advise against breeding (heritable in Belgians, Morgans).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Round dark free-floating anterior-chamber mass vs fixed fleshy iris mass
: transilluminates, floats, benign — diode laser deflation or
aspiration if obstructing vision. Iris melanoma: solid, opaque, does not

plain: Round dark free-floating anterior-chamber mass vs fixed fleshy iris mass → Uveal cyst: transilluminates, floats, benign — diode laser deflation or aspiration if obstructing vision. Iris melanoma: solid, opaque, does not transilluminate — excise/enucleate if progressive.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Pink raised ulcerated mass at limbus, third eyelid or non-pigmented eyelid
, the most common equine ocular tumor (UV, lack of pigment;
mutation). Excision (third eyelid en bloc) + adjunct
cryotherapy, β-irradiation, topical 5-FU/mitomycin C, cisplatin; locally

plain: Pink raised ulcerated mass at limbus, third eyelid or non-pigmented eyelid in a Paint/Appaloosa/Haflinger/Belgian → Ocular squamous cell carcinoma, the most common equine ocular tumor (UV, lack of pigment; Haflinger DDB2 mutation). Excision (third eyelid en bloc) + adjunct cryotherapy, β-irradiation, topical 5-FU/mitomycin C, cisplatin; locally invasive, metastasis <15% and late.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Foal normal at birth, at 1–4 days weak, icteric, hemoglobinuric after
makes colostral alloantibodies against paternal antigens (>90% Aa/

plain: Foal normal at birth, at 1–4 days weak, icteric, hemoglobinuric after nursing; multiparous mare → Neonatal isoerythrolysis — mare Aa- or Qa- negative makes colostral alloantibodies against paternal antigens (>90% Aa/ Qa; mules via donkey factor). Not "mare positive, stallion negative" — direction reversed.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

plain: NI foal management → Muzzle and withhold mare's milk 24–36 h (until gut closure), feed alternative colostrum/milk; transfuse washed dam RBCs (or Aa/ Qa-negative crossmatched gelding) if PCV <12–15%. Never sire's blood (carries the antigen); plasma does not fix anemia. Not 2–3 days — gut closes at ~24 h.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: NI prevention in a mare with known alloantibodies →
against stallion/foal RBCs late gestation or run
on colostrum; withhold colostrum 24–36 h. Risk recurs at every

plain: NI prevention in a mare with known alloantibodies → Screen mare serum against stallion/foal RBCs late gestation or run jaundiced foal agglutination test on colostrum; withhold colostrum 24–36 h. Risk recurs at every subsequent foaling.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: NI foal, bilirubin >20–27 mg/dL, seizures, opisthotonos →
(bilirubin encephalopathy); unconjugated bilirubin crosses immature BBB.
Prevent with early transfusion; grave once neurologic.

plain: NI foal, bilirubin >20–27 mg/dL, seizures, opisthotonos → Kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy); unconjugated bilirubin crosses immature BBB. Prevent with early transfusion; grave once neurologic.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Foal 24–36 h old, serum IgG <400 mg/dL (or <200) → Dx and treatment?
recheck IgG 12–24 h, repeat until >800; antibiotics if septic.

plain: Foal 24–36 h old, serum IgG <400 mg/dL (or <200) → Dx and treatment? Failure of passive transfer: <400 mg/dL failure (some references call <200 complete), 400–800 partial, ≥800 adequate. After gut closure (~18–24 h) oral colostrum is useless → IV hyperimmune plasma 1–2 L (20–40 mL/kg), recheck IgG 12–24 h, repeat until >800; antibiotics if septic. Not colostrum or whole blood at this age.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Foal <12–18 h old with low IgG →
>1.060) by bottle/tube; absorption maximal in first 6–8 h, closed by 24 h.

plain: Foal <12–18 h old with low IgG → 1–2 L good colostrum (Brix >23%, SG >1.060) by bottle/tube; absorption maximal in first 6–8 h, closed by 24 h. Check IgG at 12–24 h.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: dL); cria: IgG <800–1000 mg/dL (TP <5.5 g/dL), plasma 20–40 mL/kg IV.

plain: FPT thresholds in other species? Calf: IgG <1000 mg/dL (TP <5.2–5.5 g/ dL); cria: IgG <800–1000 mg/dL (TP <5.5 g/dL), plasma 20–40 mL/kg IV. Not 1600 for calves.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Arabian foal normal at birth, recurrent adenovirus/Pneumocystis/
Rhodococcus pneumonia from 1–3 months, lymphocytes <1000/µL, absent
mutation (no V(D)J recombination, no B or T

plain: Arabian foal normal at birth, recurrent adenovirus/Pneumocystis/ Rhodococcus pneumonia from 1–3 months, lymphocytes <1000/µL, absent IgM, thymic hypoplasia → Severe combined immunodeficiency — autosomal recessive DNA-PKcs mutation (no V(D)J recombination, no B or T cells); fatal by ~5 months as colostral antibody wanes. Not death by 2 months.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: SCID inheritance: what does it require of the parents? Both sire and dam
(~8% of Arabians); 25% affected, 50% carriers; DNA test
breeding stock, avoid carrier × carrier. Also ask Arabians about cerebellar

plain: SCID inheritance: what does it require of the parents? Both sire and dam are carriers (~8% of Arabians); 25% affected, 50% carriers; DNA test breeding stock, avoid carrier × carrier. Also ask Arabians about cerebellar abiotrophy, lavender foal syndrome.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: against SeM protein (also after influenza, EHV). Complications: skin

plain: Horse 2–4 weeks after strangles (or S. equi vaccination): fever, pitting edema of limbs/ventrum/head, mucosal petechiae → Purpura hemorrhagica — type III immune-complex leukocytoclastic vasculitis against SeM protein (also after influenza, EHV). Complications: skin sloughing, laminitis, infarctive colitis/myopathy.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: 44,000 IU/kg IV q6h) to clear residual
wraps. Do not vaccinate horses with SeM titers

plain: Purpura hemorrhagica treatment → Dexamethasone 0.05–0.2 mg/kg IV q24h tapered over 2–4+ weeks is the cornerstone, plus penicillin (22,000– 44,000 IU/kg IV q6h) to clear residual S. equi, NSAIDs, hydrotherapy, leg wraps. Do not vaccinate horses with SeM titers >1:3200. Not antibiotics alone — steroids are essential.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Horse with bilateral nasal discharge, petechiae, ecchymoses, limb edema

plain: Horse with bilateral nasal discharge, petechiae, ecchymoses, limb edema → key history question? Recent strangles exposure, infection or vaccination in the preceding 2–4 weeks (purpura hemorrhagica).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: How is regeneration assessed in an anemic horse? Bone marrow aspirate
(sternum/tuber coxae; M:E <0.5, erythroid hyperplasia) or serial PCV/MCV/
Splenic contraction (stores ~1/3 of RBC mass) masks acute loss.

plain: How is regeneration assessed in an anemic horse? Bone marrow aspirate (sternum/tuber coxae; M:E <0.5, erythroid hyperplasia) or serial PCV/MCV/ RDW rise — horses release no reticulocytes and show no polychromasia. Splenic contraction (stores ~1/3 of RBC mass) masks acute loss.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Horse with chronic infection, mild normocytic normochromic non-

plain: Horse with chronic infection, mild normocytic normochromic non- regenerative anemia → Anemia of chronic disease: low serum iron and TIBC, normal/high ferritin (hepcidin sequestration); PCV rarely <20%. Treat the cause, not with iron.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Postpartum mare PCV 11%, presumed uterine artery hemorrhage →
Whole blood or packed RBCs from a

plain: Postpartum mare PCV 11%, presumed uterine artery hemorrhage → treatment and transfusion math? Whole blood or packed RBCs from a crossmatched gelding when PCV <12–15%; ~2 mL/kg whole blood (1 mL/ kg packed cells) raises PCV ~1%.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Rouleaux on a horse blood smear? Normal in horses
suggests hyperglobulinemia). Distinguish from autoagglutination: rouleaux
disperse on 1:1 saline dilution, true agglutination does not.

plain: Rouleaux on a horse blood smear? Normal in horses (mild in cats; in dogs suggests hyperglobulinemia). Distinguish from autoagglutination: rouleaux disperse on 1:1 saline dilution, true agglutination does not.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Species whose eosinophils have very large raspberry/mulberry orange

plain: Species whose eosinophils have very large raspberry/mulberry orange granules obscuring the nucleus? Horse (cat granules rod-shaped; dog variable, vacuolated in greyhounds).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Most common equine skin tumor; verrucous/fibroblastic wart-like masses
at trauma sites on head, ventrum, limbs, paragenital skin →
(bovine papillomavirus 1/2); six forms; locally invasive, non-metastatic. A
small wound-site lesion that enlarges aggressively over weeks in a new horse is

plain: Most common equine skin tumor; verrucous/fibroblastic wart-like masses at trauma sites on head, ventrum, limbs, paragenital skin → Sarcoid (bovine papillomavirus 1/2); six forms; locally invasive, non-metastatic. A small wound-site lesion that enlarges aggressively over weeks in a new horse is fibroblastic sarcoid until proven otherwise.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Not SCC — favors pink mucocutaneous junctions in older

plain: Sarcoid: what accompanies surgical excision? Adjunct intralesional cisplatin (beads/electrochemotherapy), cryotherapy, imiquimod/5-FU, BCG (periocular), radiation — excision alone recurs in 50–60%; cisplatin needs handler protection. Not SCC — favors pink mucocutaneous junctions in older light-skinned horses.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Grey horse >15 years with firm black nodules under the tail, perineum,
grey horses >15 years (STX17 grey mutation). Slow-growing but most
eventually enlarge, ulcerate, obstruct or metastasize; excise small masses early,
cimetidine inconsistent, intralesional cisplatin, Oncept extralabel.

plain: Grey horse >15 years with firm black nodules under the tail, perineum, prepuce, parotid, lips → Melanoma (dermal melanomatosis) — ~80% of grey horses >15 years (STX17 grey mutation). Slow-growing but most eventually enlarge, ulcerate, obstruct or metastasize; excise small masses early, cimetidine inconsistent, intralesional cisplatin, Oncept extralabel. Not simply "good prognosis" — guarded long-term.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Melanoma in a bay/chestnut (non-grey) horse vs grey →
prognosis; grey-horse melanomas behave indolently for years.

plain: Melanoma in a bay/chestnut (non-grey) horse vs grey → Non-grey melanomas are uncommon but more often malignant/metastatic with poorer prognosis; grey-horse melanomas behave indolently for years.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Ulcerated 1–2 cm preputial lesions plus variably pigmented perianal
Melanoma classic for grey horses; ulcerated

plain: Ulcerated 1–2 cm preputial lesions plus variably pigmented perianal nodules in a grey stallion → Melanoma classic for grey horses; ulcerated poorly pigmented genital lesions need biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Mass on penis/prepuce of an older gelding → tumor and sedative to
non-pigmented skin; metastasizes to inguinal nodes) — excision, cryotherapy,

plain: Mass on penis/prepuce of an older gelding → tumor and sedative to examine? Squamous cell carcinoma (most common penile tumor; smegma, non-pigmented skin; metastasizes to inguinal nodes) — excision, cryotherapy, 5-FU or partial phallectomy. Acepromazine relaxes the penis for exam; avoid in breeding stallions (priapism/paraphimosis).

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Old horse with weight loss, dysphagia, ptyalism, halitosis, ventral edema;
gastroscopy or formalin specimen shows ulcerated proliferative mass in
, most common equine gastric tumor; peritoneal/hepatic metastasis
(neoplastic cells in peritoneal fluid); grave, euthanasia.

plain: Old horse with weight loss, dysphagia, ptyalism, halitosis, ventral edema; gastroscopy or formalin specimen shows ulcerated proliferative mass in the squamous (non-glandular) stomach → Gastric squamous cell carcinoma, most common equine gastric tumor; peritoneal/hepatic metastasis (neoplastic cells in peritoneal fluid); grave, euthanasia.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: Mare with stallion-like aggression, nymphomania or anestrus; one large
multicystic "honeycomb" ovary, contralateral small and inactive →
GnRH — hormones do not treat it.

plain: Mare with stallion-like aggression, nymphomania or anestrus; one large multicystic "honeycomb" ovary, contralateral small and inactive → Granulosa (theca) cell tumor, most common equine ovarian tumor; inhibin ↑ (~90%), AMH ↑ (most reliable), testosterone ↑ (~50%), progesterone <1 ng/ mL. Unilateral ovariectomy; other ovary cycles again in 6–12 months. Not GnRH — hormones do not treat it.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology

spans.text: One ovary 3× enlarged and cystic but the contralateral ovary is normal
Ovarian hematoma or hemorrhagic anovulatory follicle
examine in 2–4 weeks for regression. GTCT suppresses the opposite ovary via
inhibin, so a normal contralateral ovary argues against it.

plain: One ovary 3× enlarged and cystic but the contralateral ovary is normal and cycling → Ovarian hematoma or hemorrhagic anovulatory follicle; re- examine in 2–4 weeks for regression. GTCT suppresses the opposite ovary via inhibin, so a normal contralateral ovary argues against it.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology
section: Theriogenology — Cycle, Breeding and Early Pregnancy

spans.text: Mare: type of breeder and ovulator; cycle, estrus, ovulation timing, foal
heat, gestation? Seasonally polyestrous long-day, spontaneous ovulator
ovulation 24–48 h before end of estrus
365 days — too long; 21 days is cycle, not estrus.

plain: Mare: type of breeder and ovulator; cycle, estrus, ovulation timing, foal heat, gestation? Seasonally polyestrous long-day, spontaneous ovulator; cycle 21–22 days, estrus 5–7 days, ovulation 24–48 h before end of estrus; foal heat 5–12 (avg 9) days postpartum; gestation ~340 days (320–365). Not 365 days — too long; 21 days is cycle, not estrus.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology
section: Theriogenology — Cycle, Breeding and Early Pregnancy

spans.text: Breed every other day from day 2–3 of estrus
until ovulation, or once within 48 h before/6 h after ovulation; ovum viable ~6–

plain: Breeding timing in the mare → Breed every other day from day 2–3 of estrus until ovulation, or once within 48 h before/6 h after ovulation; ovum viable ~6– 12 h, sperm ~48 h.

chapter: Chapter 24 — Equine — Dermatology, Ophthalmology, Theriogenology, Hematology & Oncology
section: Theriogenology — Cycle, Breeding and Early Pregnancy

spans.text: Dominant follicle ≥35 mm with uterine edema → drug to induce
eCG is not used in mares; PGF2α lyses the CL. Cattle use GnRH.

plain: Dominant follicle ≥35 mm with uterine edema → drug to induce ovulation? hCG 1500–3000 IU IV (ovulates 36–48 h) or deslorelin (~40 h). eCG is not used in mares; PGF2α lyses the CL. Cattle use GnRH.

plain: Where does the mobile equine conceptus fix, and when? At the base (caudal flexure) of either horn around day 16–17, no side preference; mobility before then is required for maternal recognition of pregnancy. Vesicle visible on ultrasound from day 12–14.

plain: Mare at day 14–15 ultrasound shows two embryonic vesicles → management? Manually crush one vesicle transrectally before fixation (day 16–17), success >90%; twins are the leading non-infectious cause of equine abortion. Fixed unilateral twins at day 17–30: attempt separation; otherwise terminate with PGF2α before endometrial cups (day 35–40). Not referral for surgery.

plain: Mare with sunken anus, tipped vulva, windsucking and recurrent endometritis → procedure and rule? Caslick's vulvoplasty — suture dorsal vulvar lips to the level of the pelvic brim, leaving a ventral opening; must be opened (episiotomy) 1–2 weeks before foaling and before natural cover, then re-closed. Not for perineal tears — those need perineal body reconstruction.

plain: Several late-term (7–11 month) abortions after mild respiratory illness in young stock; fresh non-autolyzed fetus with pleural fluid, pulmonary edema, hepatic necrosis, intranuclear inclusions → EHV-1 abortion (most common infectious cause of equine late-term abortion); Dx PCR/VI of fetal tissue; isolate aborting mares. plain: Infectious causes of abortion in the mare? EHV-1 (late, storms), ascending placentitis (Streptococcus zooepidemicus), Leptospira, nocardioform placentitis, equine viral arteritis (reportable), MRLS (caterpillars). Twinning is the top non-infectious cause.

plain: Mare at 8 months with premature udder development and vaginal discharge; ultrasound shows placental thickening/separation (CTUP >12 mm at 9–10 months) → Ascending placentitis (S. zooepidemicus, E. coli). Prolong pregnancy: TMS 30 mg/kg q12h (crosses placenta), flunixin/ firocoxib, altrenogest 0.088 mg/kg PO q24h to term, ± pentoxifylline. Not C- section or termination.

plain: Late-gestation mare on endophyte-infected tall fescue: prolonged gestation, agalactia, thickened placenta/"red bag", dystocia, weak large foal → Fescue toxicosis — ergovaline (Epichloë/Neotyphodium coenophialum) is a dopamine D2 agonist suppressing prolactin. Remove from fescue 60–90 days pre-foaling; domperidone 1.1 mg/kg PO q24h from 10–15 days before due date (D2 antagonist).

plain: Mare at 9 months with mild intermittent colic; rectal: broad ligaments taut and crossing over/under the uterus → Uterine torsion (last trimester in mares, cranial to cervix so vaginal exam unremarkable; cows torse at parturition). Standing flank laparotomy preferred; rolling with plank-in-flank under anesthesia earlier in gestation; C-section near term. Mare survival ~85– 90%.

plain: Colicky mare: rectal findings separating uterine torsion from nephrosplenic entrapment → Torsion: diagonal taut broad ligament over the uterus. Entrapment: distended colon dorsal to the spleen in the nephrosplenic space, spleen displaced; ultrasound shows left kidney obscured by gas; treat phenylephrine + exercise/rolling or surgery.

plain: When is the equine placenta retained, and why urgent? >3 hours is abnormal; mares develop septic metritis → endotoxemia → laminitis (the most serious sequela) within 24–48 h. Cows: not urgent, membranes pass in days, manual removal discouraged, treat only if febrile.

plain: Mare 3–6 h post-foaling with membranes hanging → treatment of choice? Oxytocin 10–20 IU IM/IV q1–2h or 30–60 IU in 1 L saline slow IV; tie membranes above hocks, never pull forcibly (hemorrhage, inversion, retained tags). Beyond 6–8 h add broad-spectrum antibiotics, flunixin, uterine lavage, tetanus, ice feet. Not intrauterine iodine as the primary therapy.

plain: Post-foaling mare with colic, pale membranes, tachycardia, sweating (or 5 days postpartum pale with frank blood from a swollen horn) → Uterine/ broad-ligament artery hemorrhage (older multiparous mares). Quiet dark stall, no transport, minimal rectals, IV fluids/blood, aminocaproic or tranexamic acid, analgesia, antibiotics; heparin contraindicated. Not vitamin K — no clotting-factor deficiency. Toxic metritis differs: fetid discharge, fever.

plain: Foal with urine dribbling from the umbilicus → Patent urachus (congenital or secondary to omphalitis/sepsis). Ultrasound umbilical remnants, check IgG, broad-spectrum antibiotics; many close spontaneously; resect if infected or persistent; chemical cautery discouraged.

plain: Drug classically causing priapism/penile paralysis in stallions and geldings → Acepromazine (phenothiazine α-blockade); avoid in breeding stallions. Priapism is an emergency: benztropine 8 mg IV, cold hydrotherapy, massage, support, corpus cavernosum lavage.

Remove any hair ring; cold hydrotherapy, massage, hyperosmotic dressings, emollients, sling support against the abdomen, NSAIDs, replace with purse-string; chronic → phallectomy.

plain: Stallion acutely colicky and lame after breeding with swollen scrotum → Acquired inguinal/scrotal hernia with strangulated small intestine — surgical emergency; confirm by rectal palpation of bowel at the vaginal ring and scrotal ultrasound; reduce, resect, usually unilateral castration and ring closure.

plain: Stallion with unilateral cold, firm, painless scrotal enlargement → Testicular neoplasia (seminoma most common; teratoma in young/ cryptorchid testes); ultrasound then unilateral castration with histopathology. Hot painful scrotum with colic = torsion, orchitis or hernia.

plain: Unilateral cryptorchid stallion (or dog) → advice? Do not breed; remove both testes — heritable, and the retained testis has increased neoplasia and torsion risk. Not "it will recur in this animal" — the issue is transmission to offspring.

plain: Stallion with multiple 1–2 cm vesicles → pustules → ulcers on penis/ prepuce/perineum after breeding, healing with depigmented spots → Equine coital exanthema (EHV-3); heals in 2–3 weeks, no systemic illness, fertility unaffected. Sexual rest until healed, topical antiseptic, AI-equipment hygiene; no vaccine. Differentials: habronemiasis, SCC, dourine (T. equiperdum, reportable). Not melanoma — nodular black masses in greys.

plain: Several mares bred by one healthy stallion develop copious mucopurulent vaginal discharge 10–14 days post-breeding and short-cycle → Contagious equine metritis (Taylorella equigenitalis) — venereal foreign animal disease, immediately reportable. Culture clitoral fossa/sinuses and stallion urethral fossa on Amies charcoal medium or PCR; stallions are asymptomatic carriers; chlorhexidine wash + nitrofurazone 5 days, quarantine.

plain: AAEP core vaccines for every horse (rabies already given) → Tetanus, EEE/WEE, West Nile virus + rabies, all annual (arboviruses in spring before mosquito season). Risk-based: influenza, EHV-1/4, strangles, Potomac horse fever, botulism, leptospirosis, rotavirus, anthrax. Not influenza — risk-based, not core.

plain: Pregnant mare: when to booster so colostrum protects the foal; when does the foal start core vaccines? → Booster 4–6 weeks before foaling (EHV-1 at 5, 7, 9 months). Foals of vaccinated mares start core series at 4–6 months (rabies at 6 months); foals of unvaccinated mares at 3–4 months.

plain: Vaccinated horse with a fresh wound, rectal tear or surgery → tetanus prophylaxis? Toxoid booster if last dose >6 months ago; nothing if within 6 months. Unvaccinated/unknown: antitoxin 1,500–3,000 IU + toxoid at a separate site, complete series in 3–4 weeks. Antitoxin carries a small risk of serum hepatitis (Theiler's disease).

plain: Horse recovered from strangles within the year, or with a high SeM titer → vaccinate? No — defer; SeM titer ≥1:3,200 means recent exposure and vaccination risks purpura hemorrhagica (titers >1:12,800 suggest purpura/ bastard strangles). Never vaccinate during an outbreak.

plain: Horse at a show becomes dull and febrile; disease spreading → Isolate immediately (separate stall, equipment, handlers), take rectal temperatures of all horses twice daily, notify show veterinarian/state officials if reportable (EHV-1, strangles, influenza).

plain: Strangles: when are antibiotics indicated? Once lymph nodes are abscessing: hot-pack, lance, drain, no antibiotics (penicillin delays maturation, may blunt immunity). Penicillin only for early febrile cases before abscessation, dyspnea/ retropharyngeal obstruction, bastard strangles or purpura; tracheotomy for airway obstruction.

plain: Strangles outbreak on a farm → control? Stop movement; temperatures twice daily, isolate febrile horses at once (fever precedes shedding by 24–48 h); cohort into infected / exposed / clean groups; clear with 3 negative nasopharyngeal washes/PCR 1 week apart or guttural pouch endoscopy; rest premises 4 weeks. Not prophylactic penicillin or vaccinating in-contacts — purpura risk.

plain: Horse weeks–months after strangles with intermittent purulent nasal discharge; endoscopy shows pus and chondroids in the guttural pouch → Guttural pouch empyema — the carrier state (~10%) that seeds new outbreaks. Repeated lavage, chondroid removal (endoscopic basket/surgery), topical penicillin-gelatin gel; confirm clearance by PCR of pouch lavage.

plain: 2–4 weeks after strangles or vaccination: pitting edema of limbs and head, petechiae, fever → Purpura hemorrhagica — type III immune-complex vasculitis to M-protein. Dexamethasone/prednisolone, penicillin, supportive care; mortality from skin sloughing, colic, laminitis.

plain: Adult horse with chronic weight loss, intermittent fever, recurrent colic, hyperfibrinogenemia, hyperglobulinemia; firm mesenteric mass on rectal → Internal abdominal abscess (bastard strangles; R. equi in foals). Ultrasound-guided aspirate, abdominocentesis (high protein, neutrophils); months of penicillin or surgical drainage.

plain: 1–6-month-old foal on a dusty endemic farm with insidious fever, cough, tachypnea; abscessing pneumonia on ultrasound/radiographs → Rhodococcus equi (VapA-positive, facultative intracellular). Macrolide + rifampin (clarithromycin 7.5 mg/kg PO q12h or azithromycin + rifampin 5 mg/kg q12h) 4–9 weeks; watch hyperthermia, diarrhea. plain: Coggins (AGID) or ELISA positive for equine infectious anemia → required management? Reportable; confirm, then euthanasia or lifelong quarantine ≥200 yards from other equids with permanent identification (brand/freeze mark); test in-contacts. plain: Late-summer horse with fever, ataxia, head pressing/circling or muzzle fasciculations; EEE or WNV confirmed; owner asks if she can catch it → No — horses are dead-end hosts (viremia too low to infect mosquitoes); humans are infected only by mosquito bites from the bird reservoir. Reduce mosquito exposure; vaccinate other horses; reportable. Not "zoonotic, be cautious around the horse." How are EEE/WEE acquired and controlled? Mosquito bite: Culiseta melanura maintains the EEE bird cycle (Culex tarsalis for WEE), bridge vectors infect horses and people. Horse vaccination protects horses but does not reduce human risk (dead-end hosts); mosquito control does. VEE is the exception — horses amplify virus. EEE mortality 75–90%; WNV ~30%. Not bird control.

plain: Horse vaccinated for WEE, rabies, tetanus (or WNV/EHV) → which poses a direct zoonotic risk to handlers and how? Rabies — saliva contact (bite, mucous membranes, broken skin); a rabid horse presenting as colic or lameness exposes many handlers. Arboviruses: horses are dead-end hosts; tetanus not contagious; EHV not zoonotic. Rabies is the core vaccine of greatest public-health importance.

plain: Horse or cow exposed to a rabid skunk/raccoon → management by vaccination status? Currently vaccinated (USDA-licensed vaccine for the species): booster immediately + 45-day observation. Unvaccinated: euthanasia/slaughter immediately (meat usable within 7 days of exposure, bite tissues discarded) or 6-month close confinement. Overdue but documented: case-by-case, usually booster + 45 days. Not a 3-dose series — not in the compendium.

MLV may cause abortion/latency — avoid in naive pregnant cows.

Move quietly off pasture — handling can kill; supportive only (NSAIDs, furosemide).

plain: Prevention of fog fever? Monensin or lasalocid for several days before and after turnout (ionophores suppress 3-MI-producing bacteria), gradual introduction over 10–14 days, limit grazing time, feed hay first. Monensin is preventive, not a treatment for clinical cases.

Remove hay source, corticosteroids. Fog fever is acute, after lush pasture, via 3-MI.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Definitive treatment of LDA and the metabolic derangement to correct? Surgical fixation — right paramedian abomasopexy, right flank omentopexy, left flank abomasopexy, or roll-and-toggle (toggle-pin); treat concurrent ketosis/metritis. Derangement: hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (sequestered HCl, paradoxical aciduria) → NaCl + KCl fluids. Not calcium gluconate — only if hypocalcemic.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: IV fluid of choice for LDA/RDA/abomasal volvulus/vagal indigestion (abomasal outflow obstruction)? 0.9% NaCl with KCl (20–40 mEq/L; or oral KCl 60–200 g). Field alternative: hypertonic 7.2% saline 4–5 mL/kg IV over 5–10 min followed by free-choice water (20–40 L). Avoid LRS and bicarbonate (alkalinizing).

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

Prognosis worse with HR >100–120, Cl <80 mEq/L, high lactate.

plain: How is abomasal volvulus distinguished from simple RDA? By systemic deterioration — tachycardia >100, dehydration, shock, pain, marked alkalosis, ping extending cranially. Rolling is for LDA only; right pings always need surgery. Not rumen chloride — elevated in any abomasal reflux, both conditions.

plain: Why is right displacement more serious than left? RDA progresses to volvulus with vascular compromise, shock and death within hours; LDA is rarely strangulating.

plain: Cow had right flank omentopexy for LDA; one month later a right ping at ribs 11–13 and off feed → Failed/torn omentopexy with recurrent (right) displacement or volvulus → re-operate (pyloro-omentopexy). Cecal dilatation pings more caudally. Not pneumoperitoneum — bilateral dorsal ping resolving within 1–2 weeks.

Abomasal outflow/pyloric or proximal duodenal obstruction (volvulus, displacement, impaction) with reflux of HCl into the rumen ("internal vomiting"), accompanied by hypochloremic hypokalemic alkalosis and paradoxical aciduria.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine
plain: Confirmation of hardware disease? Positive withers-pinch/pole test, reticular radiography (metal, abscess gas–fluid interface), reticular ultrasound, metal detector; neutrophilia with hyperfibrinogenemia.
