plain: Treatment and prevention of hardware disease? Oral rumen magnet + procaine penicillin or oxytetracycline 3–7 days, confinement with forequarters elevated; rumenotomy if no response in 2–3 days or valuable cow. Prevent: prophylactic magnet once at 6–12 months of age, feed-line magnets. Sequelae: traumatic pericarditis (MSC, grave), vagal indigestion, diaphragmatic/liver abscess.

plain: Cow weeks after hardware disease (or late pregnancy) with chronic weight loss, "papple" abdomen (apple left dorsal, pear right ventral), bradycardia, scant feces, L-shaped rumen on rectal → Vagal indigestion (Hoflund syndrome) — functional outflow failure from reticular adhesions/ vagal damage, abomasal ulcers, lymphosarcoma, late gestation. Ping absent; rumen hypermotile or atonic. Prognosis guarded; rumenotomy/treat cause or salvage.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

omasal transport failure (frothy rumen, after TRP adhesions);

plain: Types of vagal indigestion? Type I failure of eructation (free-gas bloat); Type II omasal transport failure (frothy rumen, after TRP adhesions); Type III pyloric outflow failure/abomasal impaction (hypochloremic alkalosis); Type IV indigestion of late gestation.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Management of type II vagal indigestion? IV balanced electrolytes, oral fluids with 20–30 g KCl, transfaunation 8–16 L rumen fluid, antimicrobials; most need right-flank surgery to examine omasum/abomasum/pylorus.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Heavily pregnant cow with type III vagal indigestion (abomasal impaction) → prognosis and management? Poor. Within ~4–6 weeks of term: support (oral/IV potassium, mineral oil, magnesium hydroxide) until the calf is viable; far from term: therapeutic abortion/assisted delivery.

plain: Cow with rumen atony (<1 contraction per 2 minutes; normal 1–3 strong/2 min) → causes and approach? Hypocalcemia, grain overload, TRP, vagal indigestion, endotoxemia (mastitis, metritis), abomasal displacement, prolonged anorexia. Treat the cause, correct calcium, check rumen pH, oral alfalfa, transfaunation 5–10 L.

plain: Cow with sudden anorexia, reduced motility and mild bloat 12–24 h after a feed change; afebrile, recovers in 1–2 days → Simple indigestion. Good hay, transfaunation (5–10 L), oral fluids; change rations gradually over 7–10 days. Lacks the systemic acidosis of grain overload.

spans.text: Cattle broke into grain/corn bin; 12–36 h later depressed, ataxic/

plain: Cattle broke into grain/corn bin; 12–36 h later depressed, ataxic/ recumbent, hypothermic, dehydrated, splashy atonic rumen, profuse foul (not bloody) diarrhea, rumen pH 4.8 → Acute rumen lactic acidosis (grain overload): Streptococcus bovis then lactobacilli → lactate; rumen pH <5.5 (normal 6–7), dead protozoa, Gram-positive shift; osmotic fluid shift into rumen → systemic metabolic acidosis and dehydration.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

, thiamine, NSAIDs, transfaunation; add potassium after acidosis

plain: Treatment of grain overload? Rumenotomy or rumen lavage if severe; oral magnesium hydroxide ~1 g/kg, penicillin (oral/IV), IV fluids with isotonic bicarbonate, thiamine, NSAIDs, transfaunation; add potassium after acidosis corrects.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Sequelae in cattle surviving grain overload?
later caudal vena cava thrombosis with hemoptysis/epistaxis),

plain: Sequelae in cattle surviving grain overload? Chemical rumenitis → liver abscesses (Fusobacterium necrophorum, Trueperella pyogenes via portal vein; later caudal vena cava thrombosis with hemoptysis/epistaxis), mycotic rumenitis, laminitis, thiamine-responsive polioencephalomalacia. Prevent: gradual adaptation, roughage, buffers, monensin, tylosin in feed (VFD).

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Feedlot cattle on high grain with multiple liver abscesses at slaughter →

plain: Feedlot cattle on high grain with multiple liver abscesses at slaughter → agent? Fusobacterium necrophorum (± T. pyogenes), rumenitis–liver abscess complex; usually subclinical.

plain: First intervention for an acutely bloated, dyspneic cow or calf? Pass an orogastric tube first — relieves free-gas bloat and diagnoses choke if it will not pass; frothy bloat gets antifoaming agent through it. Trocarize at left paralumbar fossa only when the tube fails and death is imminent. Not trocar and cannula first — emergency measure only.

Relieve free-gas bloat first (tube if passable, trocar/fistula if not), then gently advance object with probang or remove by external manipulation; sedation/antispasmodic (xylazine). Risks: aspiration, pressure necrosis.

plain: Heifer with a permanent rumen fistula — indications? Chronic recurrent free-gas bloat with failed eructation — vagal indigestion, esophageal/ pharyngeal lesions, choke that cannot be relieved, mediastinal adhesions; self- retaining trocar or 2–3 cm rumenostomy vents gas and granulates closed in months. Also rumen-fluid donors.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Early-lactation high-producing dairy cow with melena, pale mucous membranes, mild colic, milk drop → Type 2 (bleeding) abomasal ulcer — concurrent LDA, ketosis, stress, or abomasal lymphosarcoma (BLV). Remove stress/concentrate, high fiber; blood transfusion if PCV <12–14%; oral antacids/H2 blockers/omeprazole have poor efficacy in adult ruminants.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Abomasal ulcer classification and location by age? Type 1

plain: Abomasal ulcer classification and location by age? Type 1 non-perforating erosions; Type 2 bleeding (melena, anemia); Type 3 perforating with localized peritonitis; Type 4 perforating with diffuse peritonitis (grave). Calves (weaning, hairballs): pyloric region; adults: fundic/body.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Three diseases that most commonly cause true colic in adult cattle?
Abomasal volvulus, cecal dilatation/volvulus, small-intestinal obstruction
(intussusception, intestinal volvulus, hemorrhagic bowel syndrome) — all
surgical emergencies. Simple LDA, TRP and vagal indigestion rarely cause

plain: Three diseases that most commonly cause true colic in adult cattle? Abomasal volvulus, cecal dilatation/volvulus, small-intestinal obstruction (intussusception, intestinal volvulus, hemorrhagic bowel syndrome) — all surgical emergencies. Simple LDA, TRP and vagal indigestion rarely cause overt colic.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Postpartum cow on high concentrate with reduced appetite/milk, mild

plain: Postpartum cow on high concentrate with reduced appetite/milk, mild colic, right paralumbar fossa ping extending caudally to pelvic inlet/tuber coxae; gas-filled blind-ended "loaf of bread" viscus palpable per rectum → Cecal dilatation (± volvulus/retroflexion) — VFA accumulation → cecal atony. Volvulus: acute colic, tachycardia, no feces.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Treatment of cecal dilatation vs volvulus?
(IV fluids + KCl, calcium, mineral oil/MgSO4, transfaunation, withhold grain).

plain: Treatment of cecal dilatation vs volvulus? Dilatation: medical trial 24–48 h (IV fluids + KCl, calcium, mineral oil/MgSO4, transfaunation, withhold grain). Volvulus or no response: right flank laparotomy with typhlotomy (evacuate, derotate); partial typhlectomy if devitalized or recurrent. Recurrence common.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Adult cow with colic, scant dark-red mucus-rich "raspberry jam" feces, distended small-intestine loops and a sausage-shaped mass on rectal → Intussusception (jejunal/ileocecal): venous congestion leaks blood and mucus into empty distal bowel. Right flank laparotomy, resection and anastomosis; fair prognosis if within 24–48 h. DDx hemorrhagic bowel syndrome, cecal/ abomasal volvulus.

plain: Most common infectious cause of diarrhea in 1–3-week-old calves? Cryptosporidium parvum; supportive care, halofuginone where available.

plain: Housed adult cattle in winter: explosive outbreak of dark bloody foul diarrhea, sharp milk drop, mild cough; 50–100% morbidity, few deaths, recovery in 1–2 weeks → Winter dysentery (bovine coronavirus); self- limiting, supportive care only, no antimicrobials. Not grain overload — foul gray not bloody diarrhea, dehydration, deaths. DDx salmonellosis (fever, deaths), BVD, coccidiosis (youngstock).

plain: Calf with several days of diarrhea, depressed, weak suckle → expected acid-base/electrolyte pattern? Metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss + D- lactate from colonic fermentation), hyperkalemia despite total-body K depletion (acidosis shifts K out of cells, reduced renal excretion → bradycardia), hyponatremia, hypochloremia, hypoglycemia, prerenal azotemia. Correcting acidosis and volume lowers K; then supplement.

plain: Fluid therapy and bicarbonate dosing for the acidotic scouring calf? Deficit (mEq) = 0.5–0.6 × BW (kg) × base deficit; give half as isotonic 1.3% NaHCO3 IV over hours, reassess. IV for calves unable to suck, recumbent or base deficit >10–15; otherwise oral electrolytes with alkalinizing agent (acetate/propionate/bicarbonate) while continuing milk. Each 0.1 pH fall raises K ~0.6 mEq/L.

plain: Calf delivered after dystocia is meconium-stained, dyspneic and weak → resuscitation? Vigor assessment (HR >100, respiratory effort, tone, nasal- stimulation response, MM color); clear nasopharynx (brief head-down — do not hang by hind legs), stimulate (cold water, straw in nostril), doxapram 1–2 mL IV/sublingual if apneic, oxygen, warmth; colostrum ≥10% BW within 6 h (tube if weak).

plain: Two of 15 lactating beef cows found dead on lush spring pasture with paddling marks; others hyperexcitable, stiff, staggering, convulsing → Hypomagnesemic tetany (grass tetany), serum Mg <1.2 mg/dL; high-K, high-N lush grass blocks rumen Mg absorption and cattle have no Mg reserve. Tx IV calcium-magnesium borogluconate slowly + 200 mL 50% MgSO4 SC; sedate convulsions first.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Daily magnesium supplementation to prevent grass tetany? ~60 g magnesium oxide per cow per day (~30–35 g elemental Mg) in concentrate, mineral, water or dusted on pasture during the risk period. 600 g causes diarrhea; 6 mg is meaningless.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Feedlot/wintered cattle on high grain or weathered hay without green forage: night blindness, convulsions, papilledema; cows deliver blind, weak or stillborn calves → Vitamin A deficiency — night blindness is the earliest sign; blindness from optic nerve constriction is permanent. Confirm low plasma/liver retinol; inject vitamin A 440 IU/kg, green feed.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

plain: Cattle on molybdenum-rich or peaty pasture: faded coat with "spectacles" around eyes (achromotrichia), diarrhea, anemia, poor growth, spontaneous fractures; lambs born with swayback → Copper deficiency (primary, or secondary to Mo, S, Fe antagonism). Cu enzymes: tyrosinase (pigment), lysyl oxidase (bone collagen), cytochrome oxidase (myelin), ceruloplasmin (iron use → nonregenerative anemia).

plain: Confirmation and treatment of copper deficiency? Liver copper (best; ~<20–25 ppm wet weight deficient) rather than serum. Copper oxide wire boluses or injectable copper glycinate; address antagonists. Sheep are prone to copper toxicity — dose carefully. Cobalt/B12 deficiency also causes ruminant anemia; iron deficiency in milk-fed veal calves.

plain: Vigorous 3-day-old calf found dead, or fast-growing calves stiff, recumbent, dysphagic with pale white streaks in muscle, on selenium-poor pasture → Nutritional myodegeneration (white muscle disease): vitamin E/ selenium deficiency → peroxidative necrosis; cardiac form fatal. Confirm ↑CK/AST, low whole-blood Se/glutathione peroxidase. Inject Se/vit E (0.055 mg Se/kg); supplement dams in late gestation.

plain: Stiff calf with ↑CK vs calf with enlarged painful joints/physes and bowed limbs → deficiency? Stiffness + ↑CK/AST → Se/vitamin E; enlarged epiphyses/bowed limbs → rickets (vitamin D/phosphorus) or copper deficiency (epiphysitis, pale coat). Exclude septic polyarthritis by arthrocentesis.

Prevent with iodized salt or EDDI in the dam's mineral through pregnancy. Avian equivalent: thyroid hyperplasia in seed-fed budgerigars.

plain: Beef heifer near term switched from grain to poor roughage, now recumbent with live fetus → problem and work-up? Pregnancy toxemia/ protein-energy malnutrition (late-gestation ketosis) — check urine/serum BHB together with Ca, P, Mg. IV dextrose, propylene glycol, calcium if low; induce/C-section if unresponsive; fix ration. True milk fever is rare in heifers before calving.

plain: Treatment of milk fever? 500 mL 23% calcium borogluconate (~10.7 g Ca) slowly IV over 10–20 min while auscultating the heart (stop if arrhythmia), ± 500 mL SC; oral acidogenic calcium chloride/sulfate bolus 12 h later. Not vitamin D3 — prepartum prevention (2–8 days before calving) only, never treatment.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

how is it prevented? Parathyroid hormone
close-up diets cause metabolic alkalosis that blunts PTH-receptor

plain: Milk fever is associated with impaired response to which hormone, and how is it prevented? Parathyroid hormone — high-K (positive DCAD) close-up diets cause metabolic alkalosis that blunts PTH-receptor responsiveness, delaying bone resorption and 1,25-vitamin D. Prevent with anionic salts (negative DCAD; urine pH 6.0–6.5) or low-calcium prepartum diets, oral calcium at calving.

plain: Separating hypocalcemia from hypomagnesemia in a recumbent cow? Milk fever: periparturient dairy cow, flaccid paresis, S-curve neck, bloat, no tetany (↓acetylcholine release). Grass tetany: lactating cow on lush pasture, hyperexcitability, tremors, tetany, convulsions (loss of NMDA inhibition). Both get IV Ca-Mg borogluconate; tetany may need sedation first.

plain: Dairy cow 2–6 weeks postpartum, dull, milk drop, refuses grain but eats hay, empty rumen, sweet acetone breath, ketonuria → Primary (type I) ketosis from negative energy balance (peak lactation precedes peak intake; oxaloacetate depleted → acetyl-CoA to ketones). Confirm blood BHB >1.2– 1.4 mmol/L; always check for LDA (secondary ketosis).

plain: Treatment and prevention of ketosis? 500 mL 50% dextrose IV + propylene glycol 300 mL PO q24h for 3–5 days; dexamethasone 20 mg IM if not pregnant. Prevent: maximize transition dry-matter intake, dry-cow BCS 3.0–3.5, monensin, bunk space. Dilution: 100 mL 50% dextrose in 900 mL saline = 5%.

plain: Over-conditioned cow 1–2 weeks post-calving: anorexia, ketonuria, depression, poor response to ketosis therapy, ↑NEFA and liver enzymes → Fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis): ruminant liver has limited VLDL export. Confirm liver biopsy triglyceride >10%; IV dextrose, propylene glycol, glucocorticoids, insulin; poor prognosis when severe. Prevent BCS ≤3.5–3.75 at dry-off.

plain: Gross liver at necropsy: icteric orange vs pale yellow greasy vs multifocal necrotic foci in a 1–6-week foal → Orange/icteric = hemolysis (anaplasmosis, leptospirosis, copper toxicity); pale yellow greasy = hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver/ketosis in cows, lipidosis in cats); multifocal necrosis in foal = Tyzzer's disease (Clostridium piliforme).

Culture mid-stream urine; procaine penicillin 22,000 IU/kg q12–24h for ≥3 weeks (C. renale) or TMS/ceftiofur (E. coli); unilateral nephrectomy if refractory; cull if bilateral/azotemic. In dogs: mainly E. coli (Staph, Proteus, Klebsiella), culture-guided 4–6 weeks.

plain: Cow with hematuria and a small firm kidney (vs enlarged) on rectal → End-stage chronic pyelonephritis (fibrosis follows the enlargement phase); in a young animal renal hypoplasia/dysplasia. Hematuria with normal kidneys and no pain → enzootic hematuria (bracken fern bladder tumors) or cystitis.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

first, then sigmoid flexure — amputating the process relieves

plain: Most common site of urethral obstruction in steers vs wethers/bucks? Steers: distal sigmoid flexure. Sheep/goats: urethral process (vermiform appendage) first, then sigmoid flexure — amputating the process relieves many small-ruminant cases. Surgical salvage: tube cystostomy or perineal urethrostomy.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

Suburethral (urethral) diverticulum at the ischial arch

plain: Why is urethral catheterization impractical in male ruminants? Suburethral (urethral) diverticulum at the ischial arch and the sigmoid flexure block retrograde passage.

chapter: Chapter 27 — Bovine — Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal, Nutrition/Metabolic, Urinary & Endocrine

spans.text: Range steers on native siliceous grasses (Nevada/

plain: Urolith type by diet → Range steers on native siliceous grasses (Nevada/ western US): silica. Feedlot high-grain: struvite (Mg ammonium phosphate). Legume/clover pasture: calcium carbonate. Prevent: water intake via salt 3– 5% of ration, Ca:P 2:1, ammonium chloride (acidifies; for phosphate stones), delay castration.

plain: Cow, sudden severe lameness, symmetric swelling above the coronet, claws separated, foul necrotic interdigital fissure, fever → Interdigital necrobacillosis (foot rot): Fusobacterium necrophorum + Porphyromonas levii (± Prevotella, T. pyogenes) invading macerated interdigital skin. Not Dichelobacter nodosus — that is the ovine footrot agent.

plain: One cow in a small herd repeatedly lame while herdmates are sound → herd or individual treatment? Individual: corrective trimming, block, topical therapy, address conformation; cull if recurrent. Herd measures (footbaths, whole-herd trimming, housing) belong to multi-animal problems such as digital dermatitis outbreaks.

plain: Where do ~90% of dairy-cow lameness lesions sit, and which lesions? In the foot, mostly the lateral hind claw (bears most load on concrete): sole ulcer and white line disease (laminitis-related), digital dermatitis, foot rot. Locomotion scoring and routine functional trimming are the control tools.

plain: Sole ulcer Tx and purpose of the block? Therapeutic trim to lower the affected claw, debride loose horn, glue a wooden/rubber block to the sound (medial) claw to unload the ulcer for 4–6 weeks, NSAID; antibiotics only for deep infection, so no milk withdrawal. Prevent with cow comfort, footbaths, controlled concentrates, biotin.

plain: Obturator paralysis management and prognosis? Hobble hindlimbs above the fetlocks 45–60 cm apart to prevent adductor rupture, non-slip footing/ deep bedding, NSAIDs or dexamethasone first days, roll every 4–6 h, hip lifters or flotation tank, check calcium. Most recover within days–2 weeks; no improvement in 5–7 days = poor prognosis. Not slaughter first-line — nursing with hobbles cures most.

plain: Downer/post-calving cow standing with hock extended and fetlock knuckled, dorsum of digits on the ground → Peroneal (fibular) nerve paralysis — cannot flex hock or extend digits (pressure in recumbency). Splint, bedding, anti-inflammatories; most recover. Not peroneus tertius rupture — a distinct equine tendon lesion (hock extends with stifle flexed).

plain: Listeriosis Tx, prognosis, public health? High-dose penicillin (~44,000 IU/ kg IM q12h) or oxytetracycline 1–2 weeks, fluids, eye protection; discard spoiled silage. Prognosis fair in cattle, poor in sheep/goats (more acute). Zoonotic (raw milk, abortion, meningitis); also causes abortion and "silage eye." Feedlot cattle on high-concentrate/high-sulfur water or distillers grains, or calves on amprolium: cortical blindness, head pressing, opisthotonus, dorsomedial strabismus → Polioencephalomalacia (cerebrocortical necrosis). Causes: thiamine deficiency/thiaminases, amprolium (thiamine antagonist), dietary sulfur >0.4% DM, lead, salt/water deprivation. Not amprolium as treatment — it causes PEM.

plain: Cow estrous cycle: length, estrus duration, ovulation timing, best time to inseminate? Cycle 21 days (18–24); standing estrus ~12–18 h; ovulation 10– 12 h after the END of estrus (~24–30 h after onset); AI ~12 h after first observed standing heat (AM/PM rule). Metestrual bleeding 24–48 h after estrus is normal. Not "12 h after ovulation" — ovulation follows estrus, not the reverse.

Summer heat stress during June–August breeding (9 months earlier): THI >68–72 shortens/silences estrus, lowers oocyte quality and conception, raises early embryonic loss. plain: Timing of Campylobacter (vibriosis) vaccination in beef cows? Two initial doses 2–4 weeks apart with the second ~4 weeks (30 days) before breeding, then annual booster before breeding; in heavily exposed herds add a mid- breeding-season booster because immunity is short. plain: Rectal palpation landmarks for bovine pregnancy: amniotic vesicle, membrane slip, fetus, placentomes, fremitus? Amniotic vesicle 30–65 d (1 cm turgid sphere at 30 d, 2 cm at 35, 3 cm at 40); membrane slip from 30–35 d; fetus 60–90 d (out of reach 4–6 mo); placentomes ~75–90 d; middle uterine artery fremitus 90–120 d gravid side, both sides after 5–6 mo.

plain: Transrectal ultrasound of bovine pregnancy: how is age estimated and when is sex determined? Age from crown-rump length (later head/trunk diameters): heartbeat 21–22 d, embryo 26–30 d, limb buds ~35 d, placentomes 35–40 d. Fetal sex at 55–70 d (optimum 55–60) by genital tubercle — near umbilicus male, near tail female.

plain: Heifer co-twin to a bull calf: short blind vagina, small vulva, infertile → Dx, mechanism, chance of being normal? Freemartin — placental vascular anastomosis makes an XX/XY chimera; male AMH and testosterone regress the Müllerian ducts, so uterus, cervix and cranial vagina are hypoplastic. ~90% affected; only 8–10% normal. Cull. Rare in sheep, goats, mares.

plain: Farm-side diagnosis of freemartinism in a heifer calf? Vaginal probe: short blind vagina ~5–8 cm vs 13–15 cm in a normal heifer calf; also hypoplastic ovaries, enlarged clitoris, prominent vulvar hair tuft. Confirm by karyotype/PCR for Y chromosome (XX/XY chimerism).

chapter: Chapter 29 — Bovine — Theriogenology, Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Which embryonic ducts form the female vs male tubular genitalia, and
what controls them? Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts → oviducts,
Müllerian ducts, testosterone maintains Wolffian ducts

plain: Which embryonic ducts form the female vs male tubular genitalia, and what controls them? Paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts → oviducts, uterus, cervix, cranial vagina; mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts → epididymis, ductus deferens, vesicular glands. Testicular AMH regresses Müllerian ducts, testosterone maintains Wolffian ducts; without testes the female pattern develops by default.

plain: White heifer disease — what is it? Segmental aplasia of the Müllerian ducts in white/roan Shorthorns: persistent hymen, blind or absent cervix/ uterine segments, uterus unicornis, fluid trapped cranial to the obstruction; ovaries normal, cow cycles (ovaries have a separate embryonic origin).

chapter: Chapter 29 — Bovine — Theriogenology, Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Late-gestation cow, tense round abdomen enlarging over 1–2 weeks; fetus
and placentomes not palpable → Dx and contrast with hydramnios?

plain: Late-gestation cow, tense round abdomen enlarging over 1–2 weeks; fetus and placentomes not palpable → Dx and contrast with hydramnios? Hydrallantois (~90% of hydrops) — placental/caruncle dysfunction, fetus usually normal, dam at risk; induce (PGF2α + dexamethasone), drain slowly, or cull; fertility poor. Hydramnios (~10%): slow over months, doughy abdomen, fetus palpable, fetal anomaly, dam rebreedable.

chapter: Chapter 29 — Bovine — Theriogenology, Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Cow with greatly prolonged gestation delivers an oversized calf that dies
within a day → fetal defect? Fetal pituitary hypoplasia/aplasia
Guernsey/Jersey, or Veratrum teratogen): no fetal ACTH–cortisol surge to
trigger parturition or mature lungs. Dam's pituitary/gonads are irrelevant —

plain: Cow with greatly prolonged gestation delivers an oversized calf that dies within a day → fetal defect? Fetal pituitary hypoplasia/aplasia (genetic in Guernsey/Jersey, or Veratrum teratogen): no fetal ACTH–cortisol surge to trigger parturition or mature lungs. Dam's pituitary/gonads are irrelevant — parturition is initiated by the fetal HPA axis.

chapter: Chapter 29 — Bovine — Theriogenology, Hematology, Immunology & Oncology

spans.text: Effect of BVDV infection on the bovine fetus by gestational stage?

plain: Effect of BVDV infection on the bovine fetus by gestational stage? <40–45 d: embryonic death. 45–125 d: persistently infected immunotolerant calf (noncytopathic strain). 100–150 d: congenital defects — cerebellar hypoplasia, hydranencephaly, cataracts, microphthalmia, brachygnathia. >150 d: immunocompetent seropositive normal calf.

section: Pregnancy termination and induction of parturition

spans.text: Cow accidentally bred by an unwanted bull → when can PGF2α terminate

plain: Cow accidentally bred by an unwanted bull → when can PGF2α terminate the pregnancy? Only once a responsive CL exists (≥day 5–7 after estrus) — so around day 7–10, not immediately or day 3; effective to ~day 150. Wear gloves when handling prostaglandins.

chapter: Chapter 29 — Bovine — Theriogenology, Hematology, Immunology & Oncology
section: Pregnancy termination and induction of parturition

spans.text: Cow 60 days pregnant, unwanted → how to abort? Cloprostenol 500 µg

plain: Cow 60 days pregnant, unwanted → how to abort? Cloprostenol 500 µg IM or dinoprost 25 mg IM; abortion in 2–5 days; effective day 5 to ~150 while the CL is the sole progesterone source. After 150 days add dexamethasone 20–25 mg (placental progesterone).

spans.text: Pregnancy termination by gestational stage: cow vs doe vs ewe?

plain: Pregnancy termination by gestational stage: cow vs doe vs ewe? Cow: PGF2α alone to ~5 months; 5–8 months PGF2α + dexamethasone 20–25 mg; last month dexamethasone ± PGF2α induces calving. Goat: PGF2α at any stage (CL-dependent throughout). Sheep: PGF2α only before ~day 50; use dexamethasone later.

spans.text: Heifer at 265 days, ultrasound shows calf larger than pelvic diameter →

plain: Heifer at 265 days, ultrasound shows calf larger than pelvic diameter → induction protocol and drawbacks? Dexamethasone 20–30 mg IM + PGF2α (25 mg dinoprost / 500 µg cloprostenol) → calving in 24–72 h, limiting fetal growth. Expect retained fetal membranes (~50%), weaker calf, poorer colostrum; elective C-section is the alternative. Glucocorticoid mimics the fetal cortisol surge.

Goats: Chlamydia, Toxoplasma, Coxiella, Brucella melitensis. Chlamydia, Coxiella and Brucella are zoonotic — pregnant women must avoid lambing/kidding.

Listeria and Leptospira also cause late abortion with RFM but less classically.

plain: Dairy herd aborting at 5–6 months; fetal brain shows non-suppurative encephalitis; farm dogs present → agent, hosts, prevention? Neospora caninum — dog (and coyote/wolf) is the definitive host shedding oocysts; cattle maintain it by endogenous transplacental transmission (infected heifers abort repeatedly). Dx fetal brain histology/IHC, dam serology. No treatment or US vaccine; cull seropositive lines, keep dog feces from feed. Pups: ascending hindlimb paralysis with rigid hyperextension.

plain: Term cow fails to progress; vaginal exam reveals spiral folds and a twisted narrowed birth canal → Dx, first step, direction? Uterine torsion (usually ≥180°, most often counterclockwise/left viewed from behind; cause unknown — large single fetus, pendulous abdomen). Correct the torsion first: rotate the calf per vaginum or roll the cast cow in the same direction as the torsion with a plank on the flank (Schaffer's), then deliver.

plain: After detorsion of a uterine torsion: when is a C-section indicated, and can the cow be rebred? C-section if detorsion fails or the cervix stays closed; an open cervix after detorsion means vaginal delivery. Torsion is not heritable and rarely recurs — rebreed unless uterine necrosis or adhesions follow. Not cull — low recurrence, not a breeding exclusion.

plain: Cow with entire uterus (caruncles visible) everted hours after calving → management and prognosis? Caudal epidural, IV calcium (hypocalcemia is the usual trigger), clean, remove placenta, shrink edema (sugar), replace in sternal frog-leg position, fully evert the horns (warm saline), then oxytocin, antibiotics ± Buhner. Not heritable, rarely recurs — survival and fertility good if replaced promptly without tears; prognosis poor with laceration, hemorrhage, shock.

plain: Late-gestation cow or ewe with recurring vaginal prolapse → retention method and long-term advice? Buhner suture (deep circumferential perivulvar, loose enough to urinate, removed at onset of parturition); caudal epidural, treat straining/hypocalcemia. Heritable, recurs each pregnancy → cull after calving/weaning, do not keep daughters. Rectal prolapse uses a purse-string suture.

plain: Dairy cow with fetal membranes hanging 24 h after calving → approach? Retained placenta (>12–24 h). Do not pull manually (caruncle trauma, delayed involution, poorer fertility); trim exposed membranes; check calcium; oxytocin helps only in the first 24–48 h. Fever/toxic → systemic ceftiofur (labeled, no milk discard) or penicillin, fluids, NSAIDs. In mares RFM is an emergency — septic metritis and laminitis within hours.

plain: Cow 3–14 days postpartum: fever, depression, foul watery red-brown discharge, cervix open → Acute puerperal (toxic) metritis (E. coli, Trueperella, Fusobacterium). Tx systemic parenteral ceftiofur (labeled, no milk withdrawal) or penicillin, plus NSAIDs and fluids; intrauterine infusions/lavage are not recommended or labeled. Not pyometra — pyometra is later, afebrile, closed cervix with a CL.

Ceftiofur (systemic; crystalline-free acid or HCl, labeled for metritis with zero milk discard); alternatives systemic penicillin/ampicillin. Intrauterine antibiotics are extralabel. Subclinical endometritis with a CL → PGF2α.

plain: Cow not seen in heat for months; persistent CL and a fluid-filled flaccid uterus, no fetal structures, closed cervix → Pyometra — progesterone from the retained CL keeps the cervix closed and suppresses uterine defenses (Trueperella usual). After natural service think Tritrichomonas foetus (classic) or Campylobacter — test the bull; also follows metritis.

plain: Treatment of bovine pyometra? PGF2α — dinoprost 25 mg IM or cloprostenol 500 µg IM; luteolysis opens the cervix and the uterus evacuates in 3–5 days; repeat in 10–14 days if needed. Fertility good if trichomoniasis is excluded.

plain: Photo: newborn calf with orange-yellow/brown stained coat after a prolonged delivery → cause and significance? Meconium staining from in- utero hypoxia/fetal distress (dystocia, prolonged stage II, breech/posterior presentation; placentitis less common) — hypoxia relaxes the anal sphincter and triggers gasping. Risk of meconium aspiration pneumonia, acidosis, FPT: clear airway, oxygen, 3–4 L colostrum within 6 h. Not icterus.

plain: Newborn calf with milk draining from the nostrils while suckling, coughing, aspiration pneumonia → Cleft palate (palatoschisis) — repair impractical in calves, chronic aspiration guaranteed → euthanasia or salvage, not elevated feeding. Causes: hereditary (Charolais, Hereford) or lupine/ poison hemlock in early gestation (crooked calf disease) — examine herdmates and pasture.

plain: Newborn calf with fixed, flexed, non-reducible joints; herdmates with cleft palate or hydranencephaly → causes? Arthrogryposis from fetal immobility: lupine (anagyrine) or poison hemlock eaten days 40–100 of gestation; viruses Akabane, Cache Valley, Schmallenberg, bluetongue (arthrogryposis-hydranencephaly); arthrogryposis multiplex (curly calf), autosomal recessive in Angus; manganese deficiency. Dystocia common.

plain: Contagious vs environmental bovine mastitis pathogens and their control? Contagious (cow-to-cow at milking): Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus agalactiae, Mycoplasma bovis (Corynebacterium bovis) → post-milking teat dip, milking order, dry-cow therapy, cull. Environmental (bedding/manure): E. coli, Klebsiella, Strep uberis, Strep dysgalactiae, Trueperella → clean dry bedding, pre-dip, J5 vaccine, teat sealant.

plain: Early-postpartum cow with hot swollen quarter, watery serum-like secretion, fever and depression → agent and treatment? Acute coliform (E. coli) mastitis — signs are endotoxin-driven. Tx is supportive: IV fluids/ hypertonic saline, flunixin, frequent stripping with oxytocin; intramammary antibiotics add little (most self-cure); systemic ceftiofur (labeled) for severe toxic cows to limit bacteremia.

plain: Does dry-cow antibiotic therapy protect against coliform mastitis? No — dry-cow antibiotics cure persistent gram-positive infections (S. aureus, S. agalactiae, environmental streps). Coliform infections are short-lived, so dry- period protection relies on internal teat sealants and clean environment.

Systemically sick cows get systemic plus intramammary therapy; prevent spread with post-dip, single-use towels, bulk-tank culture.

plain: Which contagious mastitis pathogen is reliably cured by intramammary antibiotics in lactation, and how is herd spread prevented? Streptococcus agalactiae — >90% cure with intramammary penicillin/cephapirin ("blitz therapy"); it stays in the duct lumen and is eradicable. Prevent with post- milking teat dipping, blanket dry-cow therapy, milking hygiene, treat/cull infected cows.

plain: Herd mastitis spreading at milking, multiple quarters, resists antibiotics, needs special culture media → agent and control? Mycoplasma bovis — no cell wall, so beta-lactams (ceftiofur) are useless, macrolides unreliable; also calf pneumonia, otitis, arthritis. Control: bulk-tank and individual culture/ PCR, cull or strictly segregate, milk last, do not feed waste milk to calves. Not ceftiofur or tulathromycin — no activity, and tulathromycin is not permitted in lactating dairy cows.

plain: Dry cows and heifers at pasture in summer with thick, foul purulent mastitis spread by flies → Summer mastitis — Trueperella (Arcanobacterium) pyogenes, transmitted by Hydrotaea irritans; quarter usually lost; prevent with fly control and dry-cow therapy.

plain: Methods for counting somatic cells, and the subclinical threshold? California Mastitis Test cow-side; electronic counters (Fossomatic/Coulter) or direct microscopic count in the lab; Wisconsin Mastitis Test is a gel- viscosity screening test. >200,000 cells/mL indicates subclinical mastitis.

spans.text: Which hormones control milk let-down vs maintenance of lactation?

; estrogen/progesterone build the gland but suppress

plain: Which hormones control milk let-down vs maintenance of lactation? Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) ejects milk within ~1 min of udder stimulation and is blocked by stress/epinephrine; prolactin and growth hormone (bST) maintain lactation; estrogen/progesterone build the gland but suppress secretion until parturition.

plain: Adult cows in late summer: fever, weakness, pale then icteric membranes, severe anemia, NO hemoglobinuria; some die when handled → Anaplasma marginale — extravascular (splenic) hemolysis, so urine stays clear; adults >2–3 yr most severe, calves resistant. Spread by Dermacentor ticks, biting flies and contaminated needles/instruments. Not babesiosis, leptospirosis or bacillary hemoglobinuria — those are intravascular with red urine.

plain: Confirming and treating bovine anaplasmosis? Acute: Giemsa smear — small dense bodies at the RBC margin (Babesia paired pyriform; A. centrale central). Carriers: cELISA (msp5) or PCR. Tx oxytetracycline 20 mg/kg long-acting, transfuse if PCV <12%; recovered animals remain lifelong carriers.

plain: High-producing multiparous cow 2–4 weeks after calving: red urine, pale membranes, afebrile, PCV <20% → Postparturient hemoglobinuria — hypophosphatemia (phosphorus-deficient ration; copper deficiency, cruciferous feeds contribute); ATP-poor RBCs lyse intravascularly. Tx IV sodium phosphate (60 g monosodium phosphate/300 mL saline), oral phosphorus, transfuse if PCV <12–15%. Not bacillary hemoglobinuria — C. haemolyticum after fluke damage, febrile, high mortality.

plain: Week-old calf with hypopyon, fever, swollen joints or diarrhea; serum total protein <5.0 g/dL → Septicemia secondary to failure of passive transfer (IgG <10 g/L, TP <5.0–5.2 g/dL at 24–48 h; E. coli, Salmonella seed uvea, joints, meninges). plain: Cow not milked on schedule develops urticaria, angioedema and dyspnea → cause and hypersensitivity type? Milk allergy — type I (IgE) hypersensitivity to the cow's own casein absorbed from the engorged udder; Jerseys predisposed. Milk out the udder; epinephrine/antihistamines if severe.

Coliform (E. coli) toxic mastitis — supportive care first: IV fluids/hypertonic saline, flunixin (anti-endotoxic), frequent stripping (oxytocin), calcium if hypocalcemic; systemic ceftiofur or intramammary cephapirin/ceftiofur of modest benefit (bacteria often already cleared). plain: Cattle with bloody diarrhea; lemon-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs → Trichuris (whipworm; cecum/colon). Fenbendazole or other benzimidazole (cattle meat withdrawal 8–13 days by product, no milk discard). Differentials: coccidiosis, Oesophagostomum, salmonellosis, BVD.

plain: Leaf-shaped fluke with anterior cone in cattle bile ducts → US-approved treatments? Fasciola hepatica: clorsulon (adults) and albendazole 10 mg/kg (adults); triclabendazole kills immatures but is not US-approved for ruminants. Intermediate host Lymnaea (Galba) snails. Not fenbendazole — no flukicidal activity.

chapter: Chapter 30 — Bovine — Infectious Disease, Parasitology, Toxicology, Pharmacology & Anesthesia

plain: Large operculated egg on cattle sedimentation: Fasciola vs paramphistome? Fasciola eggs oval, operculated, golden-brown, 130–150 µm; paramphistome (rumen fluke) eggs larger and clear/colorless. Adult rumen flukes are harmless; immature flukes in the duodenum cause diarrhea and hypoproteinemia.

breathing holes along the back; gadding last summer; damaged hides →

plain: Cattle in late winter/spring with subcutaneous nodules (warbles) with breathing holes along the back; gadding last summer; damaged hides → Hypoderma cattle grubs: H. lineatum (common grub) migrates via esophageal submucosa; H. bovis (northern grub) via spinal canal epidural fat. season ends (early fall, ~October), before larvae reach resting sites

plain: Timing of grub treatment, and why → Macrocyclic lactone (ivermectin, doramectin, eprinomectin, moxidectin) pour-on/injectable soon after heel-fly season ends (early fall, ~October), before larvae reach resting sites. Killing them late: H. lineatum → esophagitis, bloat, salivation, dysphagia; H. bovis → posterior paresis/paralysis. Anti-inflammatories; most recover in 48–72 h. Crushing grubs risks anaphylaxis.

plain: Housed dairy cattle in winter rubbing tail head, perineum, udder and hind legs; mildly pruritic crusting alopecia recurring after months → Chorioptes bovis (surface-feeding, non-burrowing). Pour-on eprinomectin (zero milk withdrawal) or moxidectin, or permethrin; injectable ivermectin unreliable for surface mites; treat the group. Psoroptes = whole-body intense pruritus, reportable in some states; Sarcoptes = head/neck, burrowing.

Pour- on macrocyclic lactone kills both sucking and chewing lice; injectable ivermectin misses chewing lice (no blood meal); permethrin alternative; treat whole group, repeat 2–3 weeks.

plain: Calves with access to old batteries, paint or machinery: blindness, head pressing, bruxism, bellowing, tremors, convulsions → Lead poisoning — most common bovine toxicosis. Confirm whole-blood lead >0.35 ppm (35 µg/dL), kidney/liver lead. CaEDTA 73 mg/kg/day IV/SC divided × 3–5 days, thiamine, oral magnesium sulfate, rumenotomy. Prolonged tissue residues — FARAD withdrawal. Differentials: PEM, nervous coccidiosis, rabies.

plain: Calves treated with high-dose or prolonged amprolium develop cortical blindness, head pressing, opisthotonus, dorsomedial strabismus → Polioencephalomalacia from thiamine deficiency — amprolium is a thiamine analog/antagonist. Thiamine 10 mg/kg IV then IM q6–8h × 3–5 days, dexamethasone for edema; good if treated within 24 h. Other causes: high-sulfur water/feed, grain overload, bracken. Not sulfonamides — amprolium is the thiamine antagonist.

plain: Cow with vague signs, no firm diagnosis → rule for antimicrobial selection in food animals? Use a cattle-labeled drug at label dose/route when possible; extralabel use (AMDUCA) needs valid VCPR, a diagnosis, no suitable labeled drug, extended withdrawal via FARAD, and never prohibited drugs (chloramphenicol, extralabel fluoroquinolones, nitroimidazoles, glycopeptides).

plain: Standing enucleation for ocular squamous cell carcinoma → block and what it anesthetizes? Peterson eye block (needle through the notch between supraorbital process and zygomatic arch to the orbitorotundum foramen) or four-point retrobulbar block; both desensitize CN II–VI → globe anesthesia and akinesia 1–2 h; add eyelid block. plain: Late-pregnant cow needs digit amputation for septic claw → anesthetic approach? Standing intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier block): tourniquet above fetlock/hock, 20–30 mL 2% lidocaine into a superficial distal vein, surgery within 60–90 min; ring block alternative. Avoid general anesthesia (regurgitation, bloat, fetal depression); minimize xylazine late gestation (uterine contractions).

plain: Fresh dairy cow, left-sided ping + ketosis (LDA) → Tx? Surgical fixation: right-flank omentopexy, right paramedian abomasopexy, left-flank abomasopexy, or roll-and-toggle; correct the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (saline/KCl) and the ketosis. Rolling alone recurs in most cows.

plain: LDA cow with severe ventral edema from xiphoid to udder → best surgical approach? Standing right paralumbar-fossa omentopexy (or left-flank abomasopexy) — stays dorsal to the edema. Toggle-pin and right paramedian abomasopexy need dorsal recumbency and incise edematous tissue → dehiscence, infection.

plain: Right-flank omentopexy — which structure is sutured to the body wall? The greater omentum adjacent to the pylorus ("sow's ear" fold), after decompressing and repositioning the abomasum; the abomasal wall is not entered. Not lesser omentum — too thin and too far.

Right-flank laparotomy, decompress, derotate, omentopexy/pyloropexy; IV NaCl/KCl. Not roll-and-toggle — LDA only; never roll an RDA or volvulus.

Standing right-flank laparotomy, exteriorize, typhlotomy at the apex, derotate; partial typhlectomy if devitalized or recurrent. Recurrence ~10– 25%; correct hypochloremic alkalosis.

Conservative: magnet + penicillin or oxytetracycline. Sequelae: pericarditis, vagal indigestion, liver abscess.

plain: During rumenotomy an abscess is found adhered to the reticular wall → Lance and drain it into the reticular lumen through the adhered wall (never into the peritoneum), explore for the wire, leave a magnet, broad-spectrum antimicrobials. Adhesions seal it; spillage → diffuse septic peritonitis.

plain: Why is the standing bovine C-section done through the left paralumbar fossa? The rumen fills the approach and blocks intestinal evisceration and contamination while the gravid horn is lifted to the incision; the right flank is used only when the calf cannot be reached from the left.

plain: What is a Buhner needle used for? A long blunt needle that passes a perivaginal purse-string (Buhner suture) to retain vaginal prolapse in cows and ewes — not for suturing viscera.

plain: Cow, 2-day-old laceration with swollen purple edges → management? Do not suture primarily: debride devitalized edges, lavage, systemic antibiotics (procaine penicillin or oxytetracycline) + NSAID; delayed primary closure in 2–3 days once a healthy bed forms, or second intention if heavily contaminated.

Within 6–12 h under ring block/IV regional anesthesia: debride, close 2–3 layers — mucosa/submucosa 4-0/5-0 absorbable continuous not entering the lumen, stroma, then skin fine nonabsorbable interrupted/vertical mattress; teat cannula or dry the quarter; antibiotics; sutures out 10–14 d.

plain: Bright, afebrile 1–2-month calf, soft reducible umbilical swelling ≤3 cm with palpable ring → management? Monitor and recheck in ~60 days — small rings often close spontaneously by 3–6 months (belly band optional). No antibiotics or drainage. Palpate/ultrasound the internal umbilical remnants.

plain: 3-month calf, 12 cm reducible umbilical hernia; options bandage, leave, reduce daily, operate → Herniorrhaphy: rings >5 cm, persisting beyond 4–6 months, or incarcerated do not close; bandaging and manual reduction fail. Ultrasound first — infected urachal/umbilical-vein remnants are resected at surgery. Heritable (Holsteins); advise against breeding.

plain: Calf with a firm, painful, warm or draining umbilical mass ± fever → Umbilical infection (omphalitis, omphalophlebitis, urachal abscess), not a simple hernia: ultrasound, antibiotics and surgical resection. Reducibility and absence of fever are what mark an uncomplicated hernia.

plain: Dehorning mature cattle — most common acute complication; delayed complication? Acute: hemorrhage from cornual artery branches (ligate or pull-twist). Delayed (days–weeks): frontal sinusitis, because the cornual diverticulum of the frontal sinus communicates with the horn core in older animals; also fly strike, tetanus. Disbud before 8 weeks with cornual nerve block.

plain: Dehorned older animal develops unilateral nasal discharge, head tilt, fever → Dx, Tx? Frontal sinusitis: trephine and lavage the sinus, systemic antibiotics. Prevent by covering sinus openings at dehorning and avoiding fly season.

Vaccinate pregnant dams with K99 (F5) bacterin 6 and 2 weeks before calving (annual booster thereafter), ensure colostrum within 6 h; oral K99 monoclonal antibody to calves at birth. Protection is lactogenic — immunize the dam, not the calf.

chapter: Chapter 31 — Bovine — Surgery, Husbandry, Public Health, Welfare, Regulatory & Practice Law

plain: Why are sows vaccinated 5 and 2 weeks pre-farrowing, and against what? Colostral/lactogenic immunity for the first week of life — ETEC pilus antigens (K88, K99, 987P, F41) + C. perfringens type C toxoid (often rotavirus). Pigs are the latent reservoir and do not itch; others are dead-end "mad itch" hosts. Cycle 21 d (18–24); estrus 2–3 d; ovulation ~40 h after estrus onset; wean-to-estrus 4–7 d (lactational anestrus ends at weaning); gestation 114 d (3 mo, 3 wk, 3 d); non- seasonal. plain: Diagnosis and treatment of ferret adrenal disease → Adrenal sex-steroid panel (Tennessee) + abdominal ultrasound. plain: How are chickens for human consumption killed humanely? Slaughter, not drug euthanasia: electrical water-bath or controlled-atmosphere stunning followed immediately by exsanguination before scalding. Poultry are exempt from the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act, but FSIS requires good commercial practices.

plain: Campylobacter jejuni in broilers: effect on birds and significance? Commensal — colonizes the intestine without disease; the leading cause of human bacterial foodborne enteritis (and Guillain-Barré) via undercooked or cross-contaminated carcasses; controlled by FSIS performance standards, chilling, rinses and cooking. Not carcass condemnation — Campylobacter does not condemn carcasses. C. hepaticus/bilis cause spotty liver disease in free- range layers.

plain: Which disease is acquired by eating eggs? Salmonella Enteritidis, transovarian into intact eggs (ovary/oviduct colonized before the shell forms); prevented by refrigeration, thorough cooking, NPIP/FDA Egg Rule flock testing and vaccination. Not avian influenza — spread by bird contact, not food.

plain: How often does a llama or alpaca cycle? No estrous cycle — camelids are induced ovulators, receptive whenever a dominant follicle is present (follicular waves every 12–14 days); ovulation ~ 30 h after mating, triggered by seminal β-NGF (ovulation-inducing factor). Gestation ~ 335–350 days (~11.5 months).

plain: CWD lesion and diagnostic tests? Spongiform vacuolation of neurons/ neuropil in CNS gray matter (brainstem, obex) with PrP-CWD accumulation and no inflammation. Screen ELISA, confirm IHC on obex + medial retropharyngeal lymph nodes (nodes positive earlier than brain); antemortem tonsil or RAMALT biopsy, RT-QuIC.

part: Part VI — Exotic and Non-Traditional Species

plain: Deer in a petting zoo with cattle, horses, sheep, goats, rabbits develop proliferative crusted lesions on lips/muzzle — source? Sheep and goats — contagious ecthyma (orf, parapoxvirus); deer, camelids and humans susceptible by contact. Self-limiting in 4–6 weeks; isolate, wear gloves (zoonotic).

Separate deer from domestic ruminants and their manure- contaminated pasture/water; test and cull positives (fecal PCR/culture, serology); buy from test-negative herds; protect fawns from adult feces (infection acquired young, incubates years). No deer vaccine.

Cattle are dead-end hosts (fluke encapsulated, no eggs passed, liver condemnation only); in sheep and goats it migrates unencapsulated and is often fatal.

plain: Visitor approaches a farmed deer herd — first alarm signal to herd mates? Head-high alert posture with foot stomping, followed by snort-wheeze vocalization and tail flagging before flight (contested — verify). Approach calmly from the side, avoid direct eye contact.

plain: Typical seasonal movement of northern deer and elk? Low-elevation winter range (less snow, available browse) → higher-elevation summer range in spring, returning in autumn; corridors concentrate animals and matter for CWD/TB spread.

The 3-year-old — high-risk groups are children <5, adults >65, pregnant and immunocompromised; E. coli O157 HUS is chiefly pediatric. A common cold is not a risk factor. Controls: handwashing stations, supervised contact, no food in animal areas.

Hypothyroidism is not an immune risk factor.

plain: Why did Mycobacterium bovis rise and persist in northeastern Michigan white-tailed deer and spill into cattle? Supplemental feeding and baiting concentrated deer at feed piles near farms — density-dependent nose-to-nose and feed-borne spread (M. bovis survives months on feed). Control: ban baiting/feeding, lower deer density by harvest, surveillance of harvested deer, cattle testing and feed fencing. Not Mycoplasma bovis — the agent is Mycobacterium; not overhunting of either sex.

plain: Pet snake found dead after open-mouth breathing, head elevated, bubbles at glottis; caseous lung exudate at necropsy → Hypoxia from bacterial pneumonia (gram-negative; cold husbandry). Reptiles lack a diaphragm and cannot cough, so exudate accumulates. Not starvation — gradual emaciation over weeks, no exudate.

plain: Maintenance fluid rate and time frame for a dehydrated reptile? ~10–30 mL/kg/day (far below mammals' 40–60); replace deficit over 48–72 h with warmed isotonic or slightly hypotonic crystalloids at preferred optimal temperature; no rapid boluses. Not 20–40 mL/kg/day — approaches mammalian rates.

plain: Boa with stomatitis, pharyngitis, lost teeth → Infectious stomatitis (mouth rot) secondary to cold husbandry, stress, rostral trauma → Pseudomonas/ Aeromonas overgrowth. Correct environment, debride, dilute chlorhexidine rinses, systemic ceftazidime; radiograph for osteomyelitis.

plain: Snake or iguana bloated, not defecating; radiograph shows urate/fecal mass in colon → Impaction from chronic dehydration and low temperature. Soak in shallow lukewarm (~29 °C) water 30 min–2 h daily, SC/intracoelomic fluids 10–20 mL/kg, fix humidity/heat, lubricant enema; surgery only for true obstruction.

plain: Captive iguana bloated and lethargic → differentials? Radiograph + husbandry review: follicular stasis/egg binding in females, substrate impaction, metabolic bone disease, cold/no UVB. Treat by cause (ovariectomy/ salpingotomy, calcium/UVB, fluids).

plain: Juvenile iguana fed lettuce/fruit, no UVB: soft swollen jaw, bowed limbs, tremors, pathologic fractures → Nutritional secondary hyperparathyroidism (metabolic bone disease) — low Ca:P, no vitamin D3/ UVB. Oral calcium, UVB, basking 32–35 °C, leafy greens; calcitonin only once normocalcemic; handle gently.

plain: Juvenile turtle/tortoise with soft, flexible shell → MBD from calcium/ vitamin D3 deficiency and lack of UVB (290–315 nm needed for cutaneous D3). UVB lamp, dietary Ca:P 2:1 with D3.

part: Part VI — Exotic and Non-Traditional Species
chapter: Chapter 40 — Reptiles & Amphibians — All Systems

spans.text: Correct UVB provision for a reptile enclosure?
no glass or plastic in between

plain: Correct UVB provision for a reptile enclosure? Lamp 30–45 cm (12–18 in) from basking spot, no glass or plastic in between (blocks UVB), 10–12 h photoperiod, replace every 6–12 months — output decays before visible light fails. Unfiltered sunlight is best.

part: Part VI — Exotic and Non-Traditional Species

plain: Pet lizard with hypercalcemia, calciuria, urolithiasis, soft-tissue mineralization; owner gives daily D3/calcium → Hypervitaminosis D (oversupplementation); also renal failure, neoplasia. Stop supplements, fluid diuresis. In contrast, hyperkalemia in lizards usually means renal failure/ dehydration.

plain: Green iguana fed cat food: swollen joints with chalky white deposits; white nodules on pericardium/kidneys → Gout (articular + visceral) — urate tophi from excess animal protein in a herbivore, dehydration, renal disease, aminoglycosides. normally darker; glossitis/stomatitis show swelling, caseous plaques or

plain: How often do snakes shed? Growing juveniles every 2–6 weeks, adults every 1–3 months (2–4 times a year); healthy snakes shed in one piece, lizards shed in patches.

Debride, topical povidone-iodine, systemic antibiotics, improve water quality/temperature, dry-dock periods, remove crayfish/aggressive tankmates.

plain: Snake with crusting, swelling and necrosis of facial and ventral scales → Ophidiomycosis (Ophidiomyces ophidiicola, snake fungal disease). PCR/ culture of skin biopsy; voriconazole or terbinafine plus husbandry correction.

plain: Safe blood volume from a 100 g snake? 0.5–0.8 mL — blood volume is 5– 8% of body weight and ~10% of it can be taken, i.e. 0.5–0.8% of body weight; ventral coccygeal vein or cardiocentesis.

plain: Injection site for antibiotics in a snake? IM in the epaxial muscles of the cranial half/third of the body — caudal injections pass through the renal portal system (reduced levels, concentrated nephrotoxins). Medicated water and injected prey are unreliable.

plain: Acceptable euthanasia of a turtle or iguana (AVMA 2020)? Sodium pentobarbital 60–100 mg/kg IV (jugular, subcarapacial, ventral tail vein) or intracoelomic/intracardiac after sedation; confirm with Doppler/ECG silence, then pithing or decapitation + brain destruction. Not blunt trauma or CO₂.

part: Part VI — Exotic and Non-Traditional Species

spans.text: Why must reptile euthanasia include a secondary step?

plain: Why must reptile euthanasia include a secondary step? Reptiles tolerate anoxia for hours (breath-holding, anaerobic metabolism); hearts beat long after apparent death. Therefore CO₂ alone, freezing/hypothermia, and decapitation without pithing are unacceptable; inhalants alone are unreliable in breath-holding chelonians.

plain: Order of the aquarium nitrogen cycle, and which products are toxic? Ammonia → nitrite (Nitrosomonas) → nitrate (Nitrobacter/Nitrospira) → removed by water changes/plants/denitrification. Ammonia and nitrite are acutely toxic; nitrate only chronically (target <40–50 mg/L).

Mechanical (floss, sponge, drum/bead) removes particulates; chemical (activated carbon, protein skimmer) removes dissolved organics/medications. Never rinse bio-media in chlorinated tap water.

plain: What water should fill or top up an ornamental fish tank? Dechlorinated potable tap water (sodium thiosulfate/conditioner that also neutralizes chloramine — aging alone does not), temperature- and pH-matched; change 10–25% weekly. Distilled/RO water lacks minerals and buffering → pH crash, osmotic stress unless remineralized.

plain: Anesthetic of choice for fish, route, and the mandatory preparation step? Tricaine methanesulfonate (MS-222) by immersion, 50–150 mg/L, absorbed across gills; buffer with sodium bicarbonate (~1:1–2:1) to pH 7–7.5 — unbuffered solution burns gills/skin/corneas. Recover in clean aerated water; flow anesthetic water over gills of large fish out of water.

plain: MS-222 in food fish vs ornamental fish? MS-222 is the only FDA-approved fish anesthetic — 21-day withdrawal, water >10 °C. Eugenol/clove oil is for non-food ornamentals only (no residue tolerance). Monitor opercular rate and righting reflex.

plain: Capnography: normal ETCO2 and what high, low and flat-line values mean? Normal 35–45 mmHg. High (>45–50): hypoventilation, rebreathing (exhausted soda lime, faulty valve), malignant hyperthermia. Low: hyperventilation, low cardiac output, embolism, hypothermia. Sudden zero: disconnection, esophageal intubation, apnea, obstruction or cardiac arrest.

plain: Non-rebreathing (Bain/Mapleson D) vs circle system — size cut-off, O2 flow, dead space? Bain for patients <5–7 kg: fresh gas 200–300 mL/kg/min (min 0.5–1 L/min) clears CO2 by flow, not soda lime; minimal dead space/ resistance, rapid depth changes. Circle for larger patients: 20–50 mL/kg/min maintenance (50–100 at induction) with CO2 absorbent.

plain: Reading a blood gas: how to classify the primary disorder and judge compensation? pH <7.35 acidemia, >7.45 alkalemia. pH and PCO2 move opposite → respiratory primary (PCO2 >45 acidosis, <35 alkalosis). HCO3 moves with pH → metabolic (HCO3 <20 acidosis, >26 alkalosis). Dog metabolic acidosis: PCO2 falls ~0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L HCO3 drop; compensation never normalizes pH.

plain: Low HCO3 + low pH + low PCO2 → ? Low PCO2 + high pH → ? First = metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (lactic, DKA, renal failure, diarrhea). Second = respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation: pain, hypoxemia, fear). Normal HCO3:H2CO3 ratio 20:1.

plain: How does metabolic acidosis change serum potassium? Raises it — H+ enters cells, K+ exits (~+0.6 mEq/L per 0.1 pH fall with mineral acidosis; much less with lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis).

plain: Exotic waiting room: dyspneic bird, egg-bound finch, bleeding broken blood feather, parrot with chlamydiosis, rabbit with pasteurellosis → order? plain: Class of choice for gram-negative aerobic sepsis and its toxicities? Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin): nephrotoxicity (proximal tubular necrosis — urine casts precede azotemia), ototoxicity (irreversible), neuromuscular blockade. Dose once daily, keep hydrated, avoid with furosemide/NSAIDs or in renal patients; no anaerobic activity. Gram-positives: beta-lactams first-line.

plain: Which antimicrobials cover anaerobes, and which do not? Cover: metronidazole (DOC), clindamycin, penicillin G/ampicillin, amoxicillin- clavulanate, carbapenems, chloramphenicol, cefoxitin. plain: Most effective acid suppressant / DOC for gastric ulcers; mechanism vs H2 blockers? Omeprazole (pantoprazole, esomeprazole) irreversibly blocks parietal-cell H+/K+-ATPase — the final common pathway, so all stimuli are suppressed; H2 blockers (famotidine, ranitidine) block histamine only. Horses 4 mg/kg PO q24h; dogs/cats ~1 mg/kg PO q12h. Sucralfate is a mucosal protectant.

plain: Drugs sharing a mechanism with aspirin: phenylbutazone, flunixin → All COX inhibitors (NSAIDs): anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic; aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX. Opioids — naloxone 0.01–0.04 mg/kg IV/IM/IN, onset 1–2 min but lasts only 30–60 min (shorter than most opioids → re-dose/CRI); reverses analgesia (butorphanol partially reverses mu agonists sparing some analgesia). plain: Clinical uses of PGF2α in large vs small animals? Large: luteolysis for synchronization (bovine CL responsive after day 5), pyometra, luteal cysts, mummified fetus, farrowing induction, abortion. Small: open-cervix pyometra (natural PGF2α 0.1–0.25 mg/kg SC) and pregnancy termination; panting, vomiting, defecation; canine CL relatively resistant. Not handled by pregnant women or asthmatics.

plain: Mechanism and use of activated charcoal? Adsorbs toxins in the GI lumen; repeat doses interrupt enterohepatic recirculation (NSAIDs, bromethalin, theobromine). 1–4 g/kg PO ± sorbitol (first dose only). Useless for alcohols, xylitol, heavy metals, caustics; contraindicated with aspiration risk or ileus; hypernatremia if dehydrated.

plain: Anticoagulant rodenticides (warfarin, brodifacoum, bromadiolone) — mechanism and Tx? Inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase → non-functional factors II, VII, IX, X; bleeding 3–5 days post-ingestion. Vitamin K1 2.5–5 mg/ kg/day PO with fatty meal: 2 weeks (first-generation) to 4 weeks (second- generation); recheck PT 48 h after stopping.

plain: Petting zoo or children's party with animals; food already banned from animal areas → most important remaining control? Hand-washing stations with soap and running water at every animal-area exit, before eating; supervise children <5; no strollers, pacifiers or bottles in animal areas; exclude high-risk animals (reptiles, calves with diarrhea). (NASPHV animal- contact compendium.) Is alcohol hand sanitizer enough after animal contact? No — a backup only when water is unavailable; alcohol does not kill Cryptosporidium / Giardia cysts, bacterial spores (Clostridium) or non-enveloped viruses (parvovirus, norovirus). Parvovirus surfaces: 1:30 sodium hypochlorite, 10 min contact.

plain: Extralabel drug use in a food animal → how is the withdrawal time set and where obtained? plain: How does a practice increase revenue; how is associate productivity compared? Revenue = transactions × average transaction charge: raise fees to market, improve compliance (reminders, forward booking, dentistry, diagnostics, wellness plans), add services, retain clients.
